title: From a paediatric doctor to a podium dancer: meet the 2026 stars of The Great British Bake Off | Television | The Guardian
description: Yes it’s going to be the Nigella Show – but we need to make sure the bakers get a look-in too. Here are this year’s cohort, ranked from worst to best
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Yes it’s going to be the Nigella Show – but we need to make sure the bakers get a look-in too. Here are this year’s cohort, ranked from worst to best
Content: The 2026 contestants … l-r: Gabe, Nikki, Shannon, Danni, Mo, Clara, Tom, Molly, Yannis, Gary, Moyin and Connie.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4View image in fullscreenThe 2026 contestants … l-r: Gabe, Nikki, Shannon, Danni, Mo, Clara, Tom, Molly, Yannis, Gary, Moyin and Connie.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4TelevisionFrom a paediatric doctor to a podium dancer: meet the 2026 stars of The Great British Bake OffYes it’s going to be the Nigella Show – but we need to make sure the bakers get a look-in too. Here are this year’s cohort, ranked from worst to bestStuart HeritageMon 7 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe new contestants of this year’s Great British Bake Off don’t know how lucky they are. Usually when a new intake arrives, all eyes are on them. After all, this is a show with such a long and storied history that its audience is primed for the slightest culinary mistake.But this time around the contestants will enjoy a temporary reprieve, because this is the year when Bake Off becomes The Nigella Show, and everyone will be so busy going moon-eyed over its glamorousnew judgethat they’ll barely even give the bakers a second look.Nevertheless, as is tradition, Channel 4 has just sent out its contestant biographies. Using them, and no other quantifiable data, let’s rank their chances of success from worst to best, just for the hell of it.Clara, 24, marketing graduate, HertfordshireView image in fullscreen‘A Portuguese fantasy girlie’ … Clara.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4Things aren’t looking great for Clara. A Portuguese “fantasy girlie”, it is said that her signature style is “chaotically beautiful”. As everybody knows, this is code for “Clara is not detail oriented”. What’s more, her official show biography states that she believes “the first bite of a bake is always with the eyes”. However, the first bite of anything is with the mouth. Eyes, by their very nature, cannot bite things. This failure to understand basic anatomy will almost certainly be her undoing.Mo, 21, law student, West MidlandsView image in fullscreen‘Winging it’ … Mo.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4Again, everything about Mo sounds like a whopping great red flag. In his contestant questionnaire he professes to not owning any cookbooks, calls himself “chaotic and random”, declares that he enjoys “winging it” and admits that he has never really watchedThe Great British Bake Offbefore. Worst of all, though, his description of Lawson is: “I remember my mum loved watching her growing up.” Being disorganised is one thing. Not watching Bake Off is one thing. But referring to Nigella Lawson in the past tense, as something only enjoyed by elderly people? This will not do.Danni, 25, HGV service centre administrator, DorsetView image in fullscreen‘Chaos, chaos, chaos!’ … Danni.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4Danni sounds great, but I fear they are not long for the world. Describing their baking style as “Chaos, chaos, chaos!” (there’s that red flag again), they also describe their superpower as never giving up. “Even if I fail and fail and fail and fail, I just get back up and keep going and try again in a different way.” I don’t want to appear psychic here, guys, but I’m pretty sure Danni failed.Gary, 67, retired garment technologist, NottinghamshireView image in fullscreen‘Nice older man’ … Gary.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4Bake Off has been on the air for so long now that all its contestants tend to lapse into type. As such, Gary is this year’s “nice older man”. He’s pleasingly brief with his answers in the questionnaire, and appears to live very happily with his wife and all their animals. This is all good, of course, but expect him to be quickly outflanked by all the hungry youngsters who primarily see Bake Off as a way to grow their Instagram followers.Shannon, 29, project planner and scheduler, GloucestershireView image in fullscreen‘Lovely and earnest’ … Shannon.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4Shannon is the exact opposite of Gary. By a wide margin, her questionnaire is the longest of the year, running to almost 2,000 words (for reference, Gary’s was about 500 words long). But what a wealth of information it is. For instance, we now know that she was a back-up baker on the show last year, that baking for the judges turned her stomach into “a swarm of butterflies” and that “Nigella brought this sensational presence into the tent, a kind of calm elegance that made the whole space feel homely and safe.” She seems lovely and earnest but – and I’m aware this is rich coming from me – the woman badly needs an editor.Gabe, 32, artist and drag king, West MidlandsView image in fullscreen‘Professional nuisance’ … Gabe.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4The “daddy of Birmingham drag”, Gabe describes themself as a “professional nuisance”. This may bear out. In their questionnaire, Gabe reveals that they did shots with Nigella, previously had their bum smacked by Alison Hammond and was ready to cream pie themselves in front of Noel Fielding. Every year I do these, without fail, I end up being followed on Instagram by one Bake Off contestant. I have a feeling that this year it’s going to be Gabe.Moyin, 22, political economy student, EssexView image in fullscreen‘High achiever of the group’ … Moyin.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4From what I can tell, Moyin likes to present as the high achiever of the group. He was an under-20 100m champion, could make macarons by the age of 14 and makes a point of noting that he often attends seminars on global political thought. Alas, his questionnaire has given him away, in that he gives a full-blown spoiler in it. I won’t repeat it, but it does involve Danni and genitalia. In other words, Moyin is a huge gossip and cannot be trusted.Yannis, 28, paediatric doctor, LondonView image in fullscreen‘Very thoughtful’ … Yannis.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4Yannis seems like a very composed, very thoughtful man. He is a Bangladeshi, born in Vienna but raised in London. He claims that Bake Off is the show that helped him learn to speak English. He puts great emphasis on caring for people. He is, as you will have seen, a paediatric doctor. So in that regard, I hope he does horribly here. The world needs more paediatric doctors and fewer people determined to leverage their stint on a cookery competition into semi-regular appearances on Sunday Brunch. Only instant failure can correct this cosmic unbalance.Tom, 25, hairdresser, West YorkshireView image in fullscreen‘The makings of a potential winner’ … Tom.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4Now we get to the bakers I think will actually do well. Based on his bio, Tom has the makings of a potential winner. He seems deeply unfazed by the prospect of appearing on Bake Off, not only because he describes himself as “super chill” but also because he seems to believe that it was his divine right to end up on the show. Also he claims to be obsessed by Nigella, which is the correct answer.Nikki, 50, advertising post-producer, LondonView image in fullscreen‘Certain to push through’ … Nikki.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4The primary thing to remember about Nikki is that she was once a podium dancer at Ziggy’s nightclub in Basingstoke in the 1990s. In truth, I am a little worried about Nikki, because in the questionnaire she described her baking style as “flavours, combinations and colours”, which is such a weirdly rudimentary statement that I’m worried she also describes her favourite film as “noises and shapes”. But, hey, anyone who danced on podiums in Basingstoke can almost certainly push through.Connie, 63, NHS hospital discharge lead, LondonView image in fullscreen‘The Cake Lady’ … Connie.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4Connie loves baking cakes so much that people literally call her “the Cake Lady”, and she isn’t upset by it. Plenty of the other bakers go out of their way to name Connie in their bios, too, which has to be a good sign of how well-liked she is. She also keeps a jar of fruit permanently soaking in rum, which is what poachers did in Danny the Champion of the World. What I’m trying to say is that Connie sounds like someone who could poach animals for a living, and I’m too terrified to put her lower on the list.Molly, 31, accessibility coordinator, LondonView image in fullscreen‘The woman to beat’ … Molly.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4Molly has been baking since she was six. However, that isn’t why I think she will win Bake Off this year. No, I think she will win Bake Off because her bio states that she is 25% of the way through a 350,000-stitch cross-stitch landscape of Rivendell. Can you imagine the patience, the attention to detail, the sheer bloody-minded obsessiveness required to do such a thing? Clearly this is the woman to beat.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe Great British Bake OffFood TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cravings ‘like heroin withdrawal’: what happens when weight-loss drugs don’t work? | Weight-loss drugs | The Guardian
description: GLP-1 medications have been a gamechanger in the fight against obesity. But for a minority of patients, their impact is negligible. Why?
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: GLP-1 medications have been a gamechanger in the fight against obesity. But for a minority of patients, their impact is negligible. Why?
Content: Clinical trials suggesting GLP-1 drugs can help participants lose an average of 15% to 20% of their body weight.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenClinical trials suggesting GLP-1 drugs can help participants lose an average of 15% to 20% of their body weight.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesWeight-loss drugsCravings ‘like heroin withdrawal’: what happens when weight-loss drugs don’t work?GLP-1 medications have been a gamechanger in the fight against obesity. But for a minority of patients, their impact is negligible. Why?Nicola DavisScience correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Mercedes was told by her doctor that she could be prescribed GLP-1 weight loss jabs in 2024, she broke down. “[When] she said yes, I cried in her office. And I didn’t really stop crying for a week,” she said.“Finally, after being overweight my entire life, this was going to save me. My struggle, my burden, my shame was finally going to come to an end.”But as time went on it was hope, not weight, that fell away.“I was on [Ozempic] for nine months. And then I went on Wegovy for four months, then Contrave [an oral, non-GLP-1 medication], and then Mounjaro, and that was for a few months, and then nine months ago I started on Zepbound,” said Mercedes. “Nothing has worked.”A recently retired teacher in her 50s, Mercedes is among a small proportion of people for whom the powerful new weight-loss drugs, championed by celebrities for their transformative effects, do not work.Ozempic, a type 2 diabetes medication, and Wegovy, which is licensed for weight loss, both contain a drug called semaglutide that mimics a hormone that occurs naturally in our bodies: GLP-1. These medications reduce the rate at which food is emptied from the stomach, suppresses appetite and increase the production of insulin – meaning many people lose weight.Mounjaro and Zepbound, also now household names, have an even greater weight-loss effect. They both contain the drug tirzepatide which mimics both GLP-1 and another hormone.The excitement around such “GLP-1s” has been hard to miss: the medications have grabbed headlines, with clinical trials suggesting they can help participants lose an average of 15% to 20% of their body weight.Studies suggest they could helpwith conditions ranging fromheart problemsandaddictionstofatty liver disease. In some cases experts say the effectsmay not be entirely related to weight loss.But not everyone experiences the benefits. Between 9% and a third of participants in clinical trials lose less than 5% of their body weight – depending on the type of drug and dose used.Now researchers are trying to work out why – something they say could help doctors tailor the use of the drugs, maximise cost-effectiveness and reduce side-effects.For Mercedes, the impact of non-response has been profound.“Aside from the fact that it’s not working and that it’s so expensive, to say it’s hard on the self-esteem is a humongous understatement,” said Mercedes, who lives in Canada. “It’s been a real struggle, with shame and regret and big bills and disappointment that my own body is not working the way it should.”Prof Alexander Miras, an obesity expert at Ulster University, said the efficacy of the drugs could not be blamed on patients. “If the drug does not reduce hunger and food intake for someone, it is just not going to work,” he said.Mercedes said she has tried hard to stick to lifestyle changes alongside the medications but, for her, the jabs did not suppress constant, intrusive thoughts about food.“I just thought: ‘No, I’ve got to get somewhere … I’m going to die of obesity’,” she said. “I was really strict with myself for a month – but the cravings, which I can only call like heroin withdrawal … it’s just overwhelming. And the food talk never ended.”The extreme effort paid off, to an extent. “I can honestly say I lost 20 pounds in that month, but not because of the medication,” she said.Mercedes is certainly not alone: the Guardian has heard from dozens of people for whom GLP-1 medications have had little effect.Yury K, 57, also from Canada, said he tried a number of weight loss programmes before starting Wegovy for obesity. He exercises about five days a week, mainly with kettlebells, and does not eat junk food or fast food.While Yury said he saw some improvements in his blood sugar levels and cholesterol while using the medication, as well as a reduction in food noise and appetite, he found his weight barely changed.“I started Wegovy at about 242lb and, after six months, I was still about 242lb. My weight can fluctuate a little because of water, but essentially there was no meaningful weight loss,” he said. He also experienced unpleasant side effects, including constipation and sensitive skin.“There is so much discussion about GLP-1 medications as if they work for everyone, and that was not my experience. When you put in the effort with diet and exercise, take the medication exactly as prescribed, and still see little benefit, it is difficult not to feel disappointed,” he said.Lucille*, 53, who is based in Luxembourg, told the Guardian she has been taking GLP-1 medications for four years – initially to help with insulin resistance – starting on a daily injection of a GLP-1 medication called Saxenda, before switching to Ozempic.Yet despite being effective at first, Lucille says the medications no longer help her lose weight – even after switching to Mounjaro and taking the highest dose. “It’s as if nothing is having an effect any more,” she says. “The Mounjaro 5mg [dose] is outrageously expensive and so far none of these medications have been approved by my health insurance,” she adds.At present, the reason for such variations in response remains unclear. “The short answer to why some people don’t respond is we don’t really know,” said Miras.He said research had suggested factors such as motivation, intelligence, education and socioeconomics did not predict how patients would respond to GLP-1 medications.But other characteristics might do. “We know, for example, that age plays a role – so older people lose less weight. Sex plays a role – men lose less than women,” said Miras. “[And] people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight compared to people without.”Studies have also suggested ancestry might have an impact, with the medications most effective in people of European ancestry, and least effective in people of African American ancestry.Dr Mahesh Umapathysivam, an endocrinologist and clinical researcher at Adelaide University in Australia, said it was plausible that hormones could have an effect too.“There is growing evidence that oestrogen alters GLP-1 response. We see that with the difference between male response and female response. Also, we know from some of the physiological studies that time of menstrual cycle also alters GLP-1 response,” he said.“Finally, the use of menopausal hormone replacement therapy – which contains oestrogen – is associated with greater weight loss in semaglutide users.”Then there is the matter of genetics.A recent studyhighlighted the potential role of a genetic variant that affects receptors in the brain upon which the drugs work.“People carrying the genetic variant, we found lose about an extra 0.76kg (1.6 lbs) on average, and people who carry two copies of the variant double that,” said Adam Auton, vice-president of human genetics at the 23andMe Research Institute, and the senior author of the study.“For people with two copies, this accounts for about 10% of the weight people might expect to lose on these medications.”Umapathysivam and colleagueshave recently published a studyinto two genetic variants that affect the production of an enzyme, known as PAM, that modifies many hormones including GLP-1. The team found people with such variants appear to show resistance to GLP-1.“GLP-1 resistance simply means a given amount of GLP-1 has less effect on the body,” Umapathysivam said. “The implication for treatment is that a certain dose of GLP-1 in someone with resistance might mean less weight loss, less glucose lowering, less insulin secretion or less slowing to the gastric emptying.”Despite emerging research, it is not yet possible to accurately predict who will respond to weight loss jabs and who won’t.But there are reasons for people like Mercedes to be hopeful. A series of promising new drugs are in development. “Another option is to change patients to a non-GLP-1 based drug called Mysimba [the UK brand name for Contrave]. It works in the same parts of the brain, but just slightly differently and therefore may be worth trying,” said Miras. “It is not available in the NHS, just privately.”For some who struggle to lose weight with GLP-1 medications, weight-loss surgery may be the only option left. And, Miras says, “[A] lack of response to GLP-1 based drugs does not predict lack of response to [bariatric] surgery.”And for those who lose little to no weight on GLP-1 medications, the message is clear. “It’s not your fault and it’s not the drug’s fault either, this is purely luck,” said Miras. “I’ve seen it before, it’s not very common, but it does happen.”Mercedes began GLP-1 medications with huge amounts of hope and expectation. “There was just so much publicity around it. So many people [using the drugs said]: ‘Oh, I forgot to eat lunch,’ that I suppose subconsciously I just sort of ignored the prospect that … the drugs didn’t work,” she said.“I wish I knew if there were other people out there, like me, for whom [GLP-1s] are just not effective at all.”*Some names have been changedExplore more on these topicsWeight-loss drugsObesityMedical researchfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why does the hard right have such a high tolerance for domestic abusers in their midst? | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: The ‘stop the boats’ narrative is increasingly presented as if it stems from a concern for women’s safety. This is just the laundering of thuggery
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The ‘stop the boats’ narrative is increasingly presented as if it stems from a concern for women’s safety. This is just the laundering of thuggery
Content: Patriot Platform founder Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, speaking to Zia Yusuf in Portsmouth, 7 September.Photograph: Pol Allingham/PAView image in fullscreenPatriot Platform founder Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, speaking to Zia Yusuf in Portsmouth, 7 September.Photograph: Pol Allingham/PAOpinionViolence against women and girlsWhy does the hard right have such a high tolerance for domestic abusers in their midst?Zoe WilliamsThe ‘stop the boats’ narrative is increasingly presented as if it stems from a concern for women’s safety. This is just the laundering of thuggeryMon 7 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt was a busy weekend for the insurgent and hard right, as Reform party delegates redoubled their commitment to women’s safety byphysically attacking a female protesterand Patriot Platform, a new group established by Danny Tommo, real name Daniel Thomas, arrived in Dover on Saturday, then Portsmouth on Sunday, dressed in balaclavas. No arrests were made in Dover, and therefore the protest was deemed peaceful. “A message was sent!” Thomas exclaimed later on his socials. “Now imagine how powerful the next message will be.” The next powerful message of peace the following day spurredthe issuance of a dispersal orderfrom Hampshire police, alongside some smashed windscreens (of police cars) and advice for local people to avoid the area.The “stop the boats” narrative, along with a lot of Reform’s anti-immigrant rhetoric, has become increasingly bound up with a concern for the safety of women and children. It might be aslyly vague sentiment from Robert Jenrick, in which he doesn’t want his daughters sharing a neighbourhood with men “who broke into the country illegally, about whom we know next to nothing”, or it might beZia Yusuf’s much more explicit complaintthat the nation is prepared to “sacrifice British women and girls on the altar of diversity”. Protesters outside hotels housing asylum seekers get all their righteous wrath from the danger posed to women from foreign nationals, and Thomson stated his aims straightforwardly on Instagram – posting video of Saturday’s protest, he wrote: “Protect our country! And more importantly our women and children! This is our warning!”Observers trying to remain neutral and fair-minded accept that there certainly is a crisis of violence against women in this country, but point out that more than 90% of perpetrators of rape and sexual assault in the UK areknown to their victims; anyone serious about preventing this violence would not start with the spectre of recently arrived refugees. But the Home Office’s literature for recent arrivals about the importance of consent just plays into the hands of the hard right, which then –this is Yusuf again– call this “an implicit admission that, as we all know, these undocumented fighting-age men pose a threat to the British public and women in particular”.It is pointless trying to battle this narrative with statistics, because it is cynical and strategic rather than a mistaken point of view, authentically held. It is worse than pointless trying to meet it halfway as a “legitimate concern”. And we can see that from the remarkably high tolerance these protest movements have for domestic abusers within their own midst. After the 2024 Southport riots, it later transpired that41% of the nearly 900 arrestedhad been reported for crimes associated with intimate partner violence; one police force had that figure as high as 68%.In the higher ranks of Patriot Platform, meanwhile, Thomas has served prison time fora botched kidnapping, Kevin Jones of the Thanet Patriots has pleaded guilty towounding and assaultof his partner and her mother, and Adrian Clark, also of Thanet, gavea rousing speechin August which climaxed: “We’ve all done stupid shit, but if any of these other people want to sit out there and say ‘Oh you’re a domestic abuser’, what do you think these people on the boats have a better criminal record than me? You having a laugh?” It should be stressed that only one of these lieutenants has been convicted of violence against women, and some are merely violent towards other men. It should also be stressed that nobody at Reform’s conference has been arrested, despiteviscerally unpleasant footageof one man trying to grab a woman by her neck and another apparently trying to whack her with his crutch (to be fair to West Midlands police, they have appealed to the woman to come forward).So yes, Danny Tommo is right: Patriot Platform is sending a message. Zia Yusuf is right: people should be terrified. But that message is: “Anyone taking our commitment to women’s safety seriously is a mug.” And what weshouldbe terrified of is the laundering of this thuggery by what claims to be a mainstream political party.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsViolence against women and girlsOpinionProtestReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: Colin from Accounts final season review – farewell to a blinding ray of TV sunshine  | Colin from Accounts | The Guardian
description: After season two’s mortifying ending, the charming hit comedy is back for the last time … with sex parties, extreme cringe and a final answer to the central will-they-won’t-they
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: After season two’s mortifying ending, the charming hit comedy is back for the last time … with sex parties, extreme cringe and a final answer to the central will-they-won’t-they
Content: ‘Like Friends if it had just been about Ross and Rachel’ … Patrick Brammall as Gordon and Harriet Dyer as Ashley in Colin from Accounts.Photograph: John PlattView image in fullscreen‘Like Friends if it had just been about Ross and Rachel’ … Patrick Brammall as Gordon and Harriet Dyer as Ashley in Colin from Accounts.Photograph: John PlattTV reviewColin from AccountsReviewColin from Accounts final season review – farewell to a blinding ray of TV sunshineAfter season two’s mortifying ending, the charming hit comedy is back for the last time … with sex parties, extreme cringe and a final answer to the central will-they-won’t-theyRachel AroestiMon 7 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are cliffhangers, and then there’s whatever happened at the end of Colin from Accounts’ second season. We had, by that point, witnessed protagonists Ashley and Gordon’s unconventional love story evolve from bizarre meet-cute – key stages: boob-flashing, car accident, injured dog – to soulmate-level relationship. But what starts with an exposed nipple can abruptly go tits up. On a heaving dancefloor at Ash’s best friend’s wedding, Gordon – drunk and buoyed up by the DJ dropping Slice of Heaven by Dave Dobbyn (the Oceanian equivalent of Come on Eileen, judging by the euphoric reaction) – decides to ask his girlfriend to marry him. Ash, humiliated by the circumstances, doesn’t respond. Everyone else films it and laughs. Gordon insists the whole thing was a joke and awkwardly boogies on. Then the credits roll.If you had somehow managed to wipe this eye-watering faux pas from your mind’s eye, fear not: the Aussie rom-sitcom returns for its third and final series by replaying the agonising proposal in full. It gets worse. We discover the pair split soon after and haven’t seen each other for three years. In fact, they’ve both since found other (extremely attractive) partners: the kind but dim David and the hyper-capable and efficient Chelsea. As Ash later observes, they’ve “upgraded” – but you know their respective hearts don’t really belong to their nice new beaux.View image in fullscreenNice new beaux … Ashley (Harriet Dyer) and David (Thomas Cocquerel) in Colin from Accounts.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 CBS Studios Inc., Easy Tiger Productions Pty Ltd, Foxtel Management Pty Ltd, Create NSW/Lisa TomasettiColin from Accounts – which is also the name of the dog the pair maim then adopt at the start of the show – is the sort of sitcom that runs almost entirely on charm. After all, there is no other way to convince an audience to watch two people fall in love, split up, get back together, split up again, then (I assume – the final two episodes weren’t available for review) reunite once more aside from cultivating a deep and lasting affection for them. This, however, is a mysterious art. The fact the pair are played by real-life couple and showco-creators Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyerprovides a frisson of autobiographical intrigue and obviously helps with the chemistry, but it’s hard to pin down what exactly it is about these characters that is so appealing: they’re both annoying, immature and petty, and far from morally upstanding (once they bump into each other again, it’s not long before they’ve betrayed David and Chelsea). Still, we desperately want them to find love, ideally with each other.Think of it like Friends if it had just been about Ross and Rachel, with the other characters consigned to supporting eccentrics. Among the roster of weirdos here is Ash’s stunningly awful mother Lynelle and her alarmingly creepy husband Lee, who are now deeply entrenched in the men’s rights movement. Then there’s Gordon’s thoroughly unreconstructed brother Heavy (catnip for Lynelle, then), plus his brewery colleagues – the furious yet resoundingly cool Chiara and hulking sweetheart Brett – alongside Ash’s bestie Megan and her wife Rumi. The fact that three of the last four turn out to be sex party people does later serve to make Ash and Gordon seem like relatable nerds in comparison.The real love story behind Colin from Accounts: ‘I wouldn’t want to write with anyone else’Read moreYou probably wouldn’t describe Colin from Accounts as a hard comedy: its primary objective is to make us invest in its central will-they-won’t-they, and therefore prioritises well-drawn friendships, realistic romantic messiness and amusingly sour banter over non-stop jokes. That said, it can be laugh-out-loud funny when it wants to be. This series seems to have saved all its best material for its third episode, which involves a particularly grim morning for Ashley, now a qualified GP, thanks to an old man who has brought in his stool diaryandsamples. Blessedly, she is forced to cut his appointment short when she discovers Lynelle has posted a video about her own murder on Facebook (“take your shit! Get up – go, mate!”). Later, when Ash and Gordon meet at a fancy restaurant to discuss their adulterous kiss at the latter’s birthday party, a smug waiter pours wine in excessively long, urine-like streams from a traditional Spanish pitcher in what feels like a reprise of classic 1990s sitcom silliness.Ultimately, though, this is an immensely comforting show: very sweet, very gentle, yet prevented from tipping into saccharine territory by a bass note of blokey and invariably profane Australian humour. The insults are particularly impressive – it’s difficult to choose a favourite from this series but I think I’ll go with the simple but effective “fucking cockhead” (credit: Lynelle’s ex Bernie discussing her current husband Lee). Cringe comedy – and what feels like aslightlymisjudged subplot about child abduction – aside, Colin from Accounts has been like a ray of sunshine in the schedules. It’s been a huge hit across the world, and many will mourn its ending. I hope it turns out to be a happy one at least.Colin from Accounts aired on BBC One and is on iPlayer now in the UK. In Australia, it is on Binge.Explore more on these topicsColin from AccountsTV reviewTelevisionTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: September is the real new year: 39 brilliant buys to supercharge school, work and everything in between | Life and style | The Guardian
description: From loafers to lunch boxes to fancy stationery, these picks for kids, teens and grownups will bring that new-term energy, whatever your age
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: From loafers to lunch boxes to fancy stationery, these picks for kids, teens and grownups will bring that new-term energy, whatever your age
Content: Stepping out: a few well-chosen essentials can make the return to routine feel a little brighter.Photograph: Catherine Falls Commercial/GettyView image in fullscreenStepping out: a few well-chosen essentials can make the return to routine feel a little brighter.Photograph: Catherine Falls Commercial/GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleSeptember is the real new year: 39 brilliant buys to supercharge school, work and everything in betweenFrom loafers to lunch boxes to fancy stationery, these picks for kids, teens and grownups will bring that new-term energy, whatever your ageDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereEllie Violet BramleyMon 7 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJump toThe best back-to-school buys for everyoneYoung kidsTeensWomenMenStationery and accessoriesShiny shoes. Freshly sharpened pencils. Newrucksack. Back-to-school season is here, and even for those of us no longer in full-time education, the energy of this time of year is undeniably one of fresh starts and renewed momentum.A couple of well-chosen items, from a notebook to inspire ideas to a lunch box that might encourage you to bring in your own food, are often all it takes to feel a touch more pulled together after a languorous summer. So whether you’re looking for school kit or your own stuff, here’s our pick of the best back-to-the-grind products for kids, teens and grownups.The best back-to-school buys for everyoneYoung kidsView image in fullscreenMunchkin kids’ bento box lunch box£22.99 at John Lewis£22.99 at AmazonIf your child has ever written off an entire lovingly prepared meal because of a single stray parsley leaf, this is the perfect lunch box. The enticing, rainbow-coloured compartments allow you to serve them separate snacks to power them through maths and beyond. Plus, it’s dishwasher-safe, BPA-free and comes with stainless steel cutlery.View image in fullscreenKlean Kanteen kids 355ml water bottle£15.50 at Mountain Warehouse£15.50 at RackhamsBPA-free and with a leakproof sports-style flip-cap, this bottle comes in a pattern to suit most interests – sharks, dinosaurs, unicorns, you name it. Also, crucially, it’s dishwasher-safe.For more, read ourguide tothe best water bottlesView image in fullscreenClarks shoe cleaning kit£18 at ClarksEmbarrassingly, my dad is still the only person who can be bothered to take some polish to my shoes, when he gets the chance. Courtesy, of course, of Clarks.View image in fullscreenFrugi navigator backpack£32 at John Lewis£32 at DebenhamsFun but with an expedition’s worth of pockets, this unisex Frugi backpack says start-of-term sensible but also adventure. Once your child tires of it, you can reuse it as a wash bag.View image in fullscreenLegami mushroom pencil sharpener£2.99 at Waterstones£5.68 at AmazonA pencil sharpener and an eraser in one feels like an efficiency win. But the cottagecore/goblincore aesthetic is what really sets this piece of kit apart. The most fun-gi in any kid’s pencil case.View image in fullscreenKitpascrayons, set of 12£14.95 at Cass Art£16 at the National GalleryChunky, smooth and, most importantly, washable, Kitpas crayons are a delight to colour with. Plus, they’re made from rice bran wax that would otherwise go to waste.View image in fullscreenLegami erasable pens£1.95 each at Cass Art£1.99 each at John LewisPens you can rub out once felt like the height of sophistication. These Legami ones still feel special, if not sophisticated, coming in a range of playful animal designs. They’ll liven up any desk and arerefillable.View image in fullscreenRegatta waterproof packaway jacket£15 at Regatta£12.50 at AmazonIt’s the season of mist and unexpected downpours. Kids need an anorak that can be packed away small and light, but is there when they need it. This design from Regatta comes in enough delicious colours to keep everyone happy, with sizes for ages two to 14.View image in fullscreenM&S scallop hair bow and scrunchie£12.50 at M&SPutting your hair up is a bit like pulling your socks up – it signals a readiness for knuckling down. Marks & Spencer has a great selection of accessories, including scrunchies and a bow in school uniform-adjacent coloured gingham.TeensView image in fullscreenHelix Oxford stationery set£22.49 at B&Q£20.49 at AmazonA one-and-done approach might be easiest when you need all the stationery for secondary school. Helix is a classic academic brand that provides the complete set.View image in fullscreenLeuchtturm1917 ballpoint pen£27.50 at London Graphic Centre£27.50 at AmazonBut that doesn’t mean one super special pen isn’t worth investing in. It’srefillableand comes in a few different colourways.View image in fullscreenKokuyo x Noritake Haco Haco pencil case£18.99 at London Graphics£19.99 at RymanMinimalist but fun, this pencil case is part of a series created in collaboration with Japanese illustrator Noritake. Choose between the wide orslim neckand find a hue that will make you feel happy.For more, readour review of the best travel mugs and reusable coffee cupsView image in fullscreenPenco tape writer£21.50 at London Graphic CentreI recently splashed out on one of these labellers, and it has brought order to an otherwise cluttered house (and mind), which makes it feel worth its £21.50 price tag.
