title: 25 years ago, two strangers met in the twin towers and escaped on 9/11. What happened next? | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the south tower
Author: David Smith
Headline: Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the south tower
Content: ‘In fact, we’ll be blood brothers for life. Come on, buddy. Let’s go home,’ what Brian Clark said to Stanley Praimnath when he saved him on the 81st floor of the north tower.Photograph: Courtesy Brian ClarkView image in fullscreen‘In fact, we’ll be blood brothers for life. Come on, buddy. Let’s go home,’ what Brian Clark said to Stanley Praimnath when he saved him on the 81st floor of the north tower.Photograph: Courtesy Brian ClarkSeptember 11 200125 years ago, two strangers met in the twin towers and escaped on 9/11. What happened next?Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the south towerDavid Smithin WashingtonMon 7 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 13.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe has told the story hundreds of times, but it never seems to fade. If anything, it only becomes more vivid. “Oh, gosh,” exclaims Stanley Praimnath, his voice cracking with an “ooooooh!” as if bearing a weight. “It’s like reliving that day.”Nearly 3,000 people died in theterrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DCon September 11 2001. But Praimnath and another office worker, Brian Clark, were two of only four individuals known to have survived from above the impact zone in either tower of the World Trade Center. The two strangers met in the smoke and fire of the 81st floor of the south tower, and walked down 1,620 steps into the rest of their lives.Their split-second decisions that day made all the difference. Over the next 25 years, both men moved from middle age into old age and retirement. Both enjoyed family weddings and watched children and grandchildren grow. Both saw US presidents come and go asold wars endedandnew wars began. They remained friends through it all.They also told their story –countless times– in churches, schools, TV studios and elsewhere. “It could be 800, 1,200, a number like that,” Clark estimates.Praimnath, in a separate interview, muses: “People refer to me as ‘the 9/11 guy’. It doesn’t feel repetitive. It is like unloading baggage from my shoulder, like washing my soul with tears. It is comforting to know that people out there still want to hear.”A cry for helpClark is now 79, living in retirement in northern New Jersey with his wife; he has 11 grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. Praimnath, a decade younger, lives in Valley Stream, Long Island; he is a pastor, grandfather and empty-nester who speaks of his survival not as luck, but as an act of God’s grace.Their recollections of 9/11 are still as clear as the cloudless sky over Manhattan on that September morning. Clark, a Canadian who was executive vice-president at the financial brokerage firm Euro Brokers, arrived at his office on the 84th floor around 7.15am. Down on the 81st floor, the Guyanese-born Praimnath had settled into his desk at Fuji Bank, where he worked as a loan officer.At 8.46am, the peace was shattered by a deafening double boom as the hijackedAmerican Airlines Flight 11slammed into the north tower. Clark recalls: “The lights above me flickered and I spun around in my chair and my peripheral vision caught flames against the window. It was surreal. Two or three seconds later, the flames dissipated and the airspace was filled with singed paper.”Having volunteered as a floor fire warden after the1993 World Trade Center truck bombing, Clark sprang into action. He retrieved an official torch marked “WTC fire safety team” from an overhead cabinet and began shepherding staff toward the building’s central corridor.View image in fullscreenA man stands in the rubble, calling out asking if anyone needs help, after the collapse of the first World Trade Center Tower on 9/11.Photograph: Doug Kanter/AFP/Getty ImagesCo-workers crowded against the north-facing windows, gazing up nine stories at the raging “ring of fire” consuming their twin building. Thinking the emergency was confined next door, Clark phoned his wife at home and his father in Toronto, reassuring them that he was safe.Three floors below, Praimnath was on the telephone with a colleague in Chicago who had witnessed the north tower explosion on television and begged him to evacuate. He was looking towards the Statue of Liberty when he spotted another plane – so close that he could make out the “U” on the tail ofUnited Airlines Flight 175.“On a given day, it was normal for a plane to zoom by a half a mile to a mile away,” he recalls. “But this plane is coming towards me. I made eye contact. I dropped the phone and screamed and said, ‘Lord, I can’t do this. You take over’. I don’t know why I said that – but thank God I said that.”Praimnath dived under his desk in the foetal position, weeping and praying as the Boeing 767 bore down on his window. “With the most thunderous sound, the plane came and crashed into the building,” he says.The aircraft struck diagonally at 9.03am, cutting through the 77th to 85th floors. The impact flattened entire walls, severed electrical wiring and sent a shock wave of jet fuel and debris through Fuji Bank’s offices.Praimnath says: “That big orange glow that you see there – I’m stuck in the middle of it. Upon impact, it looks like a demolition crew came with a big giant wrecking ball and ripped the entire office. Every wall is flattened. I remember a large chunk of the plane was broken off and stuck in the office doorway.“I remember flames all around me, as if somebody took a giant bag of cement, threw it in the air and I can’t breathe. The floor above me collapsed and it’s hovering over the desk and I’m like, ‘Oh, my God, I’m going to die. It’s gonna totally collapse, crush me to death, or I’m gonna get sucked out by the air pressure.’ You can hear the sound.”At the memory, he sets his teeth and blows down the phone to recreate the terrifying whoosh.View image in fullscreenThe point of impact where a plane crashed into the north tower of the World Trade Center in New York City on 9/11.Photograph: Jeff Christensen/ReutersThree floors higher, Clark was standing on the west side of the 84th floor when the aircraft sliced into the building’s eastern trading floor. “Our room exploded,” he says. “Everything came out of the ceiling – air conditioning ducts, lighting, the whole works. For five seconds the building swayed to the west and then it swayed back to vertical. For those 10 seconds I was quite terrified, thinking the building was going to roll over. But it didn’t.”When the tower steadied, Clark gathered a group of six or seven colleagues and led them toward the central core. The impact had demolished stairwells B and C, but stairwell A, tucked furthest away on the north-west side, somehow remained open.The group began descending stairwell A. On the 81st floor landing, they were halted by a man and woman coming up the stairs. “She was insistent we not go down,” Clark says. “‘No, no, no. You can’t go down,’ she said and, because she stopped us, it allowed me to hear a call for help from within the 81st floor, a muffled cry: ‘Help, I’m buried. I can’t breathe.’”Brothers for lifeClark squeezed through an opening where the door frame had been ripped from the drywall and stepped into the dark 81st floor, guided by Praimnath’s desperate shouts.Inside the office, Praimnath prayed for rescue. “I can still remember the flames encroaching and I’m screaming, ‘Lord, send somebody, I don’t want to die.’ I’m crawling away from the flames, dodging all the cables that were hanging in the ceiling, short-circuiting because the sprinkler system came on,” he recalls.“I’m like, ‘Oh my God, I’m gonna die.’ Somebody had a flashlight on the other end of the floor. The person’s saying, ‘I’ll wait for you’, but I couldn’t hear because I got temporarily deaf when the plane hit the building. As I’m crawling away, the flames are coming closer, licking up the office space.“I got to the wall. The person’s saying, ‘Bang on the wall, I know where you are’. I hit the wall and the person says, ‘Climb over there.’ It had a hollow ceiling, a 10-foot sheetrock wall, a drywall. I remember that so vividly.”Clark’s torchlighthad picked out a hand protruding from a hole in the 10-foot sheetrock wall. He grasped Praimnath’s hands and hauled him over the partition. The desk beneath Clark gave way, and both men crashed to the floor in a heap.View image in fullscreenNew York City firefighters wear face masks as they prepare to join other firefighters in battling blazes and helping injured people after the World Trade Center buildings collapse on 9/11.Photograph: Anthony Correia/ReutersClark recalls: “We fell and he gave me a big kiss. I said, ‘What’s going on, what are you doing?’ I stuck out my hand and said, ‘I’m Brian Clark.’ He says, ‘I’m Stanley Praimnath; we’ll be brothers for life.’ I said, ‘Well, I don’t have any siblings.’”Clark noticed that Praimnath had a puncture wound on his palm, while his own hand was cut and bleeding from moving debris. Clark recalls his instinctive gesture of solidarity: “I smooshed our hands together and said, ‘In fact, we’ll be blood brothers for life. Come on, buddy. Let’s go home.’”When they returned to the stairwell, Clark made the critical decision to ignore the warning of the woman on the landing. Pointing his torch down the staircase, he saw no flames. Clark and Praimnath turned downward. Most of the colleagues who had been with Clark, however, chose to head upward, believing safety lay on the roof. They died in the collapse. At Euro Brokers, 61 of Clark’s colleagues perished.Lives intertwinedWhen Clark and Praimnath finally emerged on to the street, police and emergency workers yelled at them to run. Minutes later, the south tower collapsed in a cascade of steel and concrete, sending a rolling cloud of debris surging through lower Manhattan. The two men dived inside 42 Broadway to escape the choking dust.In the chaos, Praimnath reached into his pocket and handed Clark a business card from a small home business he and his wife operated. Separated in the confusion, Clark used the number on that card to reach Praimnath late that evening, confirming that both had made it home.While Clark suffered remarkably little long-term psychological distress – describing his lack of post-traumatic stress as an unearned “gift” – Praimnath’s return to the living was fraught.Arriving home on Long Island on the evening of 9/11, Praimnath says he suffered profound memory loss. “I wanted to know what this strange woman was doing in our house with two children, not going home. I refused to go to bed because this strange woman was in that room.”View image in fullscreenAn American flag flies near the base of the destroyed World Trade Center in New York on 9/11.Photograph: Peter Morgan/REUTERSHis wife, Jennifer, quietly cared for him without judgment. “She would hobble me into the bathroom, fill the tub with warm water and Epsom salts, and tell me to soak,” he says. “Then she would put me on the couch. Every day, she would leave an apple, a sandwich, a bottle of water and a notepad. I don’t know how long I was in that state. All I know is that one day, I got up, looked at her, recognised her and snapped out of it.”When Praimnath returned to work in October at a temporary office in Jersey City, he still could not navigate on his own. “I had to draw out my commute on a map and color-code it,” he recalls. “When I got to work, people would say, ‘Stan, can you please sign this?’ I didn’t have a clue what I was signing. But they were kind, patient managers. Gradually, the pieces came back.”In the quarter-century since that Tuesday morning,the lives of Clark and Praimnathhave remained intertwined. They shared family milestones, celebrated at each other’s daughters’ weddings and phoned one another regularly.When Clark’s eldest daughter married, Praimnath and his wife were seated at the head table. Praimnath says: “Brian introduced me to all his friends and family as his blood brother. You could see people looking around, thinking, ‘Something doesn’t quite fit the picture!’ But Brian didn’t care. That’s who he is. He is the big brother I never had.”For Praimnath, surviving 9/11 opened a deep spiritual vocation. In 2006, he became a pastor, joining the staff of the church where his father-in-law was senior minister. Over the past two decades, he has travelled to churches, military bases and schools worldwide, delivering his testimony as a sermon on redemption.“On 9/11, I was crying out to the Lord under that desk, ‘Lord, let me live to walk my daughters down the aisle,’ and God answered. I walked Stephanie and Caitlin down the aisle. I’ve lived to see my grandchildren, Hannah and Ezra. They don’t call me Papa – they call me ‘Papaya’. Stephanie even bought me a shirt that says ‘Papaya’.”Yet Praimnath’s resilience has been tested repeatedly. In 1993, he narrowly escaped the first truck bombing at the World Trade Center. He was diagnosed with leukaemia and a severe bout of Covid-19 scarred his lungs with bilateral pneumonia. Then, after a trip to Europe with his wife, doctors discovered that his four coronary arteries were severely blocked, requiring emergency quadruple bypass surgery.“My question has always been: how many times do you try to kill one man?” asks Praimnath, who retired from theSumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporationtwo years ago. “I’m living by grace. I still travel. I still do exactly what I used to do before.”Blood brothersHe and Clark know they have more years behind them than lie ahead. Onthe 25th anniversary, Clark will attend a memorial service at his local town square in New Jersey, beginning at 8.45am, before spending the day quietly with his wife. Praimnath will be at a church in Virginia, telling his story once again, with gratitude.Both men find themselves speaking to a generation for whom 9/11 is not a living memory, but history. Clark, who retired in 2006, says: “I don’t have to teach history anymore – the textbooks have that covered. What textbooks don’t have is the emotional reality, the optimism that life carries on despite terrible evil. But whenever I speak at schools, 98% of the time, the very first question the kids ask is: ‘Are you still in touch with Stanley?’”Praimnath experiences the exact same phenomenon. Just recently, he addressed 700 students over Zoom at a Christian school in Tampa, Florida. “These children weren’t even alive when the towers fell,” Praimnath says. “Yet when you describe the roar of the jet engine and the wing slicing through the office, you can hear the audible gasp in the auditorium. It becomes real to them.”View image in fullscreenThe Freedom Tower rises above one of the 9/11 Memorial reflecting pools at the 9/11 Memorial museum as it prepares to mark the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks.Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesThe blood brothers look out at the contemporary US with a mixture of sorrow and perplexity. Clark has become an outspoken pacifist, dismayed by the decades of overseas conflict that followed the attacks.He says: “With 25 years of time to think about it, I realise more and more the utter futility of war. I think of Germany, Italy, and Japan being our greatest allies today. What on earth are we doing to ourselves? Dropping bombs on residential areas in Ukraine, Russia, Gaza – what a senseless waste of energy and human life.”Clark’s aversion to vengeance ran so deep that he was repulsed by thestreet celebrationsfollowing the killing of al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden in 2011. “I was disgusted when people were driving around in pickup trucks chanting ‘USA!’ and cheering for another human being’s death. Capture him, interrogate him, lock him away – fine. But taking lives and celebrating it? No. That is not who we should be.”Praimnath recalls the profound but fleeting sense of unity that blossomed after 9/11. “After that infamous day, the entire nation rallied around each other,” he reflects. “All the churches were packed. A month later, everything went back to normal.“But I still believe we are a resilient people. We may have our political differences but at the end of the day we know that, when tragedy strikes, the labels fall away. On the 81st floor, there were no Republicans or Democrats, no Black or white. We were just brothers trying to find the way out.”Explore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001New YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade ban | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Ed Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move likely to draw fierce criticism from US and Israel
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Ed Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move likely to draw fierce criticism from US and Israel
Content: Ed Miliband is expected to set out the measures in a statement to MPs on Tuesday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenEd Miliband is expected to set out the measures in a statement to MPs on Tuesday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAForeign policyUK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade banEd Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move likely to draw fierce criticism from US and IsraelPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 7 Sep 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEd Miliband will announce what he has described as abroad reset of the UK’s relations with Israelon Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause.In an intervention that is expected to draw fierce criticism from the US andIsrael, the foreign secretary will impose a UK ban on the trade in goods and some services from illegal Israeli settlements.He has also told civil society groups he is determined to reassert support for a two-state solution to the conflict with an appeal for the protection of Palestinian rights and respect for international law.In his statement to MPs, Miliband is expected to use firmer language than his recent predecessors in calling out the humanitarian injustices suffered by Palestinians in Gaza.The steps he lays out are likely to fall short of the full set of demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but they will still be seen as a sign that the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank – widely seen as intended to destroy the prospect of a Palestinian state.View image in fullscreenA Palestinian woman waits at a bus stop decked out with Israeli flags raised by settlers between Nablus and Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersIsrael has already threatened reprisals over Miliband’s previous claim that the Israeli military has held back aid into Gaza, and the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has claimed theLabourgovernment is gripped by Jew hatred. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies such as Qatar on Monday to brief them on the government’s plans in the region.Miliband’s intervention comes as polling released to the Guardian shows Britons across the political divide strongly favour banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements by a margin of more than two to one.The polling, conducted by Opinium and published by the European Council on Foreign Relations, shows that only 18% of UK adults oppose a ban on trade in goods with Israeli settlements, compared with 46% in favour. Support rises to nearly three-quarters when those who did not express an opinion are excluded.Miliband’s statement will stand by his claim that the Israel Defense Forces, in the name of security, are placing unnecessary controls on aid entering Gaza, creating a horrific situation. It is understood, however, that he is sceptical of the UK’s leverage to resolve the situation apart from calling for the restrictions to be lifted.View image in fullscreenA Palestinian woman and her children make their way through a destroyed neighbourhood of Gaza City.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersHis claim that aid had been held back was hotly denied by the Israeli foreign ministry at the weekend.Miliband is also likely to go further than his predecessors in placing the settlement measures firmly in the context of upholding international law, including the findings of two key institutions, the international criminal court and the international court of justice (ICJ), two bodies under attack by the US.The package is not likely to include sanctions over aid restrictions into Gaza, or to describe what has happened in the territory as a genocide. The UK has kept open the option of joining countries such as South Africa at the ICJ to claim Israel is in breach of the court’s previous rulings.But by acting decisively on trade, Miliband has set aside warnings that a polarising UK intervention might help Benjamin Netanyahu’s chances in Israel’s 27 October election. British sources pointed out that even Israeli military officials have warned their prime minister that the IDF will struggle to defend new settlements and outposts in the northern West Bank, because they lack basic security infrastructure and were established for political rather than security reasons.Despite US criticism of the UK stance, Washington has also been putting pressure on Netanyahu on the settlements issue to the point that he has called for some to be dismantled, saying they were not established with the necessary permits. Israel has previously demolished some outposts, but they are often rebuilt soon after.10:13British activist abducted by West Bank settlers deported by Israel - The LatestThe UK ban on trade in settlement goods, long parried by the Foreign Office as impossible to implement, is in line with the ICJ advisory opinion in 2024 requiring governments not to aid or assist an Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory, not just illegal settlements. The UK government has never formally replied to the opinion, but ministers in Keir Starmer’s government said it was broadly compliant.The measures on settlements may require primary legislation to ban the trade in goods rather than an easier statutory instrument, while the trade ban will extend to some services including financing and advertising illegal settlements.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUN expert Francesca Albanese calls for ‘true paradigm shift’ as Miliband resets policy on IsraelRead moreThe Foreign Office has previously argued that it was impossible to distinguish between products emanating from illegal settlements and those from Israel. The UK officially regards all Israeli civilian settlements built on territories captured during the 1967 six-day war as illegal under international law.Total trade in goods and services between the UK and Israel in 2025 was £6bn, and the scale of the disruption may depend on Israeli reprisals.Products produced in Israeli settlements located within the territories occupied by Israel since 1967 have not been entitled to preferential tariff treatment upon entry into the UK since 2005. The country has also issued guidance on misleading labelling and urged businesses not to trade with or be engaged in economic and financial activities in Israeli settlements. The new measures make such investments unlawful.The UK reset was made more urgent by Israel’s E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which is poised to effectively cut the occupied West Bank in two from November. But the Burnham government also feels compelled to act because of the increase in settler violence in the West Bank and the failure of Trump’s Board of Peace after six months to secure the twin objectives of Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza.View image in fullscreenIsrael’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, holds up a map showing the E1 settlement project.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APLabour is also under domestic pressure from the Greens onPalestine. The party leader, Zack Polanski, is expected to stand in the 8 October Holborn and St Pancras byelection triggered by Starmer’s resignation as an MP. The new Labour policy may give the party’s candidate some political cover against Polanski.In a sign of the potential ramifications for Miliband, Netanyahu’s older son, Yair, suggested last week that the Falkland Islands belonged to Argentina and not to Britain.He is not a minister, but after his comments Trump indicated that Washington could reconsider its position on British sovereignty over the islands.Trump said last Thursday that he would not back Britain if Argentina were to invade the islands, telling GB News: “Your country was not there to help me” when the US and Israel began their war on Iran in February.The Foreign Office declined to comment when approached by the Guardian.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyIsraelPalestineEd MilibandLabourMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Police used batons and pepper spray on far-right protesters in Portsmouth unrest | Portsmouth | The Guardian
description: Minister condemns groups behind Hampshire disorder and says officers were injured as they repelled ‘aggression’
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Minister condemns groups behind Hampshire disorder and says officers were injured as they repelled ‘aggression’
Content: An estimated 200 activists gathered in Portsmouth and clashed with riot police on Sunday night.Photograph: SuppliedView image in fullscreenAn estimated 200 activists gathered in Portsmouth and clashed with riot police on Sunday night.Photograph: SuppliedPortsmouthPolice used batons and pepper spray on far-right protesters in Portsmouth unrestMinister condemns groups behind Hampshire disorder and says officers were injured as they repelled ‘aggression’Rajeev Syal,Steven MorrisandBen QuinnMon 7 Sep 2026 15.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBatons and synthetic pepper spray were used to repel hundreds of masked, black-clad vigilantes inPortsmouthon Sunday, it has emerged, as the policing minister said officers had been injured as they repelled organised “aggression”.No 10 condemns ‘thuggish’ far-right activists after Portsmouth unrestRead moreAfter police contained the weekend’s second disruptive demonstration against asylum seekers travelling to the UK in small boats, it was claimed that officers inHampshirewere pushed off their motorbikes and pelted with bricks. Sarah Jones, the Home Office minister, condemned groups behind the disorder for promoting “racism and thuggery”.Activists wearing balaclavasclashed with police in Portsmouth on Sunday eveningafter a dinghy reached the UK from Normandy. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary have launched an investigation into potential assaults and criminal damage.Daniel Thomas, a far-right agitator closely linked to Tommy Robinson, the longtime anti-Islam figure whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, claimed to have arranged the protest.Thomas was also behind disruption in Dover on Saturday, when crowds of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road around the port for several hours.View image in fullscreenDaniel Thomas, left, speaking to the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf (right, in blue suit), has claimed to have arranged the demonstration.Photograph: Theo Shaw/PAIn a statement to MPs, Jones said: “Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary, with the support of other neighbouring forces, used a dispersal notice to ensure public safety and officers were forced to use batons and Pava spray to maintain order in the face of some aggression.”Spencer Wragg, the chair of the Hampshire police federation, said one of the officers injured was a rookie who had only finished training school three days earlier. “Those scenes in that area of Portsmouth weren’t protests, they weren’t protests at all, it was clear that some people were intent on disorder and venting their frustrations,” he said.About 120 people seeking asylum were brought to shore in Hampshire after travelling to the UK on a “mega-dinghy” which had departed from the Normandy coast and was at sea for roughly 10 hours.The landing point of the dinghy was farther west than most small boat arrivals. Officials are concerned that people smugglers are starting to target new routes across England’s south coast, with craft launched from a wider stretch of the French shoreline.View image in fullscreenAbout 120 people seeking asylum were brought to shore in Hampshire at the weekend.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersAn estimated 200 protesters gathered and clashed with riot police on Sunday night, vowing to prevent migrants leaving the port. Footage showed some chanting “send them back” as police officers with shields raised tried to maintain order.Amid concerns that police were caught unawares by the unrest in Dover on Saturday, Jones said: “Work is ongoing to establish any lessons and ensure that relevant intelligence is shared at pace across our law enforcement system.”Speaking to MPs and peers at a closed-door meeting on Monday, the prime minister Andy Burnham said Labour’s mission must be to counter “fear with positivity and hope”.Burnham is understood to have told the parliamentary Labour party (PLP) that Britain would never accept any form of racism in its communities and stood for a sense of fairness and justice.“We’ve got a fantastic opportunity in our hands to change this country for the better. We go into the autumn, in really good heart, with a spring in our step,” the prime minister said.“There’s a lot at stake and it requires us to counter fear with positivity and hope. We have a responsibility in the times that we’re living in. It’s a solemn responsibility to prevent the politics of poison seeping into our streets.“We are here to speak to the politics of hope and of positivity.”Labour and Lib Dem MPs called on the government to explain why police appeared to have been caught off-guard by the events in Dover and Portsmouth.Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and a former Home Office minister, questioned why the police were not aware of plans to block the local port. “Please ensure that the intelligence picture is strong enough so that the police can respond accordingly to future incidents,” he told MPs.The Liberal Democrat Home Office spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, asked: “How is it that far-right thugs in balaclavas were able to close Britain’s busiest port without the police receiving any prior intelligence? And how is it that then an apparently separate group with some commonalities were then able to blockade another site the next evening?”View image in fullscreenSarah Jones, the Home Office minister, said the government would learn lessons from the disorder.Photograph: House of Commons/UK Parliament/PAJones said there was “a crossover in terms of online activity” and the government would learn lessons from the disorder.In an on-camera confrontation on Monday, Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, told the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, thatthe Patriot Platform grouphe led would deliver working-class votes to Reform – but expressed anger at Nigel Farage’s criticisms of Dover demonstrators for wearing balaclavas.Thomas said: “I understand Nigel is going to be prime minister one day and I understand he has to set a standard, which will basically be that you know he can’t just come out and say, everything’s great and these guys are fantastic, but Nigel needs to be very careful with his words.”Yusuf said he would “take that message back” and added that Thomas had articulated why he and his group had organised demonstrations. “I think it’s important we listen to people. He was making his points respectfully,” he said.10:30Who is behind ‘thuggish’ far-right protests in Dover and Portsmouth? - The LatestPolice could impose a balaclava ban on future anti-migrant demonstrations after officers were injured, Whitehall sources said.Under the Crime and Policing Act, Hampshire police could apply for a ban to ensure that protesters cannot cover their faces. Facebook posts claim that a demonstration is planned for Saturday by a group called Portsmouth Patriots. Hampshire police has been approached for comment.Ministershave been criticisedfor failing to condemn far-right groups behind the disorder. Nick Lowles, the chief executive of Hope Not Hate, which charts far-right activity, told the BBC: “To have 300, 400 people with balaclavas marching down the streets, stopping traffic. You know, it’s not just good enough. We need to call these people out for their politics and for the type of Britain that they want to see.“We’ve got different ways to register our protest. We do not go on the street. We do not burn people out of their houses. We do not cause trouble and threaten to fight the police.”The Hampshire and Isle of Wight police and crime commissioner, Donna Jones, said England’s south coast was not prepared for the arrival of migrants, and ministers would have a “significant issue” if people traffickers shifted their routes farther west. She warned that places such as Portsmouth were “not set up” for the arrival of migrants.Kent police defended the force’s action after it described the highly organised protest action in Dover as “spontaneous”. Assistant chief constable Nigel Brookes said the term was used in line with national guidance and that the action had “developed rapidly”.Eight boats carrying 625 people arrived in the UK on Sunday after crossing the English Channel, Home Office data shows.Explore more on these topicsPortsmouthPoliceThe far rightImmigration and asylumHampshireEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cities in Great Britain most vulnerable to extreme heat revealed  | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: OS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperatures
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: OS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperatures
Content: The City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenThe City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAExtreme heatCities in Great Britain most vulnerable to extreme heat revealedOS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperaturesSandra LavilleEnvironment correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePortsmouth, Leicester, Exeter, Bristol andNottinghamwill be among the cities that warm the most by the end of this century as global heating turns British cities into urban heat islands, according to research.Analysis from Ordnance Survey (OS) has created a heat vulnerability index for all cities in Great Britain.Portsmouth, which sits on the south coast of England and is home to 208,000 people, is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research from the OS, the Met Office and the data analysis company 4 Earth Intelligence.Concrete, asphalt, buildings and hard surfaces in cities absorb solar radiation during the day and act like giant radiators, holding on to the heat rather than cooling down at night as in more rural areas. Cities can be up to 10C hotter than surrounding areas.Areas most at risk of extreme warming are those with the leasttree cover,green spaceand waterways.View image in fullscreenPortsmouth is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research.Photograph: Peter Titmuss/AlamyThis summer was provisionallythe UK’s hottest on record, and the research reveals which cities are suffering now from intense urban heat and which will be among the warmest in future.The research analyses 71 cities granted by royal charter across England, Scotland and Wales but excluding Northern Ireland. The OS heat vulnerability index suggests that by 2040 all 71 cities will reach high heat vulnerability. By the turn of the century, almost two-thirds could reach the most severe level. Those facing the most severe impact by the end of the century are predicted to be Portsmouth, the City of Westminster, Plymouth,Leicesterand Exeter, according to the analysis.Nick Bolton, the chief executive of Ordnance Survey, said: “Cities are where millions of people live, work and spend their everyday lives.“Extreme and sustained heat can affect people’s health and wellbeing, how comfortable our homes and workplaces are, and put additional pressure on transport, energy and emergency services. Understanding how and where this vulnerability is changing depends on an accurate view of how the country is built, based on trusted authoritative data, which is critical for planners, developers and local authorities preparing for a warmer future.”UK ‘built for climate that no longer exists’ and needs urgent changes to survive global heating, report warnsRead morePortsmouth is today the most heat-vulnerable city and will remain at the highest level for warming until the end of the century, according to the research. The city of Leicester is projected to show the biggest rise in Britain’s heat vulnerability rankings, climbing from 10th now to fourth by the end of the century, while Exeter and Nottingham also rise into the 10 most vulnerable cities, alongside Bristol andBrightonand Hove by the end of this century.Leaders in Portsmouth have identified areas including Somerstown, Portsea, Southsea and Fratton as those particularly exposed to urban heat because of their limited green areas and hard surfaces, and noted that areas with less green space overlap with those of deprivation.The City ofLondonand the City of Westminster areas rank among the most heat-retentive urban environments in the UK.The City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city, given the concentration of buildings, roads and hard surfaces as well as limited green space, trees and water. Westminster ranks third for overall heat vulnerability today and second in both future periods behind Portsmouth.View image in fullscreenTree cover, green space and waterways can help mitigate the effects of global heating.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAstudycommissioned by the mayor of London has put the total economic cost of the 2022 London heatwaves at £1.5bn, including productivity losses, health impacts, education disruption, energy demand, transport and emergency services.The OS heat vulnerability index combined current observed temperatures with the structural characteristics of Britain’s built environment and climate projections into the future to produce a score for every city on a scale of 1 to 5, where 3 to 4 is high and 4 to 5 is severe.Among cities coping the best with the changing climate is Milton Keynes, which ranks 69th out of 71 cities for heat vulnerability today. Milton Keynes has the lowest built-environment vulnerability in England and the most effective natural cooling of any city in the analysis, with 46 sq km of natural surfaces, against almost 40 sq km of hard made surfaces.Jonathan Hendry, the chief executive of 4 Earth Intelligence, said exposure varied street by street within a single city. “The areas consistently subjected to higher temperatures than their surroundings are the ones that overheat first during a heatwave,” he said.“We’re mapping how to turn thermal threats into actionable blueprints for urban resilience, supporting decisions on where heat refuges are sited and how emergency responses are planned in advance rather than in the middle of climate events.”Explore more on these topicsExtreme heatClimate crisisPortsmouthConstruction industryThe sunLondonPlymouthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Polanski faces Green rival in his pursuit of Keir Starmer’s old seat  | Green party | The Guardian
description: Hamza Chowdhury says most of his fellow Green Camden councillors back him to contest 8 October byelection
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Hamza Chowdhury says most of his fellow Green Camden councillors back him to contest 8 October byelection
Content: Hamza Chowdhury announced his candidacy for Holborn and St Pancras MP, arguing the seat does not need ‘a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet’.Photograph: Green PartyView image in fullscreenHamza Chowdhury announced his candidacy for Holborn and St Pancras MP, arguing the seat does not need ‘a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet’.Photograph: Green PartyGreen partyPolanski faces Green rival in his pursuit of Keir Starmer’s old seatHamza Chowdhury says most of his fellow Green Camden councillors back him to contest 8 October byelectionPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski is facing unexpected opposition from his own party in his attempt to fight the Holborn and St Pancras byelection for the Greens, with a local councillor saying he is also seeking the nomination, and that the seat does not need “a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet”.The intervention by Hamza Chowdhury, a Green representative on Camden council in northLondon, came as the date for the byelection was confirmed for 8 October, after Keir Starmer’s formal resignation as an MP.This is also potentially problematic for the Greens, given the vote comes just a week after their conference, meaning the final weekend of campaigning takes place as many party activists will be gathered in Brighton.Ina post on Instagramon Monday, Chowdhury said he had received nominations from six other Camden Green councillors, meaning seven of the 10 Greens on the authority oppose Polanski being selected.Among those backing Chowdhury is Lorna Russell, the group leader in Camden for theGreen party, which is the official opposition to Labour.Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, announced on Thursday thathe would seek the nomination to fight the seat vacated by Starmer, setting up a high-stakes byelection against Labour.View image in fullscreenZack Polanski canvassing in Holborn and St Pancras on 5 September.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianLocal party members will vote later this week to select a candidate, and the Guardian has been told thatthey are broadly supportive of Polanski standing.But such high-profile opposition is notable, especially given Chowdhury argued that Polanski, who lives in east London, would be unable to properly represent the area if he won.Chowdhury wrote: “I know Camden because I live it every day. I know the challenges facing our communities, our estates, our broken lifts, our unpicked bins, our unclean roads and endless housing register waiting list because these are the places I have grown up and continue to call home.“We don’t need another MP who arrives during an election campaign, puts out a few leaflets, makes a few promises and disappears once the votes are counted. We need an MP who is present, accessible and visibly part of the community all year round.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I am asking Green party members for the opportunity to represent your home truly and properly. I’m not asking you to vote for a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet. I’m asking you to choose someone who is already here.”Speaking to the Guardianwhile canvassing in the constituency at the weekend, Polanski said that even if he wins he will not move to the area, but cycle from his flat in Hackney.He said: “I can cycle to the constituency really quickly. In fact, the length of the constituency is just as fast for me to cycle,” he says. “I’d regularly be here, doing surgeries and representing people.”Polanski has said his party is the underdog in a constituency won by Starmer with an 11,000-plus majority in the 2024 election. The Greens have already flooded the area with canvassers, hoping to mimic the model usedto overturn a 13,000-plus Labour majority in Greater Manchester’s Gorton and Dentonin February.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiByelectionsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: German chancellor vows to stay in office despite AfD triumph in state election | Germany | The Guardian
description: Friedrich Merz said his conservative CDU was shaken ‘to its very foundations’ after far-right victory in Saxony-Anhalt
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Friedrich Merz said his conservative CDU was shaken ‘to its very foundations’ after far-right victory in Saxony-Anhalt
Content: ‘Giving up is not an option for me,’ said Friedrich Merz.Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Giving up is not an option for me,’ said Friedrich Merz.Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPAGermanyGerman chancellor vows to stay in office despite AfD triumph in state electionFriedrich Merz said his conservative CDU was shaken ‘to its very foundations’ after far-right victory in Saxony-AnhaltDeborah Colein BerlinMon 7 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA “shocked” and chastened Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay in office despitethe far right’s triumph in a state electionthat has brought anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin politicians within striking distance of power.The German chancellor, appearing ashen-faced in front of reporters in Berlin, said on Monday that the landslide victory by the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt had shaken his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) “to its very foundations”.The unpopular Merz, who had pledged to halve the AfD’s support at the national level, has watched the nativist party rack up electoral gains, none as convincing as its utter rout of the CDU in the eastern region on Sunday with nearly 44% of the vote.The AfD and its candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority but could yet create Germany’s first far-right state government since the Nazi period.Merz appeared contrite and willing to work on his “communication” with voters. “This is the worst electoral defeat the [CDU] has suffered in years, in decades,” he said. “Of course this will have to have consequences.”Exit polls indicated the state’s voters were driven by deep dissatisfaction with the political establishment and its stewardship of Europe’s biggest economy, with one showing thatonly 9% approved of Merz’s performance.View image in fullscreenUlrich Siegmund mocked Merz as ‘a very good campaigner’ for the AfD.Photograph: Odd Andersen/AFP/Getty ImagesSiegmund, a media-savvy former fragrance salesman, was also able to tap into a sense of grievance in the former communist east, where complaints abound that voters there are treated as “second-class citizens” more than three decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall.Siegmund, 35, mocked the 70-year-old Merz as “a very good campaigner” for the AfD.Only 16 months in office, Merz conceded his own low poll ratings had played a role in his party’s loss. “I know that I personally was a constant topic in this election campaign,” he said. “We must try – myself included – to reach people more effectively, in the full range of their emotions.”1:24‘We should have learned more from history’: Germans react to AfD win – videoThe CDU’s junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats, indicated a willingness to water down contentious measures to shore up the statutory healthcare andpension schemes.However, Merz insisted: “My determination to continue on the path of reform is unbroken,” saying a sustainable system was essential for the sake of “our children and grandchildren”. He added: “Giving up is not an option for me.”Merz said he wanted to assure Germany’s allies that “our institutions are resilient and stable” and its own vulnerable minorities that the country would stick to its values and constitution even if the AfD took power in Saxony-Anhalt. “We know that Germany carries special responsibility because of its history,” he said.He also promised to stay the course on Ukraine, stressing he would “not budge a single millimetre from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom against Russia as well”.Merz said Moscow would cheer the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt and accused it of lending support to the far right’s campaign, with another two German state elections still to come this month amidalleged Russian interference and sabotage.View image in fullscreenSven Schulze, the CDU state premier for Saxony-Anhalt, acknowledged his party now had ‘no mandate’ to govern in the state.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersAlthough the CDU rallied behind its chancellor and party leader, several influential commenters openly called for his immediate replacement – a complex step under German law.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGermany “needs a clean slate, a fresh start, and that starts with Friedrich Merz”, said theDer Spiegel editor-in-chief, Dirk Kurbjuweit. “He is evidently the wrong man for this office in these times.”The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt chapter is listed as “confirmed rightwing extremist” by the domestic intelligence service. It has pledgedmass deportations of unwelcome immigrants and asylum seekers, which critics have said would be illegal, while promising massive boosts in social welfare spending with unclear financing.The AfD has also taken aim at state support for public broadcasters and cultural institutionsit deems “unpatriotic”, sparking fears of “cultural hegemony”.The party did not win enough seats to elect Siegmund as state premier, but AfD leaders said they seek to pick off rebel lawmakers from other parties willing to play kingmaker. It is only three seats short of a majority.Theconservative-left populist BSW party, which also favours restoring ties with Russia and largely blocking immigration, signalled an openness to working with the AfD but before the election ruled out joining the state government.In the 13 years of the AfD’s existence, the mainstream parties have maintained a “firewall” against the far right, refusing any formal cooperation that would allow it take power. The strategy meant to sideline the party has appeared to backfire, however, as the permanent “outsider” role appeals to legions of voters fed up with politics as usual.The CDU state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged his party had “no mandate” to govern given its humiliating 17% result, even if it managed to cobble together an unwieldy coalition with all the other parties in the legislature.Although Saxony-Anhalt forms part of the AfD heartland as a relatively poor, ex-communist region, the party has begun makinginroads in the westas well amid alarming signs of decline in the steel, chemicals and automotive sectors.Germany faces another two regional elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in another eastern state, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the AfD is also strong.The party co-leader Alice Weidel, beaming after Sunday’s vote, said the AfD was now targeting 40% at the next general election, due in 2029. It is polling at about 28%.Explore more on these topicsGermanyFriedrich MerzAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)EuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canada’s retaliatory US tariffs set to take effect as trade dispute grows | Canada | The Guardian
description: Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
Content: Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks.Photograph: Ari Saperstein/EPAView image in fullscreenTensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks.Photograph: Ari Saperstein/EPACanadaCanada’s retaliatory US tariffs set to take effect as trade dispute growsCounter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goodsMaya YangMon 7 Sep 2026 19.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 19.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada is set to impose retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports early on Tuesday, escalating atrade fightwith its largest trading partner as tensions between US president Donald Trump and Canadian prime minister Mark Carney intensify.The tariffs, which take effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, will range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering C$27.6bn in imports from the US. The measures will target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs.The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $27.6bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian governmentsaid.“Canada’s counter-measures do not apply to US goods that are in transit toCanadaon the day on which they come into force,” it added.Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks, with Carney last week urging the Trump administration to “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions.Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” – whichCanadians have rejected.US vice-president JD Vance has also reportedly mocked Carney,apparently sayingthe Canadian prime minister “comes in and puffs his chest out and says: ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.’”Last month, Trumpannounceda new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”, adding: “We don’t need Canada, they need us!”Carney said last month Canada would not accept a US trade deal that weakened French-language protections, saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”.Quebec has long maintained laws aimed at protecting French and preserving its distinct cultural identity. Those measures have become asticking pointin the trade talks between the two countries, with American negotiators raising concerns about rules they say can disadvantage US businesses.Explore more on these topicsCanadaTrump tariffsTariffsAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bernie Ecclestone questioned after shotgun found on his private jet in Portugal | Bernie Ecclestone | The Guardian
description: The 95-year-old former Formula One chief Bernie Ecclestone said he was questioned by police in Portugal after a shotgun was found on his private jet
Author: Miguel Dantas
Headline: The 95-year-old former Formula One chief Bernie Ecclestone said he was questioned by police in Portugal after a shotgun was found on his private jet
Content: Bernie Ecclestone said he bought the gun in England, before taking it to Switzerland and on to Portugal.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersView image in fullscreenBernie Ecclestone said he bought the gun in England, before taking it to Switzerland and on to Portugal.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersBernie EcclestoneBernie Ecclestone questioned after shotgun found on his private jet in PortugalFormer F1 chief says firearm was for clay-pigeon shootingPolice quiz 95-year-old over lack of documents for gunMiguel Dantasin PortoMon 7 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBernie Ecclestone was detained in Portugal on Monday after customs authorities found him in possession of an undocumented shotgun. The Guardian has independently confirmed the incident with multiple authorities involved in the matter.The detention of the 95‑year‑old took place at Tires Aerodrome in Cascais, shortly after the formerFormula Onechief’s private jet landed. After a routine inspection of the aircraft and its passengers, authorities reportedly discovered a shotgun in Ecclestone’s possession. He was stopped for questioning by Portuguese officials and said the gun was for use in clay pigeon shooting.‘Like an AI agent’: Wolff hails Antonelli’s Italian GP victory in title chargeRead moreUnder standard procedure in such cases, the firearm is seized and the person found carrying it is formally made a defendant in criminal proceedings. It is not yet known what the outcome of Ecclestone’s case will be.Responding to reports he had been arrested, Ecclestone told the Press Association: “No. The police were very helpful and doing all they could to stop us from having to do what we had to do.”Explaining the events, Ecclestone told PA: “I was going to take part in Portugal in a clay pigeon shooting competition, which I only knew about a few days ago because Fabiana [his wife] met someone when she was coming back from Brazil to Portugal. He said he was entering into a clay pigeon competition.“So she called me and said: ‘There is something here you should go and look at. Why don’t you turn up and join?’ And I said: ‘Well, that wouldn’t be a bad idea.’ … As I have got guns already in Switzerland, which have been imported properly, because we do a bit of clay pigeon shooting there, I brought the gun in with me.“I went through customs and the people know me very well. They said: ‘Anything to declare?’ I said: ‘No, nothing really, just all the usual personal things.’“So I walked out and, as I got out, one of my people with me said: ‘The police have asked if you would go and see them.’ I went to see the police and said: ‘What can I do for you?’ And they said: ‘We would like some information on this gun you brought in.’“I didn’t even unzip the case. I said: ‘Well, it is a shotgun and this is the reason.’ And they asked where is the blue book for the gun? And I said: ‘I don’t know, I have never heard about a blue book in my life.’“They said: ‘Yes, well anyone with these guns should always have the book, it is like a passport. Incidentally, I want to look at your passport, too,’ which they took.“I said I bought the gun in England and took it into Switzerland through all the normal channels. And they said: ‘Where is the blue book?’ And I said: ‘I just told you, I don’t know about the blue book.’“There were about four police guys and they said: ‘What you have done is try to import a gun into the country.’ I said: ‘I have not tried to do that. I have come through customs, and here I am with you’.“So all this nonsense went on. We went back to the customs, and the police had complained to customs, and the customs officer said: ‘You need to surrender the gun here in Lisbon and then we will look at it there, and do you want to import it? And if so, you will have to pay duty on it and ask for a temporary import, and we will deal with it like that.’ So I said: ‘Well we’d better do that.’”This is not the first time Ecclestone has faced scrutiny from authorities over a firearm while travelling by air. In May 2022, the former F1 chief executive was arrested in Brazil for illegally possessing a gun while preparing to board a private plane bound for Switzerland.On that occasion an X‑ray of Ecclestone’s luggage revealed an undeclared LW Seecamp .32‑calibre pistol. He admitted that he owned the firearm but said he was unaware that he was carrying it.Ecclestone was taken to a facility at Viracopos Airport in Campinas, where he posted bail before being released to continue his journey.Ecclestone’s wife, Fabiana Flosi, was linked to a property purchase about 15 miles west of Lisbon. The deal was reportedly the largest private sale of a house in Portugal, with the price said to be around £35m.Ecclestone has been involved in Formula One since the 1950s, starting out as a driver and businessman before becoming a team owner and a key negotiator of the championship’s television rights.He was the sport’s most influential commercial and political figure for decades, playing a central role in securing commercial partnerships, sponsorships and agreements with racing circuits around the world.Ecclestone’s official involvement with F1 came to an end in 2017, when Liberty Media acquired the commercial rights to the championship. He has nevertheless remained an inescapable figure in the sport and is widely credited with transforming F1 into a global mass-market phenomenon.Explore more on these topicsBernie EcclestoneFormula OnenewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage still Reform’s best hope as rivals struggle to match appeal to party faithful | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Despite series of scandals, members remain loyal to their leader as questions over his successor grow
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Despite series of scandals, members remain loyal to their leader as questions over his successor grow
Content: Richard Tice and Zia Yusuf stand on either side of Nigel Farage at this year’s Reform UK conference.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenRichard Tice and Zia Yusuf stand on either side of Nigel Farage at this year’s Reform UK conference.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAReform UKFarage still Reform’s best hope as rivals struggle to match appeal to party faithfulDespite series of scandals, members remain loyal to their leader as questions over his successor growPippa CrerarandPeter WalkerMon 7 Sep 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew British politicians unleash the kind of evangelical zeal among their party faithful asNigel Farage. Despite being weighed down by weeks of scandal, last weekend’s Reform UK conference showed that – as far as the membership is concerned – the lustre has not come off their man.So it was notable that Farage felt compelled to reassure his disciples that he wasn’t going anywhere. “I’m only here because of the failure of our political class, and I am determined to lead Reform to victory at the next general election. That is my job,” he told them during his speech.While support within the party for Farage remains rock solid, the same cannot be said for the wider public. Dogged by financial controversy and with a parliamentary standards investigation hanging over him, as well as the police looking into Reform, it is unsurprising that hisratings have slumped.The steady drumbeat of speculation over his future has continued. But while he has publicly declared he intends to fight the next general election – and beyond – sources close to Farage have told the Guardian that ifReform UKloses that particular contest, it will be his last.By 2029, the likely date for the next election, Farage would be 65 years old. That would make him the same age – he tells friends – as Winston Churchill in 1940, the oldest first-time prime minister to take office in the modern era. Another five years at the helm would put Farage well ahead by that measure.Yet four out of five Reform UK members say they would want Farage to continue as leader even if the party is not in government after the next election,according to a pollof 850 members by Lord Ashcroft in June. Just 13% said he should step down if they don’t win.There are those inside the party who don’t think Farage will stick around even until the next election. “There are all sorts of reasons why Nigel could throw in the towel before then,” one Reform official said, citing family, security and money. “He’d have an easier life on the outside.”What almost everybody inside Reform agrees on, however, is that if Farage does decide to stand down, it would be on his own terms. The party base is so fervently behind him it would be virtually impossible for a rival to stage a coup.Whether Reform UK could carry on making the political weather to the extent it currently does without him at the helm is far from clear. So while any doubt remains over his plans, speculation over a possible successor will continue.One Reform insider said that if Farage did depart, the race was expected to quickly turn into a battle between Zia Yusuf and whichever “anyone but Zia” candidate seemed best placed to beat him, with the home affairs spokesperson a divisive figure even inside the party.“Everyone loves Zia when he’s on policy and focused, and when we were polling at 32%, they didn’t mind when he wasn’t,” they said. “But now it’s more like 23%, and every vote counts, there is a concern that he puts off possible switchers, especially from the Conservatives.“If you lead a party you have to be able to build internal coalitions, and he’s so combative I can’t see that happening.”Yusuf’ssocial media outburstshave prompted even party loyalists to urge him to rein it in. Nadine Dorries, the former Tory culture secretary who defected to Reform last year, said at the weekend: “I think Zia’s got a problem with Twitter and someone needs to take his phone off him.”One close ally of Farage said the party leader was “unimpressed” by some of Yusuf’s comments, which he felt distracted from Reform’s attempts to make itself look ready for government. “Nigel thinks he’s a wanker,” they added.But when asked unprompted who they would like to see as the next Reform UK leader, party members were most likely to name Yusuf, with the backing of 22%, according to the Ashcroft polling.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReform insiders believe he wants the top job – the backstory video he launched online at conference looked every bit like a veiled leadership pitch – even though party bosses have to date appeared less than enthusiastic about finding him a seat to stand for parliament.Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, was almost level, on 21%. Tellingly, just 6% suggested Robert Jenrick, the economy spokesperson, who is viewed with some scepticism among Reform activists because he defected from the Tories after losing that leadership contest, and was also a key member of the last Conservative government.“My view is there’s an acceptance that it probably can’t be a former Tory MP, and that Richard would have the authenticity to beat Zia,” one Reform insider said. “It doesn’t mean that Robert wouldn’t think about it, but if it was him against Zia, Zia would probably win.”Tice, wholed the partyfor three years until Farage’s return to frontline politics in spring 2024, probably has greater public appeal than Yusuf, and as a more moderate figure could win more votes from the Conservatives.Yet neither Yusuf’s provocative outbursts, nor Jenrick’s ruthless ambition, nor Tice’s more mainstream leanings are ever likely to deliver the same level of cut through that their boss has achieved, and so electoral success could end up eluding them.For now, despite his increasing toxicity with the general public, Farage remains Reform’s best hope.Get in touchContact Guardian Politics about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
