This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Scroll down and click onSecure Messaging. When asked who you wish to contact please select thePolitics (UK)team.EmailFor encrypted email correspondence you can create a free Proton Mail account and email us at guardian.politics.desk@protonmail.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FarageRichard TicefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sightings of Meghan at star-studded retreat fuel Cotswolds rumours | Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex | The Guardian
description: Reports of Duchess of Sussex visiting Soho Farmhouse add to speculation she could be moving to area with Prince Harry
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Reports of Duchess of Sussex visiting Soho Farmhouse add to speculation she could be moving to area with Prince Harry
Content: Meghan and her husband, Prince Harry, recently returned to Britain from the US.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/APView image in fullscreenMeghan and her husband, Prince Harry, recently returned to Britain from the US.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/APMeghan, the Duchess of SussexSightings of Meghan at star-studded retreat fuel Cotswolds rumoursReports of Soho Farmhouse visit add to speculation Duke and Duchess of Sussex could be settling in the areaHelena HortonMon 7 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the Duke and Duchess of Sussex landed back inEnglandearlier this summer, six years after they moved to California and quit as working royals, speculation was rife about where they would call home.Now, members of the luxury countryside retreat Soho Farmhouse have said they spotted Meghan arriving for an early morning coffee, sparking speculation that the couple were settling down in the exclusive countryside enclave of north Oxfordshire. The correspondent for the RoyalistTom Sykessaid the duchess was seen arriving at the Comfy Farm lounge before 9am, where she was introduced to senior staff members by name.The Cotswolds club, set in 40 hectares (100 acres) of countryside and featuring a luxury spa, 40 discreet guest cabins, and an indoor-outdoor pool, is a hotspot for celebrities.If it is true that the Sussex family are staying in a property near the club, their neighbours will include the Beckhams, who live within walking distance of Soho Farmhouse and are often seen enjoying dinners and strolls in the grounds.Paul McCartney also visits with his fashion designer daughter, Stella, who has a house nearby. Meghan and Harry previously rented a house in picturesque Great Tew, a village full of thatched chocolate-box cottages a stone’s throw from the Beckhams.Another potential neighbour is Geri Halliwell-Horner and her husband, Christian Horner, who live in a £9m former vicarage in nearby Banbury. They share a love of animals with Meghan and have a menagerie on the estate including miniature donkeys. The Telegraph reported that the Sussexesleft their rescue chickensback in Montecito but would transport their dogs over.There have been rumblings of a royal return in the Cotswolds, with thelocal papers reportingon their move. Their children, Archie and Lilibet, are enrolled at a school for the new term, and parents at a school in the area have reported being sent letters reminding them to maintain the privacy of other children and parents and not to take pictures or share any information about others there.View image in fullscreenThe village of Great Tew, where the royal couple previously rented a house.Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/AlamyAlthoughthe more than 200,000 membershave made Soho House feel less exclusive to some, Soho Farmhouse is still a favourite venue for A-list stars including Taylor Swift, Kate Moss, Tom Cruise and Harry Styles. This could be because it costs £325 a month to be a member, which screens out many members of the public, and taking photographs inside any of its venues is strictly forbidden. The chainrecently announcedit had banned Meta glasses over privacy fears.There could also be more royal reunions in the offing, as Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie are regulars at Soho Farmhouse. Eugenie was the first member of the royal family to visit the couple when they moved out to the US.King Charles wrote to the government on Monday to reiterate that the Sussexes would be private citizens in the UK. He said that would bring the couple “personal latitude … in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish”.It is a venue that is likely to feel safe to Meghan. In Harry’s memoir, Spare, he wrote that Soho House on Dean Street was “her headquarters whenever she came to London”. He added: “Sometimes she just left her luggage at Soho House for weeks. They stored it without question. The people there were like family.” The couple met there for their first date.During the same 2016 visit, Meghan was pictured cyclingaround the grounds of Soho Farmhousewith the Made in Chelsea star Millie Mackintosh. She also reportedly hosted her hen party at the Cotswolds retreat in 2018.View image in fullscreenPrince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, arriving for an awards show in London, 2020.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersMeghan is a close friend of the Soho House executive Markus Anderson, who is thought to have introduced her to high society in London when she visited in 2016. The two met in 2011 in Anderson’s home country, Canada, as she filmed the TV show Suits.Harry has several charitable events in the UK planned, including the WellChild awards in London at the end of this month. He will also be getting ready for the Invictus Games, to be held in Birmingham next summer. It has been reported that Meghan may be seeking acting roles, and she recently said she “sometimes” missed her old job and liked being around a crew when filming her Netflix cookery show.The pair “love” theOxfordshirecountryside and reportedly made the Cotswolds their base when they visited earlier this year to see King Charles. They also rented a place when they were still working royals.In Spare, Harry wrote: “We thought we could move into Oxfordshire full-time.“We loved it out there. The air fresh, the verdant grounds plus, no paps.” It seems, perhaps, they have finally achieved this.Soho House has been approached for comment. A spokesperson for the Sussexes declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsMeghan, the Duchess of SussexPrince HarryEnglandKing Charles IIIOxfordshireMonarchyTravel & leisurenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The more famous I got, the bigger my beehive got’: how Mari Wilson made Just What I Always Wanted  | Culture | The Guardian
description: ‘I was trying to bring back some glamour. The backcombed hair was like architecture really. It took more than 45 minutes to style’
Author: Jack Watkins
Headline: ‘I was trying to bring back some glamour. The backcombed hair was like architecture really. It took more than 45 minutes to style’
Content: ‘Headphones had to go under my chin’ … Mari Wilson in 1983.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Headphones had to go under my chin’ … Mari Wilson in 1983.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesHow we madeCulture‘The more famous I got, the bigger my beehive got’: how Mari Wilson made Just What I Always Wanted‘I was trying to bring back some glamour. The backcombed hair was like architecture really. It took more than 45 minutes to style’Interviews byJack WatkinsMon 7 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMari Wilson, leadand backing vocalsJust What I Always Wanted had already been in our live set, but with different verses. When we’d gone onDavid Essex’s Showcaseearlier in 1982, in the middle eight I sang “A wink from Wilbur, a kiss from Kurt, don’t tell Hank, he might get hurt” – all names of my backing band the Wilsations. But when it came to recording, I said to Tot Taylor, who wrote most of my early singles, including Love Man and Baby It’s True, “We can’t sing that because no one will know who they are. What about, ‘A mink from Paris, a ring from Rome, a whole new wardrobe in my home?’” Tot, such a brilliant writer, took it from there.We’d brought in Tony Mansfield, whose futuristicNew Musikhad enjoyed hit singles with Living by Numbers and This World of Water, to produce the song and my debut album Showpeople. He brought a modern feel but captured our warmth and sense of fun. The trumpet solo was actually a synth, as was the timpani, but Paul Bultitude recorded his very loud snare drum fills in a studio corridor. I’m at the top of my range at the end of the middle eight – something a lot of Motown artists did to make the voice sound more plaintive.double quotation markI walked from my local Post Office to Tesco – and heard the song in both placesMy older sister had a beehive which I’d loved. When I first got mine in 1980, I remember walking through Brent Cross shopping mall and everyone staring. It wasn’t long after punk and no one wanted that look. However, the more famous I became, the bigger it got! It took more than 45 minutes to style, the hair backcombed to buggery – it was like architecture really. I was trying to bring back some glamour.I’d just come from an interview when I laid down the vocal part in Pete Townshend’s Eel Pie Studios, so I was already in character. I was wearing a crimplene dress and because of my beehive, the headphones had to go under my chin.The artwork for the single and album covers was inspired by classic Julie London and Peggy Lee LPs of the 1950s. I never wanted to be just an 80s pop singer and later I shifted to jazz. Some people come to my shows and say: “I didn’t know you could sing like that.” My new album combines pop, jazz and soul – a hybrid of what I’ve been performing live all my life.My earlier singles had reflected my love of 60s soul. I remember being in a studio with the Wilsations when Just What I Always Wanted was discussed onBBC Radio 1’s Round Table. We were excited and had the broadcast relayed through the speakers, but they were saying: “She’s meant to be retro, but she’s gone synthy.” Fortunately, the public were more enthusiastic and it became my biggest seller.Tot Taylor, songwriter, backing vocals, pianoI knew something was up when I walked from my local Post Office to Tesco and heard the single playing loud and clear over the sound systems in both places. Mari and her 12-piece band had been playing live in London for around a year. We’d released a couple of – now rare – singles on my record label the Compact Organization. This operated out of a cupboard in my one-bedroom flat, with a tiny backroom office off Portland Place in London. One of Mari’s singles,Beat the Beat, was an airplay hit and we thought Just What I Always Wanted was probably a likely UK indie hit, if lucky.View image in fullscreen‘An Ashworth snap’ … Wilson in the photo shoot that provided the 1982 single’s cover.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyBut massive radio play and a Top 10 position for three weeks exceeded all expectations. The initial idea for the song came to me when the band were at the BBC for a Radio 1 live session. I sat down at their beautiful Steinway grand piano in a tea break and out of nowhere this short-phrased tune came floating by. I grabbed it, and played it over and over so I could remember it.Frankie! Eurythmics!  Tina Turner! Peter Ashworth’s 80s pop mavericks - in picturesRead moreThen, on the bus going home, I got a lyric idea for a shopping list of best things – real-life items, or examples of things that were happening to Mari. “A tune from Teddy,” came from my songwriting pseudonym, Teddy Johns. “An Ashworth snap,” referred to Pete Ashworth,the cult photographerwho took the – much imitated – photos for the sleeve.I’ve always believed the song did so well because it followed the list formula, as with Cole Porter’s You’re the Top. It brings a natural structure. Tony Mansfield’s outer space and out of sight production sounded good – and loud – on the radio. And Mari’s vocal is so figured out and “up” attitude-wise. It really shows off her velvet sound.Mari Wilson’s new album Girl About Town is out now. She plays Cadogan Hall, London on 4 October, then toursExplore more on these topicsCultureHow we madePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV has never been so nerve-jangling: 10 years of the agonising Motherland | Television | The Guardian
description: The rage, the wine, the power mums, the PTA horror – the BBC sitcom was a spot on send-up of life at the school gates. A decade on, we remember its most awkward bits
Author: Rachael Sigee
Headline: The rage, the wine, the power mums, the PTA horror – the BBC sitcom was a spot on send-up of life at the school gates. A decade on, we remember its most awkward bits
Content: ‘The most frazzled woman on television’ …Anna Maxwell Martin, centre, with Paul Ready, Lucy Punch and other cast members in Motherland.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The most frazzled woman on television’ …Anna Maxwell Martin, centre, with Paul Ready, Lucy Punch and other cast members in Motherland.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyTelevisionTV has never been so nerve-jangling: 10 years of the agonising MotherlandThe rage, the wine, the power mums, the PTA horror – the BBC sitcom was a spot on send-up of life at the school gates. A decade on, we remember its most awkward bitsRachael SigeeMon 7 Sep 2026 07.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 10.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIfUncut Gemswas about the school run instead of gambling debts, it would look like Motherland. It is now 10 years since the BBC sitcom jangled the already frayed nerves of all parents watching and turned Anna Maxwell Martin into the most frazzled woman on television in the name of skewering middle-class motherhood.Whether she was marching her children to buy school shoes the night before term started (“Don’t be closed. Pleeeeeaaaaase don’t be closed”) or having a meltdown at temporary traffic lights en route to a school drop-off that proved redundant because she’d forgotten it was half-term, Maxwell Martin’s Julia would undoubtedly have a more chilled-out time in the kitchen ofThe Bearthan raising her kids.Originally created by Sharon Horgan, Holly Walsh, Helen Serafinowicz and Graham Linehan (with Barunka O’Shaughnessy joining from series two, after Linehan departed), Motherland arrived into a TV landscape where mothers were no longer images of parenting perfection. But while the likes ofMalcolm in the Middleand Outnumbered had embraced the humour in the warts and all of child-rearing, the experience of mothering on television was still mostly centred on the kids themselves: tantrumming toddlers, precocious primary schoolers and stroppy teenagers.Motherland took a different tack. It was never about the offspring, who rarely amounted to more than the occasional school uniform bobbing into view (rare is a Motherland fan who can name all – or indeed any – of the sprogs). Instead, it was more like a workplace comedy, focusing on the adult experience of motherhood: the passive aggression, the barely disguised competition, the begged-for favours, the ulterior motives, the whingeing and the copious bottles of wine. While it had been considered progress to see women on television who were more than just mothers, Motherland acknowledged an uncomfortable truth: that the mothering bit can really take over, at least for a while there. That being a mother sometimes – often – feels like a constant fight against being flattened into two dimensions.View image in fullscreen‘Like a workplace comedy focusing on the adult experience of motherhood’ … Punch and Anna Maxwell Martin in Motherland.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyAlongside Maxwell Martin’s perma-stressed Julia was unflappable Liz (Diane Morgan), token dad Kevin (Paul Ready), long-suffering Anne (Philippa Dunne) and Amanda (Lucy Punch), a vividly heinous alpha-mum creation who always saw herself as the centre of the universe and now literally is, in spin-offAmandaland. The series two introduction of Meg (Tanya Moodie), a high-flying Black woman who appeared to have it all together, gave us a more diverse group but Motherland was carefully hyper-specific to its well-off west London demographic. The horrors here took place at interminable PTA fundraisers, joylessly non-competitive sports days and skin-crawling swimming pool birthday parties (devastatingly, not a drop-off situation).In Motherland, panic rises faster than house prices in a good school catchment area, and there is always someone to witness you making a colossal balls-up such as panicking about forgetting World Book Day and sending your child in holding an umbrella … as the novel Umbrella by Will Self. Obviously.The show gamely took on the utter weirdness of mother-to-mother relations: attempting variously to bond with, impress and one-up a group of people who just happen to have given birth around the same time as you. The thwarted efforts to join carpools and get your kids into after-school clubs, all the while doing just enough to appease this gaggle of onlookers eager to judge (if only to convince themselves they are doing OK).Amanda may be the obvious villain, but Motherland never stopped reminding us that motherhood will, at times, make sinners of us all. Having children does not suddenly wash away our foibles; if anything, it probably magnifies them. Motherland understood that being a mother frequently involves your spirit hovering somewhere above your body, watching yourself mutter Latin gibberish in an attempt to get your kids into a Catholic school, and silently screaming: “How did it come to this?”As the series progressed and the bonds formed at the school gates transitioned into real friendships, the stakes got higher. But Motherland never lost sight of the relentless nature of parenthood: even as divorce, illness and death reared their heads, lunches still had to be packed (and probably left at home).Anna Maxwell Martin looks back: ‘I was bullied a little bit, but it didn’t affect me because I was a happy weirdo’Read moreView image in fullscreen‘An act of catharsis’… Philippa Dunne with Maxwell Martin, Ready and Morgan in Motherland.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyIt’s a show that really should have had parents diving for the remote rather than spend their evenings reliving a hellish half-term cottage break or attempting to curb a nit epidemic. As Julia hissed when she ended up back at Anne’s house for an afterparty (a special bottle of cava and some dubious homemade paté): “This is my worst nightmare come true – surrounded by mums at night.”But while it’s too close to the bone to be a comfort watch, sitting down in front of Motherland is an act of catharsis – a reassurance that even when you’re trying reallyreallyhard, you still might lose someone else’s child while trick-or-treating. If you no longer identify as a Carrie or a Samantha, perhaps being a Liz or a Kevin feels more appropriate.It stands up as a triumphantly messy monument to a stage of life that passes in a blur of doctor’s appointments and sponsored bike rides and forgotten swimming kits. Less laugh till you cry and more laugh to stop yourself crying, Motherland holds out a hand to mothers watching. Not to help, of course, but to cling on to across a pub table as you try to fathom how on earth you’ve agreed to sort out the collection for the school’s poorly caretaker.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionBBCDiane MorganAnna Maxwell MartinfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘She’ll outdo herself’: Céline Dion fans camp out for glimpse of star before sold-out Paris comeback | Céline Dion | The Guardian
description: Singer has rewarded patience of hundreds waiting outside hotel with regular appearances and even some dancing
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Singer has rewarded patience of hundreds waiting outside hotel with regular appearances and even some dancing
Content: Céline Dion acknowledges fans as she arrives at her hotel in Paris for her first shows in six years.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCéline Dion acknowledges fans as she arrives at her hotel in Paris for her first shows in six years.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesCéline Dion‘She’ll outdo herself’: Céline Dion fans camp out for glimpse of star before sold-out Paris comebackSinger has rewarded patience of hundreds waiting outside hotel with regular appearances and even some dancingAngelique Chrisafisin ParisMon 7 Sep 2026 11.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNoëlla Lamy, 52, who described herself as one ofCéline Dion’s biggest fans, was preparing to spend all night on a Paris pavement without a tent but wearing a sweatshirt printed with the singer’s face for comfort.“Céline Dion is a force of bravery and an inspiration,” she said.Lamy, who works in catering for a private clinic, had travelled from her village near Amiens in northernFranceto wait for 36 hours behind a metal barrier outside the Canadian star’s Paris hotel to get a glimpse of her.Céline Dion fan Noëlla Lamy outside the singer’s Paris hotel.Photograph: Angelique Chrisafis/The GuardianHundreds of Dion fans have been gathering each day to catch sight of the singer, as she rehearses for along-awaited return to the stagein a series of sold-out Paris shows that begin this weekend.Dion, 58, announced in 2022 that she had been diagnosed with the rare and incurable autoimmune disorder,stiff-person syndrome. She took a break from performing, later describing how the condition meant she had suffered muscle spasms so strong that her ribs were broken as a result. In the 2024 documentaryI Am: Céline Dionshe provided insight into the severity of her pain from the condition, including having a seizure.Celine Dion sings with fans outside Paris hotel“She is resilient, humane and humble,” said Lamy, who had seen Dion perform several times in the US and France and has tickets for a Paris show. “I’m happy she’s back on stage and I hope it’s a gentle comeback for her. I know it won’t necessarily be the same type of shows she put on before, because of her health, but I know she’ll outdo herself and it will still be very grand.“I feel like she’s been there for me for every challenge in my life. I lost my husband around the same time she lost her husband, and her songs really helped me through. I first watched her singing on a French TV chatshow when she was 14 years old and I was eight and I’ve been a fan since then.”Dion, who grew up the youngest of 14 children in a small town near Montréal in French-speaking Quebec, has a massive fanbase in France. Although she is famous worldwide for her 1997 songMy Heart Will Go On, which featured in the Oscar-winning film Titanic and became the second-bestselling single by a woman in music history, in France she is known for her many French-language songs. Her 1995 album D’eux became the biggest-selling Francophone album of all time. In 2024, she sang an Edith Piaf song from the Eiffel Tower at theParis Olympics opening ceremony.View image in fullscreenThe Eiffel Tower illuminated in March as the singer announces her Paris shows.Photograph: Pierre Suu/Getty ImagesDion has made a point of greeting fans outside her Paris hotel, often dancing for them and chatting to them as they wait for her to come and go from evening rehearsals. She told fans a few days after arriving at the hotel that she was not going out in Paris except to rehearse because: “I’m trying to conserve my energy to give the best of myself.”The pavement outside Dion’s hotel has become a gathering place that often resembles a street party, with office workers in the next-door building putting speakers on their balcony to blast her hits while the crowd dances along.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarina, 31, a chemist for a cosmetics company, who has tickets for one of Dion’s Paris shows, said: “I thought I just have to get down here to her hotel as the mood seemed so good outside. My mother had all her CDs when I was a child and I also watched Titanic when I was small. Even if you don’t specifically listen to Céline Dion, you’re constantly surrounded by her music in France. It’s really positive that she showed her health condition so honestly. Lots of stars clearly feel they mustn’t show any difficult moments, but they’re human like us. I think it made her more real and close to her fans.”View image in fullscreenDion performing in 2017.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesSylvie Lugans, a retired cafe worker, had been a fan since Dion won Eurovision in 1988 representing Switzerland. “She’s a wonderful diva on stage, but in real life, she’s so down to earth,” Lugans said.Augustin, 21, who worked in the last remaining wallpaper factory in France, had also travelled from northern France to stand outside the hotel and had seen Dion wave at the crowd as she left.“She’s brave enough to speak about the hardest moments of her life, and that’s very moving,” he said.Explore more on these topicsCéline DionFranceEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: Harold, the halls of residence cat, who looked after me when I first left home | Cats | The Guardian
description: He was the gorgeous furry tabby who made my day, even when he waltzed into my flat just to finish my takeaway. Now he’s a campus celeb, with a part-time job guarding the doors of the village shop
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: He was the gorgeous furry tabby who made my day, even when he waltzed into my flat just to finish my takeaway. Now he’s a campus celeb, with a part-time job guarding the doors of the village shop
Content: Taking up residence … Harold at Froggatt hall in Endcliffe Village at the University of Sheffield.Photograph: Instagram/harold.theendcliffecatView image in fullscreenTaking up residence … Harold at Froggatt hall in Endcliffe Village at the University of Sheffield.Photograph: Instagram/harold.theendcliffecatThe pet I'll never forgetCatsThe pet I’ll never forget: Harold, the halls of residence cat, who looked after me when I first left homeHe was the gorgeous furry tabby who made my day, even when he waltzed into my flat just to finish my takeaway. Now he’s a campus celeb, with a part-time job guarding the doors of the village shopCharlotte SmithMon 7 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2022, when I moved into halls of residence at the University of Sheffield, my biggest concern was no longer having a furry friend to come home to, as I’d had a cat since I was 11 years old. Then I met Harold.My first encounter with this gorgeous tabby was quite unusual. One day, in our 10-bed flat, a flurry of messages appeared on the group WhatsApp chat after my fellow roommates caught an intruder on the sofa, innocently munching on my leftover pizza.As in many homes for first year university students, there were plenty of unfinished takeaways lying around the kitchen. And Harold was a smart cat with a clear goal: food. Any time he saw a snack or sensed one from a distance, he would come running. A can of tuna. A block of cheese. The occasional pancake. And I was more than happy to feed him – he probably had a better diet than me.View image in fullscreenHarold eyes up some food.Photograph: Instagram/harold.theendcliffecatWith the area housing more than 4,000 students, Harold was in high demand. He would choose a different home every night (we never found out if he had an actual owner), so I felt honoured when, from time to time, he would turn up meowing at my door. Catching him after a night out waltzing into our flat always cheered me up. It was the perfect end to an evening – as long as he stayed away from my chips.You’d often find him stretching out in the sun, eyeing up his next treat, or waiting for the lift to his third flat of the day. But, once the novelty of the university pet wore off, some of my flatmates were less keen on letting him in, as they knew his game. For me, he was too charming to refuse.At times I felt as if I was cheating on my childhood tabby, Pippa, who still lived in my family home – there was no other animal I could have a greater love for. But I cherished Harold in a different way. For a pet-loving student getting to grips with independent living, he was a home away from home.At the end of my first year of university I moved out of the buildings Harold used to roam, but I would still occasionally see him strutting from flat to flat. Later on, I became a residence mentor, supporting first year students living in university accommodation. “Do not let the cat inside any student flats,” the managers told me during my training. On a few occasions, I may have turned a blind eye.View image in fullscreenHarold guarding the doors of the village shop.Photograph: Instagram/harold.theendcliffecatToday, Harold remains a campus celeb, with 10,000 followers onInstagramas Harold the cat of Endcliffe (the name of the halls where he was found). He is always posing for the student paparazzi on social media, and even has a part-time job – guarding the doors of the village shop.I’ll always be grateful to Harold for the laughs, the late-night chats and, most importantly, for being a much-needed anchor in my first year as a student.Explore more on these topicsCatsThe pet I'll never forgetAnimalsPetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Reform UK without Nigel Farage used to be unthinkable. Not any more | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The scandals are building, his touch perhaps not quite what it was. And, most of all, his party rivals are beginning to sense an opportunity, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The scandals are building, his touch perhaps not quite what it was. And, most of all, his party rivals are beginning to sense an opportunity, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, Nigel Farage and the party’s shadow home secretary, Zia Yusuf, sing the national anthem at Reform’s conference at the NEC in Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenReform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, Nigel Farage and the party’s shadow home secretary, Zia Yusuf, sing the national anthem at Reform’s conference at the NEC in Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionReform UKA Reform UK without Nigel Farage used to be unthinkable. Not any moreGaby HinsliffThe scandals are building, his touch perhaps not quite what it was. And, most of all, his party rivals are beginning to sense an opportunityMon 7 Sep 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.42 EDTShareNigel Farage didn’t know. He wasn’t told.Sure, he was right there at the table when theundercover reporterhe believed to be a rich American’s sonspelled out very clearly how he hoped to channel his father’s money to Reform, in ways that certainly don’t sound too lawful.But hewasn’tlistening,you understand.God forbid that the man who insists his party takes compliance very seriously, and who never stops warning that the establishment is out to get him by any means possible, should actually pay attention to the details of a donation offered bang in the middle of a byelection that was fought over – of all the luck, eh? – some other questionable donations.Farage’s defence is essentially that he was present but not involved, asJeremy Corbyn once famously saidof attending an event where someone laid a commemorative wreath for members of the terrorist group behind the 1972 Munich Olympics atrocity.It didn’t work for Corbyn, any more than claiming to have tried cannabis butnever inhalingworked an age ago for Bill Clinton, in part because some people just didn’t believe it. But mostly, perhaps, because critics found it revealing even that Corbyn would be at the kind of gathering where such things might happen. Most aspirant prime ministers take good care to avoid moving in circles where someone might end up venerating terrorists, or explaining exactly how they intend to get around the law. For good reason, it turns out.What we are being asked to accept, in the instance caught on camera, is that at best Farage has been astonishingly sloppy; that he just turned up, tuned out, thanked the guy without even really knowing what for, and then went happily on his way. Take Farage at his own word and he is describing someone curiously semi-detached. Someone who, despite repeatedly claiming his enemies will stop at nothing to stitch him up, puzzlingly doesn’t seem to take such basic precautions against entrapment as noticing what’s actually going on around him. Someone for whom fighting a byelection in which nobody else of note is standing, bar a talking bin, is apparently so all-consuming that he can’t possibly be expected to concentrate on talking to donorsas well.If that degree of walking and chewing gum is a stretch, imagine what a shock running the country might be. No wonder some in Reform are starting to ask themselves if, deep down, that’s what he even wants.What would Reform look like without Nigel Farage? Once upon a time that would have been a ridiculous question – without him, it would simply fall apart – but the party now is not quite what it used to be. Among the faithful, the fact he doesn’t seem to take the job too seriously is still part of his charm, and many Reform supporters will be nothing but indignant on his behalf at the undercover tactics used to catch him out.But there are also people in Reform these days who have seen the very real possibility of seizing power to enact an agenda not seen before in Britain, just as Alternative für Deutschlandisstarting to doin Germany and as the National Rally’sJordan Bardella(the star turn at Reform’s party conference this year) and Marine Le Pen threaten to do next year in France. They won’t want to let that opportunity slip through their fingers.Having lost its lead in the polls, Reform finds itself ironically in a version of the dilemma Labour faced a few months ago: torn between those who think recovery depends on tacking left (in this case towards Tory voters who are Reform-curious but worry that it seems too extreme or sleazy) or tacking right (towards Rupert Lowe’s Restore, now consistently taking small but damaging chunks out of them, and other far-right groupings). Events like last weekend’s sinister black-shirted, paramilitary-style show of force in Dover by the previously little known Patriot Platform group – which even the government took a surprisingly long time to condemn in the decisive terms that chief secretary to the TreasuryEmma Reynolds eventually didon Monday morning, after what looked like copycat demonstrations in Portsmouth – may now start to push those tensions into the open.Are these their people, or not? Having ripped open Pandora’s box by saying what others would not on immigration, there would be a grim irony in Reform struggling to deal with the furies unleashed, if only the whole thing wasn’t so frightening for everyone else. Farage ended up calling the Dover mob “disgusting” because of their balaclavas, while suggesting he absolutely shared their anger about small boat crossings (now, of course, down to aseven-year low). But is covering your face at a protest the only line Reform won’t cross?Some of its supporters clearly do want a leader prepared to say what Farage won’t, a niche that Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesperson,evidently aims to fill. Others more recently arrived from the old Conservative party might prefer a leader who treads a hard line on immigration, welfare and woke, but with some rougher edges sanded off (or so Robert Jenrick clearly hopes). Crucially, some in both camps will see the departure ofclose aideDan Jukes – who along with head of policy, James Orr,has taken the rapfor this latest donor scandal, though both deny wrongdoing – as an opportunity to replace Farage’s loyal and protective sidekicks with people less tied to him personally.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHistorically, anyone daring to fly this close to Farage’s sun has got their wings scorched. But what if that sun doesn’t burn quite so brightly any more? What if the political judgment that always served him so well in the past is now fractionally off-key? For now, the idea that there could be an electionany minute – forced, perhaps, by some future bond market crisis – is perhaps imposing a measure of discipline on the party. But what if that imaginary snap election never materialises?For now, these are all still very much “what ifs”. Given his miraculous capacity for resurrection, it is a mistake to underestimate Farage or count him out when he is down.But until recently, even the idea of Reform without its leader seemed ridiculous; hewasReform, to the point that without him it would cease to meaningfully exist. In the current climate, that assumption may no longer be safe. Bardella, after all, got his big break when Le Pen wasbrought down by a financial scandal. It’s time the other parties thought harder about the shape Reform might take without its maker, rather than assuming the battle begins and ends with him.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsReform UKOpinionNigel FaragecommentShareReuse this content

title: Painful, unconvincing, boring: welcome to John Healey’s late show | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Chancellor has the look of a man born to announce the UK is under nuclear attack
Author: John Crace
Headline: Chancellor has the look of a man born to announce the UK is under nuclear attack
Content: John Healey delivers his speech in Coventry on Monday – after arriving 15 minutes late.Photograph: Betty Laura Zapata/ReutersView image in fullscreenJohn Healey delivers his speech in Coventry on Monday – after arriving 15 minutes late.Photograph: Betty Laura Zapata/ReutersThe politics sketchUK newsPainful, unconvincing, boring: welcome to John Healey’s late showJohn CraceChancellor has the look of a man born to announce the UK is under nuclear attackMon 7 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareMeet the new chancellor. Same as the old chancellor. Although, on reflection, that might be a little hard onRachel Reeves. At least Rachel had given the job some thought before she got it. She had had some experience working at the Bank of England and, whether you liked it or not, she had some kind of plan. John Healey? Not so much. No one can remember him ever having given the economy much thought until Andy Burnham offered the job. He was more the strong and silent type.As defence secretary, Healey had looked like a man of principle. A defender of the armed forces, a guardian of the realm. Hehad even resigned over Keir Starmer and Reeves’s refusalto guarantee increasing the defence budget to 3% of GDP by 2030.Now that he’s in charge of the purse strings, he’s remained silent. Though not so strong. It feels as if he doesn’t know what he thinks. Or if he even thinks at all. Almost as if, were he to spend too much time in deliberation, he might have to resign all over again. He doesn’t even come across as a career opportunist. A well-trodden route for cabinet ministers over the years. Instead, he’s just a rabbit caught in the headlights.There again, for your first major speech as chancellor, you’d probably prefer it if the cost of government borrowing wasn’t at a record high since the financial crash and that Jaguar Land Rover hadn’t chosen that morning to announce 4,000 redundancies. On the plus side, Healey could be guaranteed everyone’s attention. The trickier question to answer was whether he would want it.Burnham had stayed away from the Manufacturing Technology Centre in Coventry because he didn’t want to steal his chancellor’s sun. Amazingly though, Healey somehow managed to eclipse himself. It was like watching a man in negative space. The lights were off and no one was at home. One of those occasions when to have barricaded himself in the Treasury, refusing to come out, would have been a massive improvement all round. With John, less really is more. At least that way there’s the possibility of authority.You would have hoped Healey’s ability with numbers was rather better than his time-keeping. He was 15 minutes late for his own debut and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the entire Treasury ministerial team were getting decidedly fidgety before his arrival. Perhaps they were wondering whether the chancellor was going to throw a sickie. Had decided he wasn’t the right man for the gig after all. We’d have all understood. It’s a tough job and it isn’t for everyone. I’d hate to do it.It was a very nervy-looking Healey who eventually appeared. Occasionally having to grab hold of the lectern to make sure he didn’t fall over. Not the most reassuring sight. Less rock. More Northern Rock. Even when you know the news is going to be bad, you want your chancellor to appear strong and coherent. In the same way you want your doctor to tell you she has a plan and you are not going to die, in the same breath as she has said you have a life-threatening illness. A chancellor is someone you need to believe in. Not someone who will agree with you that we are probably all screwed.View image in fullscreenJohn Healey at the Manufacturing Technology Centre on Monday, where he brushed off questions with mindless waffle.Photograph: Betty Laura Zapata/PAHealey started downbeat. The global situation was terrible. The Tories had trashed the economy. Politicians don’t get to choose the time and circumstances in which they are asked to serve. It rather suggested he would have much preferred not to have landed up at the Treasury just now. But hey! We were all in it together so we might as well make the best of it. He would do what he could to make things a bit better, but if it didn’t work out he hoped there would be no bad feelings. You couldn’t help feeling it was the blind leading the blind.Then came the continuity Rachel stuff. Fiscal discipline was his priority. He would be maintaining his predecessor’s fiscal rules. He would be honest about government spending. Manifesto promises would be honoured. It made you wonder why we had changed prime minister if it was all going to be much the same. Had we been through all that psychodrama just to get someone with a little more personal charm, had twinklier eyes and who looked good in a T-shirt?Having made all his excuses, Healey turned to the good vibes stuff. The hallmark of Andy’s two months in office so far. Yes everything was terrible. Yes everything was going to stay the same. But not to worry because if we all just sat in a circle, chanted “Om” and had positive thoughts then we could turn this around. We were going all out for growth through devolution. He wanted to bring hope to every postcode. John is one of the few people who can make hope sound like a sexually transmitted disease.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was all a bit painful. Unconvincing. Boring. You longed for him to stop because the speech was as painful to listen to as it was for him to give. Healey isn’t cut out for all this positivity stuff. It dies on his lips. He was far better off where he had come from. He has the look and the gravitas of a man who had been born to make a television announcement that the UK was under nuclear attack. It was time to hide under the kitchen table with the dog and a can of baked beans and wait to die in half an hour’s time. Thank you and goodbye.The questions were no more revealing. Everything was either met with a dead bat, “You can’t expect me to comment before the budget” or was brushed aside with mindless waffle as Healey tried to fill the dead air. Still, his speech didn’t cause any extra volatility in the bond markets, so that was something. Then again, as he had spent half an hour saying nothing of interest, it would have been remarkable if the bond markets had moved. Perhaps he had sent the traders to sleep for a thousand years.They wouldn’t be the only ones. The whole of the government appeared to be in a Healey-induced sense of torpor. There was no sign of the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood. Normally, she would have been quick to crack down on the balaclava protesters in Dover and Portsmouth. But she too had been silenced. Almost as if the government wasn’t quite sure if it was OK to call out the protests.Strange that, given even Nigel Farage thought they weren’t OK. It was fine to attack migrant women and children, just so long as you did it out in the open. Take a leaf out of the Reform conference where members had been filmed apparently attacking female protesters. That was the Britain we all knew and loved.Explore more on these topicsUK newsThe politics sketchJohn HealeyAndy BurnhamRachel ReevescommentShareReuse this content

title: Friendships meant everything to me as a child. I worry today’s young people are being robbed of that | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: We sat in the park, laughing for hours, talking about nothing. Today’s childhoods are digital – and the result is an epidemic of loneliness, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: We sat in the park, laughing for hours, talking about nothing. Today’s childhoods are digital – and the result is an epidemic of loneliness, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: ‘The art of friendship is as much the art of doing nothing.’Photograph: Image Source/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The art of friendship is as much the art of doing nothing.’Photograph: Image Source/Getty ImagesOpinionFriendshipFriendships meant everything to me as a child. I worry today’s young people are being robbed of thatRhiannon Lucy CosslettWe sat in the park, laughing for hours, talking about nothing. Today’s childhoods are digital – and the result is an epidemic of lonelinessMon 7 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIsaw an old friend recently – the kind you’ve known for so long that you clear a whole day for them, as you might a family member. We laughed and laughed like we were teenagers again, and drank martinis before lunch, and it felt almost like it always did when we were young, except we could afford better than cheap cider, and he owns a house and I’m someone’s mother.Another old friend – one I’ve known even longer, since I was six – described me and the other girls who made up our little group as “fake siblings”. That is how lifelong friendships feel. There’s an easiness and acceptance that comes with longstanding intimacy. You know each other’s secrets,you’ve been inside each other’s parents’ houses, shared beds and cigarettes, witnessed heartbreak and foolishness, tears and whiteys, before the more serious stuff piles up: weddings, births, illnesses, life crises, deaths. You talk about the serious stuff, of course (there has always been some serious stuff, but teenage friendships often provide a refuge from it), but when you need it that old friendship is a portal, transporting many of us to a time of lightness and freedom that is otherwise hard to access.I don’t know where I’d be without these friendships, which is why it makes me sad to read that young people today aren’t making them, or at least not in the same way. According to a new report from the Institute for Public Policy Research titledThe Loneliest Generation, the number of young people with no close friends has risen fivefold since 2014, with 11- to 24-year-olds becoming dramatically more isolated. One in 20 16- to 21-year-olds say that they have no close friends at all.The report cites digital childhoods and austerity measures such as youth club closures as factors in eroding the foundations of a good adolescence. My own friendships owed much to the digital realm (specifically MSN Messenger), but they were still largely and crucially face to face, and that seems to be one of the things that has changed. We did not have internet childhoods, and so the skill – and I do believe it’s a skill – of making friends was crucial, and acquired young. The things that bonded us – circumstances, subcultures, music and, most of all, humour – took place mostly offline. We spent hours sitting in parks or around campfires, just talking and joking. We went to gigs and club nights and festivals. We rode our bikes or begged lifts or walked five miles home. It’s strange seeing these ways of relating to one another being idealised by younger people, spoken of wistfully in social media posts and comments as though something has been lost. I suppose we idealise the countercultures of our parents’ eras. People simply conversing without a phone present shouldn’t be seen as radical, but it’s being framed that way.We are right to be worried about this mass loneliness among young people. To spend adolescence without friends can leave a lifelong trace. Even the friendships that didn’t last affect us, even – perhaps especially – those that were not so straightforward. Therapists are fond of the phrase “rupture and repair” because it’s accurate – falling in and out and in again with friendship groups can be educative. It can teach you to be kinder to one another, to tolerate difference, and to learn what behaviour you are and aren’t willing to put up with. These are important life lessons but they are increasingly overstated –the online language of friendship, which emphasises what a friend “gives” you or “adds” to your life seems intense and transactional to those of us raised in lesspsychobabblytimes.These sorts of bonds take time and energy to establish. Many, many hours of sitting and fooling around. The art of friendship is as much the art of doing nothing. Of mooching. Hanging out. Watch an old sitcom such asSeinfeldand friends are always running errands together. When did you last go to the dry-cleaner’s with somebody?Much has been written aboutthe decline in third spacesand its impact on social relationships. Places to hang out, outside home or work, are essential to the art of real-world friendship. So is time to talk, to wander and to linger together. When it comes to the crisis in friendship,a social media ban for under-16sis a good thing: it makes relating to one another in person more of a priority, and leaves more time for those activities that bond us together.It’s only as you get older that you realise how precious those adolescent years are. People don’t talk about fun enough – how important it is to wellbeing and survival. So much about technology makes our lives smoother and quicker, but I am not sure it makes it more fun. Not like gathering four or five or six people around a campfire and drinking cider before all jumping naked into a river, or exploring an abandoned house (not something I would ever endorse, but something we used to do). Memories of adolescence and the people we spent it with have been found to be more vivid. They call itthe “reminiscence bump”. It is a crucial time for development and, as I’ve found myself, those memories carry us through our lives. In my dreams, I still explore abandoned houses with those kids, my fake siblings.What will be the long-term wellbeing impact if those years are filled instead with the flickerings of other lives on a screen, gobbled up and then swiped past, forgotten? We must preserve the art of friendship before it’s lost for ever.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsFriendshipOpinionLonelinessYoung peopleChildrenSocial mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: Jonathan Reynolds is right, Jaguar Land Rover doesn’t warrant use of public money | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: The 4,000 job cuts cannot be compared to a VW-like existential crisis and, as JLR presents them, are about staying competitive
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: The 4,000 job cuts cannot be compared to a VW-like existential crisis and, as JLR presents them, are about staying competitive
Content: JLR has had a rotten 12 months yet continues to talk bullishly about double-digit growth around the next corner as it prepares to launch five new models.Photograph: Simon Kirwan/AlamyView image in fullscreenJLR has had a rotten 12 months yet continues to talk bullishly about double-digit growth around the next corner as it prepares to launch five new models.Photograph: Simon Kirwan/AlamyNils Pratley on financeJaguar Land RoverJonathan Reynolds is right, Jaguar Land Rover doesn’t warrant use of public moneyNils PratleyThe 4,000 job cuts cannot be compared to a VW-like existential crisis and, as JLR presents them, are about staying competitiveJaguar Land Rover confirms plan to cut 4,000 jobs over two yearsMon 7 Sep 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareAdefault reaction to news of job losses in the UK car industry is to ask what the government is going to do about it. So, well done business secretary Jonathan Reynolds for giving the correct response to the question of whether public money will be used to supportJaguar Land Rover, which on Mondayconfirmed 4,000 job cuts over two years. His answer was no.It is the right stance because JLR’s cost-cutting cannot be compared to aVolkswagen-like existential corporate crisis. In common with most European carmakers, JLR has had a rotten 12 months thanks to Donald Trump’s tariffs, luxury taxes in China, inflation in the cost of raw materials and, in its case,a big cyber-attack. Yet the company continues to talk bullishly about double-digit growth around the next corner as it prepares to launch five new models.Here, for example, was the big-picture outlook assessment inMay’s full-year results: “Looking ahead, JLR remains resilient and well placed to address the geopolitical, inflationary and regulatory challenges the industry faces. Investment spend is planned to remain at £18bn over the five-year period from FY24 [full year 2024].Monday’s job losses were characterised as a major – but not exceptional – programme to keep a lid on costs by finding £1.7bn worth of annual savings. Instead of breaking even, cash-wise, when it has sold 350,000 units, JLR wants to get back to 300,000, which was the level in 2024. That seems a reasonable ambition in a trickier market, especially after a period of heavy investment. As Reynolds said, car manufacturers have always flexed the size of their workforce at different points in the business and product cycle.Note, too, that the 4,000 job losses – out of 44,000 people globally and 34,000 in the UK – will be heavily skewed towards what JLR calls “salaried and management” roles, or white-collar workers in old lingo. In other words, there will be relatively little impact on factory workers who are paid hourly. An outsider may wonder if JLR isn’t simply overpopulated with managers.Either way, the appropriate role of government is the normal one of assisting with retraining and re-employment and so on. One assumes action on that front will follow after talks with unions on Tuesday. State financial assistance might be a different matter if we were talking about new battery factories or other big capital programmes, or schemes to take the edge off the UK’s horrendous industrial electricity costs. But the job cuts, as JLR presents them, are simply about staying competitive – and there’s no reason for government to interfere in that process.The big corporate test ahead is chasing the US “luxury” market (and a starting price of £154,070 forthe new electric Range Rovermeans the vehicle definitely qualifies as a luxury item) and avoiding what the chief financial officer calls “the killing fields of mass automotive”, a reasonable shorthand for Volkswagen’s predicament under competition from China. The next couple of years will be critical for JLR.By the same token, one cannot call the job losses a blow to Andy Burnham’s ambitions for “reindustrialising” the country. They’re unwelcome, obviously, but were signalled in May and are part of a specific corporate story.Indeed, the wider reindustrialisation challenge is working out what the prime minister means. On that score, Reynolds’s early contributions on his return to his old job have been less impressive.His descriptionsof reindustrialisation have fallen into mushy “backing the industries of the future” generalities. Work to do on that score – but the position on JLR is correct.Explore more on these topicsJaguar Land RoverNils Pratley on financeAutomotive industryIndustrial policycommentShareReuse this content

title: The AfD’s win in Germany is a dark day for Europe. Time is running out to stop the far right | Cas Mudde | The Guardian
description: This party is among the most extreme in Europe. To protect our democracies, liberal parties must urgently change their tactics, says Cas Mudde, author of The Far Right Today
Author: Cas Mudde
Headline: This party is among the most extreme in Europe. To protect our democracies, liberal parties must urgently change their tactics, says Cas Mudde, author of The Far Right Today
Content: Supporters of the AfD celebrate after exit poll results were announced in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, Magdeburg, Germany, 6 September 2026.Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSupporters of the AfD celebrate after exit poll results were announced in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, Magdeburg, Germany, 6 September 2026.Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionThe far rightThe AfD’s win in Germany is a dark day for Europe. Time is running out to stop the far rightCas MuddeThis party is among the most extreme in Europe. To protect our democracies, liberal parties must urgently change their tacticsMon 7 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTShareThe far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) narrowly failed to secure an outright majority in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. But nobody should take comfort from that. The party still won by a landslide. Decades of far-right election gains have made them seem normal to the point where only the biggest victories are deemed newsworthy. But 44% of the vote for a party that is officially classified as “extreme right” is not normal. It is a black day for European democracy, even if it occurs in a small east German state.While Saxony-Anhalt (andGermanyitself) may have dodged the worst outcome because the AfD won’t automatically fulfil its ambition of forming the first far-right state government in Germany since the Nazi era, there is no reason to assume it will be so lucky at the next election. Neither will other German states, such as Mecklenburg-Vorpommern in two weeks’ time, or other countries, such as France next year. No country is immune from the far right and, perhaps even more worryingly, no far-right party or politician is too extreme for political success (as the US has shown). We must therefore update our analyses and strategies.Although Saxony-Anhalt, and east Germany in general, is an extreme case, it reflects similar trends in the rest ofEurope. Far-right parties are going from strength to strength, with old dominant parties decimated, and party systems fragmented. Consequently, coalition formation is becoming increasingly complicated, particularly if we want to keep the far right out of power. In many countries, provinces and cities, most democratic parties are having to govern together to exclude the far right. This often leads to inefficient and unstable coalitions, in turn feeding yet more political dissatisfaction and far-right support.Far-right AfD celebrate ‘dream result’ in key German state as Merz reportedly holds crisis talks – Europe liveRead moreSunday’s results will only intensify an ongoing debate in Germany about the so-calledBrandmauer(a firewall maintained by mainstream parties against cooperating with the AfD). Actually, Germany is one of the few EU countries to still have a far-rightcordon sanitaire. Throughout Europe, from Italy to Sweden, far-right parties have been normalised and integrated into the political mainstream. In most cases, the (rightwing) parties that collaborate with the far right claim that the latter have moderated and are now “conservative” – a claim that is factually wrong, but increasingly popular with the electorates and members of these parties, and much of the media.This will remain almost impossible to claim in Germany. The AfD is among the most extreme parties in Europe, and its most successful branches, including the one in Saxony-Anhalt, are among the AfD’s most extreme. This will not prevent some rightwing politicians from claiming that the AfD is less of a problem than the left, and there is even a fear that some parliamentarians from the conservative CDU in Saxony-Anhalt will defect to give the AfD a majority in the state. On the other side of the political spectrum, calls for an AfD ban will become even louder, and while this might be legally possible, it could create a massive popular backlash, going well beyond Saxony-Anhalt.Both approaches share a too-limited interpretation of the problem. The idea of maintaining theBrandmaueris that the only (or main) problem is outside the system. Yet the system is falling apart as it is. Yes, the AfD (and the far right in general) is a fundamental threat to liberal democracy, but so is the fact that a sizeable and growing part of the population no longer feels represented by its politicians. While many still come out to vote for democracy, they increasingly vote against a party rather than for one.Even worse, most mainstream politicians have accepted that they are unpopular and try to remain in power by arguing that they are the lesser evil and mobilising people to come out to vote against the far right. Ultimately, this is unsustainable. If democratic parties do not develop inspiring manifestos for what they want to achieve in government, liberal democrats will refuse to come out to vote and the far right will win a majority of votes – even if they represent only a minority of the population.Developing such manifestos will require realism from politicians, but also from the media and voters. In fragmented party systems with large far-right parties, no party will be able to implement most of its preferred policies. There are no majorities for social democratic, Christian democratic or Green parties and policies. But this should also not be the main concern at this moment. When the far right gets close to governing alone, or dominating coalitions, the main goal should be to strengthen liberal democracy – in terms of institutions and values. This should be something that all liberal democratic parties can agree on.This does not simply entail strengthening democratic institutions – the judiciary and regulating social media,for example – and promoting inclusion and tolerance. It also means listening to the many concerns and preferences of the majority of voters who do not vote for the far right. In other words, mainstream politicians need to go beyond crime and immigration and focus also on such things as increasing housing provision and public spending, limiting economic and income inequality, fighting the climate crisis and strengthening European integration.And it means accepting that you don’t get everything you want – now or in the near future.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOf course, many countries are not as close to a far-right majority as Saxony-Anhalt is. But we should not forget that in the state’s 2021 election, the AfD had “only” 20% – and the average score of the far right now isroughly 25%across Europe. In other words, there may not be much time left. And, as we can see in countries such as Hungary and the US, the democratic struggle becomes harder and less fair once the far right establishes power.Democratic politicians must therefore realise that today’s key fight is for democracy, rather than for party or power. This requires both fighting the far right and strengthening democracy. Neither the banning nor the normalisation of the far right can achieve this. Democracy neither be strengthened in isolation, nor by the politics of fear. It requires a collective effort from democratic politicians, citizens and journalists, who must show realism, resilience and restraint. And the time for that fight is now.Cas Mudde is the author of The Far Right Today, and is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of GeorgiaExplore more on these topicsThe far rightOpinionAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)GermanyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Dover and Portsmouth showed us a new kind of far right – and the authorities were caught out | Joe Mulhall | The Guardian
description: This is a new and dangerous development: a network of vigilantes who have mobilised as politicians and police have failed to act, says Joe Mulhall of Hope Not Hate
Author: Joe Mulhall
Headline: This is a new and dangerous development: a network of vigilantes who have mobilised as politicians and police have failed to act, says Joe Mulhall of Hope Not Hate
Content: On Saturday morning, balaclava-clad men piled out of the back of vans and blocked roads around Dover port.Photograph: Ay_audits/YouTubeView image in fullscreenOn Saturday morning, balaclava-clad men piled out of the back of vans and blocked roads around Dover port.Photograph: Ay_audits/YouTubeOpinionFar rightDover and Portsmouth showed us a new kind of far right – and the authorities were caught outJoe MulhallThis is a new and dangerous development: a network of vigilantes who have mobilised as politicians and police have failed to actMon 7 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.17 EDTShareSadly, we’ve become used to far-right protests in recent years. Whether it’s the vast demonstrations led by Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (AKA Tommy Robinson) in central London, or the hundreds of local protests outside hotels and HMOs housing asylum seekers, the sight of far-right activists chanting anti-migrant slogans has become all too common.What we saw in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend feels different. At roughly 7am on Saturday morning,hundreds of balaclava-clad men, dressed all in black, began piling out of the backs of vans and blocked roads around Dover port. Shockingly, the policeappear to have known nothingabout it in advance.Then, on Sunday evening, a group of mengathered near a Portsmouth beachto “block” the arrival of asylum seekers on a boat. The group had been monitoring maritime apps and tracking the progress of boats towards Britain. They put out a call for people to join them and dozens answered, including well-known activists from the neo-Nazi movement.What we have seen over the past three days marks a dangerous new development in the far right. While previous protests – many of which descended into ugly racist violence – have been worrying enough, we are now faced with a new, more clandestine and confrontational threat.Hope Not Hate was the first to identify that the Dover disturbance was organised by a far-right groupcalled Patriot Platform. The balaclava-clad men blocking roads were part of a new network founded by Tommy Robinson’s right-hand man Daniel Thomas (AKA Danny Tommo).Launched in June, the group unites a web of smaller localised anti-migrant groups into a single body. Current members hail from theKentPatriots, Watford Patriots, South London Patriots, South-East Patriots, North-West Patriots, Surrey Patriots and Chertsey Patriots, to name just a few.Patriot Platform is a self-professed Christian “army of patriots” formed to, in Thomas’s words, “reclaim our borders, restore order and send a clear message: Britain belongs to the British people”. The group functions as a vigilante unit to combat immigration and revive what it says are Christian values, ready to spring into action across the country at Thomas’s word.Worryingly, there is an unusual degree of discipline to Patriot Platform’s organising. Rather than being a single entity, it operates as a network for the local groups. These groups utilise various social media platforms, most commonly Instagram, X, Facebook and TikTok, for their promotional output.However, unlike organisers of previous public anti-migrant protests, Patriot Platform operates clandestinely, with event planning happening via closed groups and direct personal communication.Its means of operation have more in common with football hooligan gangs than with traditional anti-migrant protest groups. This is how its supporters managed to arrive in their hundreds in Dover unnoticed.Rather than being met with the usual mealy-mouthed condemnations and talk of “legitimate concerns”, these “protests” need to be called what they are: far-right vigilantism. These aren’t fearful locals, they are organised far-right activists led by Thomas, a man whopleaded guiltyto attempted kidnapping and was sentenced to two years in prison after taking part in an armed attempt to abduct a man during a drugs-related dispute.Since the riots of 2024, Thomas has repeatedly spoken about the need to take to the streets and take direct action. He has been upfront abouthis intention to createa “patriotic army that is able to take control of the United Kingdom”.Despite warnings from Hope Not Hate, the authorities have failed to act. They have allowed Thomas to agitate, organise and mobilise large groups around the country. Last weekend was the consequence of police inaction, and I fear that without decisive action things will only get worse.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClearly, the government needs to be far more robust in dealing with far-right vigilantism. The Home Office is so preoccupied with being seen to be tough on immigration that it has neglected the safety of the very migrants and asylum seekers being targeted.And the police response exposes serious failings in the authorities’ approach to far-right anti-immigrant violence more broadly. Time and again, they appear unaware of the strength of protests and unprepared for the violence that sometimes results.The events in Dover andPortsmouthshould be a wake-up call for anyone who believes that far-right extremism can be managed through inaction. This is no longer simply about angry protests or offensive rhetoric. We are seeing organised groups willing to mobilise quickly, operate covertly and confront those they see as enemies. The longer authorities fail to recognise the seriousness of this threat, the bolder these groups will become.The government must act now, before vigilantism becomes normalised and far-right activists feel they can operate with impunity on Britain’s streets.Joe Mulhall is director of research at the anti-fascism organisation Hope not HateExplore more on these topicsFar rightOpinionImmigration and asylumPolicePortsmouthKentEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Why are so many people stealing from restaurants? | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: About a quarter of British adults admit to having pilfered something from a pub or restaurant. Is it an Insta-fuelled craze, or just old-fashioned greed?
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: About a quarter of British adults admit to having pilfered something from a pub or restaurant. Is it an Insta-fuelled craze, or just old-fashioned greed?
Content: They’ll never miss it …Photograph: yacobchuk/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThey’ll never miss it …Photograph: yacobchuk/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionCrimeWhy are so many people stealing from restaurants?Emma BeddingtonAbout a quarter of British adults admit to having pilfered something from a pub or restaurant. Is it an Insta-fuelled craze, or just old-fashioned greed?Mon 7 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTShareKnives, candles, a toilet roll holder complete with screws and Rawlplugs – that’s just some of the stuff Michelin-starred restaurants in France complained about clients nicking ina recent news report. I’m not sure why the screws were presented as the ultimate absurdity – if you want to use your stolen toilet roll holder, you’ll need them – it’s just common sense!A Québécois restaurateur complained about similar theftsin July– a picnic table, a painting and even the thermostat had been pinched – and British restaurateurs confirm it happens in the UK, too. Jan Ostle of Wilsons in Bristol told the BBC’sWorld at Onethat the mother-of-pearl spoons he uses to serve herb sorbet are a particular target: “Every few months I have to buy another 28.”It’s an age-old, frequently aired story – all down to a sense of entitlement, or the desire for a souvenir, or booze-fuelled bravado – but it seems awfully retro. Wasn’ttrousering a Conran restaurant ashtraya quintessential 90s petty crime? We’re supposed to be into “experiences, not things” now, and isn’t the whole point of posting a boring Instagram carousel of seven badly litamuse-bouchesto show everyone you’ve been somewhere fancy without stealing a side plate?Every year, humans speak less and less. That’s bad news, even if you hate mindless chit-chatRead moreBut our basest instincts are still seemingly awoken by tableware in a hospitality setting:a surveyby catering equipment supplier Nisbets found 27% of British adults had nicked something from a restaurant or pub. I’m not above such crimes: there’s a dinky spoon in the drawer here we definitely didn’t buy. It must have arrived nefariously, but I just don’t remember when or how (exactly what a criminal would say). We also eat our dinners off Quick trays my husband may have liberated from the Belgian fast-food chain in the 1980s.What can restaurateurs do? Some have tried putting price tags on stuff, confronting suspected spoon smugglers (chefTom Aikens caused a kerfuffledoing this to a customer in 2012), and even amnesties (Mexican chainWahaca promised free tacosto customers who returned its covetable brightly coloured spoons).The boring solution is passing on costs with higher prices; my (marginally) more fun suggestion is bringing back branded matchboxes and matchbooks, which were a colourful, legit way to brag you’d been somewhere. They’ll need to tell clients they’re forbidden to take them, though – it’s all about the thrill, not the thing.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
