title: The Guardian view on the far right’s real weapon: it is the politics of powerlessness | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: From Dover to Saxony-Anhalt, extremists thrive when voters believe established parties can no longer deliver security, prosperity or meaningful change
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: From Dover to Saxony-Anhalt, extremists thrive when voters believe established parties can no longer deliver security, prosperity or meaningful change
Content: ‘The intimidation seen in England and the AfD’s extremism are two sides of the same coin’: an anti-migrant protest in Dover, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeView image in fullscreen‘The intimidation seen in England and the AfD’s extremism are two sides of the same coin’: an anti-migrant protest in Dover, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeOpinionThe far rightThe Guardian view on the far right’s real weapon: it is the politics of powerlessnessEditorialFrom Dover to Saxony-Anhalt, extremists thrive when voters believe established parties can no longer deliver security, prosperity or meaningful changeMon 7 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.44 EDTShareWhat links thethuggishmasked agitation in southern England this weekend and the far-right Alternative für Deutschland’s (AfD)best-ever resultin a German state – where it more than doubled the 21% vote it received five years ago? Several hundred men inbalaclavasblocking an A road are not the same as a party winning a landslide election. But both events draw on the idea that the political system has lost control. The extremists in Dover and Portsmouth dramatise this claim; the electoral result in Germany threatens to institutionalise it.The prospect of Germany’s first far-right-led state government since the second world war carries real consequences. In Saxony-Anhalt it could see power handed to a partyhostileto migrants, Islam, LGBTQ+ rights and climate policy. Alarmingly, it has seniorfigureslinked to former neo-Nazi groups. About170,000 foreign nationalslive among 2 million people in Saxony-Anhalt – and roughly a fifth of the state’s doctors were born abroad. The grim paradox is that an AfD government could oversee the very state intelligence service that has classified the party as “rightwing extremist”.In England, the “Patriot Platform” agitation is far-right vigilantism that claims it will “stop the boats” if the authorities won’t. The AfD is a political party which presents its success as arepudiationof established parties that, it claims, have failed – most notably on immigration. The intimidation seen in England and the AfD’s extremism are, however, two sides of the same coin: a broader politics in which migration is felt to embody a sense of powerlessness – not just over borders but over state institutions, economic change and national identity.View image in fullscreenUlrich Siegmund of the AfD.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAThe AfD polls highest in Germany’seastern states. These have a post-reunification history of population loss and highunemployment. Britain has its own political geography and history. The small boats are a live political issue. More than 33,000 peoplearrived by that routein the year to June 2026. Nearly all will claim asylum. But arrivals were 23% lower than the previous year. The street escalation is occurring as numbers are falling.Across Europe, the far right keepsrisingbecause immigration has become a test of whether states can still govern effectively. Cuttingmigrantnumbers orasylumclaims does not lessen the issue’s potency. Studiessuggestthat, in Germany, political alienation is more important to AfD support than deprivation. That is also why, in Britain, using facts alone – that crossings are falling, or that migrants aren’tresponsiblefor NHS waiting lists or stagnant wages – may have little electoral effect. The reality answers the far right’s argument, but doesn’t dispel the deeper belief that thecountry is becoming ungovernable.Borders, in that sense, are a symptom of a bigger problem:voters increasingly distrust democracyto make things happen for them. In Germany, politicians can point to the constitutional settlement and coalition arithmetic and say that their hands are tied. In Britain, they defer to thebond marketsand the Bank of England. The language is different, but the message can sound the same: you can vote for change, but the government is limited in what it can achieve. The answer is not to pretend that inflation or legal constraints are irrelevant. It is to show that they do not amount to a permanent veto on democratic choice.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on skin cancer: fear the heat of the sun | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: With melanoma cases rising, the UK must learn from public health campaigns elsewhere
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: With melanoma cases rising, the UK must learn from public health campaigns elsewhere
Content: ‘There is a strong case for renewed efforts to communicate the risks associated with the sun.’Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APView image in fullscreen‘There is a strong case for renewed efforts to communicate the risks associated with the sun.’Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APOpinionHealthThe Guardian view on skin cancer: fear the heat of the sunEditorialWith melanoma cases rising, the UK must learn from public health campaigns elsewhereMon 7 Sep 2026 13.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.41 EDTShareNew climate risks bring with them new health risks. An exceptionally warm and dry summer in Europe meant that outdoor workers, and those who choose to spend leisure time in the sun, were confronted more directly than usual by the need toprotect their skinfrom ultraviolet (UV) radiation, as well as avoid dehydration and overheating. In the UK, the annual total of new melanoma cases was reported tohave risen above 20,000for the first time earlier this year (the two most common forms of skin cancer, basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma, are less dangerous).As with other cancers, the increase in cases reflects an ageing and a growing population. A third of those diagnosed with cancer in the UK areover 75. But with the NHS struggling to cope with the number of those seeking treatment, and melanoma the fifth most common cancer – after prostate, breast, lung and bowel (and excluding other skin cancers) – there are growing calls for behaviour change aligned to stronger public health measures. In May, a group of MPsproposed a ban on advertising sunbeds,which – along with sunburn and tanning – are linked with a raised risk of skin cancer. Last year, a group of experts advocatedbanning their commercial usealtogether, as in Australia and Brazil.The 1981 ‘Slip, slop, slap’ campaignThere are lessons to be learned from other countries besides new laws. In Australia, melanoma is the third most common cancer, and strong public health warnings have been the norm for decades. In 1981, a cartoon seagull was the face of a“slip, slop, slap” campaignaimed at persuading people to slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen and slap on a hat. At school, children are expected to follow a “no hat, no play” rule (meaning no games in sunny outdoor spaces for those with bare heads). While some British nurseries and schools have adopted similar policies, awareness of the risks remains far lower. Many people still habitually welcome bright sunshine and high temperatures.That is partly because these remain much rarer in the UK, especially in northern areas. For good reason, melanoma is less likely to be a priority for health authorities in Scotland than in south-east England. But with global temperatures predicted to keep rising, and given their commitment to shift towards prevention in healthcare, UK ministers and local health bosses should look again at the risks of UV radiation and the factors driving it (the National Cancer Plan has already committed officials in England to seekfurther evidence on sunbeds). In Australia, doctors have objected totanning appspromoted by influencers; in the UK there has been an increase in thepopularity of tanningamong young people, due in part to promotion on social media.Personalised care for many cancers, in the form of immunotherapy, has led to the present being termed a“golden age” for oncology. Such advances deserve to be celebrated. But there aretensionsbetween the desire to focus on innovation and the need to improve access to more established services, and invest in prevention and public health. Melanoma is one of many diseases in which behaviour has a role (cancers linked to obesity are others). After a tightening of the law on tobacco and vapes, and followingthis summer’s record high temperatures, there is a strong case for renewed efforts to communicate the risks associated with the sun as well as artificial UV light – in time for summer 2027.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: A health MOT is just one step towards prevention | Health | The Guardian
description: Letters: Tackling social and economic conditions must come first, writes Dr Louise Lawson. Plus letters from James Hibberd, Bob Forster and Dr Giles Youngs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Tackling social and economic conditions must come first, writes Dr Louise Lawson. Plus letters from James Hibberd, Bob Forster and Dr Giles Youngs
Content: ‘Prevention matters, but calls for screening programmes must be matched by realistic plans for what follows.’Photograph: David Davies/PAView image in fullscreen‘Prevention matters, but calls for screening programmes must be matched by realistic plans for what follows.’Photograph: David Davies/PAHealthLettersA health MOT is just one step towards preventionTackling social and economic conditions must come first, writesDr Louise Lawson. Plus letters fromJames Hibberd,Bob ForsterandDr Giles YoungsMon 7 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTShareDevi Sridhar is right to welcome free cholesterol testing on the NHS in England and blood pressure checks in pharmacies. Such measures can help identify health risks earlier. However, I would take issue with her suggestion that a “health MOT” is “precisely what prevention is all about” (Free cholesterol tests on the NHS are great – but here’s the five-point health MOT I’d really like to see, 2 September).Sridhar’s proposed five-point health MOT is undoubtedly valuable, but it is better understood as identifying risk rather than preventing disease. Prevention is what comes next: enabling people to make changes that improve health and reduce that risk. Public health has long distinguished between upstream factors, such as poverty, housing, employment, access to affordable healthy food and safe green spaces, and downstream interventions focused on individuals. Screening and health checks sit much closer to the downstream end of that spectrum.Interventions aimed at changing behaviour emphasise individual responsibility and often assume that everyone has similar economic, social and psychological resources to adopt healthier lifestyles. Yet those living on low incomes, in insecure work or facing linguistic and cultural barriers often have far less capacity to act on health advice. Such approaches can also reinforce stigma by implying that poor health results primarily from individual choices rather than the circumstances in which people live, while diverting attention from the drivers of health inequalities.In England, people living in the most disadvantaged communities can expectabout 19 fewer years of healthy lifethan those in the least disadvantaged communities. Free testing is welcome, but a genuinely upstream approach would focus not only on identifying risk, but also on tackling the social and economic conditions that make healthy choices possible in the first place.Dr Louise LawsonLecturer in social policy, University of GlasgowProf Devi Sridhar is right to emphasise prevention and the importance of identifying cardiovascular risk early. However, screening is only the first step. As a GP in London, I worry that suggesting annual “health MOTs” risks creating expectations that the NHS currently lacks the capacity to meet. Without substantial investment in general practice and community services, what happens after we identify millions more people with pre-diabetes, obesity, mildly raised cholesterol or borderline hypertension?These patients will understandably seek advice, support and follow-up from their GP. Yet many of these conditions are driven less by a lack of diagnosis than by wider societal factors such as diet, inactivity, housing and poverty. They are not problems that can simply be solved with a prescription, or advice.Articles advocating routine health checks without this context may also encourage patients to request annual MOTs from their GP when these are not clinically indicated or commissioned. At a time when primary care is already under intense pressure, increasing demand without increasing capacity risks diverting resources from those with established illness and greatest need. Prevention matters, but calls for screening programmes must be matched by realistic plans for what follows.Dr James HibberdBarnet, LondonI always appreciate Devi Sridhar’s articles for their straightforward and sensible approach to health. However, could I humbly suggest that she reconsiders the inclusion of a press-ups test? For far too many of us, particularly those with the musculature of an anaemic grasshopper, nightmares of the school gymnasium spring to mind, with those familiar and ignominious collapses on to a sweat-speckled floor. Never to be forgotten.Bob ForsterShipton-under-Wychwood, OxfordshireI agree with Devi Sridhar that annual screening tests offer the prospect of improving the health of the nation, starting with NHS cholesterol testing for 40- to 84-year-olds. Alas, I’ve just had my 85th birthday, so I’m presumably fit only for the knacker’s yard.Dr Giles YoungsRetired consultant physician, Drinkstone, SuffolkHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Contemporary Films had a global impact and influenced my career as a director | Movies | The Guardian
description: Letters: Ross Devenish says he owes a debt to the British film distributor, while Kal Hodgson invites Mike Leigh to join the Manchester and Salford Film Society
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Ross Devenish says he owes a debt to the British film distributor, while Kal Hodgson invites Mike Leigh to join the Manchester and Salford Film Society
Content: ‘Through Contemporary Films’ distribution systems, [Johannesburg Film Society] was able to show Satyajit Ray’s film Pather Panchali, a film that has lived on in my mind while so many others have been forgotten.’ Subir Banerjee, left, and Uma Dasgupta in Pather Panchali.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Through Contemporary Films’ distribution systems, [Johannesburg Film Society] was able to show Satyajit Ray’s film Pather Panchali, a film that has lived on in my mind while so many others have been forgotten.’ Subir Banerjee, left, and Uma Dasgupta in Pather Panchali.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMoviesLettersContemporary Films had a global impact and influenced my career as a directorRoss Devenishsays he owes a debt to the British film distributor, whileKal Hodgsoninvites Mike Leigh to join the Manchester and Salford Film SocietyMon 7 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTShareWith regard to the article about 75 years of Contemporary Films by Andrew Pulver (‘Not just Hollywood crap’: Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UK, 1 September), it was not only in Britain that Charles Cooper’s impact was felt: it spread to many other parts of the world.Contemporary Films made a major impact on me in South Africa before I even went to London to study film-making in 1959. In Johannesburg, as an 18-year-old, I discovered the Johannesburg Film Society. Through Contemporary Films’ distribution systems, the society was able to show Satyajit Ray’s film Pather Panchali, a film that has lived on in my mind while so many others have been forgotten.Then, 13 years later, Charles and Kitty Cooper distributed my film Boesman and Lena, based on the play byAthol Fugardand shown in the Paris Pullman cinema, London. Years later they screened Marigolds in August, also written by Fugard, with a cast that included Fugard, John Kani andWinston Ntshona.The Coopers showed me that the word “film” was not defined by Hollywood and that there were many ways to spell film. It encouraged me to believe that we could tell our own stories without necessarily being constrained by the diktats of Hollywood. We owe the Coopers a great debt.Ross DevenishCape Town, South AfricaMike Leigh may have only watched “Hollywood and British movies” as he grew up in Manchester, but if he’d been a bit more inquisitive he could have joined the Manchester and Salford Film Society, which was at that time regularly showing world cinema; formed in 1930, it had been mentioned by the Manchester Guardian during its first year, when the paper noted its belief that “intelligent film will prosper [as] each visit to the film society shows”.Ewan MacColl, an early member, said that we presented “the cream of the world’s best films”.Our volunteer-led society is still going strong, approaching our 96th season, and currently based at the LittleTheatrein Altrincham. We are always happy to welcome new members, so perhaps Mr Leigh could join us for our showing of Tokyo Story on 12 September.Kal HodgsonHale, Greater ManchesterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Saudi deal offers a revenue boost for Exeter University that will save jobs | University of Exeter | The Guardian
description: Letter: The partnership is not funded by ‘dirty money’, as the Exeter branch of the University and College Union claims, says Prof Anthony King
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: The partnership is not funded by ‘dirty money’, as the Exeter branch of the University and College Union claims, says Prof Anthony King
Content: ‘The MA in applied security and strategy in Saudi will educate – rather than “train” – senior military officers … about strategy and decision-making.’Photograph: Mahmoud Mahmoud/EPAView image in fullscreen‘The MA in applied security and strategy in Saudi will educate – rather than “train” – senior military officers … about strategy and decision-making.’Photograph: Mahmoud Mahmoud/EPAUniversity of ExeterLettersSaudi deal offers a revenue boost for Exeter University that will save jobsThe partnership is not funded by ‘dirty money’, as the Exeter branch of the University and College Union claims, saysProf Anthony KingMon 7 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe University of Exeter’s proposed partnership with the National Defense University in Saudi Arabia is not funded by “dirty money”, as the Exeter branch of the University and College Union claims, nor is it remotely covert (Exeter University approves deal with Saudi Arabia to train military officers and officials, 29 August).Aligning with UK government policy, it is part of a legitimate strategic alliance with a leading Gulf state that, following the 7 October attacks and ongoing crisis, is playing an increasingly decisive role in Middle Eastern geopolitics.Within an ethical framework of international law and western liberal norms, the MA in applied security and strategy (MStrat) in Saudi will educate – rather than “train” – senior military officers and other officials from across the Gulf states about strategy and decision-making.Against the imputations of the UCU spokesperson you quote, the partnership with Saudi is not detrimental to academic positions in the humanities and social sciences at Exeter.On the contrary, at a time of budgetary contraction and redundancies, the Saudi MStrat is a vital new source of revenue, whose explicit purpose is to protect existing posts and create new ones.Prof Anthony KingDirector, Strategy and Security Institute, title: AI transcriptions are no time-saving measure for doctors | Doctors | The Guardian
description: Letters: Dr Mary Gibbs says there are a number of problems with AI, particularly its tendency to misunderstand, as Debbie Cameron can attest
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Dr Mary Gibbs says there are a number of problems with AI, particularly its tendency to misunderstand, as Debbie Cameron can attest
Content: ‘Turning an often complex history by the patient into a clear account that a colleague can assimilate quickly is a difficult skill to learn.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Turning an often complex history by the patient into a clear account that a colleague can assimilate quickly is a difficult skill to learn.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoDoctorsLettersAI transcriptions are no time-saving measure for doctorsDr Mary Gibbssays there are a number of problems with AI, particularly its tendency to misunderstand, asDebbie Cameroncan attestMon 7 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTShareI am an out-of-hours GP, and I am glad to see a news report on this issue, which has been causing me increasing concern at work (Doctors’ AI scribes get names of drugs and diagnoses wrong, NHS watchdog warns, 31 August). There are a number of problems with AI, particularly its tendency to misunderstand and contradict itself, which can lead to dangers for the patient, but I will concentrate on the supposed “time-saving” aspect.Many of the patients I see will have been assessed by someone else first on the phone, and I am used to reading through a triage assessment before I call in the patient. My heart sinks when I see that AI has been used – the consultation is invariably long, with duplications, and sometimes contradictions. Often, any history I take turns out to be significantly different from what is listed. So I can never trust that it is correct – I can state with certainty that I find meaningful errors far more often in AI consultations than in those typed out by colleagues.You may blame the original clinician, but anyone who has tried to proofread something they have created, particularly under time pressure, will know how difficult this is. So how can this save time, when the first clinician has to check through a long, repetitive account, and the second clinician can’t trust what is written and has to check it again?In addition, turning an often complex history by the patient into a clear account that a colleague can assimilate quickly is a difficult skill to learn, as any medical student can tell you. If we do not learn and maintain this skill, we will lose a lot, and so will our patients.Dr Mary GibbsManchesterRe the risks of AI diagnosis and medication being mistranscribed, I have first-hand experience of the problems. A consultant I worked for as a secretary had a week’s trial of voice recognition software. He gave up the idea when “I recommend two weeks on lansoprazole” turned into suggesting a two-week holiday on Lanzarote. A prescription I’m sure the patient would have been more than happy to try.Debbie CameronFormby, MerseysideHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Zheng Qinwen erases another 5-0 deficit to stun Swiatek and reach US Open quarter-finals | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Zheng Qinwen recovered from 5-0 down in the opening set to stun Iga Swiatek and reach the last eight of the US Open
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Zheng Qinwen recovered from 5-0 down in the opening set to stun Iga Swiatek and reach the last eight of the US Open
Content: Zheng Qinwen waves to the crowd after booking her spot in the last eight at Flushing Meadows.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAView image in fullscreenZheng Qinwen waves to the crowd after booking her spot in the last eight at Flushing Meadows.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Zheng Qinwen erases another 5-0 deficit to stun Swiatek and reach US Open quarter-finalsZheng makes astonishing recovery to win 7-5, 6-3Rybakina sweeps aside Osaka 6-1, 6-4 to set up clashTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsMon 7 Sep 2026 16.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe most important takeaway from 12 days at the US Open is simple: do not, by any means, lead 5-0 against Zheng Qinwen. No scoreline is as hazardous. On Friday, the former Australian Open champion Madison Keys learned this lesson the hard way as she led Zheng 5-0 in the final set of an intense tussle before Zheng, the Olympic gold medallist, rolled through seven consecutive games to win the match.Somehow, two days later, Zheng repeated the trick in her very next set against a greater opponent. Down 5-0 in the opening set of her fourth‑round match against the six-time grand slam title winnerIga Swiatek, Zheng again locked down her game and reeled off seven games in a row to take the set. Zheng refused to let it go as she pulled off one of the best wins of her career, reaching the US Open quarter‑finals with a 7-5, 6-3 victory.US Open tennis 2026: Osaka v Rybakina, Zheng stuns Swiatek, Andreeva wins and more on day nine – liveRead moreThis was a remarkable turn of events for a variety of reasons. A player winning seven games in a row from 0-5 down in consecutive sets against two different opponents is almost unheard of at the highest level; doing so against two grand slam title winners has never happened before.“In one moment, I even forgot the score in the first set at 4-5,” Zheng said. “That shows how I am focused. I guess, to come back 0-5 [again] is not lucky, that’s [what] I can say.”Swiatek was one of the tournament favourites after winning her first title of the year at the Canadian Open in Toronto and she seemed to be on the way to rediscovering the confidence that has marked her as the greatest player of her generation. However, as soon as she lost control in the first set, Swiatek’s game unravelled in a stream of erratic unforced errors. While the Pole cited difficulties with anxiety and stress as reasons for her recent troubles, here she just could not feel the ball well enough.“I wouldn’t say it had anything to do with mentality. It was more that I started making mistakes from easy balls and Qinwen stopped doing mistakes,” she said.View image in fullscreenIga Swiatek tries to return the ball on her way to a straight-sets defeat.Photograph: Seth Wenig/APMost importantly, this is a transformative result for one of the biggest talents on the tour. Coming into this match, Zheng had defeated Swiatek just once in their eight meetings, but that was a devastating loss for the Pole as it came in the semi‑finals of the 2024 Paris Olympics at Roland Garros, where Swiatek had just won her third consecutive French Open.Along with her Olympic gold medal, which instantly established her as one of the most famous athletes in China, Zheng reached the 2024 Australian Open final and rose to a career‑high ranking of No 4 last year. However, the 23-year-old underwent elbow surgery and tumbled down the rankings.Things have been incredibly difficult since. Zheng fell as low as No 160 in June and has struggled to find rhythm. Coming here, her 2026 record was 11-13. Her US Open is testament to how quickly things can come together in tennis, and after starting off this tournament having to park her ego and drop down to compete in the qualifying draw, seven wins in New York have allowed Zheng to re-establish herself as a genuine contender.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionZheng will next face Elena Rybakina, the second seed, who moved to within one win of becoming world No 1 for the first time as she comfortably defeated Naomi Osaka 6-1, 6-4. Rybakina was nearly flawless in their 66 minutes on Louis Armstrong Stadium, firing down 29 winners and just 17 unforced errors while facing just one unconverted break point in the match. Osaka needed her top level just to compete with Rybakina, but the two-time US Open champion has been struggling with achilles pain and she did not serve well enough to be competitive.The fifth seed and French Open champion, Mirra Andreeva, reached the quarter-finals at Flushing Meadows for the first time with a 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 win against Austria’s Anastasia Potapova.In the men’s draw, Alexander Blockx, the 28th seed, reached a grand slam quarter-final for the first time by defeating the 24th seed Francisco Cerundolo 6-3, 4-6, 7-5, 7-5.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Iga SwiatekUS Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maresca eyes rest for busy dad Haaland as Manchester City prepare for Porto | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City’s manager, Enzo Maresca, said Erling Haaland is a ‘complete’ person since the birth of his son and would soon need rest after a busy summer
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Manchester City’s manager, Enzo Maresca, said Erling Haaland is a ‘complete’ person since the birth of his son and would soon need rest after a busy summer
Content: Erling Haaland has matured into a complete person since the birth of his son, according to Enzo Maresca.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenErling Haaland has matured into a complete person since the birth of his son, according to Enzo Maresca.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersManchester CityMaresca eyes rest for busy dad Haaland as Manchester City prepare for PortoNorwegian forward has played every minute of seasonParenting duties have changed player’s ‘priorities’Jamie Jacksonin PortoMon 7 Sep 2026 17.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnzo Maresca believes Erling Haaland has become “complete” as his priorities have changed after the birth of theManchester CityNo 9’s son two years ago.Haaland has again started the campaign in prolific form, scoring three goals in City’s opening three Premier League victories. In three of the 26‑year‑old’s four previous seasons at City he has won the Premier League golden boot. Maresca pointed to how the birth of his son in 2024 changed the Norwegian’s motivation.Emery ready to ignite Aston Villa’s season at Club Brugge after familiar slow startRead moreThe manager said: “He’s a man now. He’s a dad. When he arrived here [in summer 2022] he was not a dad and now he’s a dad and life completely changes because the priority becomes his son. I’m happy for him because he was already top as a player and as a boy but now you can see that he is complete. He is a family man, he is still scoring goals so I’m very happy for him.”City are at Porto in the opening league‑phase game of theChampions Leagueon Tuesday. Haaland has played every competitive minute of the campaign so far, and Maresca said he will be rested at some point, particularly as as the striker was part of the Norway team that reached the World Cup quarter-finals.The Italian said: “It’s not easy for Erling or for any of the players that play for club and international teams. I think it is normal that you [may] see these players start to be tired. So, it’s correct to give them some rest. It can be one game out or one week away.“It depends on which moment we are in but the priority is to allow the players to be good and happy. When you see them tired the risk of injury increases, and we need players who are 100%.”While Maresca’s options if Haaland is rested against Porto would be selecting Antoine Semenyo at centre-forward, or fielding Phil Foden or Rayan Cherki as a false 9, he pointed to the in-game control the two latter players can give City when required.View image in fullscreenNico O’Reilly pulled up with an injury before the Coventry match but will ‘probably’ be available to face Porto.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA“There is always a gameplan and Rayan can drop a little bit to manage the tempo and the game,” the 46-year-old said.“We [also] need Rayan in the position to be dangerous – the last game against Coventry [a 1-0 win] we made contact with him five or six times between the lines and created chances.“It depends on the game. Against Coventry, it was good for him to drop a little bit and manage the tempo and not always be a reference for the other team. We need him in the right position because he gives us the quality. Phil can also do that – and the last pass between the lines is very good so we are lucky that we have two very good players that can do this.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn his first campaign as head coach, Francesco Farioli led Porto to their 31st title, and they have a maximum 15 points from their opening five Primeira Liga games.Maresca was asked if City will be favourites at the Estádio do Dragão. “We are here to do our best,” he said. “The game will dictate the favourite. This is a hard place to come. This season they started very good. In the last 14, 15 games in Europe they just lost one so we are going to try our best and try to win the game.“I know that Porto is very good in set pieces. I think it has become part of the game now so we need to do our best, defend in the right way, score goals as much as we can from set pieces because it’s part of the game and you need to be perfect because all teams are prepared for that.”Maresca said Nico O’Reilly would “probably” be available after missing the Coventry game with a late fitness problem, but the manager said he was “not sure” about Jérémy Doku’s availability after injury.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityErling HaalandChampions LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Emery ready to ignite Aston Villa’s season at Club Brugge after familiar slow start | Aston Villa | The Guardian
description: Manager remains calm despite his side taking one point and scoring no goals in opening three Premier League games
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Manager remains calm despite his side taking one point and scoring no goals in opening three Premier League games
Content: John McGinn keeps his eyes on the ball during training for Aston Villa’s match against Club Brugge.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenJohn McGinn keeps his eyes on the ball during training for Aston Villa’s match against Club Brugge.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAAston VillaEmery ready to ignite Aston Villa’s season at Club Brugge after familiar slow startManager remains calm despite his side taking one point and scoring no goals in opening three Premier League gamesBen Fisherin BrugesMon 7 Sep 2026 16.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnai Emery is not panicking. He may kick every ball on the touchline but, behind closed doors, Aston Villa’s players are used to him being the calmest person in the room, routinely more demanding after victory than defeat. John McGinn tells a story in which the Villa manager, early in his now almost four-year tenure, broke character and lost his cool during a half-time interval not owing to a lukewarm performance but because he witnessed his captain tearing into teammates. In Emery’s eyes, it was McGinn expending unnecessary energy rather than seeking solutions.Emery, McGinn and Villa have been here before. Just last season, in fact; at this point, they were pointless in the Premier Leagueand still another 157 minutes from registering their first goal. So in one sense Villa, who shook off a slow start to qualify for theChampions Leaguefor the second time in three seasons, are ahead of schedule. Villa’s goalless draw at Hull on Saturday was not the most absorbing display but there were enough green shoots to trust Emery when he says he is confident they can again exceed expectations.Maresca eyes rest for busy dad Haaland as Manchester City prepare for PortoRead moreIt is hard to disbelieve a man with Emery’s record, having overseen the most successful era in the club’s recent history. “When we started the project here, the ambition we had, it was [not even] in our highest expectations to be in Europe four years in a row,” the Villa manager says. “It was very difficult when we started working together but it was the ambition of the owner. We set our standards high with the players to be there and we are. Now is the moment to remember how we got here and the way we did. Now it is a different moment and chapter.”In these moments, Emery tends to double down on his methods. Last season they did not taste victory until their seventh game of the season in all competitions, McGinn scoring the only goal in a Europa League win against Bologna. Before that game, players assembled around 11.30am for the kind of opposition analysis meeting to which they have grown accustomed, so much so McGinn says they now walk in like robots.Emery lasers in on players’ positioning and tactical details. Jhon Durán, now on loan at Benfica from Al-Nassr after spells at Fenerbahce and Zenit St Petersburg, is famously the only player to have requested to leave mid-meeting.Villa face Club Brugge on Tuesday for the fourth time in the past two years, hoping Europe will again ignite their season.After that victory against Bologna last September, Villa embarked on an extraordinary run of 17 wins in 19 matches. Half of the 14 players involved in that game have departed but one of those who did feature, Emiliano Buendía, is hopeful that Emery’s new-look squad can put together a similar run. “It has not been the start we wanted, but we are trying to take the positive things from every match,” said the Argentinian, who has started all four Villa games this season. “We will try to change this momentum in terms of results and try to get our confidence back to perform well and [achieve] the results we want.”View image in fullscreenUnai Emery is remaining calm despite Aston Villa’s slow start to the season.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Stewart Kendall/Apl/SportsphotoAnother Champions League campaign should not be taken for granted and returning to this stage, after winning the Europa League last season, is arguably Emery’s greatest feat. The strides made under Emery will surely occupy the minds of supporters as they wander the cobbled streets of Bruges and when they explore Barcelona in November, too.Crucially, Emery is energised by the challenge, helped by the odd siesta at Villa’s Bodymoor Heath base. “Sometimes I need a good nap, after intensive work in the morning,” he said with a smile last week.For now, George Hemmings’s 13th‑minute shot against Hull represents Villa’s sole effort on target this campaign. In the same game it was the 19-year-old, who joined from Nottingham Forest aged 16, who supplied Buendía for a golden chance. It is easy to focus on the shortcomings but it would also be remiss to overlook Villa’s encouraging performance in the Super Cup against, in Emery’s view, the best team on the planet; defeat against Paris Saint-Germain was less than a month ago and Villa have only strengthened since.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne of the most exciting of their 11 summer arrivals, the 18-year-old Ibrahim Mbaye, was an unused substitute for PSG in Salzburg. Another talent signed this summer, Johan Manzambi, continues to step up his fitness after a knee injury and could feature as early as Saturday against Nottingham Forest.Only two of Villa’s new arrivals – Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson – started at Hull last time out. Matteo Ruggeri, Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho arrived from the bench. Taylor Harwood-Bellis, a £25m buy omitted from Villa’s Champions League squad, had a watching brief in Yorkshire. João Gomes was sent off on debut. Leon Goretzka, who joined on a free after leaving Bayern Munich, will not feature until at least October after a knee injury setback.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Emery often takes time to integrate signings. Youri Tielemans had to wait four months for his first Villa start before embedding himself as one of Emery’s undroppables. He demands a lot of his players and even more of himself. “In football, if you are expecting transition, maybe you are not in the right way,” he said last month.“We have to rebuild the team as fast as possible. I don’t know if we need time or not. We are progressing – still not enough because we are not getting good results – but tomorrow is a new test in Europe.”Explore more on these topicsAston VillaUnai EmeryChampions LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sale’s Courtney Lawes ‘not worried about legacy’ in drive to make England return | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Courtney Lawes is back in the Prem after two years in France and has unfinished business at international level
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Courtney Lawes is back in the Prem after two years in France and has unfinished business at international level
Content: Courtney Lawes will have to prove himself in the Prem to secure England selection.Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty Images for Sale SharksView image in fullscreenCourtney Lawes will have to prove himself in the Prem to secure England selection.Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty Images for Sale SharksPrem RugbySale’s Courtney Lawes ‘not worried about legacy’ in drive to make England returnLawes is back in the Prem after two years in France and has unfinished business at international levelGerard MeagherMon 7 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCourtney Lawes was not expecting to be named in Steve Borthwick’s pre‑season England squad over the weekend. While the 37-year-old has made clear that hisreturn to the Prem with Sale Sharksis in no small part down to his ambition to feature in a fifth World Cup next year, much like the national head coach Lawes favours action rather than words.Borthwick has explained to players such as Lawes, his fellowSalearrival Joe Marchant and Newcastle’s new No 8 Hoskins Sotutu that in order to achieve England selection they must prove themselves against the players they are now competing with in the Prem.As such, Lawes was circumspect when discussing what is privately a fierce determination to add to his 105 caps. “If I play well for Sale I’ll give myself an opportunity to play for England,” was his response, aware that Borthwick’s side have hardly kicked on since he last turned out for them at the 2023 World Cup.What fascinates most, though, is why Lawes is putting himself through it at all.‘It was tough to be Jonah Lomu’: new film sheds light on late All Blacks heroRead moreThere were times in his final years with Northampton and England that Lawes appeared bound together with gaffer tape. Peel away at the frayed edges and after years of what he describes as “balls-to-the-wall rugby” you feared he would crumple in a heap of exhausted parts. Nonetheless, the level at which he was performing at the 2023 World Cup and particularly his final, title‑winning season with Northampton was little short of stratospheric. After signing off from English rugby, winners’ medal secured, performing his valedictory press conference topless and wearing ski goggles, does his return not risk tarnishing that legacy?“I don’t feel nervous,” he says. “I’m not too worried about legacy at this point. I’d much rather come back and not be able to make it than not know whether you’ve called time a bit early. I’ll give it my best effort and the cards will lie where they lie.”To anyone with a passing interest in Lawes’s career, particularly from the point of his Test resurgence under Eddie Jones, it will come as no surprise that he worries little about legacy. He has four children but there is not the financial imperative either, even if a move to Sale – with whom his wife’s family has close ties – was brought about in part because Northampton could not afford to bring him back. There is a school of thought that worries Lawes is in for a rude awakening after two years in France’s second tier with Brive, but it is clear that he has a steely confidence that he can still perform. What has made Lawes one of the most likable England internationals of recent years is that he backs himself without any accompanying bravado.View image in fullscreenCourtney Lawes: ‘I’d much rather come back and not be able to make it than not know whether you’ve called time a bit early.’Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty Images for Sale Sharks“At Brive I don’t think I played more than three weeks on the bounce, and very often it was two weeks,” Lawes says. “So it probably prolonged my career a little bit, going out there and not having to play balls-to-the-wall rugby every single week. I wasn’t ready to retire last season. I was still playing really well and still one of the better players in the league. So I thought I’d go one more time. You’re a long time retired and I can still move really well so, why not when you’ve still got it in your legs?”Those statements will be music to the ears of Alex Sanderson and his fellow coaches at Sale. Indeed, there is an unmistakable buzz around the place after the arrival of Lawes, who demonstrated his will to win by clinching the pre‑season padel competition with Dom Hanson. Young players are in awe of him and senior pros such as George Ford have been taken aback by the levels that Lawes can still reach. Given how highly he rates Ford’s opinion, that will be music to the ears of Borthwick too.It seems inevitable then, that if he stays fit, Lawes’s return to the England fold will come in the autumn. It is a big if, but there are grounds for optimism. The season before the last World Cup, Lawes barely played for Northampton, making four appearances before mid-April. He had sustained what he thought was a head injury in September 2022 but further investigation revealed a problem with his vestibular system. He returned and performed superbly well for England during their World Cup campaign but he surprised even himself with the heights he hit in the following campaign with Saints.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBy then, however, a move to France had been agreed and international retirement had been announced. That is not to suggest Lawes regrets his move to Brive, rather that after maintaining standards across the Channel, he believes he has unfinished business with England. All the more so because Lawes has always been an advocate of scrapping the Rugby Football Union rule that prevents players based outside England being selected.View image in fullscreenCourtney Lawes made the last of his 105 appearances for England at the 2023 World Cup.Photograph: David Davies/PA“When some of your better players are out in France, I don’t see why you’d limit yourself,” he says. “No, I can see why they do it because they don’t want all their players playing abroad but I don’t think that’s necessarily going to be the case anyway. It’s important that you have the best players available for selection. If we want the game to develop and more people to watch it, I think [the rugby landscape] has to develop.”Lawes is at pains to say that moving to France is not for everyone but believes he returns with a few more strings to his bow and says the key difference in France is one of autonomy. “You’ve got to have a very specific mindset,” he says. “I see why players, take your Sextons, that are used to doing things a certain way, a certain standard, how they struggle, because you have got to be adaptable, you’ve got to be relaxed as well and have the ability to say: ‘OK, let’s do it your way.’“It’s much more individual focused rather than team focused. In terms of the players there, instead of moving the ball to space they’re expected to go for the space themselves, that kind of thing.” In other words, the kind of thing that Borthwick’s England are crying out for.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbySaleEngland rugby union teamRugby unionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kevin Pietersen must tread carefully as England mentor after life as an outspoken pundit | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: The former player’s credentials speak for themselves but the ECB has also taken a risk in employing him until the end of next year
Author: Mark Ramprakash
Headline: The former player’s credentials speak for themselves but the ECB has also taken a risk in employing him until the end of next year
Content: Kevin Pietersen is returning to the England set-up as a specialist mentor to the men’s white-ball teams.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenKevin Pietersen is returning to the England set-up as a specialist mentor to the men’s white-ball teams.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAEngland cricket teamKevin Pietersen must tread carefully as England mentor after life as an outspoken punditMark RamprakashThe former player’s credentials speak for themselves but the ECB has also taken a risk in employing him until the end of next yearMon 7 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 15.43 EDTShareFor most of the time since his retirement as a player Kevin Pietersen has worked as a pundit and commentator, encouraged to be outspoken, hold strong opinions and state them powerfully. Afterhis surprise appointmentas a specialist mentor to the England men’s white-ball teams he will have to tread a bit more carefully.He will bring positivity, as all great players initially do because of their stature within the game, but the fact that he was a great player lasts only so long, and then it’s about the words he uses and his ability to tailor his messaging.Pakistan launch player conduct investigation during dysfunctional England tourRead moreHe has not done a lot of coaching, but I have seen masterclasses on Sky that demonstrate how much hard work he put in across his career to reach the heights he did, showing strong technical understanding, and excellent communication. His credentials speak for themselves, as a world-class player with huge reserves of experience to draw on, and someone who has stayed in touch with the game. He’s got this chance on merit.But as a personality he can divide opinion: some have always sung his praises, while others might not enjoy his company so much. Normally when a consultant is brought in it’s for one tour, to see how things go. Pietersen is due to be involved with England until the end of next year. It is a big commitment, both from the England and WalesCricketBoard and from Pietersen, and also a bit of a risk.He has been quite outspoken in his criticism of Brendon McCullum’s approach to Test cricket in particular, and it might be a clever move to take a critic out of the commentary box and turn him into an ally, but I’m sure his message as a dominant player will be to encourage the batters to take a similar approach, which would probably echo McCullum’s advice. The challenge of coaching as a former player is to adapt your message to each individual. You’ve had your career, now your job is to help people to make the most of theirs, not to tell them what you would have done. Language is so powerful to players, and Pietersen will need to show a mastery of nuance that he might be unused to.View image in fullscreenKevin Pietersen was critical of England’s approach to Test cricket during Brendon McCullum’s stint as red-ball head coach.Photograph: David Gray/ReutersPakistan’s latest coaching appointments are, I think it’s fair to say, less encouraging. In fact if you want a demonstration of how not to manage an international cricket team, or for that matter any sports team, just take a look at this Pakistan set-up. In their latest brainwave theysacked their head coach and sent seven players homewhile calling up largely inexperienced replacements before the final Test this week. To me it smacks of administrators wanting to be seen to be proactive. Is it going to help? I can’t see it. But I’m not convinced that’s even their intention.Sarfaraz Ahmed, the outgoing head coach, and the bowling coach Umar Gul, who was also sacked, are two former cricketers with a lot of experience – 469 international appearances between them across the three formats – who know what the players are going through. They did not have a lot of coaching experience – Sarfaraz was appointed in April, a month after he announced the end of his international playing career – but they were appointed for a reason, and they have not suddenly lost the ability to support players.Mike Hesson, who has been Pakistan’s white-ball coach since last year and someone I’ve heard good things about, has come in and perhaps he should have been given the job in the first place, with the others working around him and learning off him, creating a unit that combined the calmness and experience of Hesson with the knowledge and respect of Sarfaraz and Gul.View image in fullscreenMike Hesson, Pakistan’s white-ball head coach, has been called in to run the Test team at Edgbaston.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAI can only imagine what the experience of being sent home mid-tour does to a player’s confidence. Irrespective of their performances, and I’m sure they will be bitterly disappointed with their lack of success, I’m sad for those players as individuals. This has been a very public humiliation for them. I wonder how this will affect the psyche of all Pakistani players who dream of representing their country. If this is the way national teams treat their best players, it will only accelerate the exodus of talent to franchise tournaments. Their replacements face a real challenge: the forecast for Birmingham this week is excellent but it’ll be cloudy and against a very good bowling attack. On potentially another juicy pitch this will not be an easy task. The Pakistan Cricket Board does not deserve its gamble to succeed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was refreshing after the second Test to hear talk from the England camp of ruthlessness, a word Ben Stokes famously hated. They are facing weak opponents who appear to have made themselves weaker, and they should be determined to make it 3-0, smelling blood. There are runs and wickets to be had. For all that Pakistan are in disarray, England have played good, sensible, grown‑up cricket and it has been a pleasure to see it.I was at Lord’s for every day of the second Test and England’s use of the conditions was outstanding. Ollie Robinson was almost unplayable, and the four seamers complement each other really well: the skill and accuracy of Robinson, the pace of Jofra Archer, the angle of Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson’s ability to swing the ball and make things happen is a thrilling combination.We have to keep a sense of proportion, because this is not the strongest batting lineup in world cricket, but I am excited for the future and intrigued to find out how they fare over the winter on the slower surfaces of Bangladesh, and with a Kookaburra ball in South Africa that can do a bit early on but after that tends to favour the batter. It’s one thing rolling through Pakistan at an overcast Lord’s and another to toil all day in the heat. But there is every reason to confidently believe that this quartet would be a handful in English conditions against any opponents, hopefully including in the Ashes next summer.And if any of the players want to know how winning the Ashes at home might feel, well, they can askKevin Pietersen.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamKevin PietersenCricketcommentShareReuse this content

title: Pakistan launch player conduct investigation during dysfunctional England tour | Pakistan cricket team | The Guardian
description: Pakistan have launched an investigation into ‘discipline and conduct’ during their highly dysfunctional tour of England, with two players understood to have had their mobile phones confiscated as part of the inquiry
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Pakistan have launched an investigation into ‘discipline and conduct’ during their highly dysfunctional tour of England, with two players understood to have had their mobile phones confiscated as part of the inquiry
Content: King Charles poses with members of the Pakistan cricket team during an audience at Clarence House earlier in September.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/ReutersView image in fullscreenKing Charles poses with members of the Pakistan cricket team during an audience at Clarence House earlier in September.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/ReutersPakistan cricket teamPakistan launch player conduct investigation during dysfunctional England tourMobile phones of players confiscated as part of inquiryNine fined during Pakistan’s recent tour of CaribbeanAli MartinMon 7 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePakistan have launched an investigation into “discipline and conduct” during their highly dysfunctional tour of England, with two players understood to have had their mobile phones confiscated as part of the probe.A spokesperson for the PakistanCricketBoard confirmed on Monday that an investigation is currently under way and while no individuals have been named, it follows the removal of seven players from their original touring party last week in response to going 2-0 down with one Test still to play.Azhar Ali: ‘Pakistan cricket cannot change in the space of a year’Read moreThe Guardian understands that, as part of this, two players had data from their mobile phones captured by PCB security officials. This is said to have occurred during the aftermath of the team’s 194-run defeat in the second Test at Lord’s.Amir Mir, the PCB head of communications,wrote on X: “The Pakistan Cricket Board has initiated an internal disciplinary inquiry following media reports concerning discipline and conduct, which are currently being reviewed internally.“The PCB handles such matters in accordance with its standard procedures. The process is being conducted under PCB regulations, ensuring that all concerned individuals are given due consideration.”The precise nature of the investigation – ie any potential wrongdoing or otherwise – is not yet clear, nor has a timeline been announced.So far only Imam-ul-Haq has drawn the public ire of the PCB – and a large section of supporters – after the opener did not bat in either innings of the Lord’s defeat due to a low-grade calf injury suffered on day one.Speaking in an interview with Geo News last week, Aaqib Javed, Pakistan’s director of high performance, said: “The Imam injury is a big question mark, and a deep disappointment.“Players in the past used to get injuries, but they used to put on casts and still tried [to play]. We’ll take action against this. How is it possible that a pulled muscle ruled you out of batting in both innings? He should have tried and fought.“He’ll have to face an inquiry; I can’t say he faked it, but a muscle pull like that cannot stop you from batting altogether.”Imam has since been released from the squad, along with Mohammad Rizwan, Salman Ali Agha, Ali Usman, Khurram Shahzad and the unused Aamir Jamal and Muhammad Awais Zafar. Sarfraz Ahmed was also stood down as head coach, with New Zealander Mike Hesson moved across from his role with the white-ball team.Speaking after training at Edgbaston on Monday, Pakistan’s newly arrived bowling coach, Ashley Noffke, said: “I don’t know too much.“I sit outside that decision-making model above us as coaches. We try to keep the players focused on what they need to worry about.“I guess that’s one thing I’ve learned about being in Pakistan and coaching for a period of time – nearly 15 months with the white-ball team – there’s always something going on in the background, whether or not it’s in or out of our control – and most of the time it’s out of the players’ control.”As well as this ongoing investigation, the upheaval has also triggered news of nine players being fined during Pakistan’s recent tour of the Caribbean.The Guardian understands this was considered a relatively minor issue. The players were supposed to stay within the Player and Match Officials Areas (PMOA) during their warm-up match in Trinidad, only for a group to break away to watch the Fifa World Cup final in a part of the ground not covered by the restrictions.Explore more on these topicsPakistan cricket teamEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Safety, security and service’: behind the scenes with police at Arsenal v Chelsea | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Facial recognition and spotters part of operation at Emirates that involved dozen incidents and two arrests
Author: Sam Dalling
Headline: Facial recognition and spotters part of operation at Emirates that involved dozen incidents and two arrests
Content: Met police officers try to defuse tension between rival fans as they leave the ground after the Premier League match between Arsenal and Chelsea.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMet police officers try to defuse tension between rival fans as they leave the ground after the Premier League match between Arsenal and Chelsea.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianSoccer‘Safety, security and service’: behind the scenes with police at Arsenal v ChelseaFacial recognition and spotters part of operation at Emirates that involved a dozen incidents and two arrestsSam DallingMon 7 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe concourses are silent when, deep in the Emirates Stadium’s bowels, Chief Inspector Pete Dearden’s briefing begins.Arsenal’s 4.30pm kick-off against Chelseais still hours away but the fixture carries significance as a London derby and because the Premier League champions are hosting a realistic challenger.Dearden is a senior officer in the Metropolitan police’s public order command and Sunday’s matchday commander. He is, to borrow football jargon, giving the pre-match team talk, running through intelligence and in-game tactics. “Set the right style and tone,” he says. After Dearden has finished, the police room becomes a pseudo-station for the afternoon, with all incidents triaged by the same crime officer. Football offences can be found in niche legislation, and the Met wants London’s matchdays to be, so far as possible, policed uniformly.Matchday is the iceberg’s tip. The Met’s 17 dedicated football officers (DFOs) each work full-time on one club, planning each fixture with the matchday commander. All 500-plus games the Met covers per season are risk-graded using factors such as risk level of supporters, proximity, recent history and kick‑off time. Dearden labels Sunday’s game “medium medium”.“Our mantra is safety, security and service,” Dearden says. “We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.”View image in fullscreenChief inspector Pete Dearden gives a briefing in the police room inside the stadium three hours before kick-off in the match between Arsenal and Chelsea.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPete Dearden: ‘We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThree police support units (PSUs), each containing an inspector, three sergeants and about 21 constables, have been assigned to the match. In addition, there are the senior team and 20 operational football officers, or “spotters”, on duty.Clubs also have their own in-house safety teams, with, in effect, both parties doing their homework before collaborating. Arsenal’s operation involves about 1,000 stewards and response team members. They are the first responders to any incidents within Arsenal’s footprint. When aChelseafan overzealously reacts to his team’s early lead, the response team remove him.Stadiums are not policed as standard, but clubs can request (and, if the request is accepted, pay for) special police services (SPS).Arsenalasked for one PSU to work within the Emirates for Chelsea’s visit but even then, police intervene only when required. Dearden estimates policing football costs the Met £23m a season, with approximately 10% recovered from clubs for SPS.The Met is looking to close that gap, with aspects such as road closures and hostile vehicle mitigation now managed, and financed, by clubs. Dearden says his department is looking at “mitigation measures to reduce risk, which means that we don’t have to have as many police resources and we don’t compromise safety and security”.Using spotters is one such measure. They work under the DFOs, are usually locally based for their day-to-day duties and operate consistently with one club. Dearden estimates that their expertise allows them to do the work of double the number of public order officers that would otherwise be needed. “They will go to pubs in the wider footprint where these people gather and try to identify what their plans are, get a good feeling for their mood and the numbers,” Dearden says.Some Chelsea spotters are in Holborn and will follow when supporters journey to Arsenal by tube. Fans being unwilling to engage with spotters may indicate they are planning something. “You can get a good idea of whether they are potentially going to cause problems at a game because of that lack of engagement,” Dearden says. “It’s that communication approach again – even with some of the supporters that cause us problems, albeit a minority, there’s still engagement to be had. There are still opportunities to say: ‘Don’t do that.’”Immediately before the match one spotter performed CPR on a supporter. The intervention was life-saving.View image in fullscreenArsenal fans walk past live facial recognition cameras on their way to the ground.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Premier League has invested millions of pounds into the intelligence-led live facial recognition pilot.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianOutside the Emirates, two blue vans contain officers monitoring the data from cameras scanning passersby as part of an intelligence‑led live facial recognition pilot. The trials were funded thanks to a multimillion-pound Premier League investment.Passing the cameras is voluntary, with signs alerting pedestrians to their presence. Faces are biometrically scanned and compared with a watchlist containing the several thousand people subject to football banning orders (FBOs) and individuals wanted for more serious crimes.“We are targeting high-harm offenders, sex offenders, those with FBOs, who, if they came to an event, could spoil it for others, commit crimes, or exploit opportunities such as crowded spaces,” Dearden says.The two-hour pilot yields six interventions, one while Guardian Sport is present. Officers intervene to speak to the individual, who is with their family. They have an FBO, although are not restricted from being around the Emirates. They have also recently been released from prison for human trafficking and are wearing a tag.Dearden feels half a dozen hits is proportional to what would be expected. “What we can’t measure is the deterrent effect,” he says.Noticeable is the relative lack of police visibility compared with recent years. That is by design, not accident. A heavy police presence does not necessarily make an event feel safe. “We don’t work on a ‘just in case’ basis these days,” Dearden says. “We deal with known knowns.” Arsenal fans in Naples on Wednesday are likely to meet a vastly different approach.Immediately before the match, the Guardian laps the ground with the day’s three-person violence against women and girls (VAWG) team. “We want to change the culture of what perhaps in the past was tolerated,” Dearden says, giving the example of staff being targeted with misogynistic abuse.“We’ve had people at football matches come forward and say: ‘I’ve heard you talk three or four times now and I’m now confident enough to report that I think I’m a victim of domestic abuse and controlling behaviour.’”The VAWG team are also watching for those who may target vulnerable individuals.View image in fullscreenA constable high-fives a young Arsenal fan as he patrols the podium level at the Emirates.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn officer acts as a spotter at the Emirates before kick-off.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianFor the match, Dearden heads to the command room with Arsenal’s safety team and the other emergency services. Proximity and open dialogue are vital. Because of the game’s risk level, there is a bronze commander, Inspector Rachel Duckett, at ground level. A half-time briefing allows all parties – including medical, the London fire brigade, the local authority, the Premier League, and British transport police – to compare notes and address issues. Dearden and Duckett then discuss the strategy for the game’s end.For all the planning, much of what happens at football is result-driven. With Arsenal 2-1 up and time running out, a late Chelsea equaliser might have changed the mood. Home and away fans cross paths after, outside the 3,000-strong Chelsea end, where there is no cordon. Arsenal supporters gloat; some Chelsea fans react. A pair of Chelsea content creators try to record in the middle of the departing crowd and receive an expletive-laden reaction from passing Arsenal fans. They are advised to move on for their own safety.Striking is the speed at which potential flashpoints are spotted and then defused. Officers are calm, not confrontational, and act as an external subconscious: “‘C’mon, think – do you really want to do that?’”View image in fullscreenA Chelsea supporter is escorted out of the ground by Arsenal stewards.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOfficers support a Chelsea content creator as he tries to record a piece after Arsenal’s 2-1 victory.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAn hour after the final whistle, the stadium is silent again, and Dearden and his senior team debrief pitchside. A dozen incidents occurred around the game, with two arrests made – one for assaulting a steward and another for racial abuse and assault. A further 10 people were reported for offences including drinking in view of the pitch, missile throwing, low-level assault of a steward, homophobic chanting and possession of drugs.Dearden says the number is “slightly higher than we’d like” but points out that it demonstrates proactivity. For example, stewards are told not to tolerate pushes as simply part of the job. Outcomes will be proportionate and consistency is key. In the days and weeks ahead, everything will be analysed, assessed, fed into data. Incremental improvement will be sought and further action may be required for the reported incidents.But, for a few hours at least, all involved can reflect on a matchday’s work completed well.Explore more on these topicsFootballArsenalChelseafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like an AI agent’: Wolff hails Antonelli’s Italian GP victory in title charge | Kimi Antonelli | The Guardian
description: Toto Wolff has compared his driver Kimi Antonelli to the greats of Formula One after the Mercedes driver’s remarkable victory at the Italian Grand Prix
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Toto Wolff has compared his driver Kimi Antonelli to the greats of Formula One after the Mercedes driver’s remarkable victory at the Italian Grand Prix
Content: Kimi Antonelli on the podium after victory in the Italian Grand Prix.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli on the podium after victory in the Italian Grand Prix.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty ImagesKimi Antonelli‘Like an AI agent’: Wolff hails Antonelli’s Italian GP victory in title chargeMercedes principal likens 20-year-old to F1 greats‘No stopping him when a driver and car are one’Giles RichardsMon 7 Sep 2026 05.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleToto Wolff has compared Kimi Antonelli to the greats of Formula One after the Mercedes driver’s remarkable victory at the Italian Grand Prix where he came backto take the flag from 19th placeon the grid.The Mercedes team principal cited the win as similar to some of the best made by Lewis Hamilton, the seven-time world champion, and said that Antonelli would likely remember the race as one of the greatest of his career.Antonelli ends Italy’s 60-year wait for home F1 win with Monza triumph from 19thRead moreAntonelli, 20 years old and in only his second season in the sport, delivered an exceptional drive to take victory in Monza, fighting his way through the field and ultimately beating his Mercedes teammate, George Russell, who had started in second on the grid, into the runner-up spot.Wolff, who had been insistent that bringing Antonelli into the team last season was the right decision despite questions being raised over his youth and relative inexperience, felt Antonelli had definitively proved himself.“We’ve seen it with other great ones in the past – Lewis, who did it at some of the races – that’s what he’s shown,” said Wolff. “There’s just no stopping when a driver and a car are one, there’s nothing that can stop them.”Antonelli now leads the world championship by 66 points from ­Russell and 76 from Ferrari’s ­Hamilton with 10 meetings remaining and is in a commanding position in the title race.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli, Oscar Piastri and Lewis Hamilton in action during the Italian Grand Prix.Photograph: Claudia Greco/ReutersIn 2024 he had made his debut for Mercedes in the first free ­practice at Monza and was left disappointed when he crashed out at the ­Parabolica corner, leaving some questioning his credentials. His win on ­Sunday, Wolff felt, had finally put the ­incident to bed.“This is one that I will remember. It’s how the circle closed,” he said. “Two years ago in first practice it was probably the toughest moment in his career for himself and his family. A moment where everyone doubted, including himself.“Then two years later, it’s the ­biggest glory, the biggest moment of his career that’s probably going to be one of his biggest moments overall in the future. Even if he wins another 200 grands prix, that one will always remain special.”Antonelli endured a difficult first season in F1 last year as he learned the ropes but has come on with extraordinary alacrity. He now has seven wins this season, including a run of five in a row, is in a strong position to close out the championship and Wolff compared his ability to learn and improve to that of advanced artificial intelligence.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli celebrates with champagne on the podium at the Italian Grand Prix.Photograph: Claudia Greco/Reuters“He came out after the winter out of the blocks in a way that no one saw coming,” Wolff said. “The ability, how he processed last year. He’s been at all the races, he’s seen the pressure of the media, the attention that he gets. It’s in a way that the system has been processed and saved.“That’s why the results that we’ve seen afterwards. But it is still surprising and amazing to see how quickly he develops. For me it’s like an AI agent that continuously self-improves and learns.”Russell, the more experienced driver at Mercedes, has a huge task ahead and admitted his teammate was all but uncatchable.“It is definitely Kimi who is in ­control of it and he is deserving to be in control, I am not even thinking about a fight or a comeback,” he said. “It is going to be exceptionally challenging to overcome that gap. I am sort of accepting that is what it is and I am going to try and enjoy it from here on in and win as many races as possible.”Explore more on these topicsKimi AntonelliFormula One 2026Formula OneMercedes GPMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: WSL talking points: Palace result in doubt after substitution nightmare, Arsenal signings shine | Women's football | The Guardian
description: Promoted side’s thrilling win may be overturned after they used four substitutions windows while Georgia Stanway show the way for Gunners
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Promoted side’s thrilling win may be overturned after they used four substitutions windows while Georgia Stanway show the way for Gunners
Content: Manchester City’s Lauren Hemp, Palace’s Lexi Lloyd-Smith and Arsenal debutant Lisa Baum.Composite: Shutterstock, GettyView image in fullscreenManchester City’s Lauren Hemp, Palace’s Lexi Lloyd-Smith and Arsenal debutant Lisa Baum.Composite: Shutterstock, GettyWomen's footballWSL talking points: Palace result in doubt after substitution nightmare, Arsenal signings shinePromoted side’s thrilling win may be overturned after they used four substitutions windows while Georgia Stanway show the way for GunnersSuzanne Wrack,Tom Garry,Sophie DowneyandRéshma RaoMon 7 Sep 2026 07.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThreat of punishment ruins Palace’s big dayKirsty Howat’s 60-second cameo deep into injury time could ruin what was a memorable day for Crystal Palace on their return to the top flight. An impressive 1-0 victory over Everton was celebrated emphatically by Jo Potter and her players but that joy would have been replaced by concern and frustration not long after. On Sunday evening WSL Football revealed that there had been a breach of the rules – the Eagles used four different substitute windows rather than the regulated three – which had not been picked up by either the coaching staff or the match officials. An investigation has now been launched with punishment to be decided (there is a potential for the result to be overturned). The needless error has put a dampener on what should have been a positive afternoon thanks to England Under-23s forward Lexi Lloyd-Smith’s winner on her WSL debut.Sophie DowneyChelsea must sharpen their clawsIt was not the first time Chelsea have struggled to kill off games under Sonia Bompastor and, on the basis ofSaturday’s 1-1 draw with Aston Villaafter an almost excessively dominant performance, it seems the issues of last season have not been put to bed. “I think in a few games we had last season we were in the same scenarios,” said Bompastor. “So, yeah, if you analyse the performance today and the statistics of the game you can say that it’s crazy we couldn’t win the game.” It felt all too familiar, with last season’s 1-0 defeat to Everton in December, which ended a 585-day unbeaten run in the WSL, particularly springing to mind. Then, Chelsea accrued 79% possession, had 30 shots and hit the woodwork three times but came away with a loss.
