The fear for Chelsea fans will be that, in the 10 months since that defeat, the issues that were becoming increasingly evident have not been resolved.Suzanne WrackMatch report:Chelsea 1-1 Aston VillaView image in fullscreenSjoeke Nüsken (left) shields the ball in Chelsea’s game against Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge.Photograph: Jermaine Addo-Yeboah/SPP/ShutterstockSignings shine on competitive debut for ArsenalMuch has been made of Arsenal’s recruitment over the summer with many believing that Renée Slegers now has a team primed to challenge for the title. Four of their new signings started in the 1-0 win over Brighton, with two standing out. Recognition of Lisa Baum’s potential came to the fore with a series of impressive showings in pre-season. The 19-year-old caught the eye on her WSL debut on Sunday not just for her well-taken goal but for her direct, positive style of play. Meanwhile, Georgia Stanway showed exactly why Slegers was so keen to bring her in. The England international has added balance to the midfield, allowing Mariona Caldentey to operate more creatively. Stanway controlled the middle of the park, ranking first for touches – at 131, she had 25 more than anyone else – joint top for accurate passes (86%), first for passes into the final third (23) and second for chances created (2).SDRole model Hemp brings up double century“Just give her the ball and then something happens!” Andrée Jeglertz said of Lauren Hemp after her 200th appearance for Manchester City. The England winger was on typically strong form during the 3-1 victory over Birmingham City and became only the fourth Manchester City player to reach that landmark of appearances. Jeglertz was full of praise for the 26-year-old and continued: “One thing that is fascinating with Lauren is, if you come and watch one of our training sessions, she has the same joy for playing football. It’s also shown in the games. Our job is to put her in situations where she can show how good she is. [She] shows young players what it’s about. They need to love to go to work and love to go to the football field. It’s not just a job. It’s also an identity.”Tom GarryMaestre masters the melting potMany believe the biggest challenges faced by theLondon City Lionessesmanager, Eder Maestre, is integrating a squad that has experienced a high turnover of players and balancing the demands of an expectant cast of superstars. There have been eight arrivals this summer and seven players have departed. Teams that have experienced a high turnover of players after a strong WSL season have previously struggled. On Friday night, however, Maestre’s team showed signs they could buck that trend with a 2-1 win over Manchester United. It wasn’t always the prettiest of performances but fledgling connections were forming in Bromley, with the individual quality of players helping to cut across any lack of cohesion. Gelling players is not easy though. “I think it’s one of the most challenging situations for any coach,” said Maestre. “We have talented players, but we have a clash of cultures. I’m trying to align everybody in the same place, trying to create something big where everybody can feel represented … I’m very happy with the performance.”SWMatch report:London City Lionesses 2-1 Manchester Unitedskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDaniëlle Van De Donk (centre) peels away after scoring London City Lionesses’ winner against Manchester United.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAre Charlton strong enough to stay up?It was a worrying start to the season for Charlton Athletic fans, as the newly promoted side were convincingly beaten on home turf by the club that finished second from bottom in the WSL last season. Not only that, Charlton failed to register a shot on target during Liverpool’s 4-0 victory and the hosts could only manage two efforts off target, as Gareth Taylor’s visitors’ enjoyed 76% of the possession. It had been a much closer-fought affair when the two sides met on the same ground on April in the Women’s FA Cup quarter-finals, when Liverpool eventually squeezed through after extra-time, but the Merseyside club appear to have strengthened significantly over the summer whereas Charlton clearly have significant work to do.TGHanson makes instant impact for Spurs with debut doubleKirsty Hanson wasted no time making her mark at Tottenham, scoring twice on her debut to secure a 3-1 victory over West Ham after joining from Aston Villa this summer. The forward opened her account with a first-time finish after an assist from Signe Gaupset and then produced a superb left-footed strike into the top corner. Hanson was the third-highest scorer in the WSL last season, behind Bunny Shaw and Alessia Russo, with 12 goals in 22 matches. She was one of several key transfers made during the window with the club believing she will add a new dimension to their attack. Speaking to Spurs Women social media about her performance, the manager, Martin Ho, said: “The movement for her first one was outstanding, and the second was a wonderful strike. When she’s in those positions with that quality and control, she’s really hard to play against. There’s lots more to come from Kirsty.”Réshma RaoSuzanne Wrack answered your questions about the WSL as part the Guardian’s new Q&A seriesConversationsExplore more on these topicsWomen's footballCrystal Palace WomenEverton WomenChelsea WomenAston Villa WomenArsenal WomenBrighton & Hove Albion WomenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, given hero’s funeral in Serbia  | Serbia | The Guardian
description: Fanfare at Belgrade funeral of man convicted of genocide raises questions from EU over Serbia’s membership plan
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Fanfare at Belgrade funeral of man convicted of genocide raises questions from EU over Serbia’s membership plan
Content: Mourners gather around the coffin of Ratko Mladić at St Luke’s church in Belgrade.Photograph: Oliver Bunic/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMourners gather around the coffin of Ratko Mladić at St Luke’s church in Belgrade.Photograph: Oliver Bunic/AFP/Getty ImagesSerbiaRatko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, given hero’s funeral in SerbiaFanfare at Belgrade funeral of man convicted of genocide raises questions from EU over Serbia’s membership planAna Milosavljevic in Belgrade andOliver HolmesMon 7 Sep 2026 07.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRatko Mladić, a Serbian general convicted of orchestrating the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war, has been given a hero’s funeral attended by thousands in Belgrade despite international alarm.Known as the “Butcher of Bosnia” for ​his role during the Balkans genocide in the 1990s,Mladić died in prisonin late August aged 84 while serving a life sentence for war crimes and crimes against humanity.Mladić was found guilty of genocide in 2017 for his role in the 1995Srebrenica massacre, in which about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed after Bosnian Serb forces overran the UN-designated enclave.But he has remained a beloved figure among many Serbs, with the president, Aleksandar Vučić, arguing last month for him to be released early from a UN detention facility in The Hague so he could die on Serbian soil.Vučić, an ultranationalist leader, has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade and is due to run again for prime minister in a snap election announced on Monday.Mladić’s coffin was flown to Serbia last week on a government plane, draped in national flags and carried from the aircraft by uniformed soldiers.On Monday morning, thousands of people gathered in front of a small church in the Serbian capital to pay their respects to Mladić. Armed forces stood guard at his casket, on top of which was laid his signature military cap, as well as a sword. A display of medals lay in front.“We know that his name will remain deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him,” said Porfirije, the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church.After the service, a street procession moved with the coffin towards the cemetery, where Mladić was buried with military honours including a three-volley rifle firing salute.View image in fullscreenMourners including Serbian veteran soldiers queue as they arrive to take part in a public memorial.Photograph: Oliver Bunic/AFP/Getty ImagesScenes of military pomp drew condemnation from the European Union’s enlargement commissioner, Marta Kos, who cancelled a forthcoming visit to Serbia on Friday. “The return of his remains to Belgrade reminds Europe of the darkest pages in our recent history,” she said on social media.View image in fullscreenPeople gather to watch the funeral service outside the church.Photograph: Darko Vojinović/APSerbia has been negotiating EU accession since 2014, but the process has stalled in recent years.“The glorification surrounding [Mladić’s] death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built,” said Kos. “That path requires confronting the past, genuine reconciliation and respecting the victims of war crimes.”View image in fullscreenThousands of people have gathered at the small church of St Luke in Belgrade.Photograph: Uros Arsic/ReutersAn EU spokesperson repeated the warning on Monday. “Any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries,” he said in a statement.On Sunday evening, ​football fans displayed a huge image of Mladić and chanted his name at a match in Belgrade.While Monday’s ceremony was not an official state funeral – probably to avoid further damaging international relations – it mirrored a state event, with large police and military delegations. Vučić said he had a prior engagement, but his son Danilo attended along with several other Serbian ministers, as well as Russia’s ambassador to the country.During the early 1990s Balkans conflict, when Mladić was a military officer, Vučić was entering politics as part of theSerbian Radical party, a far-right nationalist party that sought to secure land for a “Greater Serbia” by removing non-Serb populations.Decades later, Vučić has managed to remain in office – once as prime minister and twice as president over 12 years – while vacillating between keeping close ties with Russia and seeking EU membership. But anti-government anger was galvanised after the 2024collapse of a railway station roofthat killed 16 people, with widespread claims of corruption threatening his hold on power.On Monday, Serbia’s government said it intends to ⁠dissolve parliament and set a date for a snap election, a year ahead of a planned December 2027 vote. The current prime minister, Djuro ‌Macut, said: “If we want to mitigate tensions in society there ‌is no better way than to ask people.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe election has been seen as a chance for Vučić, who cannot legally run for president for a third term, to stay in high office, and his ruling party has nominated him for prime minister.Marko Vujić, an assistant professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences at the University of Belgrade, said he did not believe the government had planned the snap election announcement to coincide with Mladić’s funeral. “But once his death occurred, the regime took advantage of the momentum surrounding the event and used that day, among other things, for the dissolution of parliament.”View image in fullscreenSerbian military personnel pay their respects at Mladić’s coffin.Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/APMladić was one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war, which killed more than 100,000 people and displaced more than 2 million.Key among his crimes was the 1,460-day siege of the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo, where the civilian population was subjected to daily shelling and sniper attacks from Serb nationalist forces, and more than 10,000 people were killed.The three-year conflict culminated in the 1995killing of at least 8,000 Bosniak Muslimsin the town of Srebrenica, a crime that shocked governments in Europe that had spent decades working to prevent mass killings after the mid-century horrors when Nazi Germany killed 6 million Jews.View image in fullscreenGen Ratko Mladić in Sarajevo, April 1993.Photograph: Chris Helgren/ReutersIn Srebrenica, Mladić’s forces were filmed handing out sweets to children and promising their safe passage before thousands of Bosnian men and boys were rounded up, killed, and their bodies bulldozed into mass graves. “We give this town to the Serb people as a gift,” Mladić said at the time in filmed comments.Ratko Mladić obituaryRead moreThe killings have been pointed to as an international failure, especially as Srebrenica had beendesignated a “safe haven”under the protection of the UN, a global body created immediately after the second world war specifically to help prevent such bloody future global conflicts.Mladić was arrested in Serbia in 2011 after 16 years as a fugitive, and sentenced by a UN tribunal in the Netherlands to life imprisonment in 2017.While in detention, Mladić had been in ill health after having a series of strokes.The Balkan war started after the June 1991 breakup of Yugoslavia, when Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. Bosnian Serbs quickly took control of more than two-thirds of Bosnia and launched the siege of Sarajevo. After three years of bloodshed, the Dayton agreement was signed in Dayton, Ohio, ending the war and creating the independent state ofBosnia and Herzegovina.Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsSerbiaRatko MladićSrebrenica massacreEuropean UnionWar crimesEuropeBosnia and HerzegovinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Four arrested after baby dies on camping trip in Staffordshire | UK news | The Guardian
description: Two women and two men arrested on suspicion of murder after death of three-month-old girl near Great Wyrley
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Two women and two men arrested on suspicion of murder after death of three-month-old girl near Great Wyrley
Content: Police were called to the scene on Saturday morning by paramedics from the West Midlands ambulance service responding to a report of a child in cardiac arrest.Photograph: British News and Media/Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenPolice were called to the scene on Saturday morning by paramedics from the West Midlands ambulance service responding to a report of a child in cardiac arrest.Photograph: British News and Media/Alamy Live NewsUK newsFour arrested after baby dies on camping trip in StaffordshireTwo women and two men arrested on suspicion of murder after death of three-month-old girl near Great WyrleyNeha GohilMidlands correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a three-month-old girl died in Staffordshire while camping with her family.Officers said they were made aware of the death on Saturday at 8.45am after being called by paramedics from the West Midlands ambulance service, who were responding to a report of a child in cardiac arrest. An air ambulance was also sent but the child was pronounced dead at the scene.Staffordshire police said they attended the scene in woodland off Strawberry Lane near Great Wyrley and arrested four people on suspicion of murder. This includes a 42-year-old man and 30-year-old woman from south Staffordshire, a 20-year-old woman from Wolverhampton and an 18-year-old man from Walsall.View image in fullscreenThe scene of the medical emergency near Great Wyrley.Photograph: British News and Media/Alamy Live News/Alamy Live News.Officers said all four had now been bailed with conditions while the investigation continued. DI Josh Lee, from Staffordshire police’s child protection team, said: “I want to assure the local community that we are working around the clock to investigate the circumstances of this tragic incident, which has understandably caused concern.“While we can confirm that all four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder, we are still working hard to obtain further evidence and we are keeping an open mind as to the circumstances of the death at this very early stage, which we are treating as an isolated incident.“All four people were arrested at the scene of the incident and have been released on bail.“While we fully understand that speculation into the nature of this incident is likely to take place, we’d ask people to follow this page for factual, accurate updates as our investigation unfolds and to avoid sharing unconfirmed and speculative claims online.”A spokesperson for West Midlands ambulance service said: “We were called to reports of a medical emergency near to Strawberry Lane at 8.39am on Saturday. Two ambulances, two paramedic officers and a helicopter from the Midlands air ambulance charity attended the scene.“On arrival we discovered one patient, a female child. Ambulance staff immediately began administering advanced life support but sadly, despite their best efforts it became apparent nothing could be done to save her and she was confirmed dead at the scene.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump administration attacks UK plans to boost traditional media on social platforms | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: US embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: US embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’
Content: The US government warned the proposals could ‘establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content’.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe US government warned the proposals could ‘establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content’.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump administrationTrump administration attacks UK plans to boost traditional media on social platformsUS embassy says Downing Street’s plan to give BBC, ITV and other established media more online visibility carries risk of ‘censorship’Michael SavageMedia editorMon 7 Sep 2026 10.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTrump administrationhas raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force YouTube and other digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.In a pointed intervention, the US government said the proposals toboost traditional media outlets in social media algorithmscould “establish a template that authoritarian regimes could invoke to justify more control over online content”.It also warned it could undermine “independent journalists” and amount to “extraterritorial censorship of protected speech by Americans online”.The statement,made viathe US embassy in London, raises the stakes in the plans to give the likes of the BBC, ITV and other established media more visibility on increasingly dominant digital platforms.Ministers, regulators and public service broadcasters have suggested new rules are needed to counter growing misinformation online as people increasingly turn to less regulated online platforms such as X,YouTubeand TikTok.In a consultation this year, the UK government said it would consider legislating should the platforms not act to prioritise trustworthy content. However, Washington claimed such a plan risked effectively removing the content of “independent journalists” over established outlets.“Preserving a free, open internet and protecting freedom of expression online are top priorities for the Trump administration,” it said. “A framework that empowers governments to influence which sources receive preferential visibility risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship.“If the UK compels platforms to boost government-preferred media in algorithmic feeds, the effect on a government-disfavoured speaker or media source’s reach is not meaningfully different than outright removal. The US government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship.”The administration has asked what safeguards will be in place to ensure “any biases and preferences of UK government officials and third-party organisations” do not influence the plan in ways that disadvantage “independent or minority-viewpoint journalism”.A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said: “We welcome engagement and responses to our media green paper. We believe strongly in free expression and fair competition, and any action we take will ensure these are protected.”Insiders say any measures would only affect the UK. The US complaint highlights its readiness to fight for the largely US-based tech companies that run the world’s largest digital platforms.Get in touchContact Michael Savage about this storyIf you have something to share about this story you can contact Michael using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailmichael.savage@theguardian.com.Messaging appsYou can message Michael using the Signal Messenger app. Use the ‘find by username’ option and type ‘michaelsavage.01’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreDonald Trump also has a long record of attacking and bypassing the established media, regularly accusing major outlets of “fake news” and biased coverage. He often tries to reach supporters online.The US president is still engaged in hislawsuitwith the BBC over an episode of Panorama in which it spliced together one of his speeches. The BBC has apologised for the edit, but stated the show did not defame Trump.Social media companies have previously been sceptical about artificially boosting the prominence of traditional media, arguing that it goes against the principle of creator content.Online content creators have compared the proposals to state control and fear their content would be pushed down the rankings as a result.Simon Squibb, a UK YouTube creator, said he was encouraged that his concerns were shared by an “entity that I think politicians will listen to”.“This is a very dangerous potential direction for the UK to go in,” he said. “I’m happy that the USA has stepped in.”Supporters of the enforced prominence plans have couched them as a way of dealing with misinformation and preserving culturally British content.However, the government has also been clear that it wants to help public service broadcasters survive the economic turmoil created by the rise of digital platforms, which all media companies are confronting.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationDigital mediaSocial mediaYouTubeBBCITV plcTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Joey Barton to remain in custody until trial after bail application turned down | Joey Barton | The Guardian
description: The former footballer stands accused of causing grievous bodily harm with intent, with his trial now pushed back to March next year
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The former footballer stands accused of causing grievous bodily harm with intent, with his trial now pushed back to March next year
Content: Joey Barton has had a renewed bail application refused.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenJoey Barton has had a renewed bail application refused.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAJoey BartonJoey Barton to remain in custody until trial after bail application turned downFormer footballer accused of attack outside golf clubHis trial has been pushed back to March next yearPress AssociationMon 7 Sep 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 13.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former footballerJoey Bartonwill remain in custody until his trial next year after a bail application was refused.The 44-year-old had been due to stand trial at Liverpool crown court last weekaccused of causing grievous bodily harm with intentto Kevin Lynch, 51, at Fairway, Huyton, on 8 March. But on Wednesday the case was adjourned and put back to March next year.Barton, wearing a grey zip-up fleece, appeared over video link from HMP Liverpool at a hearing on Monday, when the judge David Potter refused a renewed bail application. Barton nodded as the judge remanded him in custody in advance of a pre-trial hearing on 11 December.His trial will take place exactly a year after the alleged assault, meaning the defendant, who was arrested shortly after the incident, will have spent 12 months on remand.Barton is accused of carrying out the attack on Lynch after they had been drinking together at Huyton and Prescot golf club. Lynch, a former non-league football manager and founder of the special education school NexGen Academy, was said to have sustained serious injuries to an eye.Barton, the former Manchester City and QPR midfielder, of Widnes, Cheshire, won one England cap and also played for Newcastle, Rangers, Burnley and Marseille. After stopping playing he moved into coaching and had managerial spells at Fleetwood and Bristol Rovers.Explore more on these topicsJoey BartonnewsShareReuse this content

title: French winemakers forecast 30-year low harvest after severe drought and heat | France | The Guardian
description: Estimates suggest drop in production with vineyards also concerned ‘smoke taint’ from wildfires may affect quality
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Estimates suggest drop in production with vineyards also concerned ‘smoke taint’ from wildfires may affect quality
Content: The extreme heat of the summer weather in France has caused grapes to wilt and be scalded.Photograph: sportpoint/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe extreme heat of the summer weather in France has caused grapes to wilt and be scalded.Photograph: sportpoint/AlamyFranceFrench winemakers forecast 30-year low harvest after severe drought and heatEstimates suggest drop in production with vineyards also concerned ‘smoke taint’ from wildfires may affect qualityKim Willsherin ParisMon 7 Sep 2026 11.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench vineyards hit by severe drought and heatwaves are expected to report a 30-year low in wine production after the country’s hottest ever recorded summer, according to the agriculture ministry.Initial estimates suggest winemakers will produce just under 34m hectolitres from this year’s harvest: a drop of 6% on last year, and 17% less than ‌the 2021-2025 average.Agreste, the government’s farming food, forestry and fishing statistics body, said the drop was partly caused by a reduction in the number and size of vineyards, but mostly the result ofextreme weather conditions.“The summer was particularly hot and dry: soil drought has intensified throughout the country and heatwaves have caused localised sun scald, scorching, defoliation, and wilting of the grapes, reducing harvest volumes,” it reported.View image in fullscreenA grape picker gets to work at the Trois Terres vineyard in Octon, southern France earlier this month.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPAHowever, some winemakers say with grape harvests still being conducted it is too early to make credible predictions.The disappointing forecast comes after an optimistic start to the year, with heavy spring rains that encouraged grape growth. “The hot and dry summer conditions meant a deterioration of the [harvest] forecast,” Agreste reported.A series of heatwaves brought thehighest summer temperatures recorded in Francesince records began in 1900, with averages of 24C in June, July and August. Almost half of the country recorded temperatures on or above 40C.Among the worst hit wine regions is Champagne where the grape harvest, which started unusually early in mid August, is predicted to be almost half that of last year. The Jura region in the east was the next worst hit with an estimated 37% loss. This year’s Burgundy-Beaujolais region grape production was expected to be one-third down, Agreste reported.Winemakers in Bordeaux and the Languedoc-Roussillon as well as those in the south-east and south-west reported higher harvests this year but all except the Savoie region were down on the 2021-2025 five-year average for production.However, Cécile Mathiaud of the Burgundy wine producers association said she was surprised by the government’s disastrous figures for her region’s vineyards.“We know we won’t have a full harvest this year, but we have no definite figures and there’s no suggestion the situation is a disaster,” Mathiaud said. “We have some vineyards that have reported not much this year and others where it has been higher than expected.”View image in fullscreenThe harvest under way early in the morning at Trois Terres.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPASome Burgundy vineyards began their harvest in early August but others are collecting the grapes now, she added. “Our reference is the historically low harvest of 2021 when we produced only 1m hectolitres; we think it will be higher this year, but the question is by how much? I have absolutely no idea how the ministry has come up with these figures.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAgreste said the figures were estimates and definitive results would not be known until regions made official harvest declarations later this year. It added that 2026 grape harvests were “marked by significant regional disparities”.Heatwaves and wildfires are setting back air quality improvements, UN findsRead moreWine harvests have traditionally taken place inFrancebetween September and mid October, but the climate emergency has brought dates forward slightly each year for the last four decades. This year, the harvest timetable advanced at least a week compared with last year throughout the country. Some vineyards in Bordeaux began two weeks early.There are also concerns that vines and grapes in some of France’s best-known wine producing regions, including Bordeaux, have been damaged by smoke from rampant wildfires. No major Bordeaux vineyards suffered direct damage from the flames that came within 15km (9 miles) of the city, but there is concern that smoke has entered the grape skins causing “smoke taint” and affecting the taste of the finished wine.The agriculture ministry would normally issue harvest estimates in early August, but postponed its analysis at the request of the wine industry because of what it described as “the high level of uncertainty surrounding these forecasts” caused by weather conditions and wildfires.France’s wine sector is already under pressure owing to a decline in demand. Annual wine consumption in the 1960s in France was 127 litres each year compared with 40 litres a year now.Wine drinking in the US, France’s largest export market, has also dropped and French wines have been hit by Donald Trump’s tariffs.Explore more on these topicsFranceExtreme heatEuropeWineFarmingClimate crisisFood & drink industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Glowworms shine again in North Yorkshire after larvae reared in garden shed | Insects | The Guardian
description: Volunteer ‘glow-getters’ overseeing reintroduction of endangered beetles at Nosterfield nature reserve
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Volunteer ‘glow-getters’ overseeing reintroduction of endangered beetles at Nosterfield nature reserve
Content: The much-celebrated beetles and their ‘love torches’ have vanished from the British countryside.Photograph: blickwinkel/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe much-celebrated beetles and their ‘love torches’ have vanished from the British countryside.Photograph: blickwinkel/AlamyInsectsGlowworms shine again in North Yorkshire after larvae reared in garden shedVolunteer ‘glow-getters’ overseeing reintroduction of endangered beetles at Nosterfield nature reservePatrick BarkhamMon 7 Sep 2026 06.49 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bioluminescent beams of “fairy folk” are shining again from a nature reserve inNorth Yorkshirefor the first time in a century after the successful reintroduction of endangered glowworms.Female glowworms were spotted over multiple weeks atNosterfield nature reservethis summer following a no-frills, almost zero-budget reintroduction of the much-loved invertebrates, which have vanished from the British countryside in recent decades and are notoriously difficult to re-establish.The reintroduction by volunteer “glow-getters” and the independent ecologistPete Cooperinvolved the authorised collecting of a small number of glowworms from a local donor site, breeding them in captivity and rearing hundreds of snail-eating glowworm larvae in a garden shed in Bristol.View image in fullscreenPete Cooper counting glowworm larvae before their release.Photograph: Pete CooperLarvae were transported north and first released at Nosterfield in 2024 but becauseglowwormstake two years to reach the adult stage of their life cycle – where the flightless female glows to attract feeble-flying, beamless males – it was not until this summer that the first signs of success emerged.Volunteers for theLower Ure Conservation Trustcounted up to 12 glowing females over successive weeks this summer, which was a “huge relief” for Cooper, who has spent six years mastering the complexities of breeding and releasing glowworms.“It’s a really great first indicator of initial success,” said Cooper, who gave his time to the project for free. “We know that glowworms can live out their full life cycle at this site – there is great food and plenty of mating opportunity, and it makes all that time and effort worthwhile.”Cooper is developing formal standards and guidance for glowworm breeding and release, as well as appropriate habitat management to ensure sites are suitable for glowworms to thrive.A profusion of glowworms in 1909 washailed at Nosterfield by the writer Edmund Boggas “wont to hang out their fieldstar lamps … as if lit by the hands of fairy folk”.But here, as elsewhere across Britain, the much-celebrated beetles and their “love torches” – as Samuel Taylor Coleridge put it – have been extinguished because of more intensive farming, development, electric lights and the cult of tidiness which has removed the rough and varied grassland they require.View image in fullscreenCooper releasing month-old glowworm larvae at Nosterfield in 2024.Photograph: Amy-Jane BeerIn Nosterfield, quarrying led to the glowworm’s disappearance but, since 1997, when the Lower UreConservationTrust bought its first 72 acres of disused quarry, swaths of land have gradually returned to species-rich wetland and grassland on magnesian limestone. The charity will soon be managing nearly 600 acres of former quarry for wildlife, with booming bitterns and marsh harriers now making their home on the site.Simon Warwick, the director of the conservation trust, said the project was a credit to “the raw passion and enthusiasm” of Cooper and his willingness to freely volunteer his time, as well as the 80 volunteers at the nature reserve who had tweaked habitat management for the glowworms and monitored their emergence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenGlowworm larvae released at Nosterfield in September 2024.Photograph: Amy-Jane Beer“We are very fortunate to have a lot of really knowledgable volunteers alongside our brilliant staff who are managing the land that allows the glowworms to re-establish itself in this landscape after an absence of more than 100 years,” said Warwick. “They are incredibly rare in the region and I can’t tell you how excited the volunteers have been about it.”This year, helped by glow-getter volunteers atWestbury Wildlife Park Foundation, Cooper has bred another 1,900 glowworm larvae which will be released at Nosterfield later this year.According to Cooper, they will not be certain that the reserve has a self-sustaining population of glowworms until 2030, when the offspring of this year’s wild adult glowworms will reach maturity and shine their lights.View image in fullscreen‘As if lit by the hands of fairy folk’: a 19th-century illustration of glowworms.Photograph: 19th era 2/AlamyCeilidhsfor wildlife organised by Cooper and friends have raised enough money to upgrade the breeding facilities at Westbury to ensure it is easier to captive-breed more glowworms, with growing interest from other conservation groups in glowworm translocations and reintroductions. TheUK glowworm surveyis also helping by collecting sightings of glowworms nationally to help conservationists assess where translocations would be helpful and where hidden populations of glowworms may still endure.“It will be wonderful to see this project grow bigger than me,” said Cooper.Explore more on these topicsInsectsEndangered speciesAnimalsConservationNorth YorkshireInvertebratesWildlifeShareReuse this content

title: Heatwaves and wildfires are setting back air quality improvements, UN finds | Air pollution | The Guardian
description: WMO report details extreme weather events causing climatic feedback loop with serious health consequences
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: WMO report details extreme weather events causing climatic feedback loop with serious health consequences
Content: A wildfire burning near the coast of Syracuse in Sicily, Italy, toward the end of last month.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/ReutersView image in fullscreenA wildfire burning near the coast of Syracuse in Sicily, Italy, toward the end of last month.Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/ReutersAir pollutionHeatwaves and wildfires are setting back air quality improvements, UN findsWMO report details extreme weather events causing climatic feedback loop with serious health consequencesDamien GayleMon 7 Sep 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 09.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBig increases in wildfires and heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis are hindering improvements to air quality around the world, UN experts have said.Regions that had recorded a fall in pollution emitted by cars and industrial sites are facing new threats to air quality because of exposure to smoke from wildfires, according to a new report, while rising temperatures caused by intense heatwaves are causing a surge in ground-level ozone.In turn, thepollution generated by these climate-linked eventsis itself contributing to climate breakdown, creating a feedback loop that risks dragging the world deeper into environmental catastrophe.“Air quality and climate cannot be treated as separate subjects; they are deeply intertwined and have to be treated together,” said Lorenzo Labrador, a scientific officer of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), which issued thereport.View image in fullscreenThick haze from expanding wildfires engulfs Palembang in South Sumatra.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAThe WMO publishes its air quality and climate bulletin annually, to coincide with the UN’s international day for clean air. Among its key findings was that extreme wildfires are increasing, leading to serious health consequences because of the toxicity of the smoke they are emitting.This trend, “driven by a feedback loop between climate change and fire-conducive weather conditions”, was leading to an “urgent and growing public health threat”. As well as carrying high concentrations of fine particulate matter, smoke from wildfires causes oxidative stress in people’s bodies.“Systematic reviews and experimental studies consistently link wildfire smoke exposure to increased asthma attacks, hospitalisations for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), spiked respiratory medication use, as well as impacts on mental health and birth outcomes,” the report said. According to one study cited, a tripling of wildfires since the 1990s had contributed to almost 100,000 deaths a year between 2010 and 2018.The report also raises the alarm about ground-level ozone pollution, which is exacerbated by the kinds of intense and prolonged heatwaves that have affected Europe over this past summer.“Ozone is a very powerful oxidant,” Labradorsaid. “So once it gets to the lung, it essentially oxidises lung tissue and causes inflammation and circulatory problems, and eventually heart problems.” In heavily polluted regions, roughly one in five deaths from COPD is now attributed to long-term exposure to ozone, the report said.View image in fullscreenThe Ross fire in Palo Pinto, Texas is yet to be fully extinguished after it started late last month.Photograph: Elías Valverde II/The Dallas Morning News/APEvery year the WMO includes in the report anomalies in the concentrations of fine particulate matter, referred to as PM2.5. These microscopic particles and droplets, smaller than 2.5µm suspended in the air, are a severe health hazard because they can penetrate deep into people’s lungs and bloodstream. But they also pose a significant risk to the climate.PM2.5 is emitted by fossil fuel-driven industrial activities, farming, domestic heating and transport, as well as by wildfires and dust storms. The combination of particulates and air is called aerosol. Once airborne, atmospheric aerosol can affect the Earth’s climate by modifying the properties, lifetime and brightness of clouds, affecting how they impact the planet’s climate, the report explains.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLondon’s low emission zone is working – so why are cities around the world so cautious about clean air?Read moreEventually, those particles will settle back to earth, and there they also have an impact on the climate. One example is the deposition of black carbon – or soot – on snow and ice. When such particles deposit on ice they darken the surfaces and stop it reflecting light back into space, further accelerating global heating.The report explains that this process leads to a positive feedback loop: “Increasing aridity and land-use change are expected to enhance aerosol emissions, creating a powerful climate feedback loop where a warming climate increases fires and dust emissions, which enhances deposition on snow and ice surfaces, which in turn accelerates melt, thereby ultimately reinforcing warming.”The WMO’s message was that climate and air quality must be tackled together, Labrador emphasised. “Which is not terribly hard because if you abate emissions of greenhouse gases, you are at the same time reducing emissions of air quality degrading substances,” he said.“And that leads me to the best solution that there is, which is a general abatement of global greenhouse gas emissions and fossil fuel burning.”Explore more on these topicsAir pollutionClimate crisisUnited NationsWildfiresFossil fuelsExtreme heatnewsShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: A dreadful den of murder and thievery – or is it? | Rural affairs | The Guardian
description: Lynchat, Spey Valley: So many stories fill the iron age Raitts Cave, from wild legend to the more quotidian truth of its history
Author: Merryn Glover
Headline: Lynchat, Spey Valley: So many stories fill the iron age Raitts Cave, from wild legend to the more quotidian truth of its history
Content: Raitts Cave ‘speaks of darkness, secrets, treasures and escapees’.Photograph: Merryn GloverView image in fullscreenRaitts Cave ‘speaks of darkness, secrets, treasures and escapees’.Photograph: Merryn GloverCountry diaryRural affairsCountry diary: A dreadful den of murder and thievery – or is it?Lynchat, Spey Valley:So many stories fill the iron age Raitts Cave, from wild legend to the more quotidian truth of its historyMerryn GloverMon 7 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 00.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe word “cave” is full of possibility. It speaks of darkness, secrets, treasures and escapees, all of which can be found in the stories of Raitts Cave, which lies in a field near the hamlet of Lynchat, Inverness-shire.Its Gaelic name is An Uaimh Mhor, “the great cave”, and one legend claims it was built by giants, the females hollowing out the earth and carrying the soil in their aprons to dump in the River Spey, while the males cut its massive stone slabs from the hills above. Because, in fact, it is not a natural cave, but a subterranean passage, shaped like a horseshoe and lined with stone.View image in fullscreenA subterranean passage, lined with stone…Photograph: Merryn GloverAnother tale attributes it to the 11 strapping sons of a local freebooter from the powerful 13th-centuryClan Cumming(or MacNiven), who used it to stash their loot and hide from the law (or the laird, who tricked them by disguising himself as a beggar). Justice, or vengeance, eventually caught up with them, and the brothers were hauled out and executed at the cave’s entrance.Or, it could have been the hiding place of escaping Jacobites after Culloden, who were burned alive inside. Or indeed a shelter for persecuted worshippers.The identities of the builders, the hiders and the avengers and their various fates change with each version of the story, but the evidence is scant. Officially, archaeologists first excavated the site in 1835, and called it an erd house – “earth shelter” – and later asouterrain, an underground space constructed by humans. At some point, the central roof was removed, giving access to steps and a narrow tunnel on one side, and a large covered chamber at the other.View image in fullscreenThe cave is in a field near the tiny hamlet of Lynchat.Photograph: Merryn GloverFurther digs have dated it to the late iron age (100-400 AD) and the conclusion is that it was a storeroom, probably for food, serving a roundhouse above. Bother. What about all the magic and calamity? I hearten myself that the academic’s mundane deductions do not rule out other thrilling escapades, and I explore the cave in the vivid company of giantesses, thieves, fugitives and murderers – who are, of course, much more fun in folklore than reality.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsRural affairsCountry diaryArchaeologyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Grindr pays £26m to settle UK lawsuit over allegedly sharing users’ HIV status | Technology sector | The Guardian
description: US-owned dating app allegedly allowed ad firms access to private information in breach of UK law
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: US-owned dating app allegedly allowed ad firms access to private information in breach of UK law
Content: Twelve-thousand people signed up to the action against Grindr filed by law firm Austen Hays.Photograph: Aly Song/ReutersView image in fullscreenTwelve-thousand people signed up to the action against Grindr filed by law firm Austen Hays.Photograph: Aly Song/ReutersTechnology sectorGrindr pays £26m to settle UK lawsuit over allegedly sharing users’ HIV statusUS-owned dating app allegedly allowed ad firms access to private information in breach of UK lawJulia KolleweMon 7 Sep 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrindr will pay £26m to settle a lawsuit brought by thousands of users in the UK who allege that the US dating app shared highly sensitive personal information, including in some cases their HIV status, with advertising companies.The settlement brings to an end a two-year legal battle, afterthe UK law firm Austen Hays filed a claimat the high court of England and Wales in April 2024 on behalf of Grindr users alleging violations of UK privacy laws during a period up to early 2020.The London law firm represented 12,000 people, who will receive an average compensation of £2,167 each, if the £26m is equally distributed.Grindrwas founded in 2009to make iteasier to coordinate hookups for gay men. It now claims to be the world’s largest dating app for gay, bi, trans and queer people, with nearly 15 million users around the world.Grindr said in aUS regulatory filingthat it had resolved the UK group action related to what it described as “historical data practices before 2020”, whenGrindr was owned and controlled by the Chinese gaming company Beijing Kunlun Tech.The California company said: “The settlement includes no findings or admission of liability. While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognises and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period.”As part of the UK settlement, Grindr agreed to pay £13m by the end of this year, and a further £13m by the end of March 2027.Six years ago, Grindr was sold to the investment group San Vicente Acquisition in a $608m deal and appointed new management, aftera US government national security panel raised concernsthat personal data of US users could be accessed and used by China’s government. In 2022,Grindr floated on the New York Stock Exchangethrough a merger with a Spac (special purpose acquisition company) in a deal that valuedthe appat $2.1bn (£1.55bn). It is now worth $2.65bn (£1.96bn).The company said in the filing that it had overhauled its privacy programme since 2020, “with a keen focus on the unique needs of its community”. It added that “Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control and responsible data practices”.Austen Hays’ parent firm, Gateley, said: “While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognises and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period.“We thank our clients for trusting us with this sensitive case.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGrindr, based in west Hollywood, announced in April 2018 it wouldstop sharing users’ HIV statuswith third-party companies after a report by Norwegian researchers revealed data sharing with two companies.In 2021 Norway’s data protection authorityfined Grindr65m Norwegian krone (£4.8m) – 10% of its global revenues – for violating data protection rules. GrindrappealedbutNorway’s court of appeal upheld the decision and finelast October.As Grindr shared its users’ personal data for advertising purposes, the court of appeal concluded that the company’s claim that it did “‘not sell your personal user information to third parties for advertising purposes’ is clearly misleading”.Explore more on these topicsTechnology sectorDatingAids and HIVHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oasis recordings up for auction despite band’s objections | Oasis | The Guardian
description: Guide price of archive documenting concerts, rehearsals, soundchecks and conversations between £1.2m and £1.6m
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Guide price of archive documenting concerts, rehearsals, soundchecks and conversations between £1.2m and £1.6m
Content: The archive includes recordings of candid conversations between Noel and Liam Gallagher.Photograph: Tiziana Fabi/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe archive includes recordings of candid conversations between Noel and Liam Gallagher.Photograph: Tiziana Fabi/AFP/Getty ImagesOasisOasis recordings up for auction despite band’s objectionsGuide price of archive documenting concerts, rehearsals, soundchecks and conversations between £1.2m and £1.6mNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 08.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn archive of more than 100 hours of Oasis recordings, including concerts, rehearsals and candid conversations between Noel andLiam Gallagher, is to be auctioned for up to £1.6m despite objections from the band.The collection was amassed by the band’s sound engineer Huw Richards, who worked withOasisfrom the release of their 1994 debut album, Definitely Maybe, until 2001. It comprises 209 DAT tapes, 73 analogue cassettes and three MiniDiscs, and is being sold by Richards’s son, Owain.Littleton Auctions in Evesham,Worcestershire, has given the archive a guide price of between £1.2m and £1.6m, with the sale due to take place on 3 October.Ben Homer, the auction house’s managing director, said Oasis had expressed concerns about the sale.View image in fullscreenLiam and Noel Gallagher at their Loch Lomond gig, 1996. The collection includes what is believed to be the only recording of this show.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian“The Oasis camp is aware of the auction and has expressed concerns, which is entirely understandable given the scale and significance of the material,” he said in a statement to the Guardian.Homer said the auction house was handling the sale through the appropriate legal process and the recordings were being offered with verified provenance. He said the archive would give collectors and institutions the opportunity to acquire material documenting an important period in British music.The collection includes what is believed to be the only recording of Oasis’s 1996 concert on the banks of Loch Lomond in Scotland. It also contains recordings of numerous rehearsals and soundchecks, as well as informal conversations involving the Gallagher brothers and members of the touring crew.Owain Richards, who is also a sound engineer, said he had previously been in discussions with Oasis’s management after the band sought some of the recordings.He told the Times those discussions had ultimately “fizzled away” and that the band wanted the tapes returned rather than sold elsewhere.Richards said his father had meticulously preserved the recordings, which date from a period when concertgoers were far less likely to make their own recordings on mobile phones. “It really is a piece of history,” he said.View image in fullscreenLiam (L) and Noel Gallagher at a press conference in London in August 1999.Photograph: Fiona Hanson/PARichards said the audio remained in sufficiently good condition to be mastered for a live album. The recordings cannot, however, simply be released by whoever buys them. Oasis retain the intellectual property rights, meaning the archive cannot be commercially exploited without the band’s cooperation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLittleton Auctions has described the collection as a significant record of the band’s live career and said it could be of interest to collectors, scholars and museums.The auction comes as interest in Oasis continues to grow since the band’s reunion last year, when Noel and Liam Gallagher returned to the stage together for the first time in 15 years.Oasis became one of the biggest British rock bands of the 1990s, with albums including (What’s the Story) Morning Glory? and Be Here Now. Their career was marked by the fractious relationship between the Gallagher brothers, whose arguments eventually contributed to the band’s split in 2009.The reunion saw Oasis play sold-out dates in Britain, North America, Australia and Asia. The brothers were also pictured together at the Venice film festival this weekend, whereOasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger, a film documenting their return, was premiered.The Littleton auction will also feature other Oasis memorabilia, including a pair of Adidas Kegler Super Ostrich trainers given toNoel Gallagher. Oasis were approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsOasisWorcestershirePop and rockLiam GallagherNoel GallaghernewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Mistrust’ of Palantir may affect NHS research, says health minister | Health | The Guardian
description: James Frith says patients may be less willing to share data as new figures show a rise in opt-outs
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: James Frith says patients may be less willing to share data as new figures show a rise in opt-outs
Content: Health workers protest outside the London headquarters of Palantir, in opposition to the company’s involvement with the NHS.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenHealth workers protest outside the London headquarters of Palantir, in opposition to the company’s involvement with the NHS.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAHealth‘Mistrust’ of Palantir may affect NHS research, says health ministerJames Frith says patients may be less willing to share data as new figures show a rise in opt-outsRobert BoothUK technology editorMon 7 Sep 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConcern is being raised about Palantir’s work with the NHS as new figures showed tens of thousands of patients have withdrawn their data from use in research projects.James Frith, the health innovation minister, said he was worried about “mistrust” of the US defence and health tech company and “the impact it could have on people’s willingness to share data with the NHS”.The government is deciding whether to axe the company’s £330m contract to operate the health service’s federated data platform, which is intended to improve efficiency and patient outcomes.Frith’s comment, in a letter toLayla Moran, the chair of the Commons health committee, follows a rise in patients opting out of allowing their medical data to be shared. In the two months from mid-May to mid-July, 60,000 more people withdrew their private information under a mechanism called the national data opt-out.Doctors and patients’ groups are calling for Labour to exercise a break clause in Palantir’s seven-year contract. They cite its work with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s ICE immigration agency and question the company’s claim to provide value for money.Palantir and its supporters say its AI-driven technology has cut NHS waiting lists for surgery. A spokesperson for the company said it was “helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 110,000 additional operations, a 15% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 6.8% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days”.NHS England has reported similar numbers butsaidit could not “draw conclusions about cause and effect”. The government’s statistics watchdog is investigating the data.Frith told Moran there had been an increase in NHS data opt-outs, in line with media interest in Palantir’s position.Palantir paid just £2m corporation tax in UK in 2024 despite lucrative public sector contractsRead morePalantir’s government contracts have been beset by controversy. Ministers apologised after it emerged that the company’s staff had access to identifiable patient data.London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, has also blocked the Metropolitan police from awarding Palantir a £50m contract to use its AI to support investigations. He said Londoners wanted to see public money paid only to companies that “share the values of our city”. Palantir issuingover the mayor’s decision.Frith said the rise in opt-outs was “modest” but would still be monitored. Opting out does not stop an individual’s records from being used for direct care, such as live operations. However, it prevents it being used for research and planning.Frith said: “It may not be possible to realise the benefits of the 10-year health plan if patients stop sharing their data.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFoxglove, a tech equity campaign, welcomed the minister’s acknowledgment of apparent public mistrust of Palantir. “Doctors and patients have been warning about the threat this poses to NHS care, and tens of thousands of people have opted out in just the last few months,” said Tom Hegarty, its head of communications.“People are right to be concerned given … its founder, Trump ally Peter Thiel, going on record to opine that the NHS makes people sick.”Frith indicated a policy shift on whether the Palantir-powered platform must be used by NHS trusts. In July, a health minister told parliament that health trusts would be told they “must use” parts of NHS England’s federated platform, which is controlled using Palantir technology. Now Frith has said “there is no requirement to use the FDP” and they may “prefer an alternative”.Moran, who is a Liberal Democrat MP, said she welcomed the “softened stance” on whether adoption of the FDP was mandatory but added: “We remain of the view that the government should switch provider and not extend the current contract. Given how long this process could take, ministers need to act decisively and quickly, and not put this decision off until February.”A spokesperson for the Department ofHealthand Social Care said: “There has been absolutely no change in position. The NHS federated data platform has never been mandatory and organisations have always been able to choose alternative solutions where they meet local needs.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
