Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsHealthNHSPalantirAI (artificial intelligence)Layla MoranSadiq KhannewsShareReuse this content

title: Plans for local government overhaul on hold after legal advice | Local government | The Guardian
description: Angela Rayner to announce review into local government shake-up as decisions on four areas withdrawn and 16 paused
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Angela Rayner to announce review into local government shake-up as decisions on four areas withdrawn and 16 paused
Content: The local government secretary, Angela Rayner, is expected to tell parliament review follows ‘updated and privileged legal advice’.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe local government secretary, Angela Rayner, is expected to tell parliament review follows ‘updated and privileged legal advice’.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersLocal governmentPlans for local government overhaul on hold after legal adviceAngela Rayner to announce review into local government shake-up as decisions on four areas withdrawn and 16 pausedPatrick ButlerSocial policy editorMon 7 Sep 2026 10.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlans for a large reorganisation of local government have been put on hold after the government received new legal advice that suggested they might not comply with the law.The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said the review was to ensure the process was robust and aligned with the new government’s aim to “rewire the state”, and followed “updated and privileged legal advice”.The reorganisation plans, announced in December 2024,proposed the abolition of the current two-tier systemof districts and counties in favour of a smaller number of unitary authorities – or “mega-councils” – covering large areas.At least eight councils had launched legal challenges or were considering doing so owing to opposition to the government’s choice of boundaries for new councils.Reform UK-led Kent county council is to consider a judicial review at a meeting on Tuesday after it did not receive a response from the government to a letter setting out concerns.Plans for reorganisation in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn in the light of new legal advice.Councils in Essexlaunched legal actionin June after it emerged that its own preferred option to create three unitary councils in the county was backed by senior government officials but rejected by the then communities secretary, Steve Reed.There has beenlittle appetite for theproposals within local government, with many councils regarding the changes as expensive and time-consuming, and offering little in the way of cost savings that would ease local authorities’ dire financial crisis.Decisions on 14 further areas will be reviewed and paused alongside the cases of Cambridgeshire-Peterborough and West Sussex, which are yet to have a decision confirmed.The government will also confirm that local elections in May 2027 will go ahead on existing council boundaries, saying it remains committed toeffective and sustainable local governmentand simplifying these structures.The communities secretary,Angela Rayner, told parliament on Monday: “As we are now more determined than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent, it’s only right that as a new secretary of state I make sure that everything we do is working towards that plan to change Britain, without delay.“The prime minister told the house last week he was ‘prepared to look at local government reorganisation’ and he asked me as his communities secretary to ‘do that’.“In that context, in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law.“And, secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister, and any additional considerations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I do not take this lightly. I recognise the huge amount of work that has already gone into progressing reorganisation in each of these areas and I am very grateful for it.”MHCLG said reorganisation in Surrey would not be affected by the review and the two new unitary authorities, East and West Surrey, would go live in April 2027.Cllr Sean Matthews, chair-elect of the County Councils Network, said: “Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed. For our councils that do want to proceed with reorganisation in their area, we will support them in their next steps and we will be seeking further clarity from government in the coming days.“With the government clearly listening to our concerns, we now stand ready to work with ministers. Where reorganisation is desired, this review must ensure a robust, legally compliant process in line with the original criteria. This should include establishing realistic implementation timescales and ensuring that any further decisions only create sustainable new unitary councils capable of improving local services.”Jonathan Carr-West, chief executive of the Local Government Information Unit (LGIU), said: “What began as the most ambitious change to local government in a generation now looks in danger of becoming a colossal white elephant – a huge drain on time, resources and goodwill. Those councils undergoing local government reorganisation have been trying to implement a massively complex project, under intense pressure and to very challenging timescales. Our overriding concern is that local government leaders, staff and councillors have strained every sinew to meet the deadlines set by MHCLG. Today’s announcement – whatever the reasons behind it – rides roughshod over 1,000s of hours of work.“If the prime minister is serious about his ambitions to rewire the state, then lessons must be learned from this debacle and learned fast.”Explore more on these topicsLocal governmentAngela RaynerLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border | Russia | The Guardian
description: Connection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in Ukraine
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Connection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in Ukraine
Content: Trucks drive along a road during a ceremony for the opening the first road bridge between Russia and North Korea across the Tumen River.Photograph: Oleg Kozhemyako/ReutersView image in fullscreenTrucks drive along a road during a ceremony for the opening the first road bridge between Russia and North Korea across the Tumen River.Photograph: Oleg Kozhemyako/ReutersRussiaRussia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared borderConnection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in UkrainePjotr SauerMon 7 Sep 2026 05.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia and North Korea have openedthe first road bridge across their shared border, in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine.The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang inNorth Korea, along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast.Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said.Russia and North Korea finalising first road crossing amid concerns it serves as Ukraine war supply routeRead moreThe road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group.View image in fullscreenA newly built bridge connects Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea.Photograph: Ministry of Transport of the Russian FederationAfter the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides.Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang.Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries.Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection.Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024.From ammunition to ballistic missiles: how North Korea arms Russia in the Ukraine warRead moreIn return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence.Russian and North Korean officials have alsotouted North Korea as a new holiday destinationsince the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then.Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow.During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”.Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company.At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region.During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war.“The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin.Explore more on these topicsRussiaNorth KoreaEuropeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alleged killers of Australian surfers and American friend go on trial in Mexico | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Three men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Three men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024
Content: Callum Robinson, 33, and his brother Jake, 30, from Perth, Australia, were camping in a remote beachside area when they were robbed and killed.Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGEView image in fullscreenCallum Robinson, 33, and his brother Jake, 30, from Perth, Australia, were camping in a remote beachside area when they were robbed and killed.Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGEMexicoAlleged killers of Australian surfers and American friend go on trial in MexicoThree men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024Agence France Press in EnsenadaMon 7 Sep 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe alleged killers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot in 2024 have gone on trial in the border resort where the three were murdered.The Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad wereshot dead after being robbed in Mexico’s violence-hit Baja California.They were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked. Their bodies were found hidden on a cliff.Tourist killings expose fragmentation of organised crime at the heart of Mexico’s extraordinary violenceRead moreThe Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the trial.“It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” Martin Robinson told reporters as he entered the court with his wife, Debra.“We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why,” he said.View image in fullscreenJake (left) and Callum (right) with their parents, Debra and Martin Robinson.Photograph: Callum and Jake Robinson FoundationThree men are on trial for homicide.The girlfriend of one of the accused wassentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery.The crime sparked outrage and sadness in Australia and the United States.Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad was killed a few months before he was due to marry.Other foreign tourists have previously been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.Two Australian surfers were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa.Their bodies were later burned.Explore more on these topicsMexicoWestern AustraliaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Giuliani says Mamdani should skip 9/11 ceremony during rant against Islam | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: New York City mayor confirms he will attend memorial service but declines to respond to Giuliani’s remarks
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: New York City mayor confirms he will attend memorial service but declines to respond to Giuliani’s remarks
Content: Rudy Giuliani was mayor of New York City from 1994 to 2001.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APView image in fullscreenRudy Giuliani was mayor of New York City from 1994 to 2001.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APSeptember 11 2001Giuliani says Mamdani should skip 9/11 ceremony during rant against IslamNew York City mayor confirms he will attend memorial service but declines to respond to Giuliani’s remarksEdward Helmorein New YorkMon 7 Sep 2026 16.25 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 16.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew York mayorZohran Mamdaniis set to come face-to-face withRudy Giulianiat the main September 11 memorial service, just days after the former mayor – who led the city at the time of the2001 terrorist attacks– disparaged his Muslim religion and said he should skip the ceremony.In an interview with right-leaning Newsmax at the weekend, Giulianisaid: “Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he’s coming.”Mamdani confirmed on Monday, while attending a breakfast celebrating New York’s J’ouvert and West Indian Day Paradecelebrationsin Brooklyn, that he would attend the main ceremony and multiple 9/11 events on Friday, to stand with the families of those who died and first responders – as he did last year before taking office.“I’m proud to be the mayor of this city. I love this city. I love this country,” he said. “What I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11, and a focus also on the first responders who did everything they could.”The mayor and his office have declined to respond to Giuliani’s remarks.Giuliani, the former mayor and a close ally of Donald Trump, has said he will also attend this year’s ceremony to mark the attacks by terrorists representingal-Qaida, who flew hijacked passenger planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan on September 11 2001.Reflecting pools with waterfalls constructed on the footprints of the towers and a 9/11 museum now mark the site that was dubbed Ground Zero in the aftermath of the attacks, and where each year the names of the almost 3,000 people who died are read out by survivors and loved ones, in a solemn ceremony attended by national and local leaders.In the interview with Newsmax, Giuliani was asked if Mamdani should skip the ceremony. “Well, there’s no question he should,” he said.Giuliani was mayor ofNew YorkCity from 1994 to 2001. He ran unsuccessfully for president and, more recently, has been an attorney to and a staunch ally of Donald Trump.In the convoluted tirade on air on Saturday, Giuliani threw insults and baseless comparisons. He appeared to draw parallels between Mamdani’s faith and the 9/11 hijackers acting on the extremist orders ofOsama bin Laden, the jihadist militant and terrorist leader killed by US forces during the Obama administration.He remarked that the terrorists brought their ideological opposition to the United States “in the name of the Muslim religion” and “weren’t hiding it like Mamdani is trying to hide it”. He also declared the opinion that the mayor supports a notion that Islam should be the dominant religion.Mamdani has previously spoken about how an Islamophobic backlash built after the 2001 attacks and had made anti-Muslim prejudice “a fact of life” for Muslim Americans. “It was this horrific day that was also, for many New Yorkers, the moment at which they were marked an ‘other’,”he told the New York Times last year.Last week, Mamdani issued an executive order designating 9/11 an annual official “Day of Remembrance and Service” that requires the city administration to designate a moment of silence to mourn those who were killed and affected by the attacks. A second order established a new taskforce to help the city’s emergency preparedness.Several other high-profile figures, including former New York governor George Pataki, have voiced opposition to Mamdani’s attendance at the ceremony, and an online petition arguing the same has gathered close to 100,000 signatures.Dignitaries expected to attend Friday’s commemorations include former US presidents Bill Clinton, George W Bush and Barack Obama, and some other former mayors of New York.The White House has said Donald Trump is not attending but is expected to commemorate the9/11attack on the Pentagon at that site close to Washington DC, a decision that also has also drawn criticism.US vice-president JD Vance is expected to represent the White House in New York.Explore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001Rudy GiulianiZohran MamdaniNew YorkUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Republican midterm convention will be ‘Trumpist pageantry’ – at the party’s own risk | Republicans | The Guardian
description: A historically unpopular president will take centre stage as the party seeks to sway voters with an unprecedented event
Author: David Smith
Headline: A historically unpopular president will take centre stage as the party seeks to sway voters with an unprecedented event
Content: Donald Trump speaks during an ‘End of Summer BBQ’ with Republican lawmakers in the Rose Garden at the White House on 2 September in Washington DC.Photograph: Abaca/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaks during an ‘End of Summer BBQ’ with Republican lawmakers in the Rose Garden at the White House on 2 September in Washington DC.Photograph: Abaca/ShutterstockRepublicansRepublican midterm convention will be ‘Trumpist pageantry’ – at the party’s own riskA historically unpopular president will take centre stage as the party seeks to sway voters with an unprecedented eventDavid Smithin WashingtonMon 7 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt seemed like a good idea at the time. In December 1978, Jimmy Carter, a US president besieged by inflation and energy crises, watched as thousands of Democrats descended on Memphis, Tennessee, for arare midterm convention.“It was wild,” recallsElaine Kamarck, who attended as a 28-year-old working for the Democratic National Committee.“It became a forum for Ted Kennedy to informally announce his opposition to President Carter. There was a lot of hostility to the president there. The Democrats have sworn ever since never to do anything this stupid again.”The 1978 convention took placeaftermidterm elections in which Democrats suffered losses but still maintained control of the House of Representatives and Senate. The party also held midterm conventions in1974and1982. Kamarck, who later served in the Bill Clinton administration, adds: “The Democratic party has never thought of doing this again and, whenever it has, people like me say, ‘No, are you absolutely crazy?’”Trump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited love | Sidney BlumenthalRead moreRepublicans, however, did not get the memo. This week in Dallas, Texas, the party will stage a midterm convention for the first time.Donald Trumpwill deliver a keynote address on Wednesday and closing remarks on Thursday. Other speakers include Vice-President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr and the president’s son Donald Trump Jr. The convention has been billed as a “primetime showcase” to boost morale, nationalise congressional elections and galvanise Republican voters.But success is far from guaranteed. The made-for-TV spectacleclashes directlywith the two opening games of the American football season.A Politico website surveyof more than 70 Republican candidates and members found 45 who either do not plan to go to Dallas or are still thinking about it. Some cited prior commitments while others balked at the $25,000 price of attending.Unlike conventions in a presidential election year, delegates will not be making party rules or drawing up a policy platform. “This is essentially a Trump rally that they’re calling a midterm convention,” said Kamarck, now a senior fellow in governance studies at theBrookings Institution thinktankin Washington. “They’re trying to get enthusiasm among their base because that’s what they need for November.Basically, this is a Trump show.”That ambition probably made sense when the midterm convention was first mooted. Republican voters are historically slow to turn out when Trump is not on the ballot. By putting himself on the marquee, the president – who defied the odds to win the White House in 2024 – is hoping to narrow the enthusiasm gap.Among those hoping for a boost from Trump in Texas is Senate candidate Ken Paxton, whosehistory of scandals– including an affair and securities-fraud indictment – could prove costly against the Democratic rising star James Talarico.But now it appears the plan could backfire. Trump’sapproval ratingis ‌at 33%, the lowest point of his political career, according to aReuters/Ipsos polllast week. Democrats seem more fired up about the midterms with 46% describing themselves as “very enthusiastic” ​about voting in November, compared with 31% of Republicans.double quotation markOn every issue that Trump was once strong on he is underwater, from the economy to immigrationTara SetmayerTara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, warns that building a midterm convention around a failing president is tantamount to “political suicide”.“It is an incredibly risky strategy for any Republican at this point to hitch his wagon to Donald Trump,” she explained. “On every issue that Trump was once strong on he is underwater, from the economy to immigration.”Setmayer, co-founder of the political action committee the Seneca Project, added: “The idea that he’s going to excite people is flawed at this point, given the polling numbers in Donald Trump’s own constituency. They’re not inspired and this vanity convention is not going to change that with 60 days to go to the election. If anything, it’s going to remind people of how dissatisfied they are under Donald Trump’s second term.”There are further signs that the president could be more of a curse than a blessing. Some candidates are quietly scrubbing his likeness from their websites in a tactical retreat. In Texas, candidateCarlos De La Cruzreplaced “TRUMP CONSERVATIVE” with “PROVEN CONSERVATIVE” on his homepage, erasing a line about being “ready to be President Trump’s wingman in Congress” for a platitude about “servant leaders”.In Kentucky,Ralph Alvaradopivoted to “INDEPENDENT LEADERSHIP”. In Nevada, Martin O’Donnell, a music composer best known for his work on the Halo video game series, no longer features his Trump endorsement photo on his website. In south Texas, Eric Flores replaced “SUPPORT PRESIDENT TRUMP’S AGENDA” with “LOWER THE COST OF LIVING”. In Alaska, Nick Begich edited his homepage to a simple: “We have delivered for Alaska.”double quotation markHe only cares about two things: one, that he won’t be investigated and two, that he can get his appointments through the SenateAllan LichtmanElsewhere, candidates are actively breaking ranks. The Wisconsin congressman and gubernatorial candidateTom Tiffanypublicly rebuked Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as “Lake America” and opposed importing cheaper ground beef. The Michigan congressman Tom Barrett is campaigning on his votes to limit Trump’s war in Iran, highlighting his support for the War Powers Resolution.Trump, however, appears unmoved and indifferent.Allan Lichtman, a history professor at American University in Washington, said: “He doesn’t care about any of these other candidates. He only cares about two things when it comes to the midterms: one, that he won’t be investigated and two, that he can get his appointments through the Senate. He demands loyalty for everyone else and gives loyalty to no one.”A Republican source said at least 100 members of Congress were expected to attend the convention and more than 20,000 tickets had been distributed, ensuring a packed arena.The source denied that Trump would dominate proceedings, insisting that the convention would aim to “energise our base, inform folks there is an election and highlight the contrast between whatRepublicansare offering – which is a secure border, safe communities, cutting taxes, giving Americans more freedom – and what the Democrats are offering, which is reopening the borders, repealing the tax cuts, investigating, obstructing, impeaching President Trump and not having an agenda beyond that”.The source also rejected reports that Republican candidates were distancing themselves from the president, saying: “We have Republican candidates across the country who want the president in their districts. You see it with Mike Lawler, who’s one of two Republicans left in Congress still in a district that Kamala Harris won in 2024. I believe the president has campaigned for him in his district twice. Mike Lawler does a very good job of embracing the president’s policies. He deviates on certain issues when needed.”The convention schedule will also aim to steady the ship. The first night will include segments focused on tax cuts, healthcare affordability, the border, trade and domestic manufacturing, with appearances by “workers and everyday Americans”.The second will highlight families benefiting from policies like no taxes on tips, overtime and social security, as well as overseas prisoners who have been released, border security, efforts to lower prescription drug costs and a tribute to theslain rightwing activist Charlie Kirk.The convention will also try to appeal to the “Maha” – or Make America healthy again – wing of the party, with a segment targeting corporate influence in the treatment of chronic diseases. And it will mark the 25th anniversary of theSeptember 11 terrorist attackswith families of first responders.But the program makes no mention of any programming related to foreign policy or thedeeply unpopular war in Iran.Lichtman observed: “People aren’t buying what they have to say, which is things are getting better, it’s the golden age, prices are coming down, we’re winning the Iranian war, our immigration policy is great. They’re not gonna buy it just because it’s a convention. Plus, as we know, Trump always goes off script and that’s never helpful to his party.”double quotation markThe big question is, who is going to be paying any attention to this? Who is going to be watching this other than the hardcore base?Charlie SykesBut Republicans do seem to believe they have an ace up their sleeves. Trump and his allies are expected to go in hard on a theme pointing to the primary election successes of democratic socialists and casting Democrats asgodless communists and Marxistswho pose an existential threat to the American way of life.Charlie Sykes, a conservative broadcaster and author of How the Right Lost Its Mind, said: “The midterms will either be a referendum on Donald Trump, in which case they will be disastrous for the Republicans, or Republicans will hope that they can make this a referendum on the radicalism of Democrats, so I’m guessing that will be a major theme.“The big question is, who is going to be paying any attention to this? Who is going to be watching this other than the hardcore base, the already convinced? I have a very hard time imagining independent voters tuning in to see the Trumpist pageantry.”But commentators believe that the convention, with its potential to draw primetime TV viewers and generate viral clips, could make a difference in the margins.Larry Sabato, director of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, said: “It might increase Maga’s turnout. That’s the only positive in this thing potentially for Republicans.“It’s not going to change any minds but it might convince the Maga people, ‘Well, I don’t normally vote when our hero is not on the ballot but if this is what Donald wants me to do, I’m going to pitch in and help.’ But it’s not going to help that much.”The midterm convention could have an intriguing subplot. Along with Vance, the Texas senator Ted Cruz and other potential 2028 presidential contenders will be in attendance for what could be an early audition.Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center thinktank in Washington, said: “Anybody who looks in the mirror and sees a president looking back at him or her, if those people are speakers, it will be a chance for them to make an impression.”Such aspirants would be wise to tread carefully, however, since Trump is not likely to cede the limelight willingly. Sykes added: “It is a Trump-a-palooza and once again Donald Trump insists on being – what was the old phrase aboutTeddy Roosevelt? – the bride at every wedding and the corpse at every funeral.“He wants to make the midterms all about himself despite the fact that he’s reaching the Nixon line in terms of polling unpopularity. It’s very much on brand except that right now, with every day we get closer to the midterms, Trump’s narcissism becomes a greater challenge to Republicans who want to survive what looks like a blue wave.”Explore more on these topicsRepublicansDonald TrumpUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026featuresShareReuse this content

title: Next overturns equal pay ruling that raised basic wages for shop staff | Next | The Guardian
description: Retailer wins appeal against 2024 decision forcing it to pay shop workers the same as warehouse employees
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Retailer wins appeal against 2024 decision forcing it to pay shop workers the same as warehouse employees
Content: Next said it had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse staff because of recruitment and retention pressures.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNext said it had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse staff because of recruitment and retention pressures.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesNextNext overturns equal pay ruling that raised basic wages for shop staffRetailer wins appeal against 2024 decision forcing it to pay shop workers the same as warehouse employeesJulia KolleweMon 7 Sep 2026 08.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK retailerNexthas overturned a 2024 court ruling forcing it to pay its shop staff the same higher basic pay rates as its warehouse workers under equal pay rules.The chain, led by the Conservative peer Simon Wolfson, said it had “won a landmark victory in its ongoing equal pay litigation”. It has succeeded in its appeal to the employment appeal tribunal “on the key issue of basic pay”, it said.It comes two years after 3,540 claimantswon a six-year legal fight for equal pay, which the fashion and homeware retailer then appealed against. Shop workers accused Next of paying its retail sales staff – who are predominantly female – lower hourly wages than its warehouse workers, the majority of whom are male.Since that employment tribunal ruling in Leeds, several thousand more Next staff have brought equal pay claims, bringing the total number of claimants involved in the litigation to more than 6,400. Next employs more than 20,000 store staff across 458 stores in the UK and Ireland.Next said theappeal judgmentendorsed its position that it “should not have to pay shop assistants and warehouse operatives the same amount of basic pay, in circumstances where the market and working conditions are very different”.The retailer argued that it had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse staff because of recruitment and retention pressures, which it said did not apply to the workforce in its stores. It added: “Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense.”Get in touchContact the Guardian Business teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject you can contact the Business team confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Scroll down and click onSecure Messaging.When asked who you wish to contact please select the ‘Business (UK & Global)’ team.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreThe retailer said the judgment affirmed: “Employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so.”The law firm Leigh Day, which represents Next store workers, described it as a “mixed ruling” as it rejected Next’s challenge to the tribunal’s findings that it had failed to justify lower rates of night-time pay, overtime pay and the failure to provide paid rest breaks to store workers.Next also failed to persuade the employment appeal tribunal that lower Sunday premium payments to store workers were justified. The appeal tribunal held that the issue remains to be determined and should return to the employment tribunal.The Next case, which covered the period from 2012 and 2023, explained women made up almost 78% of retail sales jobs, while men made up about 53% of warehouse staff. During that time, some warehouse staff were able to earn between 38p and £3.13 more an hour than retail sales workers, according to Leigh Day.Elizabeth George, a partner at Leigh Day representing the claimants, said: “I am pleased that the employment appeal tribunal rejected Next’s arguments that its pay practices do not disadvantage women. They plainly do and the appeal tribunal firmly recognised that. I am also pleased that the tribunal upheld the findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.“The appeal tribunal’s conclusion on basic pay is disappointing. Next pays market rates in both its stores and its warehouses in order to recruit and retain staff. The market rate is higher in the predominantly male warehouse labour market, even though the work carried out in stores has already been found to be equal work.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“While the store staff and their legal team welcome many aspects of this appeal judgment, we respectfully disagree with this approach to justification. We remain confident in our clients’ position and intend to appeal.”Next had argued that the equal pay ruling created a threat to the viability of many of its stores, and that it put retailers operating their own warehouses at a “material disadvantage” to rivals that contract out their warehouse operations.The original employment tribunal and the appeal tribunal found that there was no direct discrimination. The employment tribunalfound: “It was all about cost. Gender did not enter into the equation” when Next set pay rates.Next said it had won the vast majority of the terms challenged in the equal pay litigation, including bonus pay to warehouse staff previously, and now basic pay. It intends to seek permission to appeal in relation to other terms.“This judgment has come at the right time, the UK economy desperately needs jobs and the loss of this appeal would have represented a hammer blow to retail employment in the UK,” the company said.Explore more on these topicsNextEmployment tribunalsRetail industryEmployment lawnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jaguar Land Rover confirms plan to cut 4,000 jobs over two years | Jaguar Land Rover | The Guardian
description: Decision by carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and fallout from cyber-attack, labelled a ‘body blow for workers’
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Decision by carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and fallout from cyber-attack, labelled a ‘body blow for workers’
Content: Jaguar Land Rover’s profits have tumbled.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJaguar Land Rover’s profits have tumbled.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesJaguar Land RoverJaguar Land Rover confirms plan to cut 4,000 jobs over two yearsDecision by carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and fallout from cyber-attack, labelled a ‘body blow for workers’Nils Pratley: Jonathan Reynolds is right, Jaguar Land Rover doesn’t warrant use of public moneyRob DaviesandAlex DanielMon 7 Sep 2026 09.43 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 05.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJaguar Land Rover has announced thousands of job cuts in a “body blow for workers” as it grapples with tough trading conditions, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a cyber-attack.Britain’s largest carmaker, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata, confirmed the anticipated cuts on Monday, saying it wants to reduce its global workforce by about 4,000 over two years, as part of an effort to save £1.7bn.JLR’s employs 44,000 people globally and 34,000 in the UK. The cuts will mainly affect the 26,000 UK employees who are salaried and management workers. The company has plants in Solihull, Warwickshire and Merseyside, and is headquartered in Coventry.No bailouts for Jaguar Land Rover amid reports of thousands of job cuts, says ministerRead moreIts proposal threatens to provide an early reality check for the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, and his promise to “reindustrialise” Britain.JLR’s profits have tumbled as it wrestles with strong competition in the global car market, Trump’s US tariffs andlast year’s hack, which led to the shutdown of its factories.The JLR chief executive, PB Balaji, said: “The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty. Through our Growth Reimagined strategy, JLR is moving decisively to strengthen our competitiveness and position the business for long-term success …“As part of this transformation, we will reduce our global workforce by around 4,000 roles over the next two years. We recognise this will be difficult news for colleagues affected, and are committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect.”The Guardian understands that factory workers who are paid hourly – the vast majority of those on the shop floor – will be unaffected by the cuts, which will instead fall on salaried employees in divisions such as management, marketing, and research and development.The business minister, Jonathan Reynolds, hasruled out using taxpayers’ moneyto deter the company from pursuing the redundancies.Reynolds will hold talks with Balaji and Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, on Tuesday. Graham is expected to push for JLR to favour retraining and redeployment over compulsory job losses, if it cannot achieve enough redundancies voluntarily.The cuts will be weighted towards more senior roles in management and research and development rather than shopfloor production workers.Graham said: “While the cuts planned are not expected to impact the UK manufacturing footprint or its supply chain, we need to ensure that no stone is left unturned to mitigate these jobs losses in the highly skilled ‘white collar workforce.”JLR announced the job cuts as the chancellor, John Healey, made aneconomic speechat the Manufacturing Technology Centre in Coventry, just a few miles from the carmaker’s offices. Healey said he wanted to “draw the line” under rising business costs.A No 10 spokesperson said it was an “uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities and we know that current market conditions are challenging for the automotive sector globally”.Liam Byrne, the chair of the Commons business and trade committee, said the news was a “body blow for workers, families and communities across the West Midlands”.He added: “We now need urgent assurances that maximum support will be deployed to help everyone affected find new work.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But the troubles at JLR underline the challenge facing the government’s reindustrialisation drive. Britain is preparing to spend billions more on defence, infrastructure and new technology. But British business needs cheaper energy and government orders, not at some distant point in the future, but now, now, now.”Last year’s hack eventually cost the company about £200m and contributed to its pre-tax profit falling to just £14m, from £2.5bn a year earlier.The government last yearagreed to underwrite a £1.5bn loan to JLRto help it recover from the hack but the carmaker has not tapped the facility.JLR has also suffered the fallout from Trump’s trade tariffs, which hit sales of models such as the Range Rover and the Defender as the company seeks to expand further in the US market.JLR is in the midst of a large-scale overhaul of its products, including the launch of itsfirst fully electric Range Rover this month, which will come with a starting price of £154,070, and a new electric Jaguar. It is also considering a deal with Stellantis to make some of its cars in the US to help ease the effect of trade tariffs.Balaji said the cuts were aimed at “reducing organisational complexity” and would mean the company could break even on sales of about 300,000 vehicles a year.Europeancarmakers have faced tough trading conditions as Chinese manufacturers’ sales have surged across the UK and Europe, giving companies such as Chery and BYD a manufacturing foothold in the regions.In July, Chery, which also owns the Omoda and Jaecoo brands, accounted for nearly 8% of UK market share, up from 3% last year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders.The West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, said the job cuts were “deeply worrying” and said he will launch a £500,000 support package to help JLR workers taking voluntary redundancy find new jobs.JLR follows Volkswagen in announcing large-scale job cuts, after the German carmaker said last week that it intended to make 50,000 more people redundant as part of a turnaround plan.Explore more on these topicsJaguar Land RoverAutomotive industryJob lossesManufacturing sectorTrump tariffsTariffsJonathan ReynoldsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK house prices fall for first time since 2023, led by London and south-east | House prices | The Guardian
description: Average property cost £298,468 in August, down by 0.4% year on year amid higher interest rates, says Lloyds
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Average property cost £298,468 in August, down by 0.4% year on year amid higher interest rates, says Lloyds
Content: Many homeowners are choosing to sit tight, with sellers reluctant to accept offers, Lloyds said.Photograph: Roger Bamber/AlamyView image in fullscreenMany homeowners are choosing to sit tight, with sellers reluctant to accept offers, Lloyds said.Photograph: Roger Bamber/AlamyHouse pricesUK house prices fall for first time since 2023, led by London and south-eastAverage property cost £298,468 in August, down by 0.4% year on year amid higher interest rates, says LloydsLauren AlmeidaMon 7 Sep 2026 07.20 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 02.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK house prices have fallen for the first time in almost three years, as prospective buyers were squeezed by higher mortgage rates, geopolitical uncertainty and stretched affordability.Prices have dropped by 0.4% compared with a year ago, the first year-on-year decrease since November 2023, according to the lender Lloyds. That came in below expectations of a 0.2% annual rise, according to a poll of economists by Reuters.The average property cost £298,468 in August, falling 0.2% or £685 compared with July, the bank’s monthly index found.First annual fall in UK house prices since November 2023, led by London and the south – business liveRead moreAndrew Asaam, a director at Lloyds, said the UK’s housing market was “subdued” in the face of higher inflation, borrowing costs and geopolitical tensions.“What we’re not seeing is a rush of homeowners cutting prices,” he said. “But more are choosing to sit tight, with sellers reluctant to accept offers they feel are too low, while some buyers are waiting to see how conditions develop.”He added that the market is forecast to “remainfairly subdued in the months ahead, but this will likely only have a limited impact on house prices”.Tensions in the Middle East have stoked fears around inflation this year, feeding expectations of furtherinterest rate rises.Property buyers looking for a mortgage deal have faced months ofheightened volatility, with the average interest rate for a two-year fixed residential mortgage at 5.63% on Monday, according to the market tracker Moneyfacts, while the average five-year deal was 5.68%. Both were below 5% at the start of the year.Mortgage approvals were at their lowest level since the start of 2024, Lloyds said.Jeremy Leaf, an estate agent in north London, said the slowdown in the market reflected a “standoff” between nervous buyers and sellers who believe they have already reduced their prices by as much as they can.“There is more movement when sellers set realistic asking prices from the outset and appreciate after a period of marketing that even a cheeky offer is worth considering,” he said.“Activity is picking up now that the main holiday season is over, which is helping to improve confidence a little.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNorthern Ireland was still the best performer for house price growth across the UK, with the average home rising by 6.9% year on year to £231,245.Prices in Scotland rose by 3.5% to an average of £223,437, while in Wales prices grew by 0.6% to an average of £230,282.In England, there was a stark divide between the north and south, with the north-east and north-west recording growth of 2.7% and 2% respectively, with averages of £184,370 and £248,675.Meanwhile the south-east reported the biggest drop in house prices across the UK, down by 1.6% to an average of £381,729. In greater London, prices dropped 1.5% to £534,177.An RBC Capital Markets analyst, Anthony Codling, said the Lloyds figures paint “a picture of a market under meaningful pressure from multiple directions: elevated mortgage rates, geopolitical uncertainty pushing up energy prices, and a consumer that is both cautious and increasingly stretched.“Sellers are not panicking and cutting prices aggressively; they are simply sitting tight. Buyers, meanwhile, are waiting for clarity on the path of interest rates.”Explore more on these topicsHouse pricesPropertyHousing marketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tiny cash buffers leave small UK TV firms at risk of going bust, analysis finds | Television industry | The Guardian
description: Median £42,000 in reserve not enough to cover filming overrun or delay to series, industry body warns
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Median £42,000 in reserve not enough to cover filming overrun or delay to series, industry body warns
Content: Euston Films, the maker of the train drama Nightsleeper for the BBC, is one of a number of TV production companies to have been wound down.Photograph: Mark Mainz/BBC/Euston FilmsView image in fullscreenEuston Films, the maker of the train drama Nightsleeper for the BBC, is one of a number of TV production companies to have been wound down.Photograph: Mark Mainz/BBC/Euston FilmsTelevision industryTiny cash buffers leave small UK TV firms at risk of going bust, analysis findsMedian £42,000 in reserve not enough to cover filming overrun or delay to series, industry body warnsMark SweneyMon 7 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of small UK TV companies have so little cash in reserve that a filming overrun or a delay to a series could send them bust, an industry body has warned, asprogramme budget cuts by broadcastersthreaten their future.Analysis of the Companies House accounts filings of more than 200 of the estimated 800 independent TV production companies in the UK by the industry body Indielab has found that 40% face running out of cash within the next two years.The analysis of three years of filings made by small independent TV producers, the “indies” that make up 85% of the UK’s production sector, identified a dramatic drain on the financial reserves they use to weather tough trading periods.The reserves of more than half declined over the three-year period, with 40% registering a decline of almost a third, while the financial cushion for 31% was slashed by more than half.The analysis found that the amount held in reserves by a typical small indie – the median amount of the sample of 203 – was only £42,000 at the end of the three-year analysis period.The comparable figure at the beginning of the period was £51,000, already a slim reserve fund to rely on to bridge funding shortages.“[The £42,000] buffer would not cover the cost of a single delayed commission, a production overrun, or a series put on hold [by a broadcaster] after delivery,” said Victoria Powell, the chief executive of Indielab. “The picture is stark. Small producers are the most exposed part of the ecosystem. When commissioning spend falls, they feel it first and hardest. Our data shows the sector’s health is being eroded, year on year.”A string of high-profile TV production companies have already been wound down in the past two years.View image in fullscreenDuck Soup Films, which made the drama Lost Boys & Fairies for the BBC, has stopped active development and production.Photograph: Simon Ridgway/BBC/Duck Soup FilmsThese include Euston Films, the maker of the pre-apocalyptic thriller Hard Sun and the train drama Nightsleeper for the BBC, and Dare Pictures, which has produced Channel 4 shows including Fugitive: The Mystery of the Crypto Queen and UK Prisons Exposed: Sex, Drugs & Corruption.Other notable production closures include Leeds-based Duck Soup Films, which made the drama Lost Boys & Fairies for the BBC and Channel 4’s Dreamers, and the factual producer Proper Content, which had credits including the BBC documentary P Diddy: The Rise and Fall, the Channel 5 royal docuseries The King’s Guard and the Channel 4 show The School That Tried To End Racism.“We have seen many notable closures across the sector in the last two years,” Powell said. “We know of many more companies that have quietly closed or mothballed outside the headlines. Our data strongly suggests this trend will accelerate.”Last week, Everyone TV, the joint venture owned by the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5, released a report that warned of a “spiral of decline” affecting the production industry if broadcaster budgets continued to be cut.Despite the arrival of the deep-pocketed US streamers such as Netflix, Amazon and Disney+, the UK production industrystill relies heavily on traditional UK broadcastersfor their livelihood.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe report, by Oliver & Ohlbaum, found that public service broadcasters (PSBs) remain the leading source of UK original commissions and production for small indies, accounting for 71% of UK original content investment in 2024 and 85% of all original hours last year.However, the total amount spent on commissioning programmes by all UK-based broadcasters hasfallen from £1.99bn in 2022 to £1.73bn in 2024– the lowest level since the industry shut down during the Covid pandemic in 2020 – according to themost recent figuresfrom the industry body Pact.This fall has mainly been because of significant decreases by multichannel broadcasters, such as Sky, where spend has declined by almost 40% over that period.Figures from the British Film Institute showed that spending on prestige shows – high-end TV costing at least £1m an hour to make – by domestic broadcastershas declinedfrom £794m in 2023 to £688m last year.“PSBs with a statutory duty to support independent production need to consider what that duty really means in practice, and whether they are currently meeting it,” Powell said. “The accounts of 203 indie TV companies should be a wake-up call to the sector.”Indielab’s research focused on small indies with a turnover of less than £10m.Pact, which represents the wider industry, says it has 800 independent production company members, the majority of which are small and medium-sized with a turnover of less than £50m.Explore more on these topicsTelevision
