title: ‘It’s the Bayeux tapestry of TV!’ After six decades, the seminal series bows out with 70 Up | Television | The Guardian
description: The ‘hugely important artefact’ that’s followed 14 children since they were seven is set to air its final instalment. The now-septuagenarians and director Asif Kapadia talk about breaking new ground for 63 years – and changing TV for ever
Author: Tara Conlan
Headline: The ‘hugely important artefact’ that’s followed 14 children since they were seven is set to air its final instalment. The now-septuagenarians and director Asif Kapadia talk about breaking new ground for 63 years – and changing TV for ever
Content: The 70 Up participants.Photograph: MultiStory Media/ITVView image in fullscreenThe 70 Up participants.Photograph: MultiStory Media/ITVTelevision‘It’s the Bayeux tapestry of TV!’ After six decades, the seminal series bows out with 70 UpThe ‘hugely important artefact’ that’s followed 14 children since they were seven is set to air its final instalment. The now-septuagenarians and director Asif Kapadia talk about breaking new ground for 63 years – and changing TV for everTara ConlanMon 7 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDescribed as the Bayeux tapestry of television, the groundbreaking ITV documentary seriesSeven Upis coming to its final conclusion.In 1964, a group of randomly chosen seven-year-olds from different backgrounds were brought together and filmed in an attempt to answer questions about the effect of fate, class and environment on people’s aspirations and outcomes.Designed to test the Jesuit maxim of “give me the child until he is seven and I will show you the man”, it began as a one-off World in Action film for the regional ITV company Granada. But the producers then returned to the children every seven years, charting their progress and creating a snapshot of Britain’s social history.Viewers’ own lives, loves and losses have been reflected in the experiences of the contributors, such asNeil Hughes– the bright Liverpudlian schoolboy who dreamed of attending Oxford University but became homeless and then a local councillor – andJackie Bassett, the straight-talking Londoner who was ahead of her time in challenging conventional norms.View image in fullscreenJackie Bassett in 1978, when she was 21.Photograph: ITVNow the series is bowing out with 70 Up, which has noticeable differences from previous iterations. The Oscar-winning directorAsif Kapadiahas taken over from his long-running predecessorMichael Apted, who died in 2021. Many thought Apted’s death meant the end of Up, but the producer Claire Lewis – the custodian of the brand since 28 Up – got a call from one of the group,Nick Hitchon, who had terminal cancer and wanted to record a final interview.Hitchon died hours after Lewis recorded his thoughts, which she said was heartbreaking, so “we all decided that we should make another film and [began] looking for a director”.Knowing the concluding series needed someone skilled in archive and interviewing, she tracked down Kapadia – as his films about Ayrton Senna, Diego Maradona and Amy Winehouse “blew me away” – and discovered he was a fan of the series and that Apted had met and admired him.With Kapadia secured, Lewis then had to persuade the contributors to take part one last time. There may yet even be another incarnation of their stories, she said.Kapadia’s involvement helped convince Hughes to do 70 Up, “because I knew this was going to be a fresh start, a very different sort of enterprise”. It was also “a chance to meet some of the other participants, probably for the last time,” he said.View image in fullscreenNeil Hughes at 14 and 49.Composite: ITVBut he also reveals he feels that the portrayals of the struggles he has faced mean “I constantly try to clean up my image”. Hughes thinks Apted was very professional but “knew what he wanted”.“Michael was selectively using the material he had. Now I don’t criticise that; that is within the gift of a director.” But Hughes “relished the chance to say to people, ‘Well, I’m not quite maybe what you think I am’.“With the greatest respect to viewers of the show … they didn’t see the real me. There’s a me here who Michael never discovered.”Now living in France, Hughes does not watch TV, not even the Up series. He says it is “partly a self-defence mechanism” but also that “I’m very sensitive to screens. I don’t have a mobile phone”.Hughes has spoken before on screen about his struggles with depression and says in 70 Up: “If somebody has a mental health problem, it doesn’t mean they are odd. It doesn’t mean they have chosen to be weird or antisocial … It’s not something they chose. It’s what they are.“I’m as happy as I could be given my life … I’m still quite lonely at times, but this is a common characteristic of our age.”I ask him if he thinks his life might have been different if there had been more understanding of neurodiversity when he was younger.“Yes, I think so,” he said. Because now “it is about recognising people’s individuality”.There have been “pluses and minuses” to being in the series, he said, and he wonders existentially if television’s artifice means taking part has influenced the outcome of contributors’ lives.Overall he thinks he has benefited – notably his friendships with Lewis and fellow participant Bruce Balden. As is common in TV, the participants also were paid so “because my life’s been a struggle to keep afloat financially … the little contributions from Granada have helped from time to time”.View image in fullscreenBruce Balden in 2012.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianDuty of care to contributors has been paramount for Lewis. She says it was important to ensure she didn’t influence them at the “same time as having a relationship that was honest and trusting”. Hughes credits her for creating an “extended family” feeling among the group.For the 1964 film, “all the parents were talked to” about their children being involved, she said. “But not in the same way that they would be today”. Plus “it was completely innovative” and nobody knew it would run for so long.As British TV’s first social experiment, it paved the way for reality shows such as Big Brother and the rise of content creators.Kapadia, for whom directing 70 Up is a “dream come true”, says it is a one-off and the “most beautiful thing I’ve ever made”.“A lot of people have copied it and been inspired by it. But none of them will ever dothisever again,” he told the recent Edinburgh TV festival.His main aim has been to be “true to the series [and] answer the question that’s asked at the beginning: is your life defined at seven?”View image in fullscreenAsif Kapadia.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianBorn to Indian Muslim parents, Kapadia thinks it is “impossible not to watch it to think about your own life, your own parents, your relationships, your kids … it’s about them, but it’s about us and there’s nothing else like it”.Lewis feels Kapadia’s fresh viewpoint chimes with questions being asked about authenticity and unconscious bias in the world of television, making Apted the “15th character in the series”.Kapadia explains: “Who shoots it [and] who picks who is important” in shaping a documentary, along with “how do you cut it [and] who is judging what’s interesting or what isn’t interesting?”. Unlike Apted, he did not go to Oxbridge and “had free school meals” growing up in east London, so “what is your norm is how you always make projects”.The biggest takeaways from the participants include Hughes saying it is “remarkable, and maybe this is one of the things that Michael discovered” that he and Balden had become friends despite their different backgrounds. “It’s good for us to recognise that that can happen,” he said.Another key conclusion is some male contributors wishing they had spent less time at work. Lewis says Apted also “realised he didn’t spend as much time with his family as he should have done, and he really regretted that”.She thinks one of the most profound concluding statements comes from Symon Basterfield, who grew up in care and now fosters children. He said: “The one thing I’ve taken from this programme is my story is special because it’s been seen; not because it is special, just because it’s been seen.”A vital part of the “beautiful” and “genius” films, said Lewis, is that Apted and his original team ensured the series featured “ordinary people … they are somebody you could have been living next door to”.Bassett said: “It’s been wonderful to be part of. It’s been difficult at times, but I think we always knew that while it started about class … it ended up being about us and how different audiences relate to us.”The stories of the 14 individuals and Apted may have a new lease of life, as Lewis reveals: “What I would like to do now, because we have the material, is to make hour-long films about each person.”She is looking for funding from universities or media for the new edits, which will tell the participants’ individual stories and show how the conventions of television and our society have changed.As ITV’s factual controller, Jo Clinton-Davis, puts it, the Up series is like the Bayeux tapestry, with all who have worked on it feeling the responsibility of “looking after this hugely important artefact”.“It sort of belongs to all of us,” she said.70 Up airs at 9pm on 15 SeptemberonITV1and ITVX. All previous episodes in the Up series are streaming on ITVX in the UKExplore more on these topicsTelevisionAsif KapadiaDocumentaryFactual TVITV1newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Swiftly enchanted’: why Bedknobs and Broomsticks is my feelgood movie | Movies | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers recommending their most rewatched comfort films is a reminder that Disney’s kids fantasy is more than a Mary Poppins knock-off
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest in our series of writers recommending their most rewatched comfort films is a reminder that Disney’s kids fantasy is more than a Mary Poppins knock-off
Content: A still from Bedknobs and Broomsticks.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenA still from Bedknobs and Broomsticks.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyMy feelgood movieMovies‘Swiftly enchanted’: why Bedknobs and Broomsticks is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers recommending their most rewatched comfort films is a reminder that Disney’s kids fantasy is more than a Mary Poppins knock-offGary RyanMon 7 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 13.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Filigree, apogee, pedigree, perigee!” – the four incantatory words I blame for receiving a shonky Paul Daniels magic set as a child in the 80s. In Bedknobs and Broomsticks, it’s the spell that Angela Lansbury’s patriotic Nazi-vanquishing witch Eglantine Price casts to transform people into fluffy rabbits; a trick I yearned to pull off.‘Sometimes you just need a good cry’: why Little Women is my feelgood movieRead moreWhen it became clear I wouldn’t deter the Third Reich with three plastic thimbles, a deck of playing cards and a flaccid wand, my conjuring kit was mothballed – but my irrational love of the Disney film remains to this day. For me, it originally fell into the category of the crackling VHS that your parents taped off ITV at Christmas then would repeatedly plonk you in front of to shut you up – to the point Ican even recall the adverts.Still, Bedknobs has a flying nanny-shaped shadow over it; its ignoble reputation as a knock-off Mary Poppins was perhaps coded into its DNA. Put into production as a back-up plan when acquiring the rights to his beloved Poppins was looking shaky, Walt’s second-favourite attitude towards Bedknobs was captured by its screenwriter Don DaGradi, who sketched his boss asleep during a 1963 story conference, exaggerated zzzs tumbling out of his mouth, as the Sherman brothers previewed the rousing love song Eglantine. When it premiered in 1971, the Shermans and Lansbury felt the picture had been hobbled by cuts, while critics found the use of Nazis in a kids’ movie tonally jarring, akin to show tunes and a kick line erupting in The Hills Have Eyes.But (non-Paul Daniels-branded) cards on the table: I’m a ’Knobstruther. As a working-class nipper, turning my bed into a DFS-based Tardis and hanging out with Jessica Fletcher-with-an-English-accent appealed more than a bossy nanny healing a posho family. Even now, I prefer its more offbeat, darker tone, and how its spoonfuls of sugar are strictly wartime-rationed.Lansbury’s Miss Price is introduced to us rocking up to the village post office in a heraldic puff of luridly coloured motorcycle fumes, to collect a broomstick from a witchcraft correspondence course (a scam run by huckster magician Emelius Browne, a twinkly portrayal by Poppins alumnus David Tomlinson), only to end up reluctantly housing three London orphan evacuees. Together, they embark on a quest to locate a levitation spell to send inanimate objects into battle, thus preventing human casualties.Objectively, I realise Bedknobs is an oddly paced jamboree of set pieces and styles, but the greatest comfort feelgood movies trip the critical switch in your brain. Simply typing the song titles – the Poppins offcut The Beautiful Briny (soundtracking a dazzling underwater animated dance competition), Substitutiary Locomotion and the market-based cockney rave-up Portobello Road, featuring sailors on shore leave from HMS Choreography - means they’ll be lodged in my head. Best of all is the sumptuous sorrow of The Age of Not Believing, lamenting the receding of childhood wonder directed at sceptical 11-year-old Charlie Rawlings, which handily doubles as a midlife crisis anthem for adults. In the wake of the death of Disney in 1969, the Shermans channelled their existential angst into the number and it shows. It makes Feed the Birds resemble the Macarena.Revisiting it decades later, despite possessing a cynical anti-nostalgia firewall, I was nevertheless swiftly enchanted. It also proved funnier than I remembered. Particularly a hilarious cartoon/live action football match on an animal-ruled island, where stretcher-carrying vulture paramedics excitedly flap on to the pitch at the first sign of injury. A climactic battle where Miss Price, clad in a Brodie helmet and brandishing a sword while gliding atop a Union Jack-adorned broom, summons a phantom army of medieval suits of armour to repel a platoon of invading Nazis is played for slapstick yuks, like a bizarre cross between Went the Day Well? and the Three Stooges.In fact, the sole difference is I now snigger at eight-year-old Paul Rawlings’s exclamation of “What’s that got to do with me knob?” (I’m not proud) and understand a reference to Mr Browne’s familiarity with sex workers on Portobello Road that had previously whooshed over the innuendo no-fly zone above my head.Lately, a friend’s four-year-old son has become obsessed with Bedknobs. Talk of getting in touch with my inner child usually makes me want to find my inner King Herod, but seeing it through his eyes is like a mirror back to being a kid convinced that if he pointed at someone and reallybelieved, I could turn nemeses into nose-twitching bunnies.Bedknobs and Broomsticks is available on Disney+ in the US, UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmMy feelgood movieAngela LansburyAction and adventure filmsComedy filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias review – Slavoj Žižek goes in search of paradise | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Inserting himself into settings from Apocalypse Now to The Handmaid’s Tale, the pop-cultural critic finds it hard to locate the perfect ending – even with spoilers
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Inserting himself into settings from Apocalypse Now to The Handmaid’s Tale, the pop-cultural critic finds it hard to locate the perfect ending – even with spoilers
Content: Paradoxical … Slavoj Žižek in The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenParadoxical … Slavoj Žižek in The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias.Photograph: PRVenice film festivalReviewThe Pervert’s Guide to Utopias review – Slavoj Žižek goes in search of paradiseVenice film festival:Inserting himself into settings from Apocalypse Now to The Handmaid’s Tale, the pop-cultural critic finds it hard to locate the perfect ending – even with spoilersPeter Bradshawin VeniceMon 7 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe great pop-cultural critic and postmodern Marxist is back, with more entertaining and semi-serious provocations and deconstructive insights, notionally into the idea of “utopias”, as they appear in the movies and TV, having already done “cinema” and “ideology”.I was incidentally hoping for aSlavoj Žižekaria about how unexpectedly great and profoundly important threequels are. This is of course delivered emphatically in that amazing voice, now as universally recognised as Werner Herzog’s. Is it too late for a cameo on The Simpsons?Žižek’s trademarked and now slightly overworked way with a paradox is again in evidence. (He says that “A communist should be a convinced pessimist …” and actually describes himself as a communist though lays off the bet in his tongue-in-cheek way by saying that this he knows “this sounds crazy”.He isn’t above being a bit paradoxical himself – at one point praising The Rapture (1991) as showing the apocalypse as the literal real thing and not some lame metaphor, and then praising Last Year At Marienbad (1961) for disclosing the truth of a post-apocalyptic state of endless return.He gets big laughs with his traditional gag of recreating movie and TV settings with himself inserted in them. Žižek appears in shadow in a jungle hut like Marlon Brando in Apocalypse Now (1979), lying back in red garb submitting to conjugal violence like Elisabeth Moss in The Handmaid’s Tale (2017) and reclining in the bath like Kirsten Dunst in Melancholia (2011) – but on this last point, considering how mischievously alert Žižek is to discourses of power, I was surprised he didn’t point out that it was at a press conference for Melancholia that director Lars von Trierexpressed his sympathy with Hitler. Perhaps he thought that not mentioning it was the paradoxical thing to do.View image in fullscreenLuxuriating … Slavoj Žižek in The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias.Photograph: PRHe gets his biggest laugh at the very beginning, however, by noting that his documentary will discuss films’ endings and so delivers a warning about spoilers – if these upset you, he says, “leave the cinema now: no one will miss you”.So what and where are these utopias of his? Žižek concedes that they do not appear to be much in evidence here, but advances many subtle and nuanced arguments, from Freudian, Marxist and Hegelian perspectives, to suggest that there is a kind of utopian thinking in repressive power structures, in art as in life, which pre-empt and absorb rebellious thinking to bolster themselves and in which rebellion itself becomes unconsciously complicit in power. He has an intriguing comment on Jeanne Dielman 23 Quai Du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (1975) in which he locates the “perversion” of enjoying submission to control with Dielman’s evident orgasm in the film’s final reel. (A feminist critic might have taken Žižek aside and gently explained the possibility that Dielman was faking it.)Yet for all his ingenuity, Žižek disappointingly doesn’t address the simple issue that utopias aren’t cool. It’s all about dystopia, ironised, embittered, preferably post-apocalyptic. Unlike Sir Thomas More, our film-makers, TV writers, novelists do not find utopias interesting. (Oddly there is no mention of Sir Thomas More at all.) It is only through paradox that Žižek seems able to approach the idea of “utopia”.But he is always entertaining, riffing inexhaustibly and even, after a tiny break, actually carrying on over the final credits. Perhaps, like Kirsten Dunst in the bath, you should just lie back and luxuriate in it.The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias screened at the Venice film festivalExplore more on these topicsVenice film festivalFestivalsSlavoj ŽižekreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sharks are my film stars’: how the Jacques Cousteau of the North Sea finally unlocked its beauty  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Epic plankton blooms make filming in the North Sea notoriously difficult. But a new documentary gives a rare glimpse of the kaleidoscopic life – seals, sharks, tuna, orcas and shorthorn sculpins – lurking beneath its waves
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Epic plankton blooms make filming in the North Sea notoriously difficult. But a new documentary gives a rare glimpse of the kaleidoscopic life – seals, sharks, tuna, orcas and shorthorn sculpins – lurking beneath its waves
Content: Rare sighting … a basking shark in North Sea, Nature Untamed.Photograph: Joost van Uffelen/©Dutch Maritime ProductionsView image in fullscreenRare sighting … a basking shark in North Sea, Nature Untamed.Photograph: Joost van Uffelen/©Dutch Maritime ProductionsMovies‘Sharks are my film stars’: how the Jacques Cousteau of the North Sea finally unlocked its beautyEpic plankton blooms make filming in the North Sea notoriously difficult. But a new documentary gives a rare glimpse of the kaleidoscopic life – seals, sharks, tuna, orcas and shorthorn sculpins – lurking beneath its wavesPatrick BarkhamMon 7 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 03.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe North Sea, as even its greatest admirers will concede, often glowers an unappetising grey or brown. And we assume that its dull exterior is matched by sediment-filled waters where little life dwells. For years, the friends and family of Peter van Rodijnen wondered why the Dutch cinematographer and diving fanatic spent so much time exploring “this murky bowl of soup”. But, inspired by a childhood of watching Jacques Cousteau’s adventures in rather more enticingly temperate waters, Van Rodijnen’s dedication to North Sea diving gradually revealed its hidden wonders.Over 20 years, as camera technology improved, Van Rodijnen obtained more and more amazing footage of marine life near his home on the Netherlands coast. Nearly a decade ago, he teamed up with director Mark Verkerk. “We started with the idea,” says Van Rodijnen, “that if somebody can make a movie about the North Sea, it’s got to be us.”double quotation markIt’s no accident that there are virtually no films about the North SeaNorth Sea, Nature Untamedwill startle anyone who has ever set eyes on – or dipped a toe in – the shallow sea shared by the coastal nations of north-west Europe. Despite decades of intensive fishing, oil extraction and multiple other exploitations, parts of the North Sea are still alive with luminous pinks, purples and greens; starfish, lobsters, brittle stars, kelp forests, seals and basking sharks. This hidden wilderness may be almost as spectacular as a tropical reef, even if the Great Barrier Reef, where Van Rodijnen began his diving career, is much more accessible.View image in fullscreenRough seas … four out of five planned dives were cancelledPhotograph: Joost van Uffelen/Dutch Maritime ProductionsPart of the reason we rarely comprehend the marine riches of the North Sea is because of epic plankton blooms that, as the film explains, are actually the foundation of this living ecosystem. These annual eruptions feed its whole pyramid of marine life but, combined with the shallow waters and big tides, frequently make underwater visibility too poor to film. “It’s no accident that there are virtually no films about the North Sea,” grimaces Verkerk. “This is really one of the first big attempts. It is incredibly difficult.”Van Rodijnen, who narrates the film in a charmingly personal way, meticulously assembled his underwater stories from decades of North Sea diving. But during their seven-year shoot, the film-makers faced multiple last-minute cancellations of carefully scheduled trips to join fishers or windfarm construction sites alongside even less predictable attempts to intercept dolphin, bluefin tuna and basking sharks. Four out of every five planned dives in the North Sea were cancelled because of rough seas.“The visibility can be poor, there can be lots of currents, it is cold,” says Van Rodijnen. “You’ve got depth and the limitations of your scuba devices, so you have 20 or 30 minutes of filming per dive. It’s about patience but it’s more about persistence. You need to just keep pushing to get the shots. I had some sleepless nights, I can tell you.”Although North Sea, Nature Untamed is awash with charismatic characters – from supersmart orcas to the conscientious shorthorn sculpins that nurse neon-pink eggs until they grow eyes and squiggle out into the dark water – the documentary does not lead with obvious or familiar marine stars. “The big idea is to show the whole system working,” says Verkerk. “It’s fantastic to see the bluefin tuna come back and orcas thriving, but they only do that because of this massive system supporting all of that life.”Unlike the British natural history film-making tradition, where wild animals are often portrayed in a world without humans, people are shown as key engineers of this living system, for better and for worse. Fishing and overfishing continues to shape the North Sea, and the film reveals the impact of sand eel decline on puffins and follows Van Rodijnen on to a Dutch fishing boat. The boat is a clean, conscientious operation that prides itself on its sustainable methods, eschewing beam or bottom trawling, in which heavy beams and nets plough – and obliterate – the seabed and much of its life. But even this boat’s fishing is a challenging watch as Van Rodijnen witnesses “my subjects, my film stars” – beautiful little sharks and rays – discarded as bycatch.Later, he joins a mackerel fishing boat off Shetland, a supremely efficient, industrial enterprise. A pod of orcas recognise the sound of the vessel’s winch and pick off any mackerel that evade its vast net. While the orca pod can devour 1,000 mackerel in a day, fishers far outdo that. It is shocking to see the sheer scale of the operation: thousands of fish sucked up giant tubes into a huge steel vat.View image in fullscreenFull of life … lobsters, kelp forests and curious seals feature in North Sea, Nature Untamed.Photograph: Joost van Uffelen/©Dutch Maritime ProductionsVan Rodijnen says he still finds the images upsetting, “but once you get on the boat with those guys and you’re living together for a couple of days, you don’t always agree but you start to understand their situation”. The film is not a polemic. Van Rodijnen believes it is “naive” to hope we can “make one big Marine Protected Area out of the North Sea. That just won’t happen. There’s lots of nuance to understand.”He opposes bottom trawling and bycatch but the mackerel fishery deploys nets that don’t damage the seabed; nor does it appear to catch large quantities of non-target species. In this case, he says in the film, fishing quotas “seem to work”. However, he would still like to see marine life better protected, particularly by nations such as his own, Denmark and Norway, which he fears could revive destructive deep-sea mining proposals.For decades, the North Sea has also been challenged by extraction. While the film-makers do not turn their cameras on its oil and gas industries, they do explore the positives and negatives of the offshore windfarm boom. Underwater is “not just a world that you don’t see, but it’s also a world that you don’t hear,” says Verkerk. The film reveals the pounding noise that reverberates through the ocean during construction. “The sound is pretty deafening above the water but underwater it can be 20 times louder,” says Verkerk. “Because visibility is not so good in the North Sea, a lot of marine life is geared for sound. The impact is not just on whales but right down to the actual development of a fish egg.”View image in fullscreen‘Give nature a chance and it responds’ … Peter van Rodijnen.Photograph: Rosalie van der Does/Dutch Maritime ProductionsAs well as providing clean energy, though, there may be an unforeseen upside to the North Sea windfarms. Van Rodijnen’s most surprising dive is to some rocks that accidentally fell from a ship 30 years ago. Similar to those used at the base of windfarms, the rocks have over three decades had their grey surface transformed by multicoloured marine life – a profusion of seaweeds and sea creatures have attached itself to this artificial reef.With bottom trawling and other commercial fishing prevented within sizeable windfarm areas, de facto marine parks have been established. More mini artificial reefs could flourish over the coming decades. “Give nature a chance and it responds,” says Van Rodijnen. “It’s good to keep a constant eye on how the system reacts to these many windfarms being built. But in the end, they can absolutely have a positive effect on marine life.”Verkerk and Van Rodijnen sound surprised and delighted by the success of their film, which they have been touring for two years across the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany and even countries with no North Sea coast such as Austria and Switzerland. There’s now interest in China, Japan, Argentina and Italy, perhaps because it is ultimately a universal film about the life-giving miracle that is the sea.“It’s very much out of sight out of mind, isn’t it?” says Verkerk. “Even for those of us who live around the North Sea, it’s a little underwhelming. But it is actually an incredibly interesting sea. A lot of the problems facing seas and oceans all around the world are at their most acute here – the North Sea is leading the way in exploitation but also in solutions.”“There’s a lot of parties wanting to get something out of the oceans,” adds Van Rodijnen, “and there are a lot of discussions about the North Sea. What we’re trying to do with the film is spark wonder by showing what’s down there. Then you bring about a bit of love and understanding.”North Sea, Nature Untamedis in cinemas UK wide from 25 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsOceansEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Primetime review – Robert Pattinson’s preening TV host hunts paedophiles but real drama proves harder to target | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Venice film festival: Lance Oppenheim’s drama about controversial US reality show To Catch a Predator is unsure what it wants to say about media or morality
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Venice film festival: Lance Oppenheim’s drama about controversial US reality show To Catch a Predator is unsure what it wants to say about media or morality
Content: Pompous … Robert Pattinson as TV presenter Chris Hansen in Primetime.Photograph: A24/APView image in fullscreenPompous … Robert Pattinson as TV presenter Chris Hansen in Primetime.Photograph: A24/APVenice film festivalReviewPrimetime review – Robert Pattinson’s preening TV host hunts paedophiles but real drama proves harder to targetVenice film festival:Lance Oppenheim’s drama about controversial US reality show To Catch a Predator is unsure what it wants to say about media or moralityPeter BradshawMon 7 Sep 2026 05.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 05.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLance Oppenheim is the acclaimed documentary-maker who has made his feature debut with a strangely overwrought and heavy-footed drama-thriller, which for all its elaborate neon-lit atmosphere of noir danger isn’t at all sure what it wants to say about media or morality, or anything else.The subject is the controversial top-rated US TV reality show To Catch a Predator which ran from 2004 to 2008; that title was evidently taken from the Hitchcock movie To Catch a Thief, which in turn was inspired by the phrase “Set a thief to catch a thief”. In search of prey, the show’s researchers baited paedophiles in online chatrooms posing as children, lured them to “sting houses” where actors played underage teens on the front porch to get the abusers inside, where they can be clearly filmed expressing criminal intentions. But before anything could happen, sonorous host Chris Hansen appeared from nowhere and confronted these cringing abusers – which made for fantastic television. After this the cops made an arrest, and they and the state prosecutor did the heavy lifting of overseeing due process and presumably debating the merits of entrapment in court, although this obvious issue is not raised in the movie.Robert Pattinson certainly looks and sounds good in the role of the preening, pompous Hansen, gleefully overexcited when his show is promoted to a primetime slot, solemnly congratulating himself on cleaning up America and relishing the bizarrely melodramatic moment each week when he gets in the astonished abuser’s face, sauntering down the stairs with the insouciance of a talk show host. “Big night planned?” Merritt Wever plays Andie Bender, a hardbitten (fictional-composite) female executive in charge of Hansen’s live-ammo theatrics – Bender’s persona inherited from Faye Dunaway in Network – and Skyler Gisondo plays a needy, baby-faced wannabe actor Dan Plumb (another fictional-composite) who is the jailbait decoy that gets to lure the paedo indoors. He is persuaded to take the job by Hansen flatteringly taking him out for a drink, a scene slyly placed before us as a quasi-grooming episode.Plumb worries that this will not help his acting career long term and of course effectively invites the audience to worry that this is all just playacting anyway, all bread-and-circuses exploitation. The tension ratchets up when everyone realises they have to do something extra to maintain ratings; Hansen becomes obsessed with the rumour that there is a “whale” to be brought to justice in a righteous Texan small town – a high-ranking public figure, not just another sweaty nobody.But the movie’s own actual drama appears to reside in the backstairs office politics and gossip. Hansen is trying and failing to break off an extra-marital affair and Bender is being headhunted by a rival network prepared to offer huge bucks so she will produce a copycat version of Hansen’s show and crush it and him in the ratings. For a while, some intriguing conspiratorial possibilities present themselves. But none of that leads anywhere. Really we are just heading to the gruesome denouement which surely had to happen if paedophiles were hunted and shamed for sport; the film coasts up to a crisis, after which the drama is deemed to be at an end, although how or if Hansen has changed or conceded or learned anything is a mystery. It’s a disappointment.Primetime screened at the Venice film festival; it is out in the US on 25 September and in the UK on 30 October.Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalDrama filmsRobert PattinsonTelevisionUS televisionReality TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Imperium review – Sergei Loznitsa’s archive collage collates everyday life in cold-war Soviet Union | Movies | The Guardian
description: Venice film festival: The Two Prosecutors director cuts together documentary footage shot by a TV crew in the 1970s to try and get across what daily life in the USSR was like
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Venice film festival: The Two Prosecutors director cuts together documentary footage shot by a TV crew in the 1970s to try and get across what daily life in the USSR was like
Content: Stolidly grim … Imperium.Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMODView image in fullscreenStolidly grim … Imperium.Photograph: Essential Filmproduktion, Kino Produzioni, Société Parisienne de Production, Studio Uljana Kim - footage courtesy of AAMODMoviesReviewImperium review – Sergei Loznitsa’s archive collage collates everyday life in cold-war Soviet UnionVenice film festival:The Two Prosecutors director cuts together documentary footage shot by a TV crew in the 1970s to try and get across what daily life in the USSR was likePeter BradshawMon 7 Sep 2026 05.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 05.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is an archive-compilation documentary from Sergei Loznitsa, a hypnotic panorama of early 1970s life across the vast reaches of the Soviet Union, or maybe we should call it the Soviet empire. Loznitsa gives it the Latin title Imperium, perhaps to recall the Romans before their decline and fall. His material is taken from fascinating footage shot between 1970 and 1973 by a visiting Italian camera crew who presumably had the necessary permissions and were well enough liked by the authorities to keep coming back.The effect is part Potemkin village, part seance, part ethnographic study; there are no interviews or voiceover, just ambient footage. (The Italians may have intended this material as B-roll to be fitted into a more conventional film.) Imperium has sometimes the eerie quality of a ghost story with phantoms drifting placidly across the screen, gazing blankly into the camera, occasionally grimacing or grinning, but destined never to see the film of which they are a part. We don’t see the gulags, of course, or really anything like agencies of the state, apart from the soldiers at the October Revolution parades in Red Square. Many of the former Soviet state capitals featured here nowadays have tourist-attraction KGB museums based in their brutal former HQs; that kind of thing is obviously absent here.What we do see is a demonstration of everyday life in the big cities of Moscow, Leningrad and Kyiv, with their shops and busy avenues, heartbreakingly provincial fashion shows and pop bands – but also the very un-modern rural traditions in various countries across Asia: traditions and norms that pre-existed the Soviet Union and carry on now, very possibly looking exactly the same in 2026 as they did in the early 70s. One weirdly pagan display appears to involve setting fire to an enormous phallus. Loznitsa introduces each segment with a resounding funeral bell with the screen cutting to a vivid and symbolic red.The challenge implicit in Loznitsa’s film is how to gauge the reality of all this. Does it indirectly reveal quiet desperation? Not necessarily. Much of it looks stolidly grim, but then similar footage of Britain in the early 70s looks grim in the same way. It is placid and often dreary, without the crazed eventfulness ofAdam Curtis’s similar compilation feature about Russia in the early 90s. But the film certainly shows how colossally diverse the USSR was ethnically. Exporting the revolution was a colonial project. And the Soviet authorities were probably entirely content for these cultural displays which had nothing to do with Marxism-Leninism to be recorded because they showed the sheer range of different people who were apparently willing to embrace Soviet communism.And perhaps Imperium does, in its way, show what Soviet life was like, on the surface, at any rate for those who didn’t step out of line. But it is mysterious. What are all these people thinking and feeling? The nearest we come to discovering the answer to that question is with the shots of the children, often extreme closeups of their robust faces, scowling or smiling. Unlike the grownups, they have not learned to close their faces – although arguably that is what adults do all over the world.Imperium screened at the Venice film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsRussiaPeriod and historical filmsVenice film festivalEuropeFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: End of the Road festival review – Pulp and CMAT lead indie landmark’s joyous birthday party  | End of the Road festival | The Guardian
description: Hitting 20, this festival has grown into a warm, genre-hopping powerhouse where fringe experimental acts are greeted as warmly as the star headliners
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: Hitting 20, this festival has grown into a warm, genre-hopping powerhouse where fringe experimental acts are greeted as warmly as the star headliners
Content: Cathartic farewell … CMAT performs at the End of the Road festival.Photograph: Burak ÇıngıView image in fullscreenCathartic farewell … CMAT performs at the End of the Road festival.Photograph: Burak ÇıngıEnd of the Road festivalReviewEnd of the Road festival review – Pulp and CMAT lead indie landmark’s joyous birthday partyLarmer Tree Gardens, WiltshireHitting 20, this festival has grown into a warm, genre-hopping powerhouse where fringe experimental acts are greeted as warmly as the star headlinersDaniel Dylan WrayMon 7 Sep 2026 07.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 07.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a celebratory feeling in the air atEnd of the Road festivalthis year as it turns 20. The piano stage has been turned into a giant birthday cake with candles on top, one man is dressed as a toilet to commemorate the porcelain anniversary, and Jarvis Cocker leads a spirited singalong of Happy Birthday while wishing for 20 more years.Retaining a core identity while also expanding and evolving has been key to that longevity. While early days were centred more on alt-folk and Americana, EOTR is now a genre-hopping powerhouse, blending everything from pop fun to noisy experimentation via global grooves, and with an equal focus on the familiar and the unknown.View image in fullscreenHappy birthday … Jarvis Cocker performs with Pulp.Photograph: Burak ÇıngıRepresenting the former,Geesemanage to pull in record audience attendance levels for their Thursday headliner show, while Pulp use theirs to announce a hiatus and they bow out with a set of deep, deep cuts and B-sides (including a beautifully sprawling and pulsing live debut of Deep Fried in Kelvin). It could have backfired spectacularly – with not even a nod to a hit song until almost an hour in – but while it was steadfastly uncompromising it was also a joyous rummage through the archive of true art-pop pioneers.CMAT also announces she won’t be playing the UK for two years during her headline set, which wraps up with the singer shirtless and deep in the audience for some collective cathartic screaming to say goodbye. Angine de Poitrine’s microtonal math-rock, as though styled by Alejandro Jodorowsky on a B-movie budget, may be still firmly in the leftfield camp but they are on the main stage after their huge breakthrough year, turning their frantic and frenetic instrumental workouts into an oddly big-crowd-friendly routine.Beyond the heavy hitters, the lineup has a deeply impressive wingspan. Factory Floor are in phenomenal form as they knock out a pummeling set of industrial electro-techno. Experimental electronic duo Another Country $$$ span everything from drum’n’bass to post-rock, while Cleo Reed’s queer country-soul (cuntry, as she calls it) is playful and sweet but also angry and impassioned. James K creates swirling electronic sounds that are so richly layered, dynamic and immersive, it’s like being pulled in and out of a dream state. Model/Actriz unleash a ferocious noise that manages to be as heavy as it is groove-locked – almost recalling a sweet spot between Perfume Genius and Gilla Band – as well as theatrical, with vocalist Cole Haden either doing endless ballet twirls or down in the audience whipping them into a frenzied state. But what’s especially infectious and energising at End of the Road is how everything, big or small, weird or poppy, is proportionally and enthusiastically attended. Everything is lapped up with the same appetite and gusto.Twenty years on from its inception, the festival may be hitting a major milestone and delivering a vintage year, but it exists as a crowning achievement in a wider context. A medium-sized event (15,000 capacity) free of big corporate sponsors as money from brands and multinationals pours into identity-less festivals elsewhere, this is a rare yet deserved success story, testament to the enduring power and beauty of independent music.Explore more on these topicsEnd of the Road festivalMusic festivalsIndieFestivalsJarvis CockerPulpGeeselive music reviewsShareReuse this content

Plus, the charming Julie Andrews serenades audiences with Jane Austen’s EmmaHannah J DaviesandHollie RichardsonMon 7 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekI’m Not a Monster Presents: Where Is Austin Tice?It has been 14 years since US marine turned journalist Austin Tice went missing in Syria. Much has changed in the embattled nation since then – not least the end of Bashar al-Assad’s regime – but Tice is yet to be found. Inthis series, Josh Baker and Sara Obeidat uncover crucial new evidence, some of which has already made headlines. title: BBCSO/Oramo/Gillam/Kanneh-Mason/Goldscheider review – Simcock’s triple concerto bursts with musical interest | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Gwilym Simcock’s concerto – written for Sheku Kanneh-Mason, Ben Goldscheider and Jess Gillam (cello, horn and sax) – had problems of balance but at its best was a riot of colours and energy
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Gwilym Simcock’s concerto – written for Sheku Kanneh-Mason, Ben Goldscheider and Jess Gillam (cello, horn and sax) – had problems of balance but at its best was a riot of colours and energy
Content: Exemplary soloists … Ben Goldscheider, Sheku Kanneh-Mason and Jess Gillam.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenExemplary soloists … Ben Goldscheider, Sheku Kanneh-Mason and Jess Gillam.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewBBCSO/Oramo/Gillam/Kanneh-Mason/Goldscheider review – Simcock’s triple concerto bursts with musical interestRoyal Albert Hall, LondonGwilym Simcock’s concerto – written for  Sheku Kanneh-Mason, Ben Goldscheider and Jess Gillam (cello, horn and sax) – had problems of balance but at its best was a riot of colours and energyClive PagetMon 7 Sep 2026 07.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 07.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBBC Young Musician has produced a wholegalaxy of stars over the years, but 2016 was rather special. It was a neat idea then to commissiona 10th-anniversary triple concerto for three of its finalists– cellist Sheku Kanneh-Mason, saxophonist Jess Gillam and horn player Ben Goldscheider – each of whom has gone on to a significant career. The composer of choice wasGwilym Simcock, an eclectic artist who straddles the worlds of jazz and classical music. The result was stretched to bursting with musical interest, though not without its problems.At its best, the concerto was a riot of primary colours, with vibraphone, harp and orchestral piano – played here by Simcock himself – adding spice to the mix. The outer movements grooved, the first with a minimalist nod to Steve Reich, the finale channelling a Scottish reel. The serene central “Mesto” – the word means mournful or melancholy – was a keening lament for Simcock’s father who died during the work’s composition.All three soloists were exemplary, from Gillam’s sassy licks to the mellow ruminations of Kanneh-Mason and Goldscheider. The fly in the ointment was the busy, heavily scored orchestrations, which tended to overwhelm both cello and horn. Gillam, playing soprano saxophone, was left to ride the swells, which she did with aplomb, though too often it seemed as if the new work had been written primarily for her. The encore, a soulful arrangement of the Largo from Bach’s Trio Sonata No 5, proved that these three instruments could indeed be balanced, just not in the concerto.View image in fullscreenHigh on contrasts … BBCSO conducted by Sakari Oramo.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouBookending the concert were a pair of orchestral showcases. Sakari Oramo took a serious-minded approach to the Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra – Britten’s daredevil variations on Purcell’s musical earworm – and gave his players plenty of room to shine. Dvořák’s New World Symphony was high on contrasts, with conductor and orchestra hell-bent on extracting maximum interest from the musical narrative. Honeyed strings, light-footed winds and pealing brass lent weight to Oramo’s boldly beguiling interpretation while gossamer violins and an unselfconscious cor anglais rediscovered the sense of wonder in the famous Largo.Available onBBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicPromsGwilym SimcockSheku Kanneh-MasonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hawking by Graham Farmelo review – the dark side of genius | Biography books | The Guardian
description: A biography of the physicist recognises his achievements, but also reveals the selfish narcissist underneath
Author: Philip Ball
Headline: A biography of the physicist recognises his achievements, but also reveals the selfish narcissist underneath
Content: Stephen Hawking in 2005.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStephen Hawking in 2005.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianBook of the dayBiography booksReviewHawking by Graham Farmelo review – the dark side of geniusA biography of the physicist recognises his achievements, but also reveals the selfish narcissist underneathPhilip BallMon 7 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I wrote an unadoring review of Stephen Hawking’s final book, a collection of essays published posthumously in 2018, New Scientist suppressed some of my criticisms on the grounds that it was “too early” to voice anything other than praise for the physicist who died, aged 76, that March. It was apparently still too early in 2021, when no British publisher would touch Charles Seife’s exposé of Hawking’s bullying and self-aggrandising behaviour, Hawking Hawking.In this new biography, veteran science writer Graham Farmelo takes a different approach. It is a comprehensive and accessible portrait of a brilliant scientist and an extraordinarily determined man who also possessed deep personal flaws to which the scientific community and the public mostly turned a blind eye. The uncomfortable but unavoidable truth is that Hawking’s overweening ambition and self-promotion, his repeated failure to acknowledge the work of others, his sexism and controlling behaviour were largely ignored because of his disability. I think it is indeed going to take us years to process that.As this book was authorised by the Hawking family, and as Farmelo (whose superb biography of Paul Dirac, The Strangest Man, won a Costa award in 2009) is a generous and kind writer, I had feared the warts would be omitted. But instead Farmelo handles them mostly by letting others’ words speak for themselves.But let’s start with the science, which offers a genuinely inspirational tale. As Farmelo says, while Hawking’s longevity against all odds was surely due in part to the exceptional care and treatment he received, “it was his unconquerable will, resilience and fortitude that did most to make his remarkable career possible”. His scientific achievements would be impressive by any measure; when accomplished in the face of debilitating and ultimately paralysing motor neurone disease, they are extraordinary.Like many scientists of his calibre, Hawking was a slow and rather lackadaisical starter. But once installed at Cambridge for a PhD under the supervision of astrophysicist Dennis Sciama, his sharp intelligence emerged. It was there in early 1963 that, after a series of falls, he was diagnosed and given less than 10 years to live. Undeterred, and despite steadily declining mobility and speech, he was electrified by the work of physicist Roger Penrose, 10 years his senior, on the gravitational collapse of dead stars into what had become known as black holes.That process was predicted by Einstein’s 1915 theory of general relativity, but Penrose was the first to show convincingly that it should lead to a “singularity” where all the star’s matter condenses to zero volume: an object with mass but no matter. Hawking had the brilliant insight that this same process, happening in reverse, could explain the big bang, in which the entire universe came into being from “nothing” 13.8bn years (as we now know) ago.That was his first triumph, described in a 1970 paper with Penrose. The best came four years later, when Hawking proposed that, thanks to the peculiar quantum-mechanical nature of spacetime, black holes are not really black because they should constantly radiate a dim glow of particles – now called Hawking radiation – that will eventually lead to their evaporation. That work was a virtuosic blend of four fundamental ideas in physics: general-relativistic gravity, quantum mechanics, thermodynamics and information theory.It was the high point of his research career: Hawking’s scientific achievements were largely done by the time he became a global celebrity, appearing on Star Trek and TheSimpsons and becoming the subject of the 2014 Oscar-winning biopic The Theory of Everything. It is “as a truly great elucidator of black holes” that he will be remembered, Farmelo rightly judges.I’m not alone in thinking Hawking’s work on black-hole thermodynamics and the discovery of Hawking radiation were worthy of a Nobel prize. (Hawking became obsessed to an unseemly degree with getting one.) But let’s keep it in proportion. Anyone who compares Hawking to Einstein knows nothing about Einstein or physics. Einstein made wide-ranging contributions to the discipline, but Hawking’s expertise was narrow and his forays outside it were sometimes embarrassing. Even in the closely related field of particle physics he said things that were, as Peter Higgs (of Higgs boson fame) said, “total crap”. “He made pronouncements about things he had no understanding of,” Higgs said – in the confident knowledge that it would make newspaper headlines the next day, uncritically lapped up by reporters.Which brings us to the problematic stuff. While professional colleagues mostly spoke about Hawking with reverence and affection, it is often those closest to him who speak of another side. His father, Frank, worried that the teenaged Stephen “was developing into a selfish character … like a small boy who took everything but gave little in return”. There was evidently no love lost with his sister Mary, who called him “one of the most self-centred people I’ve ever met”. At Oxford, some friends found him rather lazy and entitled, and at Cambridge “annoyingly haughty”. His youngest son recounted how his father was “hugely competitive” and never let him or his siblings win at board games.His unsparing ridicule of his first wife Jane’s religious beliefs contributed to their marital tensions, and the sacrifices she made often went unremarked by him. The pressure of going from lover to carer would never have been easy, but Hawking’s “authoritarian” demands and indifference to Jane’s interests added to her isolation. His adoptive brother, Edward, admitted “I’ve never really felt close to Stephen … he seems very cold.” And his mother, Isobel, complained how he would ignore people when it suited him. “I suppose what in other people would just be bad manners is excusable great-mannishness in him,” she wrote bitterly in her diary.Sometimes the indulgence gets creepy. Who else’s Marilyn Monroe obsession would be pampered by hiring a lookalike to croon “I want to be loved by you” to him in a “whispery voice” on his birthday? What Farmelo calls “flirting” might have been seen as something else if Hawking had not been using a wheelchair. He does not mention the nights at Stringfellows strip club and makes light of the trip to (pre-conviction) Jeffrey Epstein’s island. But we do hear how Hawking’s victory in a scientific bet was celebrated by making his opponents deliver lectures in T-shirts showing scantily clad women. Hilarious.Hawking was scandalously bad at giving due scientific credit to others, a trait evident from the outset when he failed to indicate his debt to Penrose. Worse was his treatment of physicist Jacob Bekenstein, whose idea about the connection between the area and the entropy of a black hole he mercilessly derided before discovering for himself that Bekenstein was right – and then essentially claiming the idea as his own, which Farmelo says “disappointed some of Stephen’s friends”. Hawking could clearly be a supportive and kind adviser to his own students, but when one discovered an argument for why Hawking was wrong about a conjecture concerning black holes, he tried to get him dismissed from the Cambridge PhD programme.Some of his colleagues, Farmelo says, “believed that Stephen’s talks were ‘all about him’ and that he rarely gave much public credit to his peers”. Farmelo suspects they rarely grumbled because “such comments would have been interpreted as mean-spirited”. But mean-spiritedness rarely deters academics; what he surely means is mean-spirited about a scientist with a disability. And there’s the problem. If we were to start finally treating Hawking as we do any other scientist, it would be a positive step for disability in science (which is still poorly accommodated). The effect on Hawking’s legacy is another matter.Hawking: His Life and Work by Graham Farmelo is published by John Murray (£30). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
