title: ‘Handsome, boyish – and he can cook!’ Richard O’Sullivan landed on TV like a lovable alien | Television | The Guardian
description: It was taken as read in the 1970s that all women, given the chance, would go out with him. But the star wasn’t just a new man – he was a radical presence
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: It was taken as read in the 1970s that all women, given the chance, would go out with him. But the star wasn’t just a new man – he was a radical presence
Content: ‘Dishy but not macho’ … Richard O’Sullivan on The Sweepstakes Game, 1976.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Dishy but not macho’ … Richard O’Sullivan on The Sweepstakes Game, 1976.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockTelevision‘Handsome, boyish – and he can cook!’ Richard O’Sullivan landed on TV like a lovable alienIt was taken as read in the 1970s that all women, given the chance, would go out with him. But the star wasn’t just a new man – he was a radical presenceZoe WilliamsMon 7 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRichard O’Sullivan, who has died at the age of 82, arrived in acting by accident. As a boy, he’d come back from a family holiday in Ireland with a strong accent, and his parents sent him to the Corona Theatre School in London to soften it. This origin story was very much in keeping with his adult self-fashioning: blokey, lovable, down to earth, cheeky – not the kind of guy who would go to drama school for the purposes of drama. But his work as a child star was almost back to back. He filmed his first feature aged eight, as an extra in The Yellow Balloon, and the next role he landed was the lead in The Stranger’s Hand, released the following year (1954). He played Audrey Hepburn’s younger brother in The Nun’s Story in 1959, and Elizabeth Taylor’s in Cleopatra four years later. It’s famously not that easy, making the child-to-adult actor transition, and the higher your profile as a junior the harder it is. It was while straddling the awkward between-years that O’Sullivan appeared in two Cliff Richard flicks, The Young Ones and Wonderful Life in the early 60s, and his facility with that pastel-shaded wholesomeness fed into but only partly described the comic actor he would become.Richard O’Sullivan obituaryRead moreHis first lead role as an adult was opposite Beryl Reid in Alcock and Gander, in 1972. Creators Johnnie Mortimer and Brian Cooke found their muse in O’Sullivan. Man About the House aired the following year, with O’Sullivan playing Robin Tripp, a trainee chef. The setup sounds so unremarkable now that it’s hard to fathom it as a break from any norm: two women (played by Paula Wilcox and Sally Thomsett) are looking for a flatmate. It’s assumed it’ll be another woman who’s all ready to move in; instead, O’Sullivan appears in their bath after a party. It was almost an ET archetype – thisalienarrives, this man who can cook, and spices up all their lives, to great merriment – and they can only get him past the landlord by pretending he’s gay.View image in fullscreenUnthreatening … with Paula Wilcox (left) and Sally Thomsett in Man About the House.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThere was a timeless innocence to it all – the girls insist the flatshare must always be platonic, so there’s a lot of forbidden flirtation, like a Shakespearean subplot. But it was also distinctively second-wave feminist, which is to say, determined to shake up norms and yet the guy, mysteriously, ended up on top. Tripp was a new kind of masculine ideal – handsome, boyish, unthreatening. Happy to pretend to be gay to keep the peace, constitutionally unable to batten down his heterosexual magnetism, always in a good mood. When you put it all together, what’s not to like?In the spin-off, Robin’s Nest, he’s grown up, but only on paper. Now in a relationship with Vicky Nicholls (played by Tessa Wyatt), he’d love to make an honest woman of her but she’s not having it. This was radical, being as they were the first unmarried cohabiting couple in a British sitcom, and it was O’Sullivan’s plausibly sweet nature that made it work, managing to convey that a new era had arrived, but everyone in it was still basically OK.O’Sullivan and Wyatt were a couple in real life, which didn’t do any harm – though he’d also been going out with Thomsett during Man About the House. This seems to have been adiaphoron to O’Sullivan fans, who were legion – his on-screen relationships either could or could not have been true in real life. It was taken as given during the 70s that all women, given the chance, would go out with him. He wrote recipe books – Man About the Kitchen, Roastin’ With Richard – and he appeared in adverts for British Gas. He was the ultimate new man, who could suddenly cook, while at the same time laugh at himself.View image in fullscreenRascally … with Michael Deeks in Dick Turpin.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockWhen Robin’s Nest ended, O’Sullivan took the title role in Dick Turpin. This was a stamp of his universalism, as it’s quite a different vibe, with the derring-do and all that, but no matter – if a main guy was called for, O’Sullivan was that guy. Dick Turpin ran into the early 80s, after which came Me and My Girl. O’Sullivan never tired of the business and would take smaller roles well into the 1990s, but his leading man years were over, and he was in poor health throughout that decade, suffering a stroke in 2003.He remained the embodiment of the 70s domestic dream – rascally but not roguish, dishy but not macho. It was a transitional era, out of the sitcom past where men were mainly grumpy, into who knew what? Richard O’Sullivan persuaded a nation that, wherever it was headed, it would probably be fine.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Netflix announces production of third Inbetweeners film | Netflix | The Guardian
description: Creators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris return as writers and directors, with the original cast reprising their roles
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Creators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris return as writers and directors, with the original cast reprising their roles
Content: A scene from the first Inbetweeners film in 2011, in which the group of friends head to Crete for a post-sixth form break.Photograph: Bwark Prods/Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA scene from the first Inbetweeners film in 2011, in which the group of friends head to Crete for a post-sixth form break.Photograph: Bwark Prods/Kobal/ShutterstockNetflixNetflix announces production of third Inbetweeners filmCreators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris return as writers and directors, with the original cast reprising their rolesNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 10.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflix has announced that production has begun on a new Inbetweeners film, with the original cast members reprising their roles.It will be a continuation of the popular Channel 4 sitcom, which aired on E4 from 2008 to 2010, followed by two films in 2011 and 2014.The actors Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will star as Will McKenzie, Jay Cartwright, Neil Sutherland and Simon Cooper. The coming-of-age comedy followed the misadventures of the four teenage friends at the fictional Rudge Park comprehensive as they navigated school life, friendship and failed sexual encounters.Thetrailer announcing the new filmbegins with a garage door being opened and pairs of feet making their way towards a car, revealed to be Simon’s yellow Fiat Cinquecento. The four men are then seen in the car, and when it fails to start Simon says: “Ah, for fuck’s sake.”He gets the engine going and drives the car out of the garage with the number three written on the rear windscreen. The trailer ends with the announcement: “Now in production.”The Inbetweeners creators, Damon Beesley and Iain Morris, will return to write and direct the film. They said: “It’s been super-fun hanging out with our friends again, and we’re going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans.”In the first film, which grossed £65.1m at the box office, the group of friends head to Crete in Greece for a post-sixth form break. It made history as the biggest opening weekend for a UK comedy at the time, according to Netflix.The 2014 follow-up, which grossed £46.6m, reunited Will, Simon, and Neil as they travelled to Australia to visit Jay during his gap year.It is not known whether Emily Atack will return in her role as Charlotte Hinchcliffe, or if Emily Head will come back as Carli D’Amato.Explore more on these topicsNetflixComedy filmsComedynewsShareReuse this content

title: Rob Reiner wins posthumous Emmy for The Bear, as Widow’s Bay dominates early awards | Emmys | The Guardian
description: Reiner broke record set by his father Carl Reiner at the ceremony formerly known as the Creative Arts Emmys, with The Pitt, Pluribus and DTF St Louis also winning big
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Reiner broke record set by his father Carl Reiner at the ceremony formerly known as the Creative Arts Emmys, with The Pitt, Pluribus and DTF St Louis also winning big
Content: Rob Reiner as Albert in season three of The Bear. Reiner, who was killed along with his wife Michele Singer Reiner in December, won a posthumous Emmy for his performance on Sunday.Photograph: FXView image in fullscreenRob Reiner as Albert in season three of The Bear. Reiner, who was killed along with his wife Michele Singer Reiner in December, won a posthumous Emmy for his performance on Sunday.Photograph: FXEmmysRob Reiner wins posthumous Emmy for The Bear, as Widow’s Bay dominates early awardsReiner broke record set by his father Carl Reiner at the ceremony formerly known as the Creative Arts Emmys, with The Pitt, Pluribus and DTF St Louis also winning bigSian Cainand agenciesMon 7 Sep 2026 01.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRob Reiner has won a posthumous Emmy for his performance in The Bear, nine months after his death – breaking the record set in the exact same category by his own father, Carl Reiner.Reiner’s win for outstanding guest actor in a comedy was announced on Sunday night at the ceremony formerly known as the Creative ArtsEmmys, a two-day awards event held a week before the main ceremony and telecast.Reiner’s win prompted a long, standing ovation, with his friend and fellowThe Bearguest star Jamie Lee Curtis among those in the crowd paying tribute.The actor and film-maker was killed along with his wife, Michele Singer Reiner, in December. Their son Nick Reiner,who has pleaded not guilty, has been charged with stabbing them to death.Stand By Me at 40: Rob Reiner’s seminal coming-of-age saga remains a bittersweet triumphRead moreReiner was up against Michael J Fox and Brett Goldstein for Shrinking, Hamish Linklater for Widow’s Bay, Christopher McDonald for Hacks and Connor Storrie for Saturday Night Live.His win comes 48 years after he won the second of his two Emmys for his acting on All in the Family in 1978, the longest gap between acting wins in Emmy history. His father Carl Reiner previously held the record, having won the exact same category in 1995 for his role in Mad About You, 37 years after his first win for Caesar’s Hour.Reiner is the first posthumous Emmy winner in an acting category since Raul Julia in 1995.View image in fullscreenBetty Gilpin, who won outstanding guest actress in a comedy series for Widow’s Bay.Photograph: Lisa O’Connor/AFP/Getty ImagesElsewhere in the awards, Apple TV horror comedyWidow’s Baywon eight Emmys for its debut season, including Betty Gilpin winning outstanding guest actress in a comedy for her role on the show.Gilpin read a rapid-fire comic poem as her acceptance speech that included the lines “our business is stupid, but actors are the bomb” and “let’s all lean more toward Sam Shepard and less toward Sam Altman”.HBO medical dramaThe Pitthad a strong second-year showing with four wins, including best prosthetics, casting and outstanding guest actor in a drama for 73-year-old first-time nominee Ernest Harden Jr.Harden, who won for portraying the last days of Louie Cloverfield, a warm man struggling with alcoholism who is a constant presence in the emergency room, wept when his name was called.“I am just on cloud 25,” Harden said backstage at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. “I’m not saying it’s a complete surprise because The Pitt is such a powerful show to come from, but just to get it in your hands is unreal.”View image in fullscreenErnest Harden Jr with his Emmy for outstanding guest actor in a drama series for The Pitt.Photograph: Lisa O’Connor/AFP/Getty ImagesPluribus, another Apple TV debut, won four trophies Sunday night including editing, production design and sound mixing. Created by Breaking Bad’s Vince Gilligan,Pluribuscould challenge The Pitt in the top drama categories.DTF St Louiswon six awards in the limited series categories, with co-stars and veteran actors David Harbour and Linda Cardellini both becoming first-time Emmy winners.“Thank you to everybody who along the way through the years helped me get to this moment of a real dream come true,” Cardellini said, through tears.Shailene Woodley won her first Emmy for best guest actress in a drama for her role on Paradise.Spider-Noir, the Nicolas Cage serieswhich was cancelled after one season last week by Amazon Prime Video, won five Emmys including visual effects and stunts.TheTelevisionAcademy hands out more than 100 primetime Emmys, with most of them presented this weekend in a pair of ceremonies dedicated mostly to production crew and guest star roles. They were previously known as the Creative Arts Emmys but have now been rebranded as simply the first two nights of the 78th Emmy Awards.The primetime Emmys ceremony, also held at the Peacock Theater and hosted by Mariska Hargitay, will air live on NBC on 14 September US time.Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsEmmysRob ReinerAwards and prizesTelevisionThe PittThe BearUS television industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Susan Sarandon says she is losing movie roles because of her support for Palestine | Susan Sarandon | The Guardian
description: Oscar-winning actor says she and other outspoken critics of Israel have found it ‘impossible’ to get hired by major studios
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Oscar-winning actor says she and other outspoken critics of Israel have found it ‘impossible’ to get hired by major studios
Content: Actor Susan Sarandon at the premiere of The Echo Chamber at the Venice film festival in Italy on Sunday.Photograph: Fabio Frustaci/EPAView image in fullscreenActor Susan Sarandon at the premiere of The Echo Chamber at the Venice film festival in Italy on Sunday.Photograph: Fabio Frustaci/EPASusan SarandonSusan Sarandon says she is losing movie roles because of her support for PalestineOscar-winning actor says she and other outspoken critics of Israel have found it ‘impossible’ to get hired by major studiosReutersSun 6 Sep 2026 20.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Oscar-winning actorSusan Sarandonhas said she is still losing work because of her outspoken support for Palestinians, despite what she ⁠described as a broader shift ⁠in public opinion against ​US support for Israel.Speaking at theVenice film festival, where she is promoting her latest movie The Echo Chamber, Sarandon said some parts of the film industry continued to ⁠shun her over her activism.“I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of the historical relevance ofPalestineand the ties of Zionists with America and our politics,” ⁠she said. “That has been a major revelation for people, how much money the United States gives to Israel, nobody really ​understood that.“US opinion pollshave shown support ‌for Israel softeningand sympathy for ‌Palestinians rising since the start of the Gaza war in 2023.But the 79-year-old actor said her support for the Palestinian ‌cause continued to carry professional consequences.“I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still,” she told reporters. “But that’s the power structure. I think [among] people, certainly internationally, I feel welcome.“An Academy Award winner for Dead Man Walking, Sarandon rose to prominence in films including The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Bull Durham and Thelma and Louise.‘Many of us in Israel live in a state of shock at the savagery’: veteran director Amos Gitai returns to GazaRead moreShe wasdropped by her longstanding talent agency UTA in 2023after ‌remarks she made while attending pro-Palestinian rallies one month after the Hamas attack on Israel, including: “There are a lot of people afraid of being Jewish at this time, and are getting a taste of what it feels like to be a Muslim in this country.”The conflict has spilled into this year’s Venice film festival, with activists ​calling on organisers to raise the Palestinian flag in recognition of Palestinian directors screening at the event.The festival’s artistic director, Alberto Barbera, has said this is impossible because Italy does not formally recognise the state of Palestine, but he has pointed to several films being shown on the Lido that show the struggle of ordinary Palestinians.Sarandon said resistance to hiring outspoken critics ofIsrael⁠remained particularly strong among major studios.“If it is a major studio, I think ​it’s not just with me but with ​other people who have been told ​that that is impossible,” she said, thanking Andrea Pallaoro, the director of The Echo Chamber, for casting ​her.“I found my family, ‌I found my people ​and I’m OK,” she ​said, sparking prolonged applause at the news conference.In her latest film, adapted from the final screenplay by Italian film-maker Bernardo Bertolucci, Sarandon plays an ageing singer who hires a music producer recovering from drug addiction to work on a comeback album.The Echo Chamber is one of 21 films competing for Venice’s Golden Lion award, which will be presented on 12 September.Explore more on these topicsSusan SarandonVenice film festivalFestivalsPalestineIsraelFilm industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Work hard – nobody cares how good you used to be’: Paul Smith at 80 on love, fun and his fabulous life in fashion | Fashion | The Guardian
description: With the release of his new biography, the British designer talks about leaving school at 15, the real reason he won’t retire and why no one wears velvet trousers any more
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: With the release of his new biography, the British designer talks about leaving school at 15, the real reason he won’t retire and why no one wears velvet trousers any more
Content: ‘We were in love, we are in love still’ ... on a trip to Paris with Pauline in September 1973.Photograph: © Paul Smith/Paul Smith ArchiveView image in fullscreen‘We were in love, we are in love still’ ... on a trip to Paris with Pauline in September 1973.Photograph: © Paul Smith/Paul Smith ArchiveThe big interviewFashionInterview‘Work hard – nobody cares how good you used to be’: Paul Smith at 80 on love, fun and his fabulous life in fashionEmine SanerWith the release of his new biography, the British designer talks about leaving school at 15, the real reason he won’t retire and why no one wears velvet trousers any moreMon 7 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 07.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGo for a browse in the Paul Smith shop in Mayfair, London, on any given Saturday and you’ll likely find an older shop assistant, straight-backed in fine tailoring, approaching to help you with a new shirt, or a suit for a special occasion, perhaps a jaunty pair of socks. There aren’t many global fashion brands, Paul Smith points out, perhaps unnecessarily, “where the owner is a Saturday boy”. But working in his shop, one of more than 130 around the world, is probably Smith’s favourite part of the job. “It’s fantastic, you meet so many interesting people,” he says, smiling broadly. Smith’s whole career, he says, has always been about doing things in a different way. He’s the untrained fashion designer who created a global British brand, who put a bright lining or some stripes into classic tailoring, and who has turned down multiple substantial offers to buy his company, in order to remain in control.Sir Paul Smith has just turned 80 – and he has the enviable energy of someone less than half his age, swimming each day before 6am. He’s about to publish his memoir, Threads: My Life in Style. It’s been a good opportunity to do a stocktake. His has undoubtedly been a lucky life – right place, right time, right people (not least his wife, Pauline, whom he met at the age of 21 and who has been integral to his success) – but it’s also a story of hard work, integrity and modesty. We’ll get to whether those values are still relevant in a harsher, more competitive world, and whether Paul Smith can survive.View image in fullscreenFast fashion … Smith aged 11, practising a sprint on his first racing bike.Photograph: © Paul Smith/Paul Smith ArchiveSmith is wonderfully warm and likes to chat. We’re sitting at a table in the basement of his Mayfair shop, surrounded by beautiful and expensive mid-century furniture (he has always sold interesting objects alongside his clothes). Every so often, a staff member walks by and he’ll break off to catch up (“You all right? You had a nice time?”). Online shopping is all very well, I tell him, but I love real-life shops too, or at least those with character. Will they survive? “I hope that the 12 and 14-year-olds today will realise that there’s so much falseness out there,” and that they can find joy and surprise in “an individually owned shop, or a conversation you can have [there]”.Smith didn’t intend to become a designer. Born in 1946, he grew up in Nottingham and wanted to be a racing cyclist until he was hospitalised for eight weeks in a bad accident that ended his dream. “I suppose the nearest link with creativity was my father being an amateur photographer,” he says. Harold Smith worked as a credit draper – people would buy clothing from him in instalments – and Smith got his first job with the same company at the age of 15. Harold also co-founded a local camera club. “I used to go and listen to people talking about something called composition and lighting, and then spent time in the dark room with my father.” Funny, creative, a bit of an inventor, his father seems to have a stronger presence in his book than his mother. Was he more of an influence? “I think so, yes. The photography really taught me to look andsee. So I suppose that helped me look at things carefully. And he was a very good communicator.” Harold died at 92, still inventing fun contraptions (“I suppose a lot of that was creativity or lateral thinking”) and keeping a lot of young friends, which Smith does too. His mother, Marjorie, was loving and stable, which did a lot for Smith’s self-assurance. “I suppose the security of having a mum like that was really nice.” Later, he says, explaining his approach: “I think it’s just I’m so at ease with life.”View image in fullscreenEarly days …  Smith in his first shop in the 70s.Photograph: © Paul Smith/Paul Smith ArchiveA 21-year-old Smith was still living at home when he met Pauline, who is six years older than him and already had two children and a dog. “It was instant family,” says Smith. Pauline had trained at the Royal College of Art, had worked in London at a fashion company and was then teaching art in Nottingham. She introduced Smith to art, creativity and interesting people. All of it – this new world, and being a stepfather to two young children – was “real big stuff”, he says.In 1970, Smith was working at a Nottingham boutique. After he took some courses in clothes construction, Pauline encouraged him to open his own “shop” – a tiny back room of a building on a little lane in the city centre – which he called, with hilarious fanciness, Paul Smith Vêtements Pour Homme. “I know, that was a bit pretentious,” he says, laughing. From there, Smith gradually built a business with more than 1,200 employees, about 130 shops around the world (the brand is huge in Japan) and, at its peak, a turnover north of £200m a year.The 70s were an exciting time to be building a fashion brand. After opening a shop in New York, Smith and friends would go to Studio 54, pushing glamorous Pauline to the front and following in her slipstream. Smith remembers seeing Liza Minnelli there, among others. “[There was] Andy Warhol, there was Karl Lagerfeld, Issey Miyake, Woody Allen,” he says. “We became nocturnal for a week. At the same time there were great art galleries, and openings – [art dealer] Leo Castelli, and people like [Robert] Rauschenberg, and artists that were hot kids on the block.”View image in fullscreenSmith with David Bowie and GQ editor Dylan Jones at the 2002 GQ men of the year awards.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty ImagesIt was special, he says, “because it was a time of blank paper, being able to try things out. There was nobody to say you couldn’t do it. I think the problem we all have now is that everything’s so homogenised, everything’s so available. We’re overburdened with information, with opinions, with everything.” Back then, he says, even the smallest things could feel like a huge discovery – the rag rugs he found on a Greek holiday and brought back for the shop, a penknife from an obscure fishing store. Smith discovered the Filofax, the essential 80s yuppie organiser, made by an old east London military supplies company; he popularised it by stocking it in his shop.In the 90s, Paul Smith the brand hit its fashionable peak, worn by royalty, film stars, rock stars and anyone who’d saved up a bit of money for a wedding or to look good on a Saturday night. Smith became friends with many icons, including David Bowie, Jack Nicholson and Paul McCartney. Did he ever feel out of his depth or intimidated by them? “I suppose [it’s] lack of education,” he says. “I’m hopeless at reading, I’m dyslexic, I’m lousy at history.” He left school at 15, but then, he adds, many rock stars left school around then too. And with rock stars and royalty, “you should never assume that they don’t feel the same. My company motto is ‘never assume’, and that’s helped me enormously over the years.”The company has struggled in recent times. “We’re definitely not as relevant as we used to be,” says Smith. But longevity “is very much about hard work, continuity, reassessing, never thinking you’ve ‘made it’ because nobody cares how good you used to be”. The world may have changed, but there is still a market for beautiful clothes, says Smith. “If you were here last Saturday, [we sold] at least 10 suits for weddings, for instance. It’s my job to understand the world and how it’s changing, and the wishes and demands of the public.”Smith is surrounded by young people in the company, he says, which helps to keep him in touch. “Yes, a lot of our customers are older, but 20-odd% are not, they’re quite young, which is really exciting.” But what he has noticed, when he looks at younger people, is less individuality. “They’re not as … brave is the wrong word, but the creativity in terms of dressing is not as it used to be. I think there’s a lot of nervousness about standing out and peer pressure, and what you think you should look like. Whereas we just did whatever was part of our personality.” I think he’s getting at the idea that a slight eccentric and unique Britishness has been lost in globalisation. Remembering his own youth, “I had very long hair, I had velvet trousers.” It was silly, but fun, he says.View image in fullscreenPaul and Pauline at some friends’ wedding, Nottingham, 1969.Photograph: © Paul Smith/Paul Smith ArchiveThe company has never quite recovered after the pandemic – there’s not much need for workwear when many people work from home in the comfort of a tracksuit. Meanwhile, Brexit, he says, “was a nightmare”. Last year, Paul Smith made a loss of more than £22m and, Smith says, “we’ll lose again this year, but luckily I’ve got enough [to cover it]”. But he adds, “we’re going down the right route now. We’re on the verge of breaking even again.” The world is tough: “wars everywhere”. And unlike the energy and optimism of the 70s, 80s and 90s, it feels as if the general mood among people, he says, is worry. Smith has survived recessions and the 2008 financial crash. Does this period feel more difficult? “To me, it does. I’m not sure whether it is, but to me it does.” One reason is that independent shops are struggling – Smith has always sold to other boutiques, and they’re closing rapidly, hit by high costs and fading high streets. Is he an optimist? “I personally am, because I’m so full of joy the whole time – and positivity.”As the majority owner, Smith runs the company as he wants. “The good thing is that your expectations are your expectations, they’re not the shareholders’ expectations,” he says. “As soon as you’re in a commercial situation, it’s all about the profit, the expansion, and I’ve seen so many lovely companies die because of financial takeovers.” When he says “die”, I realise he doesn’t mean they collapse, but lose their soul – which I think, to him, is the same thing. In his book, though, he writes about feeling a pang of envy if he heard about Prada, say, opening a new shop. Less so now, though. “Over the years you make comparisons and you think: ‘Oh, should I be doing that?’ In the last two or three years I’ve grown out of that.”View image in fullscreenThe man behind the name … Smith in his Mayfair shop on Albemarle Street, London, June 2026.Photograph: Suki Dhanda and Hannah Weinstein/The GuardianSmith received many big offers to sell throughout his career. Why didn’t he? “I like my job, I love going into work. I love the fact that you can have an idea and turn it into reality, I think that’s really exciting.” Although he certainly is rich, there’s also a modesty to him. He drives his Mini to work, and while he and Pauline live in a swanky part of west London, it’s in the same home they’ve owned since 1980. He was never motivated by money, he says. “We don’t desire jets, we don’t desire grand things, and that was always it, right from the beginning.” What did he want to achieve when he set out? “This sounds crass and stupid, but just a nice life, a nice day. Pauline and I were in love, we are in love still. And luckily we’ve done well.”The DNA of the brand is so wrapped up in Smith, will it survive without him? “I don’t know. I think so, because there’s enough key people who understand it. It will change, of course it will change, but the basic DNA should stay the same. [It] should be a company that’s modest, down to earth, gives good service, respects people.” It does, sadly, sound a little old-fashioned and idealistic in our brazen capitalist age. Smith points out they have new executives, including a new managing director, who “come from very commercial backgrounds, so the wish for me is getting the balance right. I think I probably am such an oddball in today’s world that you’ve got to make sure that you’ve got a team behind you.”View image in fullscreenPaul Smith in his attic office.Photograph: © Paul Smith/Paul Smith ArchiveSmith has no intention of retiring. “I don’t think Pauline would want me at home,” he says. His latest passion is Paul Smith’s Foundation, passing on knowledge and skills – and eventually bursaries – to young designers and entrepreneurs. “All the things I didn’t know at 20 is what I’m trying to help them with.” Not just the sexy stuff like design, but essential things such as VAT and contracts. He intends to leave all his money to the foundation. “Literally everything,” he says. (Pauline has her own wealth from selling her stake in the company and will look after the family, he says.) “My wish is to just help future generations.” He is appalled at big fashion brands who employ young designers straight out of college, “draining the ideas from them” and then putting them out of a job within a few years.Smith wrote his book with these young designers in mind. “I wanted a book that helps people in the creative industry realise that you can do it a different way,” he says. But lots of us could do with being reminded, from Smith’s account, about what makes a good life – curiosity, creativity, humour, looking after people, and ambition but not greed. In a challenging world, he stays upbeat, he says, with “humour, a lovely team, not taking myself too seriously”. Plus, working in his shops, chatting to customers, taking delight in the art on the walls and the beautiful things he helps to create or find. He isn’t so different from the young man who opened his first shop 56 years ago. “I definitely think I’m still a shopkeeper.”Threads: My Life in Style by Paul Smith is published on 10 September by Macmillan, in hardback, ebook and audio, read by Bill Nighy.
