title: A new start after 60: I was always quiet – but at 82 I’m a famous, funny fashion influencer | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Vivienne Truran was a civil servant and antiques dealer, who spent most of her life in the background. At 80, she realised how outgoing she was, and started a soaringly successful new career
Author: Paula Cocozza
Headline: Vivienne Truran was a civil servant and antiques dealer, who spent most of her life in the background. At 80, she realised how outgoing she was, and started a soaringly successful new career
Content: ‘Timeless fashionista’ … Vivienne Truran.Photograph: Bethan Miller-Carey/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Timeless fashionista’ … Vivienne Truran.Photograph: Bethan Miller-Carey/The GuardianA new start after 60FashionA new start after 60: I was always quiet – but at 82 I’m a famous, funny fashion influencerVivienne Truran was a civil servant and antiques dealer, who spent most of her life in the background. At 80, she realised how outgoing she was, and started a soaringly successful new careerPaula CocozzaMon 7 Sep 2026 01.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It took me till I was 80 to realise that I’m quite an outgoing and loud person,” says Vivienne Truran. Now 82, she has 829,000 followers on Instagram, where she posts daily videos about her outfit choices, including which of her trademark glasses work best with her look, all in her lilting Cardiff accent.It all started 18 months ago. “I think I want to be an influencer,” she announced in one of her first reels. “Now, what can I influence people in?”Wasn’t Truran outgoing when she was younger? “No,” she says. “My husband, Martin, was 6ft 4in. Rugby player, good-looking chap. When he walked into the room, he took the room. So I, like a good wife, was in the background. You can’t have two noisy people in a relationship. It doesn’t work.”View image in fullscreen‘I’m just somebody who sits in a house, puts on clothes and chats a lot.’Photograph: Bethan Miller-Carey/The GuardianThey were happily married for more than 40 years; but Martin got dementia and had a number of strokes, and died in hospital during Covid. Truran has no children, and no siblings. Feeling isolated, she would make a cake and sometimes take a piece to her then neighbour – now talent manager – James Rolling, and they became friends. It was Rolling who persuaded her to get in front of the camera.He introduced her to his friends as his carer, for a joke; hence her Instagram tag @vivthecarer. They “respect each other and are a good team”, Truran says, but if she could change her tag, she would be “Viv from the Vale … like Jenny from the block”. She describes herself as a “timeless fashionista”, which she says is her third career.Truran grew up in Cardiff, Wales. She was raised by her grandmother and her mother; her parents divorced when she was three. In childhood, she says, “I thought of myself as ‘a pound a week’, because that’s what my father paid my mother in maintenance … My mother brought me up never to rely on anybody but myself.”At 16, Truran wanted to train to be a hairdresser, but her mother insisted she join the civil service “because there was a good pension. I was 16!” But, she says, “in those days you did what your parents told you to do”. She worked for the Post Office (then part of the civil service), then British Telecom, and took redundancy at 48 – before reinventing herself as an antiques dealer.View image in fullscreenGlasses to match every outfit …Photograph: Bethan Miller-Carey/The Guardian“I realised I was quite entrepreneurial,” she says. “I’d buy something and think: ‘I can sell that for a lot more.’” Back then, “rather than do Google Lens and say, ‘What’s this?’, you had to use your brain.” At her busiest, she ran three antiques stalls. “It was a gamble,” she says. “But you were gambling on yourself, your ability.”Truran thinks her mother would love her Instagram posts. Even in a care home, after she was diagnosed with cancer, “she would go down for breakfast, then she’d change to go down for lunch, then change to go down for dinner. She absolutely loved dressing up.”Historically, Truran says she was less interested in fashion, though she did take a pair of her first husband’s swimming trunks and style them as hotpants in the 1960s, and then there was her beatnik phase.Life as an influencer has given her a different identity, and a routine. “I get up every morning, have a shower, get dressed and make my video. When you’re retired and older, the best thing you can do in your life is find yourself a routine.”View image in fullscreen‘I do enjoy saying: “Look, I might be old, but I’m alive”’ … Vivienne Truran.Photograph: Bethan Miller-Carey/The GuardianTruran has become so well known that sometimes she gets stopped in the street. “It’s all surreal. People say to me: ‘You’re famous.’ Why am I famous?” she says. “I’m nobody special. I’m just somebody who sits in a house, puts on clothes and chats a lot.” Still, she hopes to reach 1 million followers.“We’ve got to make the most of what we’ve got and live to the full, because we don’t know what’s around the corner,” she says. “Don’t listen to what other people tell you. Listen to yourself.“She enjoys subverting age-related expectations. Shopping in a branch of the fashion chain Pull & Bear recently, she noticed young women looking at her in surprise when she leaned forward to pay with her Apple watch. “I do enjoy saying, ‘Look, I might be old, but I’m alive.’”Her followers have become a kind of community. “I always say to them: ‘Come on. Keep following me on this journey.’ I’m very excited about that. We don’t know where we’re going … but let’s see.”Explore more on these topicsFashionA new start after 60Social mediaDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for courgette and preserved lemon herby giant couscous | Food | The Guardian
description: A seasonal special featuring both summer vibes and autumn comfort
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: A seasonal special featuring both summer vibes and autumn comfort
Content: Georgina Hayden’s courgettes with preserved lemon and herby couscous.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden’s courgettes with preserved lemon and herby couscous.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.FoodGeorgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for courgette and preserved lemon herby giant couscousA seasonal special featuring both summer vibes and autumn comfortGeorgina HaydenMon 7 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile I dig my head in the sand at September’s arrival and the back-to-school dread, I’m trying to hold on to summer flavours for as long as possible. And this salad does just that: it’s summer and autumn, vibrant and comforting, all at the same time. It can also be served a multitude of ways: still warm, at room temperature with the feta added at the last minute, or even as leftovers (it’s great for lunchboxes, say).Courgette and preserved lemon herby giant couscousIf your courgettes are homegrown and on the larger side, use just two or three. And although it’s not a necessity, I like to cut them into irregular shapes, because that gives them more surface area to char and flavour.Prep10 minCook30 minServes44 courgettes,trimmed and roughly chopped2 preserved lemons,halved, flesh and seeds removed and discarded, peel finely chopped4 garlic cloves,unpeeled1 heaped tsp groundcoriander½ tsp sweet smokedpaprikaSea salt andblack pepperExtra-virgin olive oil200g wholewheat giant couscous, rinsed½25g packflat-leaf parsley, finely choppedA few mint sprigs, leaves picked and finely chopped1 bunch of spring onions, trimmed and finely sliced200gfetaHeat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9. Put the courgettes, preserved lemon peel, garlic cloves, ground coriander and paprika in a large roasting tray and season generously.Drizzle over two tablespoons of the oil, toss well to coat, and roast for 20 minutes, until everything is a little charred. Leave to cool a little, then press the garlic flesh into any juices in the tray, and remove and discard the skins.Meanwhile, bring a pan of salted water to a boil and cook the couscous for about eight minutes (or according to the packet instructions). Drain and rinse under cold water, then transfer to a large bowl.When everything is ready and has cooled a little, mix the courgettes and any tray juices into the couscous. Add the chopped herbs and spring onions, mix again, then taste and adjust the seasoning as required. Just before serving, finish by crumbling over the feta.Explore more on these topicsFoodSaladCheeseVegetablesSummer food and drinkFruitCereals and grainsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Cheese pie, seed crackers and prawn rolls: Ravinder Bhogal’s recipes for cooking with filo | Food | The Guardian
description: Making your own filo is notoriously faffy but, luckily, there are great ready-made versions out there that make these crunchy, golden savoury treats a doddle
Author: Ravinder Bhogal
Headline: Making your own filo is notoriously faffy but, luckily, there are great ready-made versions out there that make these crunchy, golden savoury treats a doddle
Content: Ravinder Bhogal’s cheese and spring onion pie.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.View image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s cheese and spring onion pie.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.FoodCheese pie, seed crackers and prawn rolls: Ravinder Bhogal’s recipes for cooking with filoMaking your own filo is notoriously faffy but, luckily, there are great ready-made versions out there that make these crunchy, golden savoury treats a doddleRavinder BhogalMon 7 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlove this gossamer-thin pastry for its lightness and crunch, not least because it can be used for both sweets and savouries. Once, on a trip to Athens, I learned how to make filo from scratch: it needs to be rolled very, very thin, so, unless you are skilled with a rolling pin, it’s hard and time-consuming. Luckily there are good ready-made varieties out there (if you’re using the frozen variety, make sure it’s fully defrosted). And always keep the pastry you are not working with under a damp cloth, because it dries out very quickly and will probably crack.Cheese and spring onion pie (pictured top)This boasts four varieties of cheese and a ruffly top of crisp, golden filo that requires no complicated technique.Prep15 minCook1 hr, plus coolingServes6300gfeta, crumbled250g firm ricotta, crumbled200g halloumi, grated150g gruyere or a sharp cheddar, grated150ml single cream3 eggs25g chives, finely chopped25g dill, finely chopped25g flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped1 large bunch spring onions(8-10), trimmed and finely slicedFinely grated zest of1 unwaxed lemonNutmegSea salt and black pepper125g butter, melted8 sheets filoSesame seeds, to scatterHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. In a large bowl, combine the cheeses, cream, eggs, herbs, spring onion, lemon zest and a good grating of nutmeg, then season to taste.Line the base of a 20-23cm cake tin with baking paper and grease the sides with melted butter. Lay a sheet of pastry in the bottom of the tin, allowing the excess to hang over the sides. Brush generously with butter, then lay on another sheet of pastry at a slight angle, so it doesn’t completely overlap the first sheet, and brush that with butter, too. Repeat until you have six filo sheets covering the base and sides of the tin.Spoon the filling into the pastry base and flatten it out with the back of the spoon. Brush another piece of pastry with butter, fold it in half and lay it on top of the filling, tucking in the excess pastry. Repeat with the last sheet of pastry, then fold in all the overhanging filo to create a lovely textured top. Brush with the remaining butter, sprinkle over the sesame seeds, then bake for 45 minutes, until golden. Leave the pie to rest and cool for 15 minutes before serving.Seeded filo crackersView image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s seeded filo crackers.These require no dough making or rolling: they’re simply made by layering ready-made filo pastry. They have an addictive crunch, and are ideal for swiping through your favourite dips.Prep5 minCook20 min, plus coolingServes61tbsp fennel seeds1tbsp caraway seeds1tbsp coriander seeds2tbsp sesame seeds2tbsp nigella seeds1tsppul biber½tsp onion powder1tsp flaky sea salt4 sheets filo pastry100ml extra-virgin olive oilIn a mortar, lightly crush the fennel, caraway and coriander seeds, then stir in the sesame and nigella seeds, pul biber, onion powder and salt.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Put a sheet of baking paper the size of your baking tray on a work surface, and top it with a sheet of filo. Brush with olive oil, then lay over a second sheet of filo, pressing it down lightly to get rid of any air pockets, and brush with oil. Repeat with the remaining two filo sheets, brush the top with the remaining olive oil and scatter over the spiced seed mix generously and evenly, pressing it in gently, so it sticks.Using a sharp knife, cut the filo into strips, triangles or squares – whatever you like – then slide the baking paper on to a baking tray and bake for 10 minutes. Leave to cool on the baking sheet to crisp up, then serve with your favourite dip.Saffron prawn boreksView image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s saffron prawn boreks.With the addition of saffron, these crisp prawn rolls feel rather lavish. Perfect to pass around at a party with a glass of something fizzy.Prep15 minCook40 min, plus coolingMakes16 small boreks2tbsp olive oil1 onion, peeled and very finely chopped1 red pepper, halved, pith and seeds removed, and flesh finely chopped1 carrot, coarsely grated1green bird’s eyechilli, finely chopped½tsp pul biber1 pinchsaffron threads, steeped in 1 tbsp warm water for 5-10 minutes200g raw prawns, peeled, deveined, half blitzed in a food processor, half roughly chopped25g coriander, leaves very finely choppedFinely grated zest of1 unwaxed lemon, plus the juice of ½ lemonSea salt4 sheets filo75g butter, melted1tsp fennel seeds mixed with½ tsp pul biber, to garnishPut the oil in a pan on a medium heat, then saute the onion, pepper and carrot until soft but not coloured. Add the green chilli, pul biber and saffron, stir-fry briefly, then take off the heat and tip into a bowl. Leave to cool slightly, then stir in the blitzed and chopped prawns, coriander, lemon zest and juice, and season with salt.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. On a clean surface, lay out a filo sheet and brush it with melted butter. Using a sharp knife, cut the filo into four equal rectangles. Spread a log of the filling mix along the short end of one rectangle, leaving a 1½cm gap on each side, then roll up the pastry, tucking in the ends to secure the filling. Put the roll seam-side down on a lined baking sheet and brush with more melted butter. Repeat with the remaining three sheets of filo and filling, then sprinkle over fennel seed and pul biber mix.Bake for 15-20 minutes, until golden brown and crisp, and serve hot or at room temperatureExplore more on these topicsFoodPastryVegetablesHerbs and spicesNuts and seedsCheesePierecipesShareReuse this content

title: The Gymnastics Academy changed my prepaid booking but said ‘no’ to a refund | Money | The Guardian
description: I arranged for my daughter to attend three sessions during the school holidays but the venue and one of the dates were changed
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: I arranged for my daughter to attend three sessions during the school holidays but the venue and one of the dates were changed
Content: All kitted out for three gym sessions: then the venue and dates were changed.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyView image in fullscreenAll kitted out for three gym sessions: then the venue and dates were changed.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyConsumer championsMoneyThe Gymnastics Academy changed my prepaid booking but said ‘no’ to a refundI arranged for my daughter to attend three sessions during the school holidays but the venue and one of the dates were changedAnna TimsMon 7 Sep 2026 06.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI booked my daughter for three sessions during the school summer holidays at TheGymnasticsAcademy. The reservation was made and paid for last November because of a promotional offer.In June, I received emails from The Gymnastics Academy, confirming a session for a venue I had not booked. I was concerned my account had been hacked.I emailed the company and was told the venue I had booked had since closed, and my booking had been moved to a different site. One of the dates I’d chosen had also been changed. I had not been notified of this.The new venue was too difficult to reach and the substituted date wasn’t suitable. I asked for a refund and was refused.CH,LeedsThe email you received from The Gymnastics Academy customer services team acknowledged the changes to your booking had caused “frustration and inconvenience” and apologised for “any confusion”. It concluded, however, that you do not meet the criteria for a refund, citing its booking terms.You say you signed an online form, including terms and conditions, when you booked, but have been unable to access it since. The T&Cs on the Academy’s website make no mention of entitlements if it changes the date or venue on a booking.EasyJet Holidays’ ‘spa’ resort was lacking an on-site spa or gymRead moreIn any case, a clause that rules out refunds if that happens may be unlawful under the Consumer Rights Act 2025, according to consumer expert Gary Rycroft of Joseph A Jones & Co Solicitors. “It is likely to be unfair for a trader to be able to unilaterally change fundamental aspects of the delivery of the contract, including dates and venues,” he says.“Just because a term and condition is there does not make it enforceable if it is inherently unfair on the consumer.”The Gymnastics Academy, through its lawyers, told me your account of your experience is “untrue, inaccurate and ultimately misleading”.It said that you had entered a contract with a “separate legal entity” which owned the now closed venue.It declined to specify which legal entity. It also said that you had signed T&Cs with the “relevant operating company which clearly contained provisions governing the operating company’s right to change dates, times and venues”.Of the enforceability of its terms, it said it “maintains a Primary Authority Partnership with Trading Standards, and its current terms and conditions have been vetted/approved through this relationship”.Since you paid by debit card, you were able to make a chargeback claim via your bank, which re-credited the payment while it investigated. It warned you that if the company disputed your claim, it may take the money back.It appears The Gymnastics Academy did not, so you are no longer out of pocket, although you were left trying to find and fund holiday childcare at late notice for three of your working days.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsMoneyConsumer championsConsumer affairsConsumer rightsSchool holidaysGymnasticsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Students: as cycle thefts soar, here’s how to protect your bike  | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Thefts spike during freshers’ week so make sure you choose a good lock and check your insurance
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Thefts spike during freshers’ week so make sure you choose a good lock and check your insurance
Content: Insuring your bike from the moment you arrive at university is a good idea.Photograph: Robert Evans/AlamyView image in fullscreenInsuring your bike from the moment you arrive at university is a good idea.Photograph: Robert Evans/AlamyCyclingStudents: as cycle thefts soar, here’s how to protect your bikeThefts spike during freshers’ week so make sure you choose a good lock and check your insuranceDonna FergusonMon 7 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor hard-up students, a bike is a low-cost way to travel. But with cycle theft at an all-time high, experts are urging young people not to skimp on insurance and to buy a good lock.Recent data from Aviva shows one in five (19%) of insurance claims involving student possessions relates to bicycles.James Brown, managing director ofBikeRegister, a national database used by policeto match stolen bikes to their owners, says they often get reported stolen shortly after the university term starts. “Speaking to university security teams, we know that in freshers’ week, and the weeks following, there are spikes in cycle theft,” he says.Life in bike theft Britain: ‘Afterwards, I couldn’t face going outside’Read moreHotspots are all university towns, with Oxford recording the highest number in 2025, followed by Cambridge, York and Cardiff, saysbicycle insurer Bikmo.One of the reasons, Brown says, is that some students try to save money by securing their bike with a cheap cable lock bought online, “which isn’t worth anything because it could almost be cut with a pair of scissors”.Brown recommends investing instead in a bike lock road-tested against specialist thief tools – such as angle grinders – bySold Secure, a security testing organisationowned by the Master Locksmiths Association.These are graded from bronze to diamond, but you don’t necessarily need to shell out for diamond. A gold-rated Sold Secure lock should offer a high level of protection against dedicated bike thieves, even in high-risk areas. We found some D-locks for less than £20.It is also a good idea to insure your bike the moment you arrive at university.“If you’re relying on a bike to get to class, then losing it could really affect your education,” says Kara Gammell, a personal finance expert at MoneySuperMarket.com.View image in fullscreenUniversity towns and cities are hotspots for cycle theft, with Oxford topping the list last year.Photograph: Uli_B/GettyProbably the first thing to do is check if you are covered under your parents’ existing home contents insurance policy. You may automatically be covered against theft or loss under its “temporarily removed from the home” section while you are living away in student accommodation or a shared flat.Alternatively, it may be that their policy can be extended to cover your possessions.For example, AxaInsuranceUK and Admiral will automatically cover bikes worth less than £350 that are kept both in and away from the home – including at university – as standard.While this sounds like a good deal, the problem with relying on a parent’s policy is that if their child’s bike is stolen, making a claim could affect the main policyholder’s no-claims discount and future premiums.If you also have to pay a chunky excess for an old bike, you may end up thinking whether it’s worth making a claim in the long run, says Gammell.Also, be aware that some insurers will expect students to come home every 90 days, and will refuse to cover a bike left in unoccupied student accommodation.A better option could be to shop around for specific standalone cycle insurance with a low excess – for example from Bikmo, BackPedal, Cover4Cycles or Laka.If you are moving into halls of residence, you may find the package you signed up to includes some contents insurance, but it can be basic and may not cover you if there is no forced entry.Meanwhile, if you are moving into a shared house, check with the landlord or letting agent what insurance – if any – is in place.If none of the above is a runner, you (or your parents) may have to sort out a home contents policy for your accommodation, which would insure your laptop, mobile phone and other belongings, as well as your bike.View image in fullscreenA lock that will withstand specialist thief tools is recommended.Photograph: shotbydave/GettyThe Save the Student website has a usefulguide. It says Cover4Insurance is its most-recommended student insurance provider in 2026.“Burglars know student houses aren’t always the most secure, and may have high-value items inside, like laptops, TVs and games consoles,” says Save the Student’s Tom Allingham. “So it really is worth insuring your goods.”Bear in mind insurers may specify what type of lock you need and require a bike to be locked to an immovable object, even in communal areas (such as the hallway of a student house). “It’s key to double-check your policy and the small print,” says Gammell.Registering its frame number for free on property databases, such as BikeRegister and Immobilise, is another good idea.Brown also recommends uploading time-stamped photos, any distinguishing marks and relevant receipts to the entry. That way, he says, you can easily prove ownership and value for a claim. It also helps police to return it.Registering it on a property database can also act as a deterrent to thieves if you prominently mark the frame with its newly registered database ID – perhaps by using a tamper-proof QR code sticker or permanent marking kit.Experienced thieves know that this will point any future buyer – or police officer – straight to the entry, Brown says, so they will pick another bike to steal.“They will know it’s going to be difficult to sell on and, if they are caught in possession of the bike, it can be linked back to an original owner, and they can be charged with – at the least – handling stolen goods,” he says.Favour Samuel, the NUS England president, says: “Bike theft is at an all-time high in our cities, and when thieves are unable to steal whole bikes, they’ll steal just the wheels. But don’t let that put you off cycling – it is a great and sustainable way to travel.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingStudent financeUniversitiesConsumer affairsInsuranceStudentsCrimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pixel 11 review: Google sets the bar for standard flagship phones | Google | The Guardian
description: Longer battery life, faster chip, actually useful AI tools and better cameras keep quality Android ahead of competition
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Longer battery life, faster chip, actually useful AI tools and better cameras keep quality Android ahead of competition
Content: The latest Google phone is most refined yet, offering the best balance of price and features for base-model flagship handsets.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe latest Google phone is most refined yet, offering the best balance of price and features for base-model flagship handsets.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.GoogleReviewPixel 11 review: Google sets the bar for standard flagship phonesLonger battery life, faster chip, actually useful AI tools and better cameras keep quality Android ahead of competitionSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 7 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle’s Pixel 11 continues to set the standard for what you should expect from the base model of a flagship phone with class-leading cameras, long software support and almost all the bells and whistles of its most expensive phones.The regular Pixel 11 costs £879 (€999/$899/A$1,499) making it £80 or equivalent more expensive than last year’s model as the cost ofRAMageddon continues to bite. It’s not cheap by any stretch of the imagination, but it comes with 256GB of storage and is £200 less than the Pixel 11 Pro, matching rivalSamsung’s Galaxy S26.At a glance the Pixel 11 looks very similar to theprevious twoGooglephone iterations: glass front and back with flat aluminium sides and large pill-shaped bar at the back, which is much slimmer this time. Stick it in a case and the protruding camera all but disappears.View image in fullscreenThe Pixel 11’s camera bar depth has been reduced by 40% compared with previous models for a sleeker look that doesn’t catch on your pocket quite as much.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 6.3in OLED screen is crisp and super bright with up to a 120Hz refresh rate to keep your scrolling smooth. The in-screen fingerprint scanner is fast and accurate, while thecamera-based face recognitionworks well during the day and is secure enough for use with banking apps, unlike similar systems on most Android rivals.SpecificationsScreen:6.3in 120Hz FHD+ OLED (422ppi)Processor:Google Tensor G6RAM:12GBStorage:256 or 512GBOperating system:Android17Camera:48MP+ 13MP UW + 10.8MP 5x tele; 10.5MP selfieConnectivity:5G, eSIM, wifi 6E, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6 and GNSSWater resistance:IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes)Dimensions:152.8 x 72.0 x 8.6mmWeight:197gFaster and more efficient Tensor G6 chipView image in fullscreenThe Pixel 11 takes less than 90 minutes to fully charge using a 30W or greater power adaptor (not included) hitting 53% in half an hour. It also supports 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThePixelhas a new generation of Google’s chip, the Tensor G6, which is up to 20% faster in tests. It significantly lags top-end rivals from Qualcomm and Apple, so won’t win any raw performance awards, but feels snappy in daily tasks and can handle mid-level gaming just fine.The battery life is also improved over previous models, lasting about 54 hours of light use between charges. That includes actively using the screen for more than seven hours for browsing, messaging, apps and photos across a mix of 5G and wifi.Gaming and more demanding use hits the battery harder, but the Pixel should be able to see out even the heaviest of use days.Android 17 with more proactive AIView image in fullscreenGoogle’s proactive AI tools pop up with timely information in chats and other situations to save you manually having to check your calendar, search for a restaurant or schedule an event.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Pixel 11 runs the latest Android 17 out of the box with operating system and security updates provided untilAugust 2033.The software is slick, nicely animated and well optimised, with plenty of colourful customisation if you want it. As with previous Pixels, it is a showcase for some of Google’s most advanced AI systems, many of which run on-device, making them fast.The most interesting of the tools remains Google’s proactive AI systems, which vary a bit depending on where you live. In the UK the expandedMagic Cuefromlast yearpops up in messages and a few other apps with information such as your schedule, flight or order details, and suggestions for good local restaurants from Google maps or photos to share in a chat. In the US, Canada, Australia and a few other regions, the feature is called “Gemini Proactive Assistance” but has similar powers. If you use a supported app, such as Google Messages, the suggestions are low-key great. Unfortunately it doesn’t work in WhatsApp, Signal or other third-party apps I’ve tried, which limits its usefulness.In the UK and US, Gemini can go further, proactively taking action for you, such asbooking a restaurant via OpenTable, which is the type of assistance that has long been promised by various AI agents.Another useful AI feature is built directly into Google’s keyboard called Rambler, which is voice typing on steroids. You can speak naturally to it and the system will remove your ums and ers and other deviations to produce a succinct, fully formed sentence or paragraph. It makes trying to dictate a rushed messaged while hustling for public transport a lot easier, although it doesn’t show your text until after you hit the stop button, unlike most other dictation tools.CameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app is fairly simple to use while being feature rich with plenty of tools and modes to make the best of your photography.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Pixel 11 has three cameras on the back and a solid 10.5-megapixel selfie camera in the screen.The improved main 48MP camera captures excellent photos across a range of lighting conditions, including low light where its larger sensor helps capture more of what’s available. The 13MP ultra-wide camera is one of the best on a phone of this class, helpful for fitting more in the shot or providing a different perspective. But it is the 10.8MP 5x telephoto camera that sets it apart from the competition, capable of meaningfully closing the distance to objects. In bright light it can digitally zoom to 30x magnification with surprisingly good results.Entirely new for the Pixel camera this year is the“Looks” feature, which allows you to customise how the phone captures and processes your photos for very different styles far beyond simple filters applied after the fact.There are three versions of the default look available – natural, vanilla and shadows – plus six more-distinctive looks, including “digi” that replicates the look of the old digital cameras that has recently become popular. Each look can be customised in colour, tone, grain and sharpness, so you can get arty or replicate a particular film style.If you are a Pixel user who has ever thought its photos look a little too cold, dramatic or overly processed, this is for you.The Pixel shoots great video at up to 4K at 60 frames a second. The newMagic Capturefeature is a one-button shooting mode that records video and photos automatically that is best used during events such as birthday parties where you want to be more in the moment but still capture the scene.Google has also added a “Creator Suite” mode to the video capture, which shoots straight to a folder you can quickly storyboard and trim to create a video. It also has a teleprompter mode for shooting face to camera, a social media grid to get the alignment correct and speech enhancement that cuts out background noise.All these features are in addition to Google’s popular Auto Best Take, Add Me and Camera Coachfrom last year, which makes the new Pixel camera one of the most feature rich available.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe Pixel 11 is available in a range of colours including the standard mat black (obsidian).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe batteryis rated to lastin excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repairwith manualsandparts available.The Pixel 11 is contains 33% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down thephone’s environmental impactin its report and willrecycle old devicesfor free.PriceThe Google Pixel 11 costs from£879(€999/$899/A$1,499) in a choice of four colours.For comparison, thePixel 10acosts£499, the Pixel 11 Pro costs£1,079, the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs£1,279, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from£1,799, theSamsung Galaxy S26costs£879and theApple iPhone 17costs£799.VerdictThe Pixel 11 isn’t the most advanced Google phone, nor is it the cheapest. But this middle-ground model offers more than enough to beat the competition and question whether you really need to spend more on a Pro phone.It offers, yet again, a very high-quality experience, great triple camera, long software support and very good battery life. It won’t win any raw performance awards, so those looking for a gaming phone should look elsewhere, but it feels fast and responsive in daily use.Google’s AI tools are second to none, particularly its Rambler dictation feature in the keyboard and the proactive Gemini features, which offer genuinely useful help even if they are not available in every third-party app.The new camera looks feature provides more control over photos than ever before on a Pixel, so you can tailor it to your preferences or get creative far beyond simple filters.It may not have changed all that much from last year’sequally excellent Pixel 10, and it isn’t quite thebargain the Pixel 10ais, but the Pixel 11 is the best phone you can get under £900.Pros:seven years of software updates, great camera with 5x telephoto, great screen, impressive local AI features, Qi2.2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, long battery life, good size, fast fingerprint and face recognition, 256GB starting storage.Cons:face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance short of rivals, no physical SIM card slot in the US, heavier than rivals, not a big upgrade on previous model, no wifi 7.View image in fullscreenThe combination of fast face recognition and in-screen fingerprint scanner with the slick screen keep the Pixel 11 feeling responsive in use.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsGooglePixelSmartphonesAlphabetMobile phonesAndroidreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Is it true that … hard water damages hair? | Hair care | The Guardian
description: Mineral deposits can accumulate, making hair drier, but removing them can cause different problems
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: Mineral deposits can accumulate, making hair drier, but removing them can cause different problems
Content: Illustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianIs it true that …Hair careIs it true that … hard water damages hair?Mineral deposits can accumulate, making hair drier, but removing them can cause different problemsKate LloydMon 7 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom hair treatments to shower filters, a wave of products have been launched promising to protect hair from the “problems” caused by living in a hard-water area. But are they really necessary? “Hard water has a higher concentration of dissolved minerals, especially calcium and magnesium,” says Desmond Tobin, professor of dermatological science at University College Dublin. “These are naturally occurring in water, particularly water that is not rainwater.”When water moves through soil and rocks, such as limestone, minerals dissolve into it and remain there when it comes out of your tap. These minerals are responsible for the limescale that builds up in your kettle.double quotation markCalcium and magnesium can accumulate on hair washed in hard water“You know you’re living in a hard‑water area by how easy it is to lather up soap,” says Tobin. “If it is really difficult, and it forms a kind of scum rather than bubbles, you’re in a hard-water area. It’s healthy to drink, but it can trigger some issues.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs it true that … you need to detox your scalp?Read moreWashing your hair in hard water can leave mineral deposits on the hair shaft, which some believe make it look duller and feel rougher.There is evidencethat calcium and magnesium can accumulate on hair washed in hard water, although the evidence that this causes damage is less clear.Removing this buildup can cause problems, though, especially for those with dry or brittle hair. Tobin says the best shampoos for doing so are high lather and contain ingredients such as sulfates, which can be harsh on those hair types. “It’s this balancing act between removing the buildup and leaving enough oil in the system to condition the hair,” says Tobin.If you live in a hard-water area and notice your hair getting drier, Tobin recommends installing a water softener in your home.Explore more on these topicsHair careIs it true that …Men's hairWomen's hairBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Going for gold: an early autumn road trip across Finland’s sparkling lake district | Finland holidays | The Guardian
description: On a self-drive break in search of Lake Saimaa’s autumn colours, we encountered blue skies, cosy lakeside cabins and saunas, great food – and lots of stubbornly green trees
Author: Annabelle Thorpe
Headline: On a self-drive break in search of Lake Saimaa’s autumn colours, we encountered blue skies, cosy lakeside cabins and saunas, great food – and lots of stubbornly green trees
Content: Finland’s Lake Saimaa at sunriseView image in fullscreenFinland’s Lake Saimaa at sunriseFinland holidaysGoing for gold: an early autumn road trip across Finland’s sparkling lake districtOn a self-drive break in search of Lake Saimaa’s autumn colours, we encountered blue skies, cosy lakeside cabins and saunas, great food – and lots of stubbornly green treesAnnabelle ThorpeMon 7 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 02.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwasn’t sure what to expect from an autumn trip to Finland, my first ever to the country, but spending an afternoon sprawled on a deck chair beneath blazing blue skies certainly wasn’t part of it. After a morning walking beneath the leafy canopy at theMustila Arboretum– the oldest, most extensive botanical garden in the country – and a lunchtime wine-tasting (more of which later), my friend Sara and I pitched up at the Sahanlahti resort, deep in the FinnishLakeland, only to find sun-drenched scenery that felt far more Mediterranean than Nordic.Sahanlahti was the second stop on a mid-September road trip from Helsinki to the shores of Lake Saimaa; a journey in search ofruska, the spectacular autumn colours that blaze for a few short weeks before the long Finnish winter sets in. However, on our opening drive east from the airport to the Radalla resort, set on Lake Urajärvi, most of the thousands of trees we drove past were resolutely green, with just the very tips of the leaves tinged with auburn, like a foliage balayage.View image in fullscreenEnjoying the peace at Sahanlahti resort on Lake Saimaa.Photograph: Annabelle Thorpe“You’re too early,” the waitress told us, cheerfully, after we had checked in to our chic waterfront cabins, and were tucking into hefty plates of crispy garlic chicken, scattered with freshly picked chanterelles, in Radalla’s quiet dining room. “But you might get some sun tomorrow.” Later, walking back to our cabins through thick drizzle, we agreed she was most probably just being kind.The Radalla resort is just one of dozens of lakeside hotels scattered across southern Finland – many with self-catering cabins, sauna complexes and gleaming metal steps that lead from wooden piers down into the chilly waters of the lake. The grey drizzle we awoke to made a dip less than appealing, and instead we decided to set off for our next stop, taking in the arboretum en route before finding a place for lunch.double quotation markResolutely green trees rolled past us for mile after mile, until slowly the fields began to melt into lakesDriving in southern Finland turned out to be quite different from other countries. Most settlements fringe the lakesides, so they tend to be tucked away down side roads leading off from the main highway. Instead, trees – those resolutely green trees – rolled past us for mile after mile, until slowly the fields began to melt into lakes, one after another, the road snaking alongside the blue-grey waters, or stitching together small islets that lay scattered between them.Googling somewhere for lunch, Sara came across theOllinmäki winery, an unexpected find in a country that grows absolutely no grapes. Instead, berry wines are hugely popular, and once settled in at our table, we were persuaded to try a flight of six, accompanied by a bowl of hearty elk soup (which tasted considerably better than it looked) and a leaf salad with local cheese. One wine, the white currant and berry Myllärin Matti was particularly delicious, with the tang of a crisp sauvignon – although I wouldn’t want to find out what a Finnish hangover feels like.From the winery it was an easy drive to Sahanlahti, by which time the weather had cleared and pin-sharp blue skies gleamed above the shores of Lake Saimaa. The main house – painted butterscotch-yellow and dating back to the mid-18th century, when the owners presided over the local sawmill – had a languidly old-fashioned air, but dinner at theKoskivahti restaurantwas anything but: rich mushroom soup, slivers of goose confit with lingonberry sauce, wafer-thin beetroot carpaccio with tangy goat’s cheese.View image in fullscreenAnnabelle Thorpe and friend foraging for wild mushrooms.Photograph: Annabelle ThorpeIt might have been too early for the leaves to turn, but we had arrived right in the middle of harvest season, when heading out into the fields and islands to pick wild mushrooms and berries (of which there are 35 different varieties) is practically a national sport. We had barely set down our bags at our final stop, Järvisydän resort, before we were whizzing out across Saimaa on a small motor boat, baskets tucked between our feet, to hunt for chanterelles and look for rare ringed seals and ospreys.double quotation markWe had arrived in the middle of harvest season, when heading out into the fields and islands to pick wild mushrooms and berries is practically a national sportThe sky was flawlessly blue as we whipped across the water, disembarking first to pick the mushrooms – slashes of bright yellow among the green undergrowth. We were guided in our harvesting by Sebastian, the 12th generation of the Heiskanen family to be running Järvisydän. “Back in 1654,” he told us, “my family were given a portion of land by the Russian tsar, to build a tavern on the route between St Petersburg and Helsinki.” More than 350 years later, the tavern has morphed into a 100-room resort, offering everything from starkly modern glass-walled cabins, high in the forest, to hexagonal log houses with bedrooms set off a central, fire-lit atrium, and camping pods.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe ‘Hobbit-like spa’ at Järvisydän resortIt’s an extraordinary place: everything – from the vast reception, dwarfed by a replica Viking longship hull hung above reception, to the restaurants, bar and the Hobbit-like spa – is built entirely from local stone and timber. A visit to the spa seemed the perfect way to warm up after our chilly boat trip, with six different saunas to dip into – although the “sunken log” sauna, where the temperature reached 70C, gave me some sense of how an ice-cream might feel if left out in the sun.Of the three resorts we visited, Järvisydän was the standout – for its history, for the spectacular scenery of Lake Saimaa that surrounds it, for the delicious mushroom soup and for the long, sunlit walk we took on our final afternoon, through the dense pine forest, where red squirrels skittered around in the branches above. It was a wrench to leave on our last morning, but as we sped back along quiet roads to Helsinki, we agreed Finland had – in spite of our foliage fail – outstripped our expectations. It was more beautiful, more peaceful, more sunkissed than we could ever have imagined.Ruska(the vibrant colours of autumn foliage) begins in the northof the country in early to mid-September, reaching the Lake Saimaa region in the south by early October.The trip was provided byDiscover the World. A four-nightbespoke self-drive tripstaying atRadalla,SahanlahtiandJärvisydänresorts startsat £794pp, including B&B and car hire, but not flights.Explore more on these topicsFinland holidaysScandinavia holidaysRoad tripsScandinavian food and drinkEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The death of ‘hello’: how gen Z – and scammers – put paid to the greeting | Social etiquette | The Guardian
description: If you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you’re sure there’s a human being on the line. Is this the end of an era?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: If you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you’re sure there’s a human being on the line. Is this the end of an era?
Content: With caller ID, gen Z don’t bother with the charade of a greeting.Photograph: Posed by model /Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWith caller ID, gen Z don’t bother with the charade of a greeting.Photograph: Posed by model /Getty ImagesPass notesSocial etiquetteThe death of ‘hello’: how gen Z – and scammers – put paid to the greetingIf you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you’re sure there’s a human being on the line. Is this the end of an era?Mon 7 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Hello.Age:200 years old.Status:Under threat of extinction.That’s ridiculous –we’ve been saying hello to each other for millions of years.Well, that isn’t true. As I just mentioned, the word appeared in print a couple of hundred years ago. But it’s a deviation of“holla”, “hollo”, “halloo” or “hillo”, all of which were used in English as attention-grabbing noises since at least the 16th century.But we use it all the time now.Only because of the telephone. After the phone’s invention by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876, Thomas Edison decided that a newstandardised greetingneeded to be invented.Why?Because previously people tended to greet each other with time-based salutations, such as “good morning” or “good evening”. But the telephone could instantly cross time zones, which made these redundant.But why hello?Because Edison preferred it to Bell’s favoured “Ahoy-hoy”.Shame.I know. Anyway, forget all that, because nobody says hello any more.But I like hello.Too late. Technology has marched on again: everyone has a smartphone with caller ID now. Why go through the charade of a “hello?” when you already know who’s calling you?I don’t know, basic politeness?Tell that to gen Z. The New York Times hasreportedon the death of hello, stating that young people now prefer to answer the phone with “Hi”, “What’s up?” or “Yeah?”.This sounds spurious.It isn’t. Asurveylast year revealed that 40% of 18-24 year-olds feel that it is acceptable to answer the phone without any form of greeting whatsoever.Isn’t that a bit weird?It sort of makes sense, though. Conversations have become free-form things spread across multiple formats. If you’ve just been texting, or DMing, or emailing with someone, a phone call is just a continuation and arguably doesn’t require anything as formal as a hello.Still, it’s nice.Only if you love AI scammers.What the hell? Where did that come from?You didn’t hear about this? Apparently scammers can now replicate your voice with AI, cloning it from your telephone greeting, and use it to beg your loved ones for money. This is a real thing that has been covered by theconsumer watchdog Which?, the BBC andthe Guardian.This is genuinely nightmarish.Guess what the best way to beat it is.I’ll guess rudeness.Correct! If you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you are sure that a friendly human being is on the other end of the line. Not saying hello first could save you a whole heap of trouble.Well, it looks like this is goodbye to hello.Don’t say goodbye. Say au revoir.Because it’s romantic?No, because the terrifying hordes of robot scammers might clone you into a French person, and your family would be confused.Do say:“Hello is becoming obsolete.”Don’t say:“Ahoy-hoy!”Explore more on these topicsSocial etiquettePass notesLanguageTelecommunications industryYoung peopleScamsCrimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China | China | The Guardian
description: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat
Content: Rescue workers evacuate residents amid flooding in Minhou county, Fuzhou, Fujian province.Photograph: cnsphoto/ReutersView image in fullscreenRescue workers evacuate residents amid flooding in Minhou county, Fuzhou, Fujian province.Photograph: cnsphoto/ReutersWeather trackerChinaAnalysisWeather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east ChinaAlice Nightingale-Smith for MetDeskTorrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heatMon 7 Sep 2026 04.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareTyphoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-eastChinalast week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and theMississippivalley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s celsius (high 90s fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.Explore more on these topicsChinaWeather trackerSouth AfricaMississippiAsia PacificAfricaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Canada’s retaliatory US tariffs set to take effect as trade dispute grows | Canada | The Guardian
description: Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
Content: Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks.Photograph: Ari Saperstein/EPAView image in fullscreenTensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks.Photograph: Ari Saperstein/EPACanadaCanada’s retaliatory US tariffs set to take effect as trade dispute growsCounter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goodsMaya YangMon 7 Sep 2026 19.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 19.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada is set to impose retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports early on Tuesday, escalating atrade fightwith its largest trading partner as tensions between US president Donald Trump and Canadian prime minister Mark Carney intensify.The tariffs, which take effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, will range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering C$27.6bn in imports from the US. The measures will target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs.The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $27.6bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian governmentsaid.“Canada’s counter-measures do not apply to US goods that are in transit toCanadaon the day on which they come into force,” it added.Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks, with Carney last week urging the Trump administration to “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions.Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” – whichCanadians have rejected.US vice-president JD Vance has also reportedly mocked Carney,apparently sayingthe Canadian prime minister “comes in and puffs his chest out and says: ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.’”Last month, Trumpannounceda new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”, adding: “We don’t need Canada, they need us!”Carney said last month Canada would not accept a US trade deal that weakened French-language protections, saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”.Quebec has long maintained laws aimed at protecting French and preserving its distinct cultural identity. Those measures have become asticking pointin the trade talks between the two countries, with American negotiators raising concerns about rules they say can disadvantage US businesses.Explore more on these topicsCanadaTrump tariffsTariffsAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alleged killers of Australian surfers and American friend go on trial in Mexico | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Three men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Three men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024
Content: Callum Robinson, 33, and his brother Jake, 30, from Perth, Australia, were camping in a remote beachside area when they were robbed and killed.Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGEView image in fullscreenCallum Robinson, 33, and his brother Jake, 30, from Perth, Australia, were camping in a remote beachside area when they were robbed and killed.Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGEMexicoAlleged killers of Australian surfers and American friend go on trial in MexicoThree men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024Agence France Press in EnsenadaMon 7 Sep 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe suspected murderers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot have gone on trial, two years after their killings in a suspected robbery.Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state.They had been camping in a remote beachside area when they were allegedly attacked in April 2024.Their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft several days after they went missing.View image in fullscreenJake (left) and Callum (right) with their parents, Debra and Martin Robinson.Photograph: Callum and Jake Robinson FoundationThey bore gunshot wounds to their heads. Three men are on trial over their killings.The Robinsons’ parents traveled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the proceedings on Monday.Bereaved mother Debra Robinson stared at the accused before bursting into tears in the courtroom.“It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” her partner, Martin Robinson, had earlier told reporters.“We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why.”Authorities allege the men were murdered during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was found burned near their bodies.Three witnesses appeared before the court on Monday, including the stepson of one of the defendants, who described his stepfather as violent.Testifying from an adjoining room with his face concealed, he said he accompanied the accused to the crime scene, waiting nearby when the “commotion” began.“I heard a lot of noise,” he said, explaining that he had run away but rejoined the group after they called him.He said they warned him that “the same thing that happened to the gringos would happen to him” if he said anything.The crime sparked outrage and grief in Australia and the US, where the surfers’ friends and families galvanized a major search on social media for their bodies.Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine.Tourist killings expose fragmentation of organised crime at the heart of Mexico’s extraordinary violenceRead moreRhoad was killed a few months before he was set to marry.Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn’t usually affect tourists.Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa in the north-west. Their bodies were later burned.Explore more on these topicsMexicoWestern AustraliaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border | Russia | The Guardian
description: Connection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in Ukraine
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Connection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in Ukraine
Content: Trucks drive along a road during a ceremony for the opening the first road bridge between Russia and North Korea across the Tumen River.Photograph: Oleg Kozhemyako/ReutersView image in fullscreenTrucks drive along a road during a ceremony for the opening the first road bridge between Russia and North Korea across the Tumen River.Photograph: Oleg Kozhemyako/ReutersRussiaRussia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared borderConnection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in UkrainePjotr SauerMon 7 Sep 2026 05.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia and North Korea have openedthe first road bridge across their shared border, in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine.The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang inNorth Korea, along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast.Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said.Russia and North Korea finalising first road crossing amid concerns it serves as Ukraine war supply routeRead moreThe road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group.View image in fullscreenA newly built bridge connects Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea.Photograph: Ministry of Transport of the Russian FederationAfter the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides.Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang.Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries.Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection.Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024.From ammunition to ballistic missiles: how North Korea arms Russia in the Ukraine warRead moreIn return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence.Russian and North Korean officials have alsotouted North Korea as a new holiday destinationsince the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then.Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow.During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”.Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company.At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region.During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war.“The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin.Explore more on these topicsRussiaNorth KoreaEuropeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: NSW Greens MP pleads with federal colleagues not to back National party motion to block koala park deal | Australian Greens | The Guardian
description: Federal Greens partyroom split over plan for NSW to get millions of dollars’ worth in carbon credits for creating a koala national park
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: Federal Greens partyroom split over plan for NSW to get millions of dollars’ worth in carbon credits for creating a koala national park
Content: NSW Greens MP Sue Higginson has urged federal colleagues not to vote with the Coalition and One Nation to block a carbon credit plan for koalas.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenNSW Greens MP Sue Higginson has urged federal colleagues not to vote with the Coalition and One Nation to block a carbon credit plan for koalas.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPAustralian GreensNSW Greens MP pleads with federal colleagues not to back National party motion to block koala park dealFederal Greens partyroom split over plan for NSW to get millions of dollars’ worth in carbon credits for creating a koala national parkFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAdam MortonClimate and environment editorMon 7 Sep 2026 18.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 19.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA New South Wales Greens MP has pleaded with her federal colleagues not to vote with the Coalition andOne Nationto block a plan for the NSW government to get millions of dollars’ worth in carbon credits for creating a koala national park.Sue Higginson, a former lawyer and forest campaigner turned NSW upper house MP, is the first member of the minor party to speak in detail about a dispute that has split the Greens and environmentalists.The disagreement is over a federal regulation, known as a carbon credit method, that allows state governments that protect native forests on public land to earn credits from logging.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe Nationals want to kill the regulation on behalf of the forestry industry through a disallowance motion and a Senate vote is scheduled next week.The federal Greens will discuss on Tuesday whether to back the pro-logging Nationals’ motion on the grounds the koala park should be created, but not this way.Among their considerations will be the political fallout for the environmental party if it is accused of standing in the way of a nature protection. None have spoken publicly on the issue.The meeting follows weeks of lobbying by conservationists, including in full-page newspaper advertisements and email drives. The Australia Institute, which wants the method killed, has declared the issue the “first big climate test” of Larissa Waters’s leadership of the party.Each Australian carbon credit is said to represent one tonne of greenhouse gas emissions that has been prevented from being released or drawn down from the atmosphere. Their use is contentious, partly because polluting companies can buy an unlimited number of credits – also known as offsets – to count as their own cuts while continuing to pollute.Peer-reviewed studies have found some existing carbon credit methods have not effectively reduced emissions and scientists say limiting the climate crisis requires rapid direct emissions cuts and offsetsshould be used sparingly.Those who want the regulation killed, including the Bob Brown Foundation and the Wilderness Society, say NSW Labor proposed a koala park near Coffs Harbour a decade before announcing it was dependent on carbon credit revenue, and the offsets created would not represent real emissions reductions. They say the method sets a precedent for other state governments to withhold environment protection unless they get carbon credits.On the other side are NSW conservation and Indigenous groups, national groups including WWF, Greenpeace and the Ken Henry-led Australian Climate and Biodiversity Foundation, and some senior ecologists. They say there is no guarantee the park would go ahead as promised if the method was disallowed, and that critics are too dismissive of what protecting 176,000 hectares of additional forests home to more than 100 threatened species would mean for forests that have been devastated by decades of logging and how hard local campaigners have fought over decades for this win.Higginson said allowing carbon credits from protecting public forests to be used as offsets polluters was “deeply offensive to me” and that initially opposed what is known as the “improved native forestry method”. Her position shifted after the the method forced a substantial reduction in logging across NSW forests. She said it could “end the native forest logging industry”.Greens criticise Labor after former IDF officer’s ‘reprehensible’ comments on Zomi Frankcom strikeRead more“The numbers that matter most in this fight are how many hectares of forest can we save, how big can we make our national park estate, how many First Nations’ people we can get working on country, how much carbon can we draw down and sequester in our forests as they grow big old, how many fires we can protect our forests from, how many greater gliders, forests owls, swift parrots and koalas we can save and how much can we make climate polluters pay to charge them out of existence,” she said.Higginson said forestry industry leaders planned a separate, less environmentally friendly carbon credit method that would “lock in native forest logging for many more years and see the generation of carbon credits of far less integrity”.“I utterly reject that the protection of any forest should be contingent on carbon credits, but this isn’t the question that’s been put in front of the Greens to decide … This is about winning the forests,” she said.“If our fight is about destroying carbon credits, let’s do that. Let’s tear down the entire system together. [But] the National party’s disallowance will do the opposite of that.”Higginson’s position is broadly backed by some independent senators, including David Pocock and the former Green Lidia Thorpe. But it puts her on the opposite side of the issue to her mentor, and the person who asked her to run for parliament, the formerAustralian Greensleader Bob Brown.Higginson said she was “devastated” when she learned their policy split over the issue given Brown’s legacy, but they continue to campaign together, including at an event for Sydney’s southern forests on Saturday.Brown said he understood the desperation of “very good people” who believed they had no option other than to support the method, but said the NSW premier, Chris Minns, had broken an election promise and joined Anthony Albanese in “putting capitalism before the environment”.He said Australia had created about 600 national parks, none before had needed carbon credit revenue and the method would be “letting polluters off the hook”. “It’s absolutely the wrong thing to do,” he said. “My view is if the disallowance motion goes through [Minns] would have to go back to his initial position to protect the park.”He called on Greens senators “not to be coerced by Labor’s anti-environmental gimmick”. But he said he would still support them if they ultimately disagreed.“Labor is the villain here,” he said.Explore more on these topicsAustralian GreensOne NationAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stolen Generations survivors have more health challenges than other First Nations people  | Indigenous Australians | The Guardian
description: Indigenous Australians forcibly removed under government policies more likely to have severe or profound disability, report finds
Author: Sarah Collard
Headline: Indigenous Australians forcibly removed under government policies more likely to have severe or profound disability, report finds
Content: A new report reveals the long-term intergenerational impacts of the forced removal of Indigenous children, a policy adopted by all Australian governments up to the 1970s.Photograph: AAPView image in fullscreenA new report reveals the long-term intergenerational impacts of the forced removal of Indigenous children, a policy adopted by all Australian governments up to the 1970s.Photograph: AAPIndigenous AustraliansStolen Generations survivors have more health challenges than other First Nations peopleIndigenous Australians forcibly removed under government policies more likely to have severe or profound disability, report findsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSarah CollardIndigenous affairs correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe tens of thousands ofIndigenous Australiansand their descendants who were forcibly removed under government assimilation policies have far greater physical and health challenges when compared with the wider Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations, according to a new report.The report by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) was commissioned by peak advocacy body the Healing Foundation, which supportsStolen Generationssurvivors and their families, and builds on existing data released in 2023.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailReleased on Tuesday, the report reveals the stark inequities and the long-term intergenerational impacts of forced removals, a policy adopted by all Australian governments up to the 1970s under racist assimilation laws.Valerie and her siblings were taken from their mother and placed in institutions during Australia’s Stolen Generations. Two didn’t surviveRead moreChildren were put into institutions, or were fostered or adopted out to non-Indigenous families, where many of them suffered harsh, degrading treatment and sexual abuse after being taken from their families. It is estimated at least one in 10 and possibly as many as one in three Indigenous children were removed from their families between 1910 and 1970.The report uses survey data from 2022 and 2023 of Stolen Generation members, who are now all over the age of 50, and their descendants.About 200,000 people – or 45% of Indigenous Australians aged over 18 – have a parent, grandparent, aunt or uncle who was removed from their family, the report said.Survivors were 2.7 times more likely to have severe or profound disability than other Indigenous Australians, and 1.7 times as likely to have been admitted to hospital in the past 12 months even when differences such as age, sex and remoteness of location were taken into account.Compared with non-Indigenous Australians, survivors were six times more likely to have kidney disease, 4.8 times more likely to have a severe or profound disability, and 3.9 times more likely to report high psychological distress.6:55Seven First Nations Australians tell us their worries and hopes for future generations – videoThe report also found that Stolen Generations survivors experienced greater socioeconomic challenges and distress, such as being less likely to be able to pay for unexpected emergency costs, or experiencing more days where they were unable to afford their essential needs.“The collective pattern indicates that Stolen Generations survivors experience generally more challenging socioeconomic circumstances than other Indigenous people,” the report said.The report also found that Stolen Generations survivors were nearly twice as likely as other Indigenous peoples to report high levels of psychological distress, and 1.6 times likely to report experiencing mental or behavioural health conditions.
