Their descendants were 1.3 times more likely both to report high psychological distress and to be diagnosed with a mental health condition.Dr Martin Edvardsson, the acting head of First Nations health at AIHW, said Australia lacked comprehensive data on the experiences and needs of Stolen Generation survivors and their families.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Understanding the needs of Stolen Generations survivors through the existing data sources will be increasingly challenging as survivors grow older and become less well represented in household surveys,” Edvardsson said.Leonie Williamson, the deputy CEO of the Healing Foundation said the report lays bare the devastating long term impacts of removing children from their family and communities.“I think what this report really does is highlight how you know these race-based policies conducted over decades are still very much with us,” she says.Williamson saida recent reportfound just six percent of recommendations from the 1997 Bringing them Home inquiry had been fully implemented saying much of the way forward has been outlined by community.The Gubbi Gubbi and Butchulla woman told Guardian Australia the report points to the dire need for trauma-informed holistic support for survivors and their descendants from state and territory governments.“It is such a missed opportunity. We can clearly see that if you target services for Stolen Generation survivors and descendants, you could make a real leap in outcomes for the whole of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community.”This article was updated on 8 September, 2026. There are an estimated 200,000 Indigenous Australians over the age of 18 descendant from the Stolen Generations, not two million.Indigenous Australians can call13YARNon 13 92 76 for information and crisis support; or call Lifeline on 13 11 14, Mensline on 1300 789 978 or Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636Explore more on these topicsIndigenous AustraliansStolen GenerationsHealthInequalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Record strength El Niño could mean bigger supermarket bills for Australians, experts warn  | Australian economy | The Guardian
description: Predicted hot and dry weather in growing areas in eastern Australia identified as ‘one of the key issues’ that will affect food prices over next 12 months
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: Predicted hot and dry weather in growing areas in eastern Australia identified as ‘one of the key issues’ that will affect food prices over next 12 months
Content: RBA officials are concerned a severe El Niño could drive food prices higher and create a further headache later this year, when the central bank is contemplating whether it needs to hike interest rates again.Photograph: Sam Mooy/AAPView image in fullscreenRBA officials are concerned a severe El Niño could drive food prices higher and create a further headache later this year, when the central bank is contemplating whether it needs to hike interest rates again.Photograph: Sam Mooy/AAPAustralian economyRecord strength El Niño could mean bigger supermarket bills for Australians, experts warnPredicted hot and dry weather in growing areas in eastern Australia identified as ‘one of the key issues’ that will affect food prices over next 12 monthsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPatrick ComminsEconomics editorMon 7 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 16.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe most severe El Niño weather event on record threatens to push food prices higher this year, experts say, piling pressure on households already struggling with the post-pandemic spike in grocery bills and complicating the Reserve Bank’s efforts to bring inflation back under control.The Bureau of Meteorology has forecastEl Niño will peak in late spring or summer and “reach levels above the warmest observed since reliable records began in 1950”.Michael Harvey, a consumer food analyst at Rabobank research, said the predicted hot and dry weather in key growing areas in eastern Australia was “clearly one of the key issues that will have an impact on food pricing over the next 12 months”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe Food and Agricultural Organisationin its latest updatereported rising weather-related threats are already being reflected in high and climbing global commodity prices.BoM forecasts strongest El Niño on record as research points to ‘alarming’ climate change influenceRead more“It’s a very volatile time, and there are lots of risks around cost re-escalation in the food system,” Harvey said. “There is absolutely risk of food inflation coming through at the consumer end.”Not all commodities are heading in the same direction, however. For example, dairy and meat prices are beginning to ease after a big recent rise as the underlying fundamentals in those markets shift independently of the looming weather event.In Australia El Niño created a risk for what is still expected to be a strong winter wheat crop this year, Harvey said.Temperature anomalies graph“That will be the big thing to watch, as well as the spillover effects of that into things like feed grains,” he said, adding that the ultimate impact would be clear by the final quarter of the year.Even absent hotter and drier weather, overseas shocks have already pushed commodity price benchmarks higher this year, which are linked to local markets through the export trade.Dennis Voznesenski, CBA’s agricultural economist, said global wheat prices are up by about a third since the start of July, versus about 9% in Australia.The extreme weather warnings also come as the global oil benchmark, Brent crude, pushed past US$97 a barrel on Monday afternoon to be 35% higher since the start of July.With diesel prices on the rise again – a key cost for farmers – fertiliser suppliers have also warned of ongoing supply disruptions that will keep prices structurally higher.Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine’s record grain harvests are struggling to find their way to international markets after tit-for-tat attacks on critical Black Sea ports.Australian ski resorts to close up to a month early due to global heating and El NiñoRead more“A third of global grain exports are stuck right now,” Voznesenski said.The past five years have seen rapid increases in prices across a range of supermarket goods, contributing to an entrenched cost-of-living crisis across Australia.In the five years to June, for example, the cost of staples such as breads and cereals, dairy, and other products such as jams and eggs, jumped by between 28% and 30%.In comparison, in the preceding five-year period to mid-2021, the cumulative increase in these supermarket shelf items was 3-6%, according to analysis of quarterly Australian Bureau of Statistics data.Food and drink pricesRBA officials are concerned that a particularly severe El Niño could drive food prices higher and create a further headache later this year, at a time when the central bank is already contemplating whether it needs to raise interest rates again.But Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said it was not easy to show a clear link between El Niño events and higher food prices, saying there were a range of costs – from labour to freight and packaging – that often played a bigger role in determining how much Australians pay at the checkout.“It won’t be a first-order influence on overall inflation, but if you get a little bit extra from food prices, then it’s unhelpful,” Kearns said.Explore more on these topicsAustralian economyAustralia weatherClimate crisisEl Niño southern oscillationCost of living crisisRetail industryInflationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Grassroots Labor group urges Albanese government to chart course away from ‘American war machine’ | Australian military | The Guardian
description: Pressure follows revelations US military and weapons manufacturers control or have access to more than 100 bases across Australian continent
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: Pressure follows revelations US military and weapons manufacturers control or have access to more than 100 bases across Australian continent
Content: The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, told the Senate on Monday the US military presence in the country is ‘at Australia’s invitation’, and that the defence sites were ‘Australian bases under Australian command’.Photograph: Darren England/AAPView image in fullscreenThe foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, told the Senate on Monday the US military presence in the country is ‘at Australia’s invitation’, and that the defence sites were ‘Australian bases under Australian command’.Photograph: Darren England/AAPAustralian militaryGrassroots Labor group urges Albanese government to chart course away from ‘American war machine’Pressure follows revelations US military and weapons manufacturers control or have access to more than 100 bases across Australian continentWhy can the US access so many Australian military bases? – podcastFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBen DohertyMon 7 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 16.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has “led Australia into wars of aggression” for 50 years, internal party campaign group Labor Against War has argued, urging the government to chart a foreign policy independent “from the American war machine”.The Australian government has defended the growing presence of theUS militaryon the Australian continent, insisting the defence sites “are Australian bases under Australian control”, despite evidence the US military controls more than a dozen bases on Australian territory.On Monday, the Guardian published data showing the US military, and US weapons manufacturers, control or have access tomore than 100 bases across the Australian continent.The US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war?Read moreThe Guardian has detailed 17 military facilities on Australian soil that are controlled by the United States military. The military has access to 75 more Australian-run bases, and US defence corporations access to 18 more.In total, the US military and American defence corporations have control of or access to 110 facilities on Australian territory, well over half of all the military installations in Australia. That analysis has not been contradicted. Thedata was compiledby Dr Richard Tanter, senior research associate with the US-based Nautilus Institute.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe publication of the database has exposed disquiet within theLabor partyover growing US military presence across the continent.Marcus Strom, the national convener of the grassroots Labor Against War group, said “the latticework of US bases and facilities across our continent should alarm anyone that values Australia’s independence from the American war machine”.“For more than 50 years the US has led Australia into wars of aggression,” Strom said.“Labor Against War calls on the Albanese government to chart a new course for Australia’s foreign and defence policy that is suited to the future, not clinging to the fading guarantees of the past.”Strom said the governmentshould abandon the Aukus nuclear submarine agreementas a first step.In question time in the Senate, Greens senator David Shoebridge asked the foreign affairs minister,Penny Wong, why the government had chosen to “sign us up to the next US war”.Wong said the government would resolutely defend the US alliance and that “everything the government is doing is working to deter and avert conflict”.7:00US military presence in Australia, mapped – video“We are of the view that the US alliance contributes to Australian sovereignty. It enables us to have access to a range of capability that Australia would not have access to,” she said.Wong told the Senate the US military presence in the country is “at Australia’s invitation”.“These are Australian bases under Australian command.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShoebridge said Australians living near US military facilities in Australia feared they could be targets in the event of conflict in the region, citing attacks on US bases in the Middle East in the current war with Iran.“These bases obviously make Australia a target when the US decides to start its next forever war, don’t they?”Shoebridge asked Wong to specify one instance where Australia had said no to the US having access to anAustralian militarybase.“Access to and use of Australian facilities … is on a rotational basis, mutually determined and at Australia’s invitation,” Wong said.A remote spy base and a ‘criminal’ blockade raise questions about Australia’s complicity in Gaza warRead morePine Gap, the best known of the US-Australia “joint defence facilities” on Australian territory, was established by the CIA in the 1960s near Alice Springs. US National Security Agency documents, leaked by whistleblower Edward Snowden, show the “chief of facility” at Pine Gap is always an American, whoreports directly the US National Reconnaissance Office. The deputy is a senior Australian Signals Directorate official.Former defence minister Christopher Pyne described Pine Gap in a public hearing as “more American than Australian”. There are numerous other bases on the Australian mainland that are controlled by the US rather than Australia, including the GPS monitoring station at RAAF Edinburgh base in South Australia, and the Learmonth solar observatory in Western Australia.The defence minister, Richard Marles, travelled to the US last week, agreeing with the US secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth, “toaccelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics, and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”.Marles said:“American force posture is growing in Australia, and that’s across all the domains.“We think that’s really important in terms of providing deterrence in the Indo-Pacific, providing for stability and peace in the Indo-Pacific, and that’s very much in Australia’s national interest.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian militaryAustralian foreign policyPenny WongUS militaryAustralian politicsLabor partyAukusnewsShareReuse this content

title: German chancellor vows to stay in office despite AfD triumph in state election | Germany | The Guardian
description: Friedrich Merz said his conservative CDU was shaken ‘to its very foundations’ after far-right victory in Saxony-Anhalt
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Friedrich Merz said his conservative CDU was shaken ‘to its very foundations’ after far-right victory in Saxony-Anhalt
Content: ‘Giving up is not an option for me,’ said Friedrich Merz.Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Giving up is not an option for me,’ said Friedrich Merz.Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPAGermanyGerman chancellor vows to stay in office despite AfD triumph in state electionFriedrich Merz said his conservative CDU was shaken ‘to its very foundations’ after far-right victory in Saxony-AnhaltDeborah Colein BerlinMon 7 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA “shocked” and chastened Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay in office despitethe far right’s triumph in a state electionthat has brought anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin politicians within striking distance of power.The German chancellor, appearing ashen-faced in front of reporters in Berlin, said on Monday that the landslide victory by the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt had shaken his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) “to its very foundations”.The unpopular Merz, who had pledged to halve the AfD’s support at the national level, has watched the nativist party rack up electoral gains, none as convincing as its utter rout of the CDU in the eastern region on Sunday with nearly 44% of the vote.The AfD and its candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority but could yet create Germany’s first far-right state government since the Nazi period.Merz appeared contrite and willing to work on his “communication” with voters. “This is the worst electoral defeat the [CDU] has suffered in years, in decades,” he said. “Of course this will have to have consequences.”Exit polls indicated the state’s voters were driven by deep dissatisfaction with the political establishment and its stewardship of Europe’s biggest economy, with one showing thatonly 9% approved of Merz’s performance.View image in fullscreenUlrich Siegmund mocked Merz as ‘a very good campaigner’ for the AfD.Photograph: Odd Andersen/AFP/Getty ImagesSiegmund, a media-savvy former fragrance salesman, was also able to tap into a sense of grievance in the former communist east, where complaints abound that voters there are treated as “second-class citizens” more than three decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall.Siegmund, 35, mocked the 70-year-old Merz as “a very good campaigner” for the AfD.Only 16 months in office, Merz conceded his own low poll ratings had played a role in his party’s loss. “I know that I personally was a constant topic in this election campaign,” he said. “We must try – myself included – to reach people more effectively, in the full range of their emotions.”1:24‘We should have learned more from history’: Germans react to AfD win – videoThe CDU’s junior coalition partner, the Social Democrats, indicated a willingness to water down contentious measures to shore up the statutory healthcare andpension schemes.However, Merz insisted: “My determination to continue on the path of reform is unbroken,” saying a sustainable system was essential for the sake of “our children and grandchildren”. He added: “Giving up is not an option for me.”Merz said he wanted to assure Germany’s allies that “our institutions are resilient and stable” and its own vulnerable minorities that the country would stick to its values and constitution even if the AfD took power in Saxony-Anhalt. “We know that Germany carries special responsibility because of its history,” he said.He also promised to stay the course on Ukraine, stressing he would “not budge a single millimetre from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom against Russia as well”.Merz said Moscow would cheer the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt and accused it of lending support to the far right’s campaign, with another two German state elections still to come this month amidalleged Russian interference and sabotage.View image in fullscreenSven Schulze, the CDU state premier for Saxony-Anhalt, acknowledged his party now had ‘no mandate’ to govern in the state.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersAlthough the CDU rallied behind its chancellor and party leader, several influential commenters openly called for his immediate replacement – a complex step under German law.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGermany “needs a clean slate, a fresh start, and that starts with Friedrich Merz”, said theDer Spiegel editor-in-chief, Dirk Kurbjuweit. “He is evidently the wrong man for this office in these times.”The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt chapter is listed as “confirmed rightwing extremist” by the domestic intelligence service. It has pledgedmass deportations of unwelcome immigrants and asylum seekers, which critics have said would be illegal, while promising massive boosts in social welfare spending with unclear financing.The AfD has also taken aim at state support for public broadcasters and cultural institutionsit deems “unpatriotic”, sparking fears of “cultural hegemony”.The party did not win enough seats to elect Siegmund as state premier, but AfD leaders said they seek to pick off rebel lawmakers from other parties willing to play kingmaker. It is only three seats short of a majority.Theconservative-left populist BSW party, which also favours restoring ties with Russia and largely blocking immigration, signalled an openness to working with the AfD but before the election ruled out joining the state government.In the 13 years of the AfD’s existence, the mainstream parties have maintained a “firewall” against the far right, refusing any formal cooperation that would allow it take power. The strategy meant to sideline the party has appeared to backfire, however, as the permanent “outsider” role appeals to legions of voters fed up with politics as usual.The CDU state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged his party had “no mandate” to govern given its humiliating 17% result, even if it managed to cobble together an unwieldy coalition with all the other parties in the legislature.Although Saxony-Anhalt forms part of the AfD heartland as a relatively poor, ex-communist region, the party has begun makinginroads in the westas well amid alarming signs of decline in the steel, chemicals and automotive sectors.Germany faces another two regional elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in another eastern state, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the AfD is also strong.The party co-leader Alice Weidel, beaming after Sunday’s vote, said the AfD was now targeting 40% at the next general election, due in 2029. It is polling at about 28%.Explore more on these topicsGermanyFriedrich MerzAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)EuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s centre fears nationalist wave after AfD victory but only has itself to blame | The far right | The Guardian
description: Saxony-Anhalt win part of wider trend driven by mainstream policy failures and gradual normalisation of far right ideas
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Saxony-Anhalt win part of wider trend driven by mainstream policy failures and gradual normalisation of far right ideas
Content: ‘It starts here’: is the AfD’s win in Saxony-Anhalt just the beginning for the far-right’s European resurgence?Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APView image in fullscreen‘It starts here’: is the AfD’s win in Saxony-Anhalt just the beginning for the far-right’s European resurgence?Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APThe far rightAnalysisEurope’s centre fears nationalist wave after AfD victory but only has itself to blameJon HenleyEurope correspondentSaxony-Anhalt win part of wider trend driven by mainstream policy failures and gradual normalisation of far right ideasMon 7 Sep 2026 12.13 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.32 EDTShareThe numbers speak for themselves: Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), a party that dabbles in Nazi imagery, distinguishes between “biological” and “passport” Germans, and is too extreme even for France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen, nearly doubled its score in Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt to 43.8% of the vote.Meanwhile, the centre-right CDU of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, collapsed to 17.2%, less than half its total in the same race five years ago, and the centre-left SPD – Germany’s other main party of government for the past 60-odd years – scraped 9.3%. The least that can be said is that the centre did not hold.It is not yet clear whether the AfD, whose local branch in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt is officially classified by the country’s domestic intelligence service as“confirmed rightwing extremist”, will be able to form a government: it has 39 lawmakers in the 83-member parliament, just short of an outright majority.But the score is the party’s strongest-ever state result and puts it closer to governing a German state than any far-right party since the second world war. It has sent shock waves round Europe, with nationalists cheering a “historic win” that is “just the beginning” andmainstream leaders warningof a “grave moment” for Europe.Sweden holds legislative elections next weekend. France faces a crunch presidential ballot next spring. Key parliamentary races will follow there, as well as in Italy, Spain and Poland, later in the year. Far-right parties are polling strongly in all of them, and Europe’s centre fears a continent-wide nationalist wave.1:24'We should have learned more from history': Germans react to AfD win – videoIt would be wise not to read too much into one election result in one quite particular German state. Saxony-Anhalt, analysts note, is home to barely 1.8 million voters and has long been a far-right stronghold: in federal and state elections over the past decade, support for the AfD there has consistently been double the national average.“A far-right party winning a regional election in Germany is not more scary than a far-right party winning a regional election in France, the UK or the Netherlands,”said Tarik Abou-Chadi, a professor of European politics at Oxford University. “Saxony-Anhalt should not be the basis for sweeping conclusions about the electoral sociology of the AfD.”Nonetheless, the AfD leads in national polls. It is also ahead – although in a far tighter race, with the SPD – in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where state elections are due later this month, and it is lying second even in liberal Berlin. Its rise is part of a decade-long march by far-right parties across Europe.View image in fullscreenThe AfD is polling second even in liberal Berlin, and leading polls nationwide.Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPAAlmost one in four voters in Europenow cast their ballot for far-right parties, according to research led byMatthijs Rooduijn, a political scientist at the University of Amsterdam, a proportion that has grown nearly fivefold since the mid-1990s and climbed particularly steeply over the past three years.Thisanalysis, by more than 150 political scientists in 31 countries, found that the proportion of Europeans voting for a far-right party in their country’s most recent national elections had risen in 2026 to more than 23%, from about 10% a decade ago and roughly 5% in 1995.Far-right populist parties are now in government as part of ruling coalitions in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, propping up a rightwing minority government in Sweden, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany (and, until very recently, the UK).They have also suffered recent defeats, including in the Netherlands, where Geert Wilders’s Freedom party (PVV) lost nearly a third of its seatsto finish second last year, and Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz wascomprehensively beatenby his centre-right rival in April.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe AfD’s win in Germany is a dark day for Europe. Time is running out to stop the far right | Cas MuddeRead moreBut the trend seems clear. AsCas Muddeof the University of Georgia, a leading expert on Europe’s far right,put it after Orbán’s defeat: “The far right is here to stay, and many of its parties are as established as the (former) ‘mainstream’ parties. Like other parties, their electoral support fluctuates.”That steady electoral advance has been achieved despite a refusal by mainstream parties in countries such as France and Germany to collaborate with far-right parties, prompting some commentators to argue that the“cordon sanitaire” or “firewall” has now failed, or even been counterproductive.By keeping the AfD out, they argue, Germany’s mainstream parties have actually boosted it: the party has been protected from the compromises and failures inherent in government. At the same time, the centre has been “hollowed-out”: forced into uncomfortable, unstable alliances that agree on and – vitally – accomplish little, further frustrating voters and driving support for the extremes.“There’s a self-reinforcing political dynamic that feeds the AfD’s rise,” saidMujtaba Rahman, of the Eurasia Group risk consultancy. “The weaker the election results, the less common ground in the coalition, the fewer the policy results. The fewer results, the bigger the frustration in the electorate, the bigger the AfD’s share of the vote.”Many political scientists, however, say blaming the firewall is an excuse, and data suggests far-right parties do not in any case get weaker when they are in government, but become stronger: one recent study of more than 1,300 different governments in 57 countries found far-right parties that entered governmentaveraged a score six percentage points highercome the next election.Besides the persistent inability of mainstream governments to deliver for disillusioned voters hit by a spiralling cost of living crisis, it is above all the gradual mainstreaming and normalisation of the far right’s ideas that has driven – and continues to drive – its steady advance, political scientists argue.Research suggests voter attitudes towards core far-right themes such as immigration have not changed significantly over time, but have become much more significant in their voting decisions: normalisation by the media and by mainstream parties that readily embrace far-right framing have legitimised far-right views.“The entire debate about whether thecordon sanitaireis ‘successful’ or contributes to strengthening the far right completely misses the point,”said Gabriela Greilinger, an Austrian-Hungarian political scientist. “Far-right politics and policies already constantly take centre stage, whether or not the far right is in power. There is no cordon around their ideas.”Explore more on these topicsThe far rightGermanyEuropeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)analysisShareReuse this content

title: Merz says ‘shock’ AfD victory in key German state ‘is an election result we cannot simply move past’ – as it happened | Germany | The Guardian
description: German chancellor says vote for far-right party ‘will have repercussions’ across the country
Author: Martin Belam
Headline: German chancellor says vote for far-right party ‘will have repercussions’ across the country
Content: 07.39 EDTMerz concedes 'most severe election defeat' in 'years, or decades'Merz begins by saying “we are all deeply shocked” by the result in Saxony-Anchalt.“We did not expect it to turn out this way,”he says.He says the vote “will have repercussions” and says even a glance at who congratulated the AfD shows “the level of international attention this result has garnered.”He says that “when nearly 60% of voters … cast their ballots for political parties that fundamentally call into question our country’s democratic institutions …it is an election result we cannot simply move past as if nothing happened.”He concedesthis is “the most severe election defeat the CDU has suffered in years, indeed in decades.”Share

title: French winemakers forecast 30-year low harvest after severe drought and heat | France | The Guardian
description: Estimates suggest drop in production with vineyards also concerned ‘smoke taint’ from wildfires may affect quality
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Estimates suggest drop in production with vineyards also concerned ‘smoke taint’ from wildfires may affect quality
Content: The extreme heat of the summer weather in France has caused grapes to wilt and be scalded.Photograph: sportpoint/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe extreme heat of the summer weather in France has caused grapes to wilt and be scalded.Photograph: sportpoint/AlamyFranceFrench winemakers forecast 30-year low harvest after severe drought and heatEstimates suggest drop in production with vineyards also concerned ‘smoke taint’ from wildfires may affect qualityKim Willsherin ParisMon 7 Sep 2026 11.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench vineyards hit by severe drought and heatwaves are expected to report a 30-year low in wine production after the country’s hottest ever recorded summer, according to the agriculture ministry.Initial estimates suggest winemakers will produce just under 34m hectolitres from this year’s harvest: a drop of 6% on last year, and 17% less than ‌the 2021-2025 average.Agreste, the government’s farming food, forestry and fishing statistics body, said the drop was partly caused by a reduction in the number and size of vineyards, but mostly the result ofextreme weather conditions.“The summer was particularly hot and dry: soil drought has intensified throughout the country and heatwaves have caused localised sun scald, scorching, defoliation, and wilting of the grapes, reducing harvest volumes,” it reported.View image in fullscreenA grape picker gets to work at the Trois Terres vineyard in Octon, southern France earlier this month.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPAHowever, some winemakers say with grape harvests still being conducted it is too early to make credible predictions.The disappointing forecast comes after an optimistic start to the year, with heavy spring rains that encouraged grape growth. “The hot and dry summer conditions meant a deterioration of the [harvest] forecast,” Agreste reported.A series of heatwaves brought thehighest summer temperatures recorded in Francesince records began in 1900, with averages of 24C in June, July and August. Almost half of the country recorded temperatures on or above 40C.Among the worst hit wine regions is Champagne where the grape harvest, which started unusually early in mid August, is predicted to be almost half that of last year. The Jura region in the east was the next worst hit with an estimated 37% loss. This year’s Burgundy-Beaujolais region grape production was expected to be one-third down, Agreste reported.Winemakers in Bordeaux and the Languedoc-Roussillon as well as those in the south-east and south-west reported higher harvests this year but all except the Savoie region were down on the 2021-2025 five-year average for production.However, Cécile Mathiaud of the Burgundy wine producers association said she was surprised by the government’s disastrous figures for her region’s vineyards.“We know we won’t have a full harvest this year, but we have no definite figures and there’s no suggestion the situation is a disaster,” Mathiaud said. “We have some vineyards that have reported not much this year and others where it has been higher than expected.”View image in fullscreenThe harvest under way early in the morning at Trois Terres.Photograph: Guillaume Horcajuelo/EPASome Burgundy vineyards began their harvest in early August but others are collecting the grapes now, she added. “Our reference is the historically low harvest of 2021 when we produced only 1m hectolitres; we think it will be higher this year, but the question is by how much? I have absolutely no idea how the ministry has come up with these figures.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAgreste said the figures were estimates and definitive results would not be known until regions made official harvest declarations later this year. It added that 2026 grape harvests were “marked by significant regional disparities”.Heatwaves and wildfires are setting back air quality improvements, UN findsRead moreWine harvests have traditionally taken place inFrancebetween September and mid October, but the climate emergency has brought dates forward slightly each year for the last four decades. This year, the harvest timetable advanced at least a week compared with last year throughout the country. Some vineyards in Bordeaux began two weeks early.There are also concerns that vines and grapes in some of France’s best-known wine producing regions, including Bordeaux, have been damaged by smoke from rampant wildfires. No major Bordeaux vineyards suffered direct damage from the flames that came within 15km (9 miles) of the city, but there is concern that smoke has entered the grape skins causing “smoke taint” and affecting the taste of the finished wine.The agriculture ministry would normally issue harvest estimates in early August, but postponed its analysis at the request of the wine industry because of what it described as “the high level of uncertainty surrounding these forecasts” caused by weather conditions and wildfires.France’s wine sector is already under pressure owing to a decline in demand. Annual wine consumption in the 1960s in France was 127 litres each year compared with 40 litres a year now.Wine drinking in the US, France’s largest export market, has also dropped and French wines have been hit by Donald Trump’s tariffs.Explore more on these topicsFranceExtreme heatEuropeWineFarmingClimate crisisFood & drink industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Why is the far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics? | Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) | The Guardian
description: Aftershocks of party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt will ripple across Germany, with two more state elections this month
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Aftershocks of party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt will ripple across Germany, with two more state elections this month
Content: Ulrich Siegmund said before the vote he would only stand for election as premier with a clear majority.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAView image in fullscreenUlrich Siegmund said before the vote he would only stand for election as premier with a clear majority.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)ExplainerWhy is the far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics?Aftershocks of party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt will ripple across Germany, with two more state elections this monthDeborah Colein BerlinMon 7 Sep 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany is reeling from the biggest far-right victory in a state election since the Nazi period after voters in Saxony-Anhalt in the former communist east gave the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) partya thumping first-place finish of 44%, just short of an absolute majority.What happened and why is it significant?For the first time since the second world war, a German state is on the brink of electing a far-right government after a big win in Saxony-Anhalt, described by the news magazine Der Spiegel as a magnitude 9.0 “political earthquake”.Coming in nearly 27 points ahead of the co-ruling Christian Democrats (CDU), the conservative party of the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, the AfD pulled off a coup whose aftershocks will ripple across Germany and beyond its borders. The AfD will have broad powers over education, culture and ‌domestic security if it manages to take power in the state. Among other policies, it has promised to start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools, and halt the building of new windfarms. It now has a strong wind at its back for the two state elections yet to come this month.Its triumph also raised doubts whether the unpopular Merz could hold on in the face of such a clear rejection of his policies and leadership after just 16 months in power. The AfD co-leader Alice Weidel told reporters in Berlin that her party was targeting a 40% result at the next general election, scheduled for 2029. It is currently polling in first place at 28%.View image in fullscreenAlice Weidel (right, with Ulrich Siegmund, centre, and her AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, left) said the AfD was targeting a 40% vote at the next general election.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAWhat might happen next?The AfD’s national leaders and the chief candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, the media-savvy former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, said the state’s voters had given the party a clear mandate to govern. However, without an absolute majority in the state parliament, the party would need partners or supporters to either join a coalition or “tolerate” a minority government. Siegmund said repeatedly before the vote he would only stand for election as premier with a clear majority. The remaining parties ruled out playing kingmaker to Siegmund by lending formal support. However, the BSW, a small “left-conservative” populist party which narrowly cleared the 5% hurdle to representation, has hinted at tacit cooperation.Prior to the election, some Christian Democrats in the state openly questioned the “firewall” policy. Siegmund indicated he would spend the coming days and weeks “with an outstretched hand”, testing the hitherto resolute opposition to helping the AfD into power. If Siegmund fails to build a coalition, he suggested holding a new election, something that would require a two-thirds majority in the state legislature.1:24'We should have learned more from history': Germans react to AfD win – videoWhat does the result say about the firewall approach?The stunning outcome in Saxony-Anhalt has underscored doubts about the viability of the policy of mainstream parties to exclude the AfD from power. The only other time the AfD won in a state, in neighbouring Thuringia in 2024, its victory was less decisive, allowing the remaining parties to cobble together an ideologically awkward, cross-spectrum coalition. Given the AfD’s margin of victory in Saxony-Anhalt, it is difficult to imagine how the humiliated CDU could form such a “Frankenstein” alliance of disparate parties this time. The state premier, Sven Schulze, acknowledged the party no longer had a mandate to try.View image in fullscreenSiegmund has suggested a new election if he fails to build a coalition.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAWhat does the result mean for the CDU and Friedrich Merz?Sunday’s election amounted to a stinging rebuke of Merz and his CDU. The stony-faced chancellor admitted he was “deeply shocked” by the result. Exit polls showed voters were furious about his broken promises to revive the economy and shore up fiscal discipline. Energy prices, stoked by inflation and the Iran war, have hit voters hard in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany’s poorest state. Cost of living issues appeared to far outweigh immigration, the AfD’s trademark call to arms, as a mobilising issue. Although support for the AfD has been strongest in the ex-communist east, the party also made strong gains in two elections in western states earlier this year amid fears over deindustrialisation.The Social Democratic party (SPD), a junior partner in Merz’s alliance, indicated on Monday it would be willing to water down planned changes to Germany’s costly and creaking social welfare system in order to placate disgruntled voters. Merz insisted the measures to shore up the healthcare and pension systems were necessary and vowed to remain and fight for them “in the interest of our children and grandchildren”.View image in fullscreenFriedrich Merz has been ‘deeply shocked’ by the result.Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPAWhat about the next two state elections?Voters in the German capital, Berlin, and the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, two of Germany’s 16länder,will go to the polls on 20 September. The obvious momentum for the AfD, as well as widespread German dissatisfaction with Merz and his right-left government with the SPD, mean those polls are also fraught with risk for the parties in the federal coalition. The AfD currently has a narrow lead ahead of the co-ruling SPD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but for now looks unlikely to win an absolute majority. The situation in Berlin – once divided between east and west – looks muddled, with the CDU, far-left Linke and the AfD all jockeying for first place. Even if the CDU managed to hold on to its lead on election day, it would struggle to form an ideologically coherent coalition, dealing Merz and his party another stinging blow that could further destabilise his government.Explore more on these topicsAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)GermanyThe far rightEuropeexplainersShareReuse this content

title: UK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade ban | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Ed Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move likely to draw fierce criticism from US and Israel
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Ed Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move likely to draw fierce criticism from US and Israel
Content: Ed Miliband is expected to set out the measures in a statement to MPs on Tuesday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenEd Miliband is expected to set out the measures in a statement to MPs on Tuesday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAForeign policyUK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade banEd Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move likely to draw fierce criticism from US and IsraelPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 7 Sep 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEd Miliband will announce what he has described as abroad reset of the UK’s relations with Israelon Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause.In an intervention that is expected to draw fierce criticism from the US andIsrael, the foreign secretary will impose a UK ban on the trade in goods and some services from illegal Israeli settlements.He has also told civil society groups he is determined to reassert support for a two-state solution to the conflict with an appeal for the protection of Palestinian rights and respect for international law.In his statement to MPs, Miliband is expected to use firmer language than his recent predecessors in calling out the humanitarian injustices suffered by Palestinians in Gaza.The steps he lays out are likely to fall short of the full set of demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but they will still be seen as a sign that the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank – widely seen as intended to destroy the prospect of a Palestinian state.View image in fullscreenA Palestinian woman waits at a bus stop decked out with Israeli flags raised by settlers between Nablus and Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersIsrael has already threatened reprisals over Miliband’s previous claim that the Israeli military has held back aid into Gaza, and the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has claimed theLabourgovernment is gripped by Jew hatred. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies such as Qatar on Monday to brief them on the government’s plans in the region.Miliband’s intervention comes as polling released to the Guardian shows Britons across the political divide strongly favour banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements by a margin of more than two to one.The polling, conducted by Opinium and published by the European Council on Foreign Relations, shows that only 18% of UK adults oppose a ban on trade in goods with Israeli settlements, compared with 46% in favour. Support rises to nearly three-quarters when those who did not express an opinion are excluded.Miliband’s statement will stand by his claim that the Israel Defense Forces, in the name of security, are placing unnecessary controls on aid entering Gaza, creating a horrific situation. It is understood, however, that he is sceptical of the UK’s leverage to resolve the situation apart from calling for the restrictions to be lifted.View image in fullscreenA Palestinian woman and her children make their way through a destroyed neighbourhood of Gaza City.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersHis claim that aid had been held back was hotly denied by the Israeli foreign ministry at the weekend.Miliband is also likely to go further than his predecessors in placing the settlement measures firmly in the context of upholding international law, including the findings of two key institutions, the international criminal court and the international court of justice (ICJ), two bodies under attack by the US.The package is not likely to include sanctions over aid restrictions into Gaza, or to describe what has happened in the territory as a genocide. The UK has kept open the option of joining countries such as South Africa at the ICJ to claim Israel is in breach of the court’s previous rulings.But by acting decisively on trade, Miliband has set aside warnings that a polarising UK intervention might help Benjamin Netanyahu’s chances in Israel’s 27 October election. British sources pointed out that even Israeli military officials have warned their prime minister that the IDF will struggle to defend new settlements and outposts in the northern West Bank, because they lack basic security infrastructure and were established for political rather than security reasons.Despite US criticism of the UK stance, Washington has also been putting pressure on Netanyahu on the settlements issue to the point that he has called for some to be dismantled, saying they were not established with the necessary permits. Israel has previously demolished some outposts, but they are often rebuilt soon after.10:13British activist abducted by West Bank settlers deported by Israel - The LatestThe UK ban on trade in settlement goods, long parried by the Foreign Office as impossible to implement, is in line with the ICJ advisory opinion in 2024 requiring governments not to aid or assist an Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory, not just illegal settlements. The UK government has never formally replied to the opinion, but ministers in Keir Starmer’s government said it was broadly compliant.The measures on settlements may require primary legislation to ban the trade in goods rather than an easier statutory instrument, while the trade ban will extend to some services including financing and advertising illegal settlements.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUN expert Francesca Albanese calls for ‘true paradigm shift’ as Miliband resets policy on IsraelRead moreThe Foreign Office has previously argued that it was impossible to distinguish between products emanating from illegal settlements and those from Israel. The UK officially regards all Israeli civilian settlements built on territories captured during the 1967 six-day war as illegal under international law.Total trade in goods and services between the UK and Israel in 2025 was £6bn, and the scale of the disruption may depend on Israeli reprisals.Products produced in Israeli settlements located within the territories occupied by Israel since 1967 have not been entitled to preferential tariff treatment upon entry into the UK since 2005. The country has also issued guidance on misleading labelling and urged businesses not to trade with or be engaged in economic and financial activities in Israeli settlements. The new measures make such investments unlawful.The UK reset was made more urgent by Israel’s E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which is poised to effectively cut the occupied West Bank in two from November. But the Burnham government also feels compelled to act because of the increase in settler violence in the West Bank and the failure of Trump’s Board of Peace after six months to secure the twin objectives of Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza.View image in fullscreenIsrael’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, holds up a map showing the E1 settlement project.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APLabour is also under domestic pressure from the Greens onPalestine. The party leader, Zack Polanski, is expected to stand in the 8 October Holborn and St Pancras byelection triggered by Starmer’s resignation as an MP. The new Labour policy may give the party’s candidate some political cover against Polanski.In a sign of the potential ramifications for Miliband, Netanyahu’s older son, Yair, suggested last week that the Falkland Islands belonged to Argentina and not to Britain.He is not a minister, but after his comments Trump indicated that Washington could reconsider its position on British sovereignty over the islands.Trump said last Thursday that he would not back Britain if Argentina were to invade the islands, telling GB News: “Your country was not there to help me” when the US and Israel began their war on Iran in February.The Foreign Office declined to comment when approached by the Guardian.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyIsraelPalestineEd MilibandLabourMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Syrian reactor could have been used for nuclear weapons if completed, UN says | Syria | The Guardian
description: Chief of nuclear watchdog says secret Assad-era facility would have been able to produce fissile material
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Chief of nuclear watchdog says secret Assad-era facility would have been able to produce fissile material
Content: People stand near a ripped poster of Bashar al-Assad in Aleppo, Syria, in November 2024.Photograph: Mahmoud Hassano/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople stand near a ripped poster of Bashar al-Assad in Aleppo, Syria, in November 2024.Photograph: Mahmoud Hassano/ReutersSyriaSyrian reactor could have been used for nuclear weapons if completed, UN saysChief of nuclear watchdog says secret Assad-era facility would have been able to produce fissile materialGuardian staff and agencies in ViennaMon 7 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA nearly complete nuclear reactor built secretly during the rule of the toppled Syrian leaderBashar al-Assadwould have been able to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons, the chief of the UN nuclear watchdog has revealed.Inspectors from the International AtomicEnergyAgency (IAEA) last month visited two sites, one in Deir ez-Zor and a second in an undisclosed location identified to them by Syrian authorities.The IAEA head, Rafael Grossi, said on Monday it was “obvious that the previous government was pursuing a number of clandestine” activities.“They didn’t want the world to know what they were doing,” he told reporters after opening the Vienna-based agency’s quarterly board of governors meeting.“Given the configuration, the technical features of that type of reactor, this is a reactor that is very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be used directly for the fabrication of nuclear weapons,” he said, adding that building the reactor was a “very important step”.Syria was believed to have operated an extensive undeclared nuclear programme under Assad that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in the eastern Deir ez-Zor province.After Assad was ousted in December 2024, the new government agreed to give IAEA inspectors access to suspected former nuclear sites.During a visit to Syria in August, IAEA inspectors confirmed that “the cooling infrastructure which has now been uncovered is consistent with that of a nuclear reactor”. Grossi and a team of senior inspectors also visited a previously undeclared site in the country.In 2018, Israel admitted carrying out a top-secretair raid on the site 11 years earlier.In 2008, less than a year after the strike, US officials accused Syria of having sought to build a secret nuclear reactor and acknowledged that Israel had destroyed it in the raid.View image in fullscreenAn image from a video released in April 2008 by the CIA showing a photo of a covert nuclear reactor being built in Syria’s eastern desert, according to the narrated video.Photograph: APSyria notified the agency of the site’s existence in a 17 July letter and invited the IAEA “to cooperate with the Syrian authorities in the inspection and verification of the site and of any nuclear material to be potentially found”.The IAEA said in its confidential report circulated to member states last Tuesday and seen by the Associated Press that this new site contained “natural uranium metal in the form of fuel rods with cladding”. The agency verified the material and confirmed “the presence of around 73 tonnes of natural uranium metal”.Grossi said that when the inspectors visited the site in August they had to “tear down walls” and go through “very difficult and narrow passages” to reach the nuclear material that had been hidden. The site had boxes scattered all over the place, he said.Grossi said “the important thing is that this material now is under safeguards” of the IAEA, adding that agency inspectors had managed to install cameras at the location.Asked if the nuclear material would remain in Syria or be removed, Grossi said this was “a matter that the Syrian government will have to decide”. He added: “We are not requesting them to do this or to do that. For us what’s important is that we know all the time where this [material] is until the last gram.”Logan Mintz, a director for nuclear materials security at the Washington-based Nuclear Threat Initiative, said natural uranium metal was not directly usable for a nuclear weapon but could be “diverted to a covert weapons programme that further processes it into plutonium for a nuclear weapon”.She said that once deemed safe to move, the material could be “transported in certified containers” to a third country that could “safely and securely disposition it into a more chemically stable and more widely used form” for possible use in nuclear power plants.“As with any transport of nuclear material, this movement would require robust security from theft or sabotage,” she said.Associated Press and Agence France-Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsSyriaNuclear weaponsNuclear powerBashar al-AssadEnergyMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: UN expert Francesca Albanese calls for ‘true paradigm shift’ as Miliband resets policy on Israel | Israel | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: UN special rapporteur on occupied territories says ban on goods from settlements ‘important’ but must go further if it is to amount to more than a ‘press release’
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Exclusive: UN special rapporteur on occupied territories says ban on goods from settlements ‘important’ but must go further if it is to amount to more than a ‘press release’
Content: Francesca Albanese, UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, said she would not join people dismissing policy as ‘theatre’ before details announced.Photograph: Jordi Ruiz Cirera/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFrancesca Albanese, UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, said she would not join people dismissing policy as ‘theatre’ before details announced.Photograph: Jordi Ruiz Cirera/The GuardianIsraelUN expert Francesca Albanese calls for ‘true paradigm shift’ as Miliband resets policy on IsraelExclusive: UN special rapporteur on occupied territories says ban on goods from settlements ‘important’ but must go further if it is to amount to more than a ‘press release’Patrick WintourDiplomatic EditorMon 7 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s planned ban on trade with unlawful Israeli settlements is a welcome, if overdue, first step and must be judged according to its practical impact, a UN expert has told the Guardian.The UK foreign secretary,Ed Miliband, has vowed to act more decisively against Israeli settlements, as well as continued restrictions of aid into Gaza, prompting the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, to claim on Saturday that Downing Street was motivated by “Jew hatred”.Miliband said what he had been told about restriction on aid into Gaza had reinforced the need for more decisive action. But Huckabee, writing on X in support of the Israeli foreign ministry’s own criticisms, said: “The Brits have lost it. The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts.”Huckabee did not mention in his statement that Miliband is himself Jewish. The Israeli foreign ministry had said: “Had the foreign secretary been interested in facts rather than stories, he would have known that there are no restrictions whatsoever on bringing medicines into the Gaza Strip, and that no medicine is being blocked.”Ed Miliband promises ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK policy toward IsraelRead morePalestinian groups in the UK are holding judgment until they see the fine detail of Miliband’s policy, due to be announced on Tuesday, but are expecting the most significant shift since a previous foreign secretary, David Lammy, withdrew most arms export licences in September 2024.Speaking to the Guardian, Francesca Albanese, the UN’s special rapporteur on the occupied territories, said a “ban on settlement goods was a change in UK government stance and absolutely important”. She added she would “not join those dismissing it as theatre before the details had been announced”.She said a settlement trade ban would have to be part of “a true paradigm shift to Israel-Palestine that ultimately seeks to implement theinternational court of justice advisory opinion in 2024”, which stated that Israel’s presence in the occupied territories was “unlawful in its entirety”. The opinion, she added, said that “all states carry an obligation – not a preference of an obligation – not to recognise the situation as legal, and not render aid and assistance in maintaining it”.UK must end all trade with Israel, says co-founder of BDS movementRead moreAlbanese also said the trade ban could not be narrowly confined to goods – such as agricultural products and cosmetics – since “they are a fraction of what sustains the occupation, and a fraction that Israel can absorb without difficulty”.The package should also aim to include trade in services, she said, progressively suspending British intelligence cooperation, all arms licensing and the unexamined flights out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Albanese warned that if the steps were not taken or were “completely off the table”, the changes would “over time come to be seen as not amounting to a reckoning, but a press release”.She said that a state banning “dates from Ma’ale Adumim [a city in the West Bank]” while “continuing to licence the equipment used to enforce the checkpoints around it” had not “changed its relationship with the occupation … It has rearranged its communication strategy.”Albanese added that, “because the 2024 ICJ advisory opinion declares the entire Israeli presence in the occupied territories as unlawful, third states’ obligations ‘not to render aid or assistance’ extends to everything that sustains that unlawful presence as a whole.”View image in fullscreenIsraeli finance minister Bezalel Smotrich standing near the settlement of Ma’ale Adumim, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, holding a map showing the E1 settlement project.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APAlbanese said the UK needed to end any ambiguity around the tender for the E1 settlement that will sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank and cut the territory in two, adding: “Since bids close a week before Israel’s elections on 27 October, there is nothing that London can realistically do in September that can change that calendar.”But she warned the government could not let the tenders simply pass, pointing out that Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, had already said E1 was designed to “bury the idea of a Palestinian state”.“There is a difference between the tenders closing and the settlement getting built and financed,” she added. “Construction on this scale needs finance, insurance and construction firms, and since E1 amounts to annexation and not just settlement expansion, sanctions or similar have to be threatened against those firms that seek to cooperate with the building of E1.”Albanese also called on the UK government to join South Africa before the ICJ, and also support Nicaragua on Monday when the ICJ hears preliminary oral objections from Germany over claims filed by the Central American country that Berlin’s continued arms sales to Israel makes it complicit in genocide.She said: “Britain is not a party to that case. It can still choose which side of the argument it stands on: whether it treats participation in international accountability mechanisms as a threat to an alliance, or recognises that an alliance built on anything other than principle and the rule of law is not an alliance at all. It is an arrangement of convenience, honoured only until convenience changes.”Finally she urged the UK to issue guidance to UK-based firms not to overcomply with sanctions imposed by the US on the international criminal court prosecutor, the deputy prosecutors, eight judges and an increasing number of others, including herself and Palestinian human rights groups that have cooperated with the court. “This has frozen bank accounts, everywhere, for people doing nothing other than their judicial function or providing evidence lawfully requested by an international court,” she said.Explore more on these topicsIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaWest BankEd MilibandForeign policyIsrael-Gaza warnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cities in Great Britain most vulnerable to extreme heat revealed  | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: OS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperatures
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: OS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperatures
Content: The City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenThe City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAExtreme heatCities in Great Britain most vulnerable to extreme heat revealedOS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperaturesSandra LavilleEnvironment correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePortsmouth, Leicester, Exeter, Bristol andNottinghamwill be among the cities that warm the most by the end of this century as global heating turns British cities into urban heat islands, according to research.Analysis from Ordnance Survey (OS) has created a heat vulnerability index for all cities in Great Britain.Portsmouth, which sits on the south coast of England and is home to 208,000 people, is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research from the OS, the Met Office and the data analysis company 4 Earth Intelligence.Concrete, asphalt, buildings and hard surfaces in cities absorb solar radiation during the day and act like giant radiators, holding on to the heat rather than cooling down at night as in more rural areas. Cities can be up to 10C hotter than surrounding areas.Areas most at risk of extreme warming are those with the leasttree cover,green spaceand waterways.View image in fullscreenPortsmouth is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research.Photograph: Peter Titmuss/AlamyThis summer was provisionallythe UK’s hottest on record, and the research reveals which cities are suffering now from intense urban heat and which will be among the warmest in future.The research analyses 71 cities granted by royal charter across England, Scotland and Wales but excluding Northern Ireland. The OS heat vulnerability index suggests that by 2040 all 71 cities will reach high heat vulnerability. By the turn of the century, almost two-thirds could reach the most severe level. Those facing the most severe impact by the end of the century are predicted to be Portsmouth, the City of Westminster, Plymouth,Leicesterand Exeter, according to the analysis.Nick Bolton, the chief executive of Ordnance Survey, said: “Cities are where millions of people live, work and spend their everyday lives.“Extreme and sustained heat can affect people’s health and wellbeing, how comfortable our homes and workplaces are, and put additional pressure on transport, energy and emergency services. Understanding how and where this vulnerability is changing depends on an accurate view of how the country is built, based on trusted authoritative data, which is critical for planners, developers and local authorities preparing for a warmer future.”UK ‘built for climate that no longer exists’ and needs urgent changes to survive global heating, report warnsRead morePortsmouth is today the most heat-vulnerable city and will remain at the highest level for warming until the end of the century, according to the research. The city of Leicester is projected to show the biggest rise in Britain’s heat vulnerability rankings, climbing from 10th now to fourth by the end of the century, while Exeter and Nottingham also rise into the 10 most vulnerable cities, alongside Bristol andBrightonand Hove by the end of this century.Leaders in Portsmouth have identified areas including Somerstown, Portsea, Southsea and Fratton as those particularly exposed to urban heat because of their limited green areas and hard surfaces, and noted that areas with less green space overlap with those of deprivation.The City ofLondonand the City of Westminster areas rank among the most heat-retentive urban environments in the UK.The City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city, given the concentration of buildings, roads and hard surfaces as well as limited green space, trees and water. Westminster ranks third for overall heat vulnerability today and second in both future periods behind Portsmouth.View image in fullscreenTree cover, green space and waterways can help mitigate the effects of global heating.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAstudycommissioned by the mayor of London has put the total economic cost of the 2022 London heatwaves at £1.5bn, including productivity losses, health impacts, education disruption, energy demand, transport and emergency services.The OS heat vulnerability index combined current observed temperatures with the structural characteristics of Britain’s built environment and climate projections into the future to produce a score for every city on a scale of 1 to 5, where 3 to 4 is high and 4 to 5 is severe.Among cities coping the best with the changing climate is Milton Keynes, which ranks 69th out of 71 cities for heat vulnerability today. Milton Keynes has the lowest built-environment vulnerability in England and the most effective natural cooling of any city in the analysis, with 46 sq km of natural surfaces, against almost 40 sq km of hard made surfaces.Jonathan Hendry, the chief executive of 4 Earth Intelligence, said exposure varied street by street within a single city. “The areas consistently subjected to higher temperatures than their surroundings are the ones that overheat first during a heatwave,” he said.“We’re mapping how to turn thermal threats into actionable blueprints for urban resilience, supporting decisions on where heat refuges are sited and how emergency responses are planned in advance rather than in the middle of climate events.”Explore more on these topicsExtreme heatClimate crisisPortsmouthConstruction industryThe sunLondonPlymouthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police used batons and pepper spray on far-right protesters in Portsmouth unrest | Portsmouth | The Guardian
description: Minister condemns groups behind Hampshire disorder and says officers were injured as they repelled ‘aggression’
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Minister condemns groups behind Hampshire disorder and says officers were injured as they repelled ‘aggression’
Content: An estimated 200 activists gathered in Portsmouth and clashed with riot police on Sunday night.Photograph: SuppliedView image in fullscreenAn estimated 200 activists gathered in Portsmouth and clashed with riot police on Sunday night.Photograph: SuppliedPortsmouthPolice used batons and pepper spray on far-right protesters in Portsmouth unrestMinister condemns groups behind Hampshire disorder and says officers were injured as they repelled ‘aggression’Rajeev Syal,Steven MorrisandBen QuinnMon 7 Sep 2026 15.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBatons and synthetic pepper spray were used to repel hundreds of masked, black-clad vigilantes inPortsmouthon Sunday, it has emerged, as the policing minister said officers had been injured as they repelled organised “aggression”.No 10 condemns ‘thuggish’ far-right activists after Portsmouth unrestRead moreAfter police contained the weekend’s second disruptive demonstration against asylum seekers travelling to the UK in small boats, it was claimed that officers inHampshirewere pushed off their motorbikes and pelted with bricks. Sarah Jones, the Home Office minister, condemned groups behind the disorder for promoting “racism and thuggery”.Activists wearing balaclavasclashed with police in Portsmouth on Sunday eveningafter a dinghy reached the UK from Normandy. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary have launched an investigation into potential assaults and criminal damage.Daniel Thomas, a far-right agitator closely linked to Tommy Robinson, the longtime anti-Islam figure whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, claimed to have arranged the protest.Thomas was also behind disruption in Dover on Saturday, when crowds of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road around the port for several hours.View image in fullscreenDaniel Thomas, left, speaking to the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf (right, in blue suit), has claimed to have arranged the demonstration.Photograph: Theo Shaw/PAIn a statement to MPs, Jones said: “Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary, with the support of other neighbouring forces, used a dispersal notice to ensure public safety and officers were forced to use batons and Pava spray to maintain order in the face of some aggression.”Spencer Wragg, the chair of the Hampshire police federation, said one of the officers injured was a rookie who had only finished training school three days earlier. “Those scenes in that area of Portsmouth weren’t protests, they weren’t protests at all, it was clear that some people were intent on disorder and venting their frustrations,” he said.About 120 people seeking asylum were brought to shore in Hampshire after travelling to the UK on a “mega-dinghy” which had departed from the Normandy coast and was at sea for roughly 10 hours.The landing point of the dinghy was farther west than most small boat arrivals. Officials are concerned that people smugglers are starting to target new routes across England’s south coast, with craft launched from a wider stretch of the French shoreline.View image in fullscreenAbout 120 people seeking asylum were brought to shore in Hampshire at the weekend.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersAn estimated 200 protesters gathered and clashed with riot police on Sunday night, vowing to prevent migrants leaving the port. Footage showed some chanting “send them back” as police officers with shields raised tried to maintain order.Amid concerns that police were caught unawares by the unrest in Dover on Saturday, Jones said: “Work is ongoing to establish any lessons and ensure that relevant intelligence is shared at pace across our law enforcement system.”Speaking to MPs and peers at a closed-door meeting on Monday, the prime minister Andy Burnham said Labour’s mission must be to counter “fear with positivity and hope”.Burnham is understood to have told the parliamentary Labour party (PLP) that Britain would never accept any form of racism in its communities and stood for a sense of fairness and justice.“We’ve got a fantastic opportunity in our hands to change this country for the better. We go into the autumn, in really good heart, with a spring in our step,” the prime minister said.“There’s a lot at stake and it requires us to counter fear with positivity and hope. We have a responsibility in the times that we’re living in. It’s a solemn responsibility to prevent the politics of poison seeping into our streets.“We are here to speak to the politics of hope and of positivity.”Labour and Lib Dem MPs called on the government to explain why police appeared to have been caught off-guard by the events in Dover and Portsmouth.Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and a former Home Office minister, questioned why the police were not aware of plans to block the local port. “Please ensure that the intelligence picture is strong enough so that the police can respond accordingly to future incidents,” he told MPs.The Liberal Democrat Home Office spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, asked: “How is it that far-right thugs in balaclavas were able to close Britain’s busiest port without the police receiving any prior intelligence? And how is it that then an apparently separate group with some commonalities were then able to blockade another site the next evening?”View image in fullscreenSarah Jones, the Home Office minister, said the government would learn lessons from the disorder.Photograph: House of Commons/UK Parliament/PAJones said there was “a crossover in terms of online activity” and the government would learn lessons from the disorder.In an on-camera confrontation on Monday, Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, told the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, thatthe Patriot Platform grouphe led would deliver working-class votes to Reform – but expressed anger at Nigel Farage’s criticisms of Dover demonstrators for wearing balaclavas.Thomas said: “I understand Nigel is going to be prime minister one day and I understand he has to set a standard, which will basically be that you know he can’t just come out and say, everything’s great and these guys are fantastic, but Nigel needs to be very careful with his words.”Yusuf said he would “take that message back” and added that Thomas had articulated why he and his group had organised demonstrations. “I think it’s important we listen to people. He was making his points respectfully,” he said.10:30Who is behind ‘thuggish’ far-right protests in Dover and Portsmouth? - The LatestPolice could impose a balaclava ban on future anti-migrant demonstrations after officers were injured, Whitehall sources said.Under the Crime and Policing Act, Hampshire police could apply for a ban to ensure that protesters cannot cover their faces. Facebook posts claim that a demonstration is planned for Saturday by a group called Portsmouth Patriots. Hampshire police has been approached for comment.Ministershave been criticisedfor failing to condemn far-right groups behind the disorder. Nick Lowles, the chief executive of Hope Not Hate, which charts far-right activity, told the BBC: “To have 300, 400 people with balaclavas marching down the streets, stopping traffic. You know, it’s not just good enough. We need to call these people out for their politics and for the type of Britain that they want to see.“We’ve got different ways to register our protest.
