We do not go on the street. We do not burn people out of their houses. We do not cause trouble and threaten to fight the police.”The Hampshire and Isle of Wight police and crime commissioner, Donna Jones, said England’s south coast was not prepared for the arrival of migrants, and ministers would have a “significant issue” if people traffickers shifted their routes farther west. She warned that places such as Portsmouth were “not set up” for the arrival of migrants.Kent police defended the force’s action after it described the highly organised protest action in Dover as “spontaneous”. Assistant chief constable Nigel Brookes said the term was used in line with national guidance and that the action had “developed rapidly”.Eight boats carrying 625 people arrived in the UK on Sunday after crossing the English Channel, Home Office data shows.Explore more on these topicsPortsmouthPoliceThe far rightImmigration and asylumHampshireEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Policing minister makes statement on ‘intimidating and thuggish’ anti-migrant protests – as it happened | Politics | The Guardian
description: Sarah Jones tells MPs ‘those responsible should expect to face the consequences’
Author: Andrew Sparrow
Headline: Sarah Jones tells MPs ‘those responsible should expect to face the consequences’
Content: 12.48 EDTMinister says some agitators were 'intimidating and thuggish'Some protestors showed “intimidating and thuggish behaviour” this weekend, Sarah Jones, the policing minister said.But she added she did not seek to “minimise” legitimate concerns people had about small boat crossings.“This government has taken action to fix the broken system we inherited and crack down on the people smugglers,” Jones said, pointing out that system-wide arrests were up 70%.ShareUpdated at12.55 EDT

title: Polanski faces Green rival in his pursuit of Keir Starmer’s old seat  | Green party | The Guardian
description: Hamza Chowdhury says most of his fellow Green Camden councillors back him to contest 8 October byelection
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Hamza Chowdhury says most of his fellow Green Camden councillors back him to contest 8 October byelection
Content: Hamza Chowdhury announced his candidacy for Holborn and St Pancras MP, arguing the seat does not need ‘a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet’.Photograph: Green PartyView image in fullscreenHamza Chowdhury announced his candidacy for Holborn and St Pancras MP, arguing the seat does not need ‘a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet’.Photograph: Green PartyGreen partyPolanski faces Green rival in his pursuit of Keir Starmer’s old seatHamza Chowdhury says most of his fellow Green Camden councillors back him to contest 8 October byelectionPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski is facing unexpected opposition from his own party in his attempt to fight the Holborn and St Pancras byelection for the Greens, with a local councillor saying he is also seeking the nomination, and that the seat does not need “a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet”.The intervention by Hamza Chowdhury, a Green representative on Camden council in northLondon, came as the date for the byelection was confirmed for 8 October, after Keir Starmer’s formal resignation as an MP.This is also potentially problematic for the Greens, given the vote comes just a week after their conference, meaning the final weekend of campaigning takes place as many party activists will be gathered in Brighton.Ina post on Instagramon Monday, Chowdhury said he had received nominations from six other Camden Green councillors, meaning seven of the 10 Greens on the authority oppose Polanski being selected.Among those backing Chowdhury is Lorna Russell, the group leader in Camden for theGreen party, which is the official opposition to Labour.Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, announced on Thursday thathe would seek the nomination to fight the seat vacated by Starmer, setting up a high-stakes byelection against Labour.View image in fullscreenZack Polanski canvassing in Holborn and St Pancras on 5 September.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianLocal party members will vote later this week to select a candidate, and the Guardian has been told thatthey are broadly supportive of Polanski standing.But such high-profile opposition is notable, especially given Chowdhury argued that Polanski, who lives in east London, would be unable to properly represent the area if he won.Chowdhury wrote: “I know Camden because I live it every day. I know the challenges facing our communities, our estates, our broken lifts, our unpicked bins, our unclean roads and endless housing register waiting list because these are the places I have grown up and continue to call home.“We don’t need another MP who arrives during an election campaign, puts out a few leaflets, makes a few promises and disappears once the votes are counted. We need an MP who is present, accessible and visibly part of the community all year round.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I am asking Green party members for the opportunity to represent your home truly and properly. I’m not asking you to vote for a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet. I’m asking you to choose someone who is already here.”Speaking to the Guardianwhile canvassing in the constituency at the weekend, Polanski said that even if he wins he will not move to the area, but cycle from his flat in Hackney.He said: “I can cycle to the constituency really quickly. In fact, the length of the constituency is just as fast for me to cycle,” he says. “I’d regularly be here, doing surgeries and representing people.”Polanski has said his party is the underdog in a constituency won by Starmer with an 11,000-plus majority in the 2024 election. The Greens have already flooded the area with canvassers, hoping to mimic the model usedto overturn a 13,000-plus Labour majority in Greater Manchester’s Gorton and Dentonin February.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiByelectionsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: No 10 condemns ‘thuggish’ far-right activists after Portsmouth unrest | Portsmouth | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of men, some in balaclavas, try to prevent asylum seekers’ processing, two days after similar scenes in Dover
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Hundreds of men, some in balaclavas, try to prevent asylum seekers’ processing, two days after similar scenes in Dover
Content: 0:57Riot police clash with far-right protesters in Portsmouth – videoPortsmouthNo 10 condemns ‘thuggish’ far-right activists after Portsmouth unrestHundreds of men, some in balaclavas, try to prevent asylum seekers’ processing, two days after similar scenes in DoverPeter WalkerandJessica ElgotMon 7 Sep 2026 11.34 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDowning Street has condemned the “thuggish and intimidating behaviour” of far-right activistswho blocked roadsin Portsmouth when a boat carrying asylum seekers arrived in the city, two daysafter similar scenesin Dover.Hundreds of men, some dressed in black and wearing balaclavas, tried to stop the arrivals from being transported for processing until 3am, when police removed them with threats of arrest.Hampshire police said later that a number of police, coastguard and Border Force vehicles had been damaged, and a few officers had suffered minor injuries. It said the force was investigating possible offences of assaults on officers and criminal damage.10:30Who is behind ‘thuggish’ far-right protests in Dover and Portsmouth? - The LatestThe crowd was seemingly organised by Daniel Thomas, a far-right agitator closely linked toTommy Robinson, the longtime anti-Islam and far-right figure whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.Thomas was also behind the scenes in Dover on Saturday, when crowds of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road around the port.Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “The intimidating and thuggish behaviour we saw over the weekend in Dover andPortsmouthis absolutely unacceptable. We condemn it unreservedly. We’ll always respect the right to peaceful protest but not where it crosses the line into disorder.”On Monday night, Burnham said Labour had a “solemn responsibility” to stop the “politics of poison seeping into our streets”.Speaking to the parliamentary Labour party at a closed-door meeting in Westminster, the prime minister said there was “a lot at stake” and that the party must “counter fear with positivity and hope”.View image in fullscreenDamage to a police car windscreen at the scene of the far-right protest in Portsmouth on Sunday night.Photograph: SuppliedThomas, who uses the name Danny Tommo on social media, was recorded telling the crowd that Portsmouth was “now ground zero” for the arrival of asylum seekers on boats from France, saying “enough is enough” and “Dover was a dummy run”.Later on Monday he interrupted media interviews in Portsmouth with Zia Yusuf, the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, to tell reporters that the use of balaclavas and masks was not intended to intimidate, but to stop supporters of his self-styled Patriot Platform group from being targeted by leftwing protesters.Thomas was jailed in 2016 for the attempted kidnapping of a man connected to claims of drugs being sold, but now describes himself as a committed Christian.1:02Far-right activists wade through sea to film asylum seekers in Portsmouth – videoThe government had come under some pressure to condemn the events in Dover and Portsmouth as de facto vigilantism.Nick Lowles, the chief executive of Hope Not Hate, which charts far-right activity, told the BBC: “To have 300, 400 people with balaclavas marching down the streets, stopping traffic. You know, it’s not just good enough. We need to call these people out for their politics and for the type of Britain that they want to see.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’ve got different ways to register our protest. We do not go on the street. We do not burn people out of their houses. We do not cause trouble and threaten to fight the police.”chartReform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, condemned the use of masks and paramilitary-style black outfits, but said the road blockades showed the UK was “on the edge of serious civil disturbance” over small boats carrying asylum seekers, even though the number arriving has fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year.“Masked marches on the streets of Dover, and a huge, spontaneous protest on the streets of Portsmouth last night,” he said in a video posted on X. “You’d be right in thinking that this country is now on the edge of serious civil disturbance.“But let me please say this: people wearing masks, dressed up in a similar type uniform to a paramilitary, is not going to solve this problem … Remember, peaceful protests good, uniforms and masks bad.”Despite the fall in small boat arrivals, ministers will be alarmed by the apparent use of different routes by people smugglers, moving beyond the Dover area.Donna Jones, the Conservative police and crime commissioner for Hampshire, said a boat carrying 140 people left somewhere near Cherbourg in France at about 1am on Sunday morning, before entering the Solent, near Portsmouth, about 10 hours later.She said the town did not have the infrastructure in place to process arrivals, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “My big concern now is that Portsmouth does not become a destination of choice for the people traffickers who are trying to bring people across to Britain.”She did not condemn the far-right activists, saying: “Largely they were peaceful. They were there making their point, but they don’t want Portsmouth to become a destination.”Explore more on these topicsPortsmouthTommy RobinsonImmigration and asylumHome OfficeFar rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: US woman charged with killing son ‘very invested’ in Lindsay Clancy trial, prosecutors say | US news | The Guardian
description: Corie Walsh charged with murder after two-year-old Barrett found dead in basement of Illinois family home last week
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Corie Walsh charged with murder after two-year-old Barrett found dead in basement of Illinois family home last week
Content: Lindsay Clancy with her lawyer Kevin Reddington in court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, last week.Photograph: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/ReutersView image in fullscreenLindsay Clancy with her lawyer Kevin Reddington in court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, last week.Photograph: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/ReutersUS newsUS woman charged with killing son ‘very invested’ in Lindsay Clancy trial, prosecutors sayCorie Walsh charged with murder after two-year-old Barrett found dead in basement of Illinois family home last weekAssociated PressMon 7 Sep 2026 19.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Illinois woman charged with killing her two-year-old son had been closely following the murder trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy and was texting friends about the case just hours before her son was found dead, prosecutors said.Corie Walsh, 40, was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after her son, Barrett, was found dead in the basement of the family’s suburban Chicago home last Tuesday, according to court records obtained by NBC Chicago.Prosecutors said Walsh had become “very invested” in Clancy’s nationally watched trial and was discussing it with friends until about 12:30pm. that day. A neighbor found Barrett less than four hours later.Walsh was found elsewhere in the home with injuries authorities said were self-inflicted. Prosecutors said she later told investigators that she killed her son because she believed he was the “devil” and the “anti-Christ”. Her attorney, Andrea Lyon, told reporters Walsh was experiencing a psychotic episode and called the boy’s death a tragedy for the entire family.Police were called to Walsh’s home in Frankfort, about 35 miles south-west of Chicago, shortly before 4pm after a neighbor discovered Barrett in the basement, according to prosecutors’ petition seeking to keep Walsh jailed before trial.The neighbor found the boy and began CPR while calling 911, prosecutors said. He was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. An autopsy determined that he died from asphyxia caused by ligature compression of the neck.Police searching the house found Walsh fully dressed in a bathtub containing bloody water, prosecutors said. She had cuts to her wrists and thighs and was taken to a hospital with injuries authorities described as not life-threatening.The disclosure that Walsh had been following Clancy’s trial came days after a Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in that case when jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict.Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, was accused of killing her three young children in 2023. Her lawyers argued that she was legally insane and suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors maintained that Clancy understood what she was doing and knew it was wrong.Authorities in Illinois have not alleged that Clancy’s trial played a role in the killing of Walsh’s son, and no evidence made public so far establishes a connection beyond her discussion of the case.Frankfort police and prosecutors in Will county did not respond to calls for comment on Monday.Explore more on these topicsUS newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Federal investigators search for cause of Amazon cargo jet crash that killed five | Florida | The Guardian
description: Focus likely on whether plane touched down too late in its glide path on to tarmac to enable it to stop safely
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Focus likely on whether plane touched down too late in its glide path on to tarmac to enable it to stop safely
Content: A view of an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane that overran a runway at Miami international airport, in Miami, Florida, on Sunday.Photograph: Marco Bello/ReutersView image in fullscreenA view of an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane that overran a runway at Miami international airport, in Miami, Florida, on Sunday.Photograph: Marco Bello/ReutersFloridaFederal investigators search for cause of Amazon cargo jet crash that killed fiveFocus likely on whether plane touched down too late in its glide path on to tarmac to enable it to stop safelyEdward HelmoreandMaya YangMon 7 Sep 2026 17.49 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 10.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederal investigators have started collecting evidence, including a flight data recorder, following the Sunday crash of anAmazoncargo jet at Miami international airport that killed five people and injured five others.Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Jennifer Homendy, chair of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), announced a preliminary investigation into the Amazon Air flight 7598 accident involving a Boeing 767-33 Alpha operated by 21 Air, an all-cargo airline.“What we know so far is the flight was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, with two crew members on board. This was the third flight for the aircraft. That aircraft yesterday went from Cincinnati toMiami, Miami to San Juan, and San Juan back to Miami,” Homendy said.She added: “[It] overran runway 30 on landing, struck navigational aids and equipment, then impacted a 2012 white Ford Econoline van that was owned by Professional Ocean Service Corporation, which is a contract cleaning company for the airline. In the van were seven persons on board.“The aircraft then traveled through a perimeter fence and impacted a Toyota Corolla Cross LE, which was traveling on Northwest 67th Avenue, and then continued into the grass and impacted another fence line, which separated an area where Tesla robotaxis were stationed. In total, it was about 1,300ft past the paved surface.”Homendy described the Ford Econoline van as “torn apart”, and noted that for the Corolla Cross LE, “you can see airbags … you can see components from vehicles, both passenger vehicles and the aircraft itself”.Federal investigators are expected to focus on several areas, including operations and human performance, flight crew experience, as well as 21 Air’s policies and contractual relationship with Amazon.Other areas of focus include air traffic services, radar data, aircraft performance and structure, meteorology, as well as the “lack thereof of an engineered materials arresting system, or EMAS … a crushable, lightweight material that’s at the end of a runway that safely stops an aircraft”, Homendy said.She added that although the NTSB would remain on scene for at least a week, its focus during that time will not be on determining probable cause, but rather on documenting the scene and collecting perishable evidence.Video footage from Sunday showed the Boeing 767 jet wobbling slightly, coming in fast and flying relatively far along the runway before it touched down.After the aircraft overshot the runway, coming to rest in a parking lot with its nose tipped forward, flames burst out of part of the jet and thick, dark smoke began billowing into the air.The crash trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade rescue fire chief Ray Jadallah said. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.Jadallah described the incident as a “very complex situation” where the plane crashed into multiple vehicles as it ran off the tarmac, trapping several people inside their vehicles.Video of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767-33A, operated by contractor 21 Air,postedto social media show it touching down far along the runway. Otherposted footageshows the plane with a left hand wheel of the landing gear still a little above the ground as the jet speeds down the tarmac, apparently abnormally fast, and then it overruns the end of the runway, where the right undercarriage collapsed and the wing caught fire.Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 ft (914m) of a runway. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said if it was beyond that area, the plane should normally have aborted the landing and gone around for another attempt.Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the transportation department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.Storm clouds can be seen in the area and strong winds reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.Miami airport is not equipped with “arresting beds”, systems of lightweight, crushable material that the federal aviation authority (FAA) says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide at the end of runways to help safely stop planes that overshoot.Some 200 emergency personnel responded to the incident, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the fire department said.The flight operators, 21 Air, is a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Flights later resumed, although two runways at the busy airport remained out of service on Monday morning.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsFloridaMiamiAmazonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Giuliani says Mamdani should skip 9/11 ceremony during rant against Islam | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: New York City mayor confirms he will attend memorial service but declines to respond to Giuliani’s remarks
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: New York City mayor confirms he will attend memorial service but declines to respond to Giuliani’s remarks
Content: Rudy Giuliani was mayor of New York City from 1994 to 2001.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APView image in fullscreenRudy Giuliani was mayor of New York City from 1994 to 2001.Photograph: Ted Shaffrey/APSeptember 11 2001Giuliani says Mamdani should skip 9/11 ceremony during rant against IslamNew York City mayor confirms he will attend memorial service but declines to respond to Giuliani’s remarksEdward Helmorein New YorkMon 7 Sep 2026 16.25 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 16.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew York mayorZohran Mamdaniis set to come face-to-face withRudy Giulianiat the main September 11 memorial service, just days after the former mayor – who led the city at the time of the2001 terrorist attacks– disparaged his Muslim religion and said he should skip the ceremony.In an interview with right-leaning Newsmax at the weekend, Giulianisaid: “Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he’s coming.”Mamdani confirmed on Monday, while attending a breakfast celebrating New York’s J’ouvert and West Indian Day Paradecelebrationsin Brooklyn, that he would attend the main ceremony and multiple 9/11 events on Friday, to stand with the families of those who died and first responders – as he did last year before taking office.“I’m proud to be the mayor of this city. I love this city. I love this country,” he said. “What I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11, and a focus also on the first responders who did everything they could.”The mayor and his office have declined to respond to Giuliani’s remarks.Giuliani, the former mayor and a close ally of Donald Trump, has said he will also attend this year’s ceremony to mark the attacks by terrorists representingal-Qaida, who flew hijacked passenger planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan on September 11 2001.Reflecting pools with waterfalls constructed on the footprints of the towers and a 9/11 museum now mark the site that was dubbed Ground Zero in the aftermath of the attacks, and where each year the names of the almost 3,000 people who died are read out by survivors and loved ones, in a solemn ceremony attended by national and local leaders.In the interview with Newsmax, Giuliani was asked if Mamdani should skip the ceremony. “Well, there’s no question he should,” he said.Giuliani was mayor ofNew YorkCity from 1994 to 2001. He ran unsuccessfully for president and, more recently, has been an attorney to and a staunch ally of Donald Trump.In the convoluted tirade on air on Saturday, Giuliani threw insults and baseless comparisons. He appeared to draw parallels between Mamdani’s faith and the 9/11 hijackers acting on the extremist orders ofOsama bin Laden, the jihadist militant and terrorist leader killed by US forces during the Obama administration.He remarked that the terrorists brought their ideological opposition to the United States “in the name of the Muslim religion” and “weren’t hiding it like Mamdani is trying to hide it”. He also declared the opinion that the mayor supports a notion that Islam should be the dominant religion.Mamdani has previously spoken about how an Islamophobic backlash built after the 2001 attacks and had made anti-Muslim prejudice “a fact of life” for Muslim Americans. “It was this horrific day that was also, for many New Yorkers, the moment at which they were marked an ‘other’,”he told the New York Times last year.Last week, Mamdani issued an executive order designating 9/11 an annual official “Day of Remembrance and Service” that requires the city administration to designate a moment of silence to mourn those who were killed and affected by the attacks. A second order established a new taskforce to help the city’s emergency preparedness.Several other high-profile figures, including former New York governor George Pataki, have voiced opposition to Mamdani’s attendance at the ceremony, and an online petition arguing the same has gathered close to 100,000 signatures.Dignitaries expected to attend Friday’s commemorations include former US presidents Bill Clinton, George W Bush and Barack Obama, and some other former mayors of New York.The White House has said Donald Trump is not attending but is expected to commemorate the9/11attack on the Pentagon at that site close to Washington DC, a decision that also has also drawn criticism.US vice-president JD Vance is expected to represent the White House in New York.Explore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001Rudy GiulianiZohran MamdaniNew YorkUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Legal veterans lead fightback against Trump’s ‘full-out assault on democracy’ | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Advocacy groups expand legal challenges and condemn president’s ‘self-serving attempts to take over midterms’
Author: Peter Stone
Headline: Advocacy groups expand legal challenges and condemn president’s ‘self-serving attempts to take over midterms’
Content: Trump at an event at the White House last month.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersView image in fullscreenTrump at an event at the White House last month.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersDonald TrumpLegal veterans lead fightback against Trump’s ‘full-out assault on democracy’Advocacy groups expand legal challenges and condemn president’s ‘self-serving attempts to take over midterms’Peter Stonein WashingtonMon 7 Sep 2026 15.59 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and ex-judges have expanded legal challenges to Donald Trump’s authoritarian executive orders on voting and other presidential actions they see as a “war” on the rule of law in the US.Heavy legal opposition to Trump’s two executive orders on elections to curb voting rights and supplant the authority of states on election matters has come from the Democracy Defenders Fund, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and kindred groups.These legal outfits and like-minded allies have won key lawsuits on election issues, plus litigation thwarting Trump’s moves to end birthright citizenship and a $1.8bn slush fund that could have paid money to allies including January 6 rioters he deemed were unjustly charged.Since Trump returned to power, for instance, Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center have jointly filed lawsuits against Trump’s 2025 and 2026 executive orders on voting, challenging their constitutionality to set new voting rules that by law are run by the states.Key legal briefs they filed together include an August one on behalf of several voting rights groups and local officials in two states to block Trump’s March 2026 executive order that would restrict voting by mail and authorize the US Postal Service to implement rules to that end.Other groups that have accelerated their legal challenges to Trump’s moves to thwart voting rights and expand his executive powers in other ways, include the Brennan Center for Justice, Democracy Forward, members of the Democratic Attorneys General Association and the Washington Litigation Group.Last month, for instance, 24 Democratic attorney generals and other plaintiffs filed suit to block USPS from moving forward with rules to curb mail voting and in late August won a temporary 14-day restraining order from federal judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts.In response, the DoJ’s solicitor general John Sauer on Thursday appealed to the supreme court to lift the injunction, arguing in heated words that the freeze would create “serious, irreparable harm on the federal government, the states themselves, and the voting public”.On 4 September Talwani made her injunction permanent, writing that implementing Trump’s order so close to the election “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail.” She also stressed that “the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation.”Sauer on 6 September responded with another emergency appeal to the high court urging it permit the new USPS rules to go into effect, claiming that it “does not seize control of states’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail.”In a related twist, a detailed whistleblower complaint that Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut released last week alleged that the USPS has been proceeding with a “secretive, rushed” effort to implement Trump’s order that could lead to “catastrophic failure” with this year’s mail-in voting.About 50 million Americans, the majority of whom are Democrats, vote by mail, according to reports.With the elections about two months away, the legal groups are stepping up efforts to thwart “self-serving attempts to take over the midterms”, said a former DoJ lawyer, which experts fear may create chaos and disenfranchise millions of voters.Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at the Campaign Legal Center, told the Guardian: “The CLC and the DDF have worked closely together on two ongoing lawsuits challenging the president’s unlawful voting executive orders that attempt to dictate election rules. We’ve teamed up in the supreme court on a brief filed by former state and federal judges, including noted conservative judges, that emphasized just how unlawful and dangerous the president’s efforts to dictate election rules are.”Baldwin, who spent 14 years in the justice department’s civil rights division, said the CLC and the DDF have also “worked together in federal cases filed in Oregon and California to make sure that the DoJ isn’t able to seize voters’ sensitive data by making false claims about non-citizen voting. In cases around the country, the Campaign Legal Center is pushing back on the DoJ’s lawless efforts to vacuum up and aggregate sensitive data to create a national voter file of some sort.”Further, former ambassador Norm Eisen, the executive chair of the Democracy Defenders Fund, which he co-founded in 2023, told the Guardian that since its inception the DDF has been involved in more than 300 legal cases and matters in three primary areas: elections, the rule of law and anti-corruption.Eisen said the group, whose board boasts former federal judge and conservative stalwart J Michael Luttig and liberal-leaning ex-federal judge Nancy Gertner, likes to work in conjunction on cases with other ideologically diverse and nonpartisan groups like the CLC and the WLG because “they both have strong bipartisan credibility. It’s a big-tent approach we’ve taken with our election work.”Eisen said Luttig and Gertner were instrumental in helping recruit dozens of former judges with bipartisan credentials to file amicus briefs on multiple matters including an August one to the supreme court opposing Trump’s 2026 executive order to curb mail voting.For its part, the WLG this summer hired about half a dozen new lawyers to handle election-related litigation. “As the midterms approach with growing concerns about potential federal interference in elections, we’ve brought on more attorneys to be even more prepared to litigate sensitive matters under acute time pressure,” said James Pearce, a principal with the WLG.View image in fullscreenA Kentucky voter in Louisville casts her ballot.Photograph: Bryan Woolston/ReutersElsewhere, Sophia Lin Lakin, who leads the ACLU Voting Rights Project, said the group had been “pushing back” on administration efforts to seize personal voting data from states, and said the ACLU has been involved in 26 of 30 legal challenges to the administration on the issue. To date, the administration has lost 23 cases where rulings have been made.Critics say Trump, the DoJ, the USPS and the Department of Homeland Security seem to be laying the groundwork for further attacks on the nation’s election rules, citing Trump’s false claims about election fraud and his radical plans to change voting rules.In July in a televised speech, Trump falsely portrayed the nation’s voting system as riddled with fraud and condemned voting by mail and non-citizen voting. “Mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt,” Trump claimed without evidence, even though he voted twice by mail this year.Trump, who continues to blame voting fraud for his 2020 loss to Joe Biden, also charged that non-citizen voting, which is illegal and historically minuscule, poses a “crisis of election security”. Trump’s fixation on noncitizen voting is belied by a database from the rightwing Heritage Foundation that only cites 100 cases over a quarter-century.But according to documents reviewed by the New York Times, hundreds of DHS agents have been engaged in a hunt to find noncitizens among registered voters. The chief of the DHS has said ICE agentscould be sent to polling places“if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant”.The DoJ has helped to amplify Trump’s bogus election claims with legal threats and actions.In July, Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the department’s civil rights division, wrote to officials in 50 states warning that “any election officer, including the chief election officer of the state, who knowingly retains noncitizens on the state’s [voter list] or facilitates noncitizens in receiving and casting ballots could be subject to criminal liability”.In August, the DoJ announced plans to send a larger-than-usual contingent of 1,000 lawyers to monitor voting nationwide, raising concerns that such large efforts could lead to voter intimidation.And in a harbinger of coming legal fights, Trump announced on his Truth Social platform last month that the DoJ’s Ed Martin, a key election denialist in charge of pardons, was leaving to handle election-related litigation.Former DoJ lawyers say administration threats to voting rights make opposition from legal advocates crucial.Stacey Young, a lawyer who left the department at the start of 2025 after 18 years to found Justice Connection, a group of more than 3,000 ex-DoJ lawyers and other alumni, denounced Trump’s moves “to interfere” with elections.“The constitution makes clear that the president has no authority over the administration of our elections, but that hasn’t stopped this president, or those he put in power at the justice department, from trying to interfere,” Young said in a statement. “We’re taking these threats seriously and leveraging our collective strengths to protect election integrity, which is key to maintaining a functioning democracy.”Justice Connection is working with experts in its alumni network to engage with the media, Congress and the public to highlight the justice department’s traditional role in election security and ensuring compliance with federal voting laws.Other DoJ alumni agree that opposition to Trump’s election agenda is critical.“These organizations are doing critical work in protecting the ability of people to vote and make their voices heard – a cornerstone of democracy,” said Michael Bromwich, a former DoJ inspector general. “The full-out assault on democracy must be addressed through the courts because Congress has proven itself unwilling and unable to check the undemocratic steps taken by the administration.”Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney for eastern Michigan who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, said: “Large law firms sent armies of young attorneys to our nation’s airports to represent individuals caught up in Trump’s travel ban. That is not happening any more because of the ‘deals’ they negotiated with the Trump administration in his second term to support his pet causes.“Thank goodness for groups like the Democracy Defenders Fund, which are attracting top legal talent and challenging some of Trump’s lawless activities. Their work is protecting the rights of all Americans.”Further, Nick Brown, Washington state’s attorney general, who chairs an election protection group for the Democratic Attorneys General Association, said it has teamed up with some legal advocacy groups such as the Brennan Center, States United and the DDF to hold “strategy sessions” to prepare for potential disruptive moves by the Trump administration in the November elections.Brown also attacked the administration’s appeal to the supreme court to move forward with Trump’s executive order on voting by mail, despite Judge Talwani’s strong concerns and Democratic attorney generals’ litigation against it.He said: “As the court said, states’ compliance with this illegal order would be ‘practically impossible’ before the November elections given the unprecedented demands it would put on state and local elections officials. The chaos that would cause is exactly what Trump wants. That’s why we continue to fight for a fair and properly administered election.”Baldwin too raised strong concerns about the DoJ’s push to get the supreme court to issue a ruling that would expedite Trump’s executive order on voting by mail.She said: “The DoJ’s slapdash effort at getting the supreme court’s blessing to turn the USPS into a gatekeeper for mail would be a farce, if it didn’t put our fundamental right to vote in the crosshairs. Given the importance of what is at stake, the DoJ’s continued efforts are nothing more than an attempt to foist chaos on the electoral process. But they will fail.”Other lawyers engaged in key election legal battles and other litigation voice optimism they will prevail.Tianna Mays, the legal director of the DDF, said: “The Trump administration has declared war on the rule of law, yet our democratic guardrails are still holding. We refuse to stand by idly while this administration flouts the constitution and attempts to eviscerate our institutions.”This article was updated on 7 September 2026 to reflect that members of the Democratic Attorneys General Association have filed suit, not the Daga itself.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: First Thing: German far-right leader thanks Elon Musk after landmark election win praised by Russia | US news | The Guardian
description: The populist, far-right, anti-immigration AfD won the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt
Author: Martin Belam
Headline: The populist, far-right, anti-immigration AfD won the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt
Content: Top candidate of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), Ulrich Siegmund, who thanked Elon Musk.Photograph: Liesa Johannssen/ReutersView image in fullscreenTop candidate of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), Ulrich Siegmund, who thanked Elon Musk.Photograph: Liesa Johannssen/ReutersFirst Thing newsletterUS newsFirst Thing: German far-right leader thanks Elon Musk after landmark election win praised by RussiaPopulist, far-right, anti-immigration AfD wins vote in eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. Plus, 50 years since The Muppet Show first hit our screensDon’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up hereMartin BelamMon 7 Sep 2026 07.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 07.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood morning. A far-right leader who has won an important state election in Germany hasthanked Elon Musk for his support, as voices in Europe warn the result is a serious moment for the continent. No far-right party has led or formed a government in Germany since the defeat of nazism at the end of the second world war.Ulrich Siegmund, the Alternative für Deutschland’s lead candidate, thanked Musk on X after the tech billionaire said “Well done!” in German to the AfD co-founder Alice Weidel. The populist, far-right, anti-immigration party won the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.During its campaign, the AfD sought to capitalise on a mood of nostalgia for the communist East Germany and discontent among east Germans. The party has promised a remigration and deportation offensive, to ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms. It wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and reintroduce the singing of the country’s national anthem in schools.Will the AfD be able to form a state government?Despite its resounding victory, the party fell just short of a majority. It was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called “firewall” of the mainstream parties, which refuse to work with it. The final results showed the AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member legislature.What has been the reaction in Washington and Moscow?Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the election projection without comment on his Truth Social site. The Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump’s post and praised a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”. The AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians in Germany to no longer receive refugee status.Iran war likely to drag on for another six months,former US defense secretary warnsView image in fullscreenLeon Panetta said the Iran conflict risked becoming another ‘forever war in the Middle East’.Photograph: Paul Buck/EPADonald Trump’s war with Iran islikely to drag on for another six months, the former US defense secretary Leon Panetta has said, adding that it risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight.“It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama. “I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added.Who else has been saying Trump’s war may not achieve its aims?The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, said on Sunday morningWashington might not be able to reach an agreement with Tehranthat would prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons. “We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said.Lindsay Clancy murder trial ends in dramatic deadlockView image in fullscreenThe case against Lindsay Clancy has ceased for the moment, but the legal wrangling is not over and a second trial could now be on the horizon.Photograph: Greg Derr/ReutersLindsay Clancy, prosecutors, defense lawyers, the judge and the millions watching on wereback where they startedafter her five-week trial over the murder of her three children ended in a mistrial. The case has ceased for the moment, but the legal wrangling is not over and a second trial could now be on the horizon, prolonging and repeating an agonizing spectacle that has gripped the US and the world.What will Clancy’s defense team most likely do?They will almost certainly push to have the charges against their client dropped, aggressively lobby against another trial and make a case to the district attorney’s office along the lines of: “Why are you doing this to this poor woman? She’s still clearly obviously suffering. She’s been punished with her paralysis and, worse than that, the loss of her three children.”Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlashView image in fullscreenThere are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans a month.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersGrowing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US arepushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda.There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans a month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk former lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently used by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.In other news …View image in fullscreenThis satellite image shows three storms, from left, Hurricane Lowell, Hurricane Karina and Tropical Storm Marie in the Pacific Ocean.Photograph: CIRA/NOAA/APHawaii hasdeclared a state of emergencyas powerful Hurricane Lowell makes its way toward the islands.The Trump administration renewed its appeal to the US supreme court toallow restrictions on mail-in voting, after a federal judge had blocked new limits.More voters are identifying as Democratsand shying away from calling themselves Republicans, according to the latest quarterly data.Falling ceiling debris at the Kennedy Center hasrenewed debateover much-needed renovations, with preservationists worried the board may seize on the incident to close the institution.The UK government has condemned balaclava-clad far-right activists whoblocked roads in the south of Englandafter a boat carrying asylum seekers arrived in Portsmouth.Stat of the day: At least five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airportView image in fullscreenThe Amazon car plane overshot the runway at Miami, striking several vehicles.Photograph: Lynne Sladky/APAn Amazon cargo plane crashedat Miami international airport in Florida after the flight overshot the runway, striking several vehicles and resulting in at least five deaths. Three people were left in critical condition and two more were hospitalized as operations at the airport were brought to a halt.Building Power: Even in safe-haven Massachusetts, trans care is at risk, but young people are fighting to protect itView image in fullscreenYoung trans activists protest in the building containing the office of Massachusetts’ state attorney general in BostonPhotograph: Alexa B Wilkinson/courtesy of Gender Liberation MovementOrganizers with the youth-led group Protect Trans Futures (PTF) havestaged an occupation, refusing to leave without a commitment to protect civil rights for trans children.Don’t miss this: Tennessee says child rapists deserve to die – now it prepares to execute one of their victimsView image in fullscreenOn Wednesday, Christa Pike’s lawyers filed a 226-page clemency petition with Tennessee’s Republican governor, Bill Lee.Photograph: APAged just 18, Christa Pike was sentenced to death for murder. But what if the jury knew she had suffered years of sexual abuse as a child?Ed Pilkington reports.… or this: Graphic novel aims to remember the history and horror of genocideView image in fullscreenPortraits in the Holocaust Memorial Center for the Jews of North Macedonia, Skopje.Photograph: Georgi Licovski/EPADana Mashoian Walrath’s The Book of Genocides is an audacious and personal new look at genocides from Germany to Palestine.David Smith speaks to the author, who expects to get banned from Israel as a result of her work.Climate check: The heat crisis has mayors of major cities all facing the same questionView image in fullscreenThe mayor of Phoenix, Arizona, is working with her counterparts in other parts of the world.Photograph: John Sirlin/AlamyWriting for the Guardian, the mayors of Paris, Milan and Phoenixexplain how they areworking jointly to find solutions that protect vulnerable residents, communicate risk, and redesign neighborhoods in preparation for hotter summers.Last Thing: How the Muppets rocked the world with anarchy, nonsense and the inimitable Miss PiggyView image in fullscreenElton John performs on The Muppet Show, which first hit screens in September 1976.Photograph: David Dagley/ShutterstockWho doesn’t love the The Muppet Show, which first hit our screens 50 years ago?Darren Richman looks backat that incredible burst of creativity from Jim Henson and company.Sign upSign up for the US morning briefingFirst Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. title: ‘The most anti-union president’: how Trump turned his back on US workers | US unions | The Guardian
description: Labor experts stunned at how anti-worker Trump has been with actions since last Labor Day that have hurt unions
Author: Steven Greenhouse
Headline: Labor experts stunned at how anti-worker Trump has been with actions since last Labor Day that have hurt unions
Content: A portrait of President Donald Trump hangs from the Department of Labor headquarters in Washington DC ahead of Labor Day on 31 August 2026.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA portrait of President Donald Trump hangs from the Department of Labor headquarters in Washington DC ahead of Labor Day on 31 August 2026.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockUS unions‘The most anti-union president’: how Trump turned his back on US workersLabor experts stunned at how anti-worker Trump has been with actions since last Labor Day that have hurt unionsSteven GreenhouseMon 7 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has repeatedly vowed to champion US workers. Shortly before Labor Day last year, he said: “Every policy of the Trump administrationis designed to lift up the American workerand “promote great-paying blue-collar jobs”. But in the year since last Labor Day, Trump has taken many actions that have hurt US workers and unions, with some labor experts saying they’ve been stunned at how anti-worker Trump has been.In the months after Trump returned to office, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) cut workplace inspections by 20%, compared with Joe Biden’s last year in office. Even though Trump campaigned as a champion of coal miners, his administration has repeatedlydelayed implementation of a rule to limit silica dust, which has afflicted and killed many coal miners with black lung. The United Mine Workers union hasurgently called for “immediate enforcement”of the stalled silica dust rule.With regard to wages, workers haven’t been doing so well under Trump. While the White House boasts that wages have risen, the problem for workers is that prices – pushed up by Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war –have risen faster than wagesover the past year, helping fuel the affordability crisis. In a move that will cut pay for many low-wage workers, the Trump administration has proposed eliminating federal minimum wage and overtimeprotections for 3 million often low-paid homecare workerswho take care of seniors and the disabled.Despite several court rulings to slow or stop this anti-union effort, Trump has pushed aggressively ahead with his unprecedented campaign to strip 1 million federal employees of their ability to bargain collectively – a move that Liz Shuler, president of the AFL-CIO, the nation’s main labor federation, called, “the largest single act of union-bustingin our history”. Trump has moved to end collective bargaining for hundreds of thousands of workers at the Transportation Security Agency, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Department of Agriculture, the Environmental Protection Agency and other agencies.In another unprecedented move, Trump fired Gwynne Wilcox, the pro-union chair of the National Labor Relations Board – the first time a president has fired an NLRB member. Trump has since named numerous pro-business officials to the labor board.“Trump’s actions make him by far the most anti-union president in our modern history,” Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants and a leading progressive voice in the labor movement, said in an interview. “His administration has been massively anti-worker, anti-union and anti-working class.”White House officials take sharp issue with critics who say Trump is anti-worker. Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson, said: “President Trump will always put American workers first, which is why he signed the largest middle-class tax cuts in history, secured trillions in investments into our country, and negotiated historic trade deals to reshore our manufacturing industry and protect American jobs. Thanks to President Trump, American workers are prioritized over illegal aliens and foreign-born workers once again.”Heidi Shierholz, president of the Economic Policy Institute, a progressive thinktank, said she was stunned by some of Trump’s anti-worker actions, especially by his order last yearchopping the minimum wage that federal contractorsmust pay their employees, to $13.30 an hour from $17.75. That move caused some workers to lose over $9,000 a year in pay.This year, Trumprescinded a Biden-era regulation that made overtime payavailable to more salaried workers. As a result, 4.3 million workers will no longer qualify for time-and-a-half overtime. (Two federal courts in Texashad ruled against Biden’s overtime regulation.) In his years as president, Trump has never pushed to raise the $7.25-an-hour federal minimum wage, which has greatly eroded in value since it last increased in 2009.“TheTrump administrationis systematically weakening policies and institutions that give workers a voice, that give workers protections and that hold employers accountable,” Shierholz said. “He’s been doing that from day one, and since then it has absolutely continued and accelerated. You see attacks on every kind of worker protection from safety and health to wage and hour protections. Policy after policy after policy goes directly against the interests of workers.”Trump has helped some groups of workers by getting Congress to enact no tax on tips and a significant cut in taxes on overtime pay. The White House boasts that Trump also helped cuts taxes for working families, but Trump’s critics say those cuts overwhelmingly favor the ultra-wealthy, while giving just modest cuts to workers.President Biden had proposed a landmark regulation to protect workers against extreme heat, but the Trump administration, pushed hard by corporate America, is seeking toseriously weaken Biden’s effortto require rest breaks for workers and access to water and shade when it is very hot. The Trump administration also wants to undo Biden’s plans to codify extreme heat as a workplace hazard.This past February, after intense lobbying by corporations, the Trump administration moved to scrap a Biden-era rule and make it far easier for employers toclassify workers as independent contractors, be they construction workers or Uber drivers. This move will significantly lower many employers’ labor costs by removing any obligation to pay minimum wage and overtime and to contribute to those workers’ Social Security, Medicare and unemployment insurance benefits.Although Trump boasts that theUS economyis in the best shape ever, monthly job growth under Trump is down significantly compared with Biden. Young workers are having a hard time finding jobs, while Trump has been an outspoken cheerleader for AI and datacenters, which are fueling huge fears about many jobs disappearing. Trump promised to use tariffs and other means to make American manufacturing great again. But ever since Trump returned to office, the US has lost 35,000 manufacturing jobs, partly because of all the chaos and uncertainty Trump’s tariffs created, although in the past few months there have been modest gains in factory jobs.The Trump administration has shown hostility to unions in a way that shocked many Americans. As part of an investigation into opposition to ICE’s operations in Minnesota, Trump’s Department of Homeland Security got hold of financial records from two leading unions, the Service Employees International Union and the Communications Workers of America, saying that this was part of an inquiry into “domestic terrorism financing”.Further showing how much Trump officials dislike and distrust organized labor, Trump’s prosecutors even told a grand jury that the AFL-CIO, the nation’s main union federation, representing 15 million American workers and retirees, and several unionswere part of a criminal conspiracyto obstruct the efforts of ICE agents in Minnesota.“It’s terrible that they’re going after labor activists and unions in Minnesota for merely standing up for their neighbors,” Nelson said. “It’s outrageous that this administration called union members who are fighting for their neighbors ‘domestic terrorists’.”Explore more on these topicsUS unionsTrump administrationUS economyDonald TrumpUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Grindr pays £26m to settle UK lawsuit over allegedly sharing users’ HIV status | Technology sector | The Guardian
description: US-owned dating app allegedly allowed ad firms access to private information in breach of UK law
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: US-owned dating app allegedly allowed ad firms access to private information in breach of UK law
Content: Twelve-thousand people signed up to the action against Grindr filed by law firm Austen Hays.Photograph: Aly Song/ReutersView image in fullscreenTwelve-thousand people signed up to the action against Grindr filed by law firm Austen Hays.Photograph: Aly Song/ReutersTechnology sectorGrindr pays £26m to settle UK lawsuit over allegedly sharing users’ HIV statusUS-owned dating app allegedly allowed ad firms access to private information in breach of UK lawJulia KolleweMon 7 Sep 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrindr will pay £26m to settle a lawsuit brought by thousands of users in the UK who allege that the US dating app shared highly sensitive personal information, including in some cases their HIV status, with advertising companies.The settlement brings to an end a two-year legal battle, afterthe UK law firm Austen Hays filed a claimat the high court of England and Wales in April 2024 on behalf of Grindr users alleging violations of UK privacy laws during a period up to early 2020.The London law firm represented 12,000 people, who will receive an average compensation of £2,167 each, if the £26m is equally distributed.Grindrwas founded in 2009to make iteasier to coordinate hookups for gay men. It now claims to be the world’s largest dating app for gay, bi, trans and queer people, with nearly 15 million users around the world.Grindr said in aUS regulatory filingthat it had resolved the UK group action related to what it described as “historical data practices before 2020”, whenGrindr was owned and controlled by the Chinese gaming company Beijing Kunlun Tech.The California company said: “The settlement includes no findings or admission of liability. While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognises and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period.”As part of the UK settlement, Grindr agreed to pay £13m by the end of this year, and a further £13m by the end of March 2027.Six years ago, Grindr was sold to the investment group San Vicente Acquisition in a $608m deal and appointed new management, aftera US government national security panel raised concernsthat personal data of US users could be accessed and used by China’s government. In 2022,Grindr floated on the New York Stock Exchangethrough a merger with a Spac (special purpose acquisition company) in a deal that valuedthe appat $2.1bn (£1.55bn). It is now worth $2.65bn (£1.96bn).The company said in the filing that it had overhauled its privacy programme since 2020, “with a keen focus on the unique needs of its community”. It added that “Grindr is and remains a safe space for users, committed to transparency, user control and responsible data practices”.Austen Hays’ parent firm, Gateley, said: “While Grindr disputes the allegations, it recognises and acknowledges the distress and loss of trust expressed by some of its UK users regarding that pre-2020 period.“We thank our clients for trusting us with this sensitive case.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGrindr, based in west Hollywood, announced in April 2018 it wouldstop sharing users’ HIV statuswith third-party companies after a report by Norwegian researchers revealed data sharing with two companies.In 2021 Norway’s data protection authorityfined Grindr65m Norwegian krone (£4.8m) – 10% of its global revenues – for violating data protection rules. GrindrappealedbutNorway’s court of appeal upheld the decision and finelast October.As Grindr shared its users’ personal data for advertising purposes, the court of appeal concluded that the company’s claim that it did “‘not sell your personal user information to third parties for advertising purposes’ is clearly misleading”.Explore more on these topicsTechnology sectorDatingAids and HIVHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Belichick denies he has lost control of UNC football program amid off-field turmoil | College football | The Guardian
description: North Carolina football coach Bill Belichick said on Monday he believes his program ‘totally’ has an atmosphere of following rules
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: North Carolina football coach Bill Belichick said on Monday he believes his program ‘totally’ has an atmosphere of following rules
Content: Bill Belichick’s Tar Heels won their opening game of the season.Photograph: David G McIntyre/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBill Belichick’s Tar Heels won their opening game of the season.Photograph: David G McIntyre/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockCollege footballBelichick denies he has lost control of UNC football program amid off-field turmoilFormer general manager has resigned postBelichick’s son Steve is on medical leaveSchool has launched investigation into programAgenciesMon 7 Sep 2026 16.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorth Carolina football coach Bill Belichick said on Monday he believes his program “totally” has an atmosphere of following rules amid an investigation into its conduct.“Obviously everybody’s responsible, including me, for doing things properly,” Belichick said. “And we intend to do that.”The Tar Heels were off following their season-opening win against TCU in Ireland on 29 August. But during that open week, general manager Michael Lombardi resigned after being put on paid administrative leave in late July amid the university’s investigation into his conduct.The same day, Raleigh TV station WRAL cited anonymous sources in reporting the type of questions asked of some interviewees. Some focused on Belichick’s son Steve, the Tar Heels’ defensive coordinator, who is currently on medical leave. There havealso been allegationsthat Steve Belichick has been questioned by lawyers over issues related to drug use.Additionally, Lombardi attorney Tom Mars told The Athletic that the school’s investigation now included questions into potential “inappropriate” relationships that didn’t involve his client. Two people with knowledge of the situation had previously told the AP that a human resources complaint from a former employee was tied to Lombardi originally being placed on leave as the investigation launched.Those developments have only added to a year’s worth of unwanted headlines off the field to go with shaky play on it under Belichick.By Monday, reporters spent roughly the first 13 minutes of Belichick’s 20-minute game week news conference asking questions that had nothing to do with Saturday’s upcoming home game against East Tennessee State. That included whether his program had an atmosphere of rule compliance and if Belichick had “control” over the program.“If you’re around here every day, I think you’d see it,” Belichick said.Belichick was also asked whether he had spoken to chancellor Lee Roberts and athletic director Steve Newmark about his job security. He responded by looking ahead to the ETSU game, though he later elaborated more on his relationship with school officials when asked whether they had asked him to change anything in running the program.“They’ve been very supportive, a great working relationship with those people,” he said. “In the end, look, we want to run the program in the very best way. And if there’s things we need to do to correct it, then we’ll obviously do them.”Later on Monday, a school spokesman issued a statement backing the 74-year-old Belichick, who won six Super Bowl titles with the NFL’s New England Patriots.“The University continues to support Bill Belichick and the Carolina football program,” said Dean Stoyer, UNC’s vice chancellor for communications.The Tar Heels tallied more losses by double-digit margins (five) than wins (four) in Belichick‘s debut season, along with distractions such as an assistant coach being briefly suspended for violating NCAA rules. Belichick said in July he hoped lessons learned would lead to more success this season.The Tar Heels got that with the 15-10 win against TCU after losing to the Horned Frogs by 34 in Belichick’s UNC debut. But the past week take some glow off that victory.“We’re so focused on everything internal and getting better on the field and getting better in the meeting room that we could care less about what we see in the headlines or what’s on the news,” running back Benjamin Hall said. “It’s not going to affect this team.”Explore more on these topicsCollege footballCollege sportsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zheng Qinwen erases another 5-0 deficit to stun Swiatek and reach US Open quarter-finals | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Zheng Qinwen recovered from 5-0 down in the opening set to stun Iga Swiatek and reach the last eight of the US Open
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Zheng Qinwen recovered from 5-0 down in the opening set to stun Iga Swiatek and reach the last eight of the US Open
Content: Zheng Qinwen waves to the crowd after booking her spot in the last eight at Flushing Meadows.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAView image in fullscreenZheng Qinwen waves to the crowd after booking her spot in the last eight at Flushing Meadows.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Zheng Qinwen erases another 5-0 deficit to stun Swiatek and reach US Open quarter-finalsZheng makes astonishing recovery to win 7-5, 6-3Rybakina sweeps aside Osaka 6-1, 6-4 to set up clashTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsMon 7 Sep 2026 16.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe most important takeaway from 12 days at the US Open is simple: do not, by any means, lead 5-0 against Zheng Qinwen. No scoreline is as hazardous. On Friday, the former Australian Open champion Madison Keys learned this lesson the hard way as she led Zheng 5-0 in the final set of an intense tussle before Zheng, the Olympic gold medallist, rolled through seven consecutive games to win the match.Somehow, two days later, Zheng repeated the trick in her very next set against a greater opponent. Down 5-0 in the opening set of her fourth‑round match against the six-time grand slam title winnerIga Swiatek, Zheng again locked down her game and reeled off seven games in a row to take the set. Zheng refused to let it go as she pulled off one of the best wins of her career, reaching the US Open quarter‑finals with a 7-5, 6-3 victory.US Open tennis 2026: Osaka v Rybakina, Zheng stuns Swiatek, Andreeva wins and more on day nine – liveRead moreThis was a remarkable turn of events for a variety of reasons. A player winning seven games in a row from 0-5 down in consecutive sets against two different opponents is almost unheard of at the highest level; doing so against two grand slam title winners has never happened before.“In one moment, I even forgot the score in the first set at 4-5,” Zheng said. “That shows how I am focused. I guess, to come back 0-5 [again] is not lucky, that’s [what] I can say.”Swiatek was one of the tournament favourites after winning her first title of the year at the Canadian Open in Toronto and she seemed to be on the way to rediscovering the confidence that has marked her as the greatest player of her generation. However, as soon as she lost control in the first set, Swiatek’s game unravelled in a stream of erratic unforced errors. While the Pole cited difficulties with anxiety and stress as reasons for her recent troubles, here she just could not feel the ball well enough.“I wouldn’t say it had anything to do with mentality. It was more that I started making mistakes from easy balls and Qinwen stopped doing mistakes,” she said.View image in fullscreenIga Swiatek tries to return the ball on her way to a straight-sets defeat.Photograph: Seth Wenig/APMost importantly, this is a transformative result for one of the biggest talents on the tour. Coming into this match, Zheng had defeated Swiatek just once in their eight meetings, but that was a devastating loss for the Pole as it came in the semi‑finals of the 2024 Paris Olympics at Roland Garros, where Swiatek had just won her third consecutive French Open.Along with her Olympic gold medal, which instantly established her as one of the most famous athletes in China, Zheng reached the 2024 Australian Open final and rose to a career‑high ranking of No 4 last year. However, the 23-year-old underwent elbow surgery and tumbled down the rankings.Things have been incredibly difficult since. Zheng fell as low as No 160 in June and has struggled to find rhythm. Coming here, her 2026 record was 11-13. Her US Open is testament to how quickly things can come together in tennis, and after starting off this tournament having to park her ego and drop down to compete in the qualifying draw, seven wins in New York have allowed Zheng to re-establish herself as a genuine contender.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionZheng will next face Elena Rybakina, the second seed, who moved to within one win of becoming world No 1 for the first time as she comfortably defeated Naomi Osaka 6-1, 6-4. Rybakina was nearly flawless in their 66 minutes on Louis Armstrong Stadium, firing down 29 winners and just 17 unforced errors while facing just one unconverted break point in the match. Osaka needed her top level just to compete with Rybakina, but the two-time US Open champion has been struggling with achilles pain and she did not serve well enough to be competitive.The fifth seed and French Open champion, Mirra Andreeva, reached the quarter-finals at Flushing Meadows for the first time with a 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 win against Austria’s Anastasia Potapova.In the men’s draw, Alexander Blockx, the 28th seed, reached a grand slam quarter-final for the first time by defeating the 24th seed Francisco Cerundolo 6-3, 4-6, 7-5, 7-5.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Iga SwiatekUS Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Will hordes of influencers, weed smokers and mid-point talkers bring down the US Open? | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: This year, the noise at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center has officially become A Problem. But changing it would mean changing society
Author: Aaron Timms
Headline: This year, the noise at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center has officially become A Problem. But changing it would mean changing society
Content: The price of cocktails and food have become an annual talking point at the US Open.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe price of cocktails and food have become an annual talking point at the US Open.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesUS Open Tennis 2026Will hordes of influencers, weed smokers and mid-point talkers bring down the US Open?This year, the noise at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center has officially become A Problem. But changing it would mean changing societyAaron Timmsat Flushing MeadowsMon 7 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 07.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first thing you notice while sitting in the upper tiers of Arthur Ashe Stadium is the noise. A persistent exterior hum filters up from ground level, fed by the massive ventilation and cooling units that sit outside the stadium, the clack of the Long Island Rail Road to the north, and the forklifts receiving goods from the refrigerator trucks that keep the USTA Billie Jean King NationalTennisCenter flush with its essential supplies of Evian, champagne, and premium IPA. Overhead, planes descending toward LaGuardia airport ensure the auditory assault takes place by land and air simultaneously. In the lower rakes of the stadium, the babble of the spectators is incessant; it’s not unusual to overhear full-volume conversations on various non-tennis topics – work, family, romance, last night’s dinner – that continue without interruption for the duration of an entire match.New York is famously noisy, and the US Open, as the most glamorous annual sporting event in town, has always been loud in sympathy with its environment. Indeed, the brashness of the American grand slam has historically been its major selling point, the signature that distinguishes it from the Australian Open (the “happy slam”), Wimbledon (strawberries and cream, all-white attire, the home of tennis), and the French Open (French). People have been complaining about the volume of theNew Yorkcrowd for decades. But this year the noise at the US Open feels different. This year noise at the noisy slam has become A Problem.Influencers have been fingered as the main culprit: one “creator” filming with a ring lightcauseda brief stoppage in Naomi Osaka’s first-round match; another group of dancing TikTokers went viral with theirbalcony routineduring a match last week; various players have griped about ticketholders more interested in filming themselves than watching the tennis causing distractions during play. But influencers are not solely to blame, and there have also been more general grievances about fan behavior: Jakub Menšik got a drunk spectator ejected during his loss to Learner Tien, while Aryna Sabalenkacomplainedabout the persistent smell of weed invading the court during her victory over Kamilla Rakhimova. “It’s become a bit of a zoo,”saidjourneyman Adrian Mannarino last week when describing the atmosphere at this year’s Open, and there’s now an abiding sense that measures must be taken to arrest the lawlessness that has taken hold among the crowds.‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka halts US Open match due to cannabis smellRead moreHow bad are things really, though? It’s true that the grounds at the US Open this year have felt at times oppressively crowded. But the shoving obliviousness of the fans – the constant staring at phones, the almost universal lack of spatial awareness, the inconsiderate jostling in the interminable lines for the courts and the drinks and the $38 French dip sandwiches and the tiny free canisters of Dove deodorant – reflects nothing more than the poisonous effect of tech and commerce on culture at large. The tournament is drenched in commercial influence: more than it is a series of tennis matches, the US Open is a showcase for brands shilling everything from yogurt to $100,000 cars.Tournament organizers have no standing to complain about all those naughty influencers when they themselves have so cravenly courted the very commercial dollar that brings influencers through the gates; a tournament built on brand activations and clammy promotional partnerships, with all its associated chaos, is very much a creature of their own making. If the USTA was actually serious about reducing the impact of influencers at the Open, it would reduce its own dependence on the brands that solicit them. But that, of course, will never happen.View image in fullscreenA fan takes a photo of the court during a night session at the US Open.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesThen there’s the question of the actual disruptiveness caused by all this noise. Tennis, like golf, is unusual among the big professional sports in its insistence on a respectful silence during play; there’s none of the mockery and jeering throughout points that might greet, say, a basketball player looking to drain a free-throw in front of a hostile crowd. Is it time for tennis to change? On the outer courts at Flushing Meadows, doubles teams and lower-ranked singles competitors lash the ball at each other with a ferocity that seems entirely undiminished by the crush of spectators gabbing and milling about in their vicinity. If these players are unbothered by the bickering couples, wayward kids, and visor-wearing dads loudly discussing their 401ks all around them, why can’t the thoroughbreds on the fancy courts learn to shut out the noise and stay focused?But also: we live in a society! Yes, the smell of weed is unavoidable on the streets of New York, and sometimes (though I’ve never smelled it personally on the grounds of the National Tennis Center) that trademark skunk will waft on to the courts at the US Open.
