So what? Part of making a substance legal – as marijuana is in New York state – is that the odor of that substance is also legal. This city has always been an intensely odiferous place, and the land on which the US Open is now held has its own rich olfactory heritage; the ash heaps that used to dominate the point where the National Tennis Center now stands – made famous as the “Valley of Ashes” in F Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby – were probably not, one imagines, all perfume and roses. As a nod to local tradition, what could be more appropriate than a US Open that’s consistently smelly?I’m joking, of course, but part of coexisting with other humans is dealing with the externalities they generate – their sounds, their smells, their movements and outbursts. The debate over odor, noise, and influencer inanity exposes a deeper crisis in tennis and organized sport more generally. Every US Open now begins with a week of hand-wringing over ticket prices, hundred-dollar chicken-and-caviar nuggets, and the prospect of tennis’s flashiest tournament turning into a compound for the super-rich; the USTA then goes into crisis mode and activates all its standard messaging about “access” during the pre-tournament fan week, the underappreciated democratic benefits of demand-driven dynamic pricing, and the important work done to reinvest the windfall generated by the Open into grassroots development of the sport.But then the tournament begins and the narrative shifts: what, the tennis purists immediately demand to know, is this boozy, stoner rabble stumbling through the gates and why are they making so muchnoise? Have they norespect for the sport? Suddenly, a public conversation that was about accessibility becomes a policing operation centered around heritage and etiquette; brands havereportedlyalready begun the work of influencer re-education, and during Sunday morning’s pre-match coverage therewasmuch excitable conversation on the Tennis Channel about the example of Wimbledon, which isconsideringintroducing a kind of finishing school for influencers to make sure the ring-light crowd behaves itself while taking in matches on the hallowed grounds of SW19. Well, which one is it going to be: do we want grand slam tennis to be a sport of the people, or the exclusive entertainment of a well-behaved, stupid-monied few? If tennis wants more fans, inevitably it will have to make peace with the fact that not all of them will be model spectators.View image in fullscreenFans look at their phones during the 2025 US Open.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesAs annoying as a lot of the fans at the US Open are, it would be a mistake for the USTA to use the backlash against influencers, weed smokers, mid-point talkers, and various other behavioral deviants in the stands as the pretext for a restriction of access to the sport; if anything, a more affordable and democratic tournament might even dilute the impact of the reel-filming set. “You want people to continue to grow the sport,” Osakaarguedwhen quizzed on this year’s influencer controversy. “I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette.”That seems like the most diplomatic and sensible line for players to take on the issue, but there’s ultimately a limit to how much etiquette and re-education campaigns can really achieve. I despise influencers as much as anyone, but it’s not up to me – or the USTA, or the players on tour, or anyone else – to decide who gets to buy a ticket to the US Open; the sole criterion of entry to the grounds at Flushing Meadows is the ability to pay the price of admission. Sporting crowds, even at expensive events like the Open, are necessarily a reflection of society – and the society of dancing TikTok buffoons, Honey Deuce selfie takers, and casual fansaskingAI to explain who is contesting the match they are watching with their own eyes, as hideous as it may be, is simply the world that we live in now.But nothing is inevitable. Tennis, like everything else in sport, like everything else in culture, can be whatever we want it to be. One of the most instructive walks you can take at the US Open is once you leave the grounds. Exiting to the south and west, you’ll find groups of mostly Hispanic families and friends having the time of their lives on the vast fields of Flushing Meadows Corona Park, playing football and volleyball and grilling and drinking long into the night; from one of the park vendors, a giant skewer of chicken giblets, served on a paper plate with roasted potatoes and red onion and doused in salsa picante, will set you back $6, a far better deal than anything you’ll find on the US Open’s miserable menu of overpriced “viral” culinary abominations.Continuing west you’ll eventually land in Corona, a densely populated working-class neighborhood with a significant presence of Mexican and Ecuadorian immigrants. Here the contrast with the hordes at the US Open is genuinely fascinating. The streets are clamorous and intense, filled with the clatter of the elevated 7 train, the pop and sizzle of the food trucks, the chatter of twilight conversations on stoops and sidewalks, and the slap-slap-slap of the games of dominoes that crowd every corner. But there are no phone-gazing zombies meandering across pavements; there’s none of the greedy insensitivity of the masses at the Open; there aren’t even many devices visible. These streets are packed with people and thrumming with life, but their vibrancy is neighborly, uplifting, and welcoming, rather than hectoring, selfish, and bland as is the case for the hyperactivity beyond the entrance gates of the National Tennis Center.I’m not suggesting, of course, that the US Open should relocate to 37th Avenue in North Corona, but the juxtaposition of these two ideas of urban coexistence is powerfully informative. Changing the crowds at the US Open would mean changing society – throwing away the phones and the chatbots and the Bluetooth microphones, rejecting the delusions of the attention economy, saying once and for all that no, in fact, you will not “get ready with me”. It would mean embracing a life of community and human contact and non-screen-mediated concern for each other. But until the distant day when that happens, we’re stuck, I fear, with more of the same – and the US Open will continue to reflect our profoundly stupid and ugly cultural present.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisUS sportsNew YorkTennisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: For baseball’s Black and Latino players, it’s always 1926 somewhere | MLB | The Guardian
description: From home-run celebrations to tilted caps, players embracing joy continue to collide with an old guard devoted to Dust Bowl grimness
Author: Howard Bryant
Headline: From home-run celebrations to tilted caps, players embracing joy continue to collide with an old guard devoted to Dust Bowl grimness
Content: Oliver Marmol and Doug Eddings argue during Friday’s game.Photograph: David Zalubowski/APView image in fullscreenOliver Marmol and Doug Eddings argue during Friday’s game.Photograph: David Zalubowski/APMLBFor baseball’s Black and Latino players, it’s always 1926 somewhereHoward BryantFrom home-run celebrations to tilted caps, players embracing joy continue to collide with an old guard devoted to Dust Bowl grimnessMon 7 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 15.58 EDTShareOver the last several years, simultaneously lauded and paralyzed by its ironclad traditions, baseball has undergone various forays into reinvention, trying to free itself from itsunwritten rules of retaliation, its seeming aversion to joy, its demand that every generation of player of every culture and background play the game with the grimness of a Dust Bowl farmer.The sport even attempted to change those customs by promoting a cultural shift withan industry-wide motto:Let the Kids Play.But in a time of intense division within the aggressive backdrop of Trumpism, the result is a racial clash that is actually a generational and cultural one that predates current politics by a century.On Saturday night, Braves superstar Ronald Acuña Jr hit a third-inning home run off Zack Wheeler of the Phillies andfloated around the bases, arms wide, imitating an airplane, Euro-stepping past third base as if he were Manu Ginobili, and infuriating Wheeler and his manager Don Mattingly with his apparent disregard for the accepted customs of the game.A week before, in the midst of what would be a 16-1 rout, Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm swiped two meaningless bases in a blowout win over the Red Sox when the defense had conceded his presence – according to a 150-year-old custom, runners are expected to respect this courtesy by not advancing. Chisholm’s breach of protocol prompted Red Sox radio announcer Will Flemmingto suggest on the airthat a Yankee player drill one of Chisholm’s teammates for his insolence.‘I felt like Babe Ruth’: baseball’s 3ft 7in pinch-hitter, 75 years onRead moreFor the trifecta, during a Colorado-St Louis series this weekend, neither the Cardinals nor the Rockies had a problem with each other – but umpire Doug Eddings did, stopping the game to tell Cardinals rookie Hancel Rinconto adjust his hat. Eddings determined the rookie’s hat was too crooked (despite his later admission that Rincon had not violated any official rules) and Rincon would not disrespecthis gameonhis field.Eddings then issued a time violation to the Cardinals when manager Oli Marmol complained,thenejected Marmol, andthenmissed an obvious call at the plate against the Cardinals.In each of the incidents, the offended – Eddings, Wheeler (and to a lesser extent Mattingly), and Flemming – were white, while the alleged offenders – Acuña, Chisholm, Rincon, and Marmol – were Black or Latino. Periodically this season, baseball has found its way into the repellent culture wars, first during the World Baseball Classic earlier this year when the Americans soured the proceedings with their militia-like grimness when therest of the world was having fun. Maybe war is all America has to offer these days.In June, when participation was optional, several players decided to exercise their religious freedoms by crashing Pride Night bywriting Bible passages on their hats. When the players were warned over the incident, the Department of Justicethreatened to investigatewhether baseball was discriminating against Christians.If, however, it appears that baseball is an extension of Maga – and it very well may be – what Eddings and company have really resurfaced over the past is not exactly Trumpism per se, but what Trumpism tacitly demands: an incessant imposition of whiteness on American institutions, and an aggressiveness that emboldens the gatekeepers like Eddings to put the coloreds in their place.No league forces its historical whiteness on its players like Major LeagueBaseball. That whiteness is also known as “tradition,” ofplaying the game the right way.That tradition is practiced by players Black, white and Latino, who were raised in the old-school American baseball tradition with its ethnic, Depression-era seriousness. Other sports adjust to the new generations of players who enter the game. The NBA’s Nikola Jokić and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander are not expected to play like George Mikan and John Havlicek. In baseball, Bob Gibson and Pedro Martínez are proudly the spiritual extensions of Rube Waddell and Walter Johnson.Mattingly, wasn’t happy with Acuña, but judging by his postgame comments his conflicts were not racial, or racist, but instead resigned to a baseball becoming unrecognizable to him – a carnival of bat flips and unprofessionalism masquerading as fun. Mattingly has been in the game nearly 50 years. He was teammates with the ultimate showman, Rickey Henderson, whose on-field expressions were loathed, but Mattingly knew Henderson was no clown. He also managed Yasiel Puig, who was electric but whose respect for his craft wavered. Mattingly knows the difference between being professional and not, joy and disrespect, and seemed to be lamenting the desperate blurring of the two at the encouragement of the people who run the sport.In better times, when it didn’t appear umpires were looking for a fight, and when baseball especially did not appear to enlist itself in harassing players of color – Eddings might have been shrugged off as another power-tripping umpire having a bad day and taking it out on a kid making his big-league debut and the manager telling him to “fucking grow up,” as Marmol did.These are not better times. Eddings looked small and petty, and baseball’s strain of “playing the right way” is usually code for its eternal conflicts with how Black and Latino players express themselves in competition, how they dress, celebrate, emote. Even in 2026, somewhere in baseball – as evidence by Flemming’s comments and subsequent apology – it is always 1926.What, it should be asked, is this all about? It is an example of just how frayed the nerves of the country are, and what abuses of authority look like, especially as baseball in the backdrop of a Maga country feels like a hostile place. The Cardinals responded by protecting their player, and thumbing their nose at Eddings bytilting their hats as a team in solidarity. The small moments can provide the kind of kindling that can bring a team together (after five months of mediocrity, the Cardinals are trying to snag an 11th-hour playoff spot.)As for Eddings, who later apologized, he resembled the doomed, peacocking general surrounded by enemy forces. Umpires have few friends these days. The humorous YouTube channel Jomboy, once an innocuous value-add for Yankee fans for its clever lip-reading of on-field incidents, became a viral sensation, and MLB, desperate to attract a younger audience, realized the telegraph isn’t going to make a comeback andbought an equity stake in the company, transforming Jomboy from a clever fan site to an arm of MLB, which is not so innocuously trying to rid the game of human umpiring. In addition to Jomboy, numerous unofficial social media users virally spread umpires’ worst calls, intensifying the drumbeat that umpiring in its current form needs to go the way of the flannel uniform.Eddings spent this Labor Day weekend making another case for the robots, contributing simultaneously to baseball’s 100-year culture war and to the umpires’ digging of their own graves.Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America.He writes at Substack.Explore more on these topicsMLBBaseballUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: Bernie Ecclestone questioned after shotgun found on his private jet in Portugal | Bernie Ecclestone | The Guardian
description: The 95-year-old former Formula One chief Bernie Ecclestone said he was questioned by police in Portugal after a shotgun was found on his private jet
Author: Miguel Dantas
Headline: The 95-year-old former Formula One chief Bernie Ecclestone said he was questioned by police in Portugal after a shotgun was found on his private jet
Content: Bernie Ecclestone said he bought the gun in England, before taking it to Switzerland and on to Portugal.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersView image in fullscreenBernie Ecclestone said he bought the gun in England, before taking it to Switzerland and on to Portugal.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersBernie EcclestoneBernie Ecclestone questioned after shotgun found on his private jet in PortugalFormer F1 chief says firearm was for clay-pigeon shootingPolice quiz 95-year-old over lack of documents for gunMiguel Dantasin PortoMon 7 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBernie Ecclestone was detained in Portugal on Monday after customs authorities found him in possession of an undocumented shotgun. The Guardian has independently confirmed the incident with multiple authorities involved in the matter.The detention of the 95‑year‑old took place at Tires Aerodrome in Cascais, shortly after the formerFormula Onechief’s private jet landed. After a routine inspection of the aircraft and its passengers, authorities reportedly discovered a shotgun in Ecclestone’s possession. He was stopped for questioning by Portuguese officials and said the gun was for use in clay pigeon shooting.‘Like an AI agent’: Wolff hails Antonelli’s Italian GP victory in title chargeRead moreUnder standard procedure in such cases, the firearm is seized and the person found carrying it is formally made a defendant in criminal proceedings. It is not yet known what the outcome of Ecclestone’s case will be.Responding to reports he had been arrested, Ecclestone told the Press Association: “No. The police were very helpful and doing all they could to stop us from having to do what we had to do.”Explaining the events, Ecclestone told PA: “I was going to take part in Portugal in a clay pigeon shooting competition, which I only knew about a few days ago because Fabiana [his wife] met someone when she was coming back from Brazil to Portugal. He said he was entering into a clay pigeon competition.“So she called me and said: ‘There is something here you should go and look at. Why don’t you turn up and join?’ And I said: ‘Well, that wouldn’t be a bad idea.’ … As I have got guns already in Switzerland, which have been imported properly, because we do a bit of clay pigeon shooting there, I brought the gun in with me.“I went through customs and the people know me very well. They said: ‘Anything to declare?’ I said: ‘No, nothing really, just all the usual personal things.’“So I walked out and, as I got out, one of my people with me said: ‘The police have asked if you would go and see them.’ I went to see the police and said: ‘What can I do for you?’ And they said: ‘We would like some information on this gun you brought in.’“I didn’t even unzip the case. I said: ‘Well, it is a shotgun and this is the reason.’ And they asked where is the blue book for the gun? And I said: ‘I don’t know, I have never heard about a blue book in my life.’“They said: ‘Yes, well anyone with these guns should always have the book, it is like a passport. Incidentally, I want to look at your passport, too,’ which they took.“I said I bought the gun in England and took it into Switzerland through all the normal channels. And they said: ‘Where is the blue book?’ And I said: ‘I just told you, I don’t know about the blue book.’“There were about four police guys and they said: ‘What you have done is try to import a gun into the country.’ I said: ‘I have not tried to do that. I have come through customs, and here I am with you’.“So all this nonsense went on. We went back to the customs, and the police had complained to customs, and the customs officer said: ‘You need to surrender the gun here in Lisbon and then we will look at it there, and do you want to import it? And if so, you will have to pay duty on it and ask for a temporary import, and we will deal with it like that.’ So I said: ‘Well we’d better do that.’”This is not the first time Ecclestone has faced scrutiny from authorities over a firearm while travelling by air. In May 2022, the former F1 chief executive was arrested in Brazil for illegally possessing a gun while preparing to board a private plane bound for Switzerland.On that occasion an X‑ray of Ecclestone’s luggage revealed an undeclared LW Seecamp .32‑calibre pistol. He admitted that he owned the firearm but said he was unaware that he was carrying it.Ecclestone was taken to a facility at Viracopos Airport in Campinas, where he posted bail before being released to continue his journey.Ecclestone’s wife, Fabiana Flosi, was linked to a property purchase about 15 miles west of Lisbon. The deal was reportedly the largest private sale of a house in Portugal, with the price said to be around £35m.Ecclestone has been involved in Formula One since the 1950s, starting out as a driver and businessman before becoming a team owner and a key negotiator of the championship’s television rights.He was the sport’s most influential commercial and political figure for decades, playing a central role in securing commercial partnerships, sponsorships and agreements with racing circuits around the world.Ecclestone’s official involvement with F1 came to an end in 2017, when Liberty Media acquired the commercial rights to the championship. He has nevertheless remained an inescapable figure in the sport and is widely credited with transforming F1 into a global mass-market phenomenon.Explore more on these topicsBernie EcclestoneFormula OnenewsShareReuse this content

title: Mauricio Pochettino wants the US to become ‘one of the most powerful countries in soccer’ | Mauricio Pochettino | The Guardian
description: As he prepares for the upcoming international window, the US head coach spoke about Folarin Balogun, the LA Olympics and dual national players
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: As he prepares for the upcoming international window, the US head coach spoke about Folarin Balogun, the LA Olympics and dual national players
Content: Mauricio Pochettino recently signed a contract extension with the US.Photograph: Abbie Parr/APView image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino recently signed a contract extension with the US.Photograph: Abbie Parr/APMauricio PochettinoMauricio Pochettino wants the US to become ‘one of the most powerful countries in soccer’As he prepares for the upcoming international window, the US head coach spoke about Folarin Balogun, the LA Olympics and dual national playersPablo Iglesias MaurerMon 7 Sep 2026 13.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s been two months since the US men’s national teamcrashed out of the World Cupin disappointing fashion, and their head coach, Mauricio Pochettino, is back at work.The former Tottenham and PSG manager was largely viewed as a short-term hire when he joined the US in 2024, brought on to help the team capitalize on their first home World Cup in more than three decades. Along the way, Pochettino and US Soccer warmed to the idea of a contract extension,one they finalized in August.The US will play four friendlies in late September and early October against Peru, Chile, Mexico and Canada, but that stretch of games pales in comparison to the larger task at hand. Pochettino must guide the US to qualification for the 2030 World Cup, of course, but the Argentinian – and the federation – have more ambitious goals that involve reshaping the structure of soccer in the United States.In Zavier Gozo, Crystal Palace land a US prospect living up to the hypeRead moreThe US will also play at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, and it’s been widely reported they may feature in the Copa América that same summer. On Monday, Pochettino joined a small circle of reporters to talk about the task at hand. His quotes have been lightly edited for clarity and length.Pochettino’s expanded rolePochettino has said that choosing to remain with the US for another World Cup cycle is a chance for him to “have a lasting impact on the sport in the country that has welcomed us so warmly – and for that impact to extend beyond results on the field.” Indeed US Soccer’s announcement of Pochettino’s contract renewal came with an interesting wrinkle – the federation said the Argentinian would take a more prominent role steering the direction of youth development and coaching education, and would advise on professional league collaboration and a handful of other areas.That sort of broad influence isn’t exactly an alien concept in international soccer, but no US coach has ever taken such a prominent role in steering the direction of the program as a whole. He will not have to wait long to make his mark, as US Soccer is undergoing a significant restructuring and is in the process of filling two new director roles for the men’s and women’s senior and youth programs. On Monday, Pochettino said he’s made it clear he’s happy to help with that process – “but it can’t [just] be my guy,” he said, laughing.“This is the future of the USA,” said Pochettino. “We want to try to perform in the World Cup and to create something special with the fans. And now it’s about being a part of the legacy that the federation wants to create – becoming one of the most powerful countries in soccer. That is a dream, no? It’s amazing. If we can be part of that, we are so excited and so happy.”On Folarin Balogun’s deadline day dramaThis summer’s transfer window was a decidedly quiet one for the USMNT. Aside from a few notable moves – Gio Reyna to Strasbourg, Sebastian Berhalter to Middlesbrough and Zavier Gozo’sleap from MLS to Crystal Palace– many players stayed put.The list includes Monaco forward Folarin Balogun, who seemed poised for a big-money move after a breakout World Cup. Instead, Balogun saw a move to Evertonfall apart at the last moment, with the Premier League club citing a potential fitness issue, something Monaco (and Balogun) both contested.Balogun is far from the first player to suffer a deadline day letdown, and Pochettino offered support for the 25-year-old on Monday.“Yes, it’s difficult because you cannot influence that decision,” said Pochettino. “You need to support what they are doing with the people making the decisions. In some special cases, like Flo’s, I will call in the next few days. I wanted to give him a little bit of space after that situation in Everton. I want to know from him what happened. But we are always offering our support, and that’s it. I think he’s an important player for us, he was an important player in the World Cup and I hope that he can find being in Monaco, or in another place, his best place to perform in the best way.”Dual nationalsPochettino said little about the 26-man roster he’ll call into camp later this month. One player we know will not be there, though, is Augsburg center-back Noahkai Banks. The German-American remains undecided about his international future and will not feature for the US this window.The 19-year-old has said he wants to make a decision by “the next international break, or at the latest by the international break after next.” German media has reported that newly appointed Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp has gone so far as to scout Banks in person.“We are in contact with all the potential dual nationals,” said Pochettino. “I think it’s important for us, of course, because that is the human connection that is so important. Even if they, like in that case, Noki, didn’t change his mind and is waiting still, no decision, and of course we cannot consider him for the next camp … But the organization is working with all the dual nationals and players with the possibility to make a decision. That human connection is important because if one day they feel that they can defend and they want to fight and to be part of our national team … Of course, if they deserve it, and we consider that they deserve to be involved, of course we are going to call [them up].”Los Angeles 2028Olympic soccer, as it always has, takes a backseat to any number of global and continental competitions. Still, the 2028 Games in Los Angeles present a massive opportunity to the USMNT, who will once again look to captivate a home audience after this summer’s World Cup.The Games, Pochettino said on Monday, are a top priority to his staff, who are working in concert with U-23 head coach Steve Cherundolo. Curiously, Pochettino mentioned making use of this coming window to examine a handful of younger players who could feature at the 2028 Olympics.“I think we have a core of young players that need to play the Olympic Games because I think an objective for our federation and for the country … is to try to be a contender for the gold medal. [The Games are] going to be in our country, and we are going to support that. And always the decision on the first team with the players that are in that process – we are going to take the best decision altogether, always, and to try to protect those players in the best condition, and to help them to arrive, not only being important for the first team, but important for [the] type of competition that is important for the country.”On those young playersPochettino has been a frequent critic of the mentality of some American players. During the buildup to the 2026 World Cup, he expressed frustration with players who he felt did not prioritize national team call-ups and sometimes seemed to struggle with soccer’s place in American culture.On Monday, Pochettino seemed eager to change the mentality of coaches and young players who decline call-ups, sometimes citing fitness or load management concerns.“[It’s important that young players] want to be involved,” said Pochettino. “[When a player in MLS or elsewhere] has the possibility to join the under-18 or under-19 national teams, or the Olympic Games, it’s so important to be part of them. That is another habit that we need to change. Sometimes the coaches say, you know, ‘I have a 17-year-old guy that plays in MLS,’ but when the under-19 national team calls they say: ‘No, they need to rest.’ If you’re 17 and need to rest? Ay, ay, ay. You have a big problem.He added: “You cannot rest at 17. When I was 17, 16, or 15, all of my teammates, when we played in Newell’s Old Boys, sometimes you play two, three games in the same day. You cannot treat a 17- or 18-year-old player like a 30-year-old player. Sometimes we [treat younger players like older players], rather than settling the good principles and good habits. We make 18-year-old players like [28- or 30-year-olds]. That is amazing, no? Physically, when you are 18, the possibility to recover from one effort to another is different when you are 32. Sometimes [young] players come with the older mindset, and that is the evolution that we need to change in [American soccer.]”Explore more on these topicsMauricio PochettinoUSAUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: CBS’s Champions League studio panel are back and ready to irritate each other | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Kate Scott, Thierry Henry, Jamie Carragher and Micah Richards discuss their oft-viral approach to covering soccer for a US audience
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: Kate Scott, Thierry Henry, Jamie Carragher and Micah Richards discuss their oft-viral approach to covering soccer for a US audience
Content: Kate Scott anchors the Champions League panel for US viewers on CBS and Paramount+.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKate Scott anchors the Champions League panel for US viewers on CBS and Paramount+.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueCBS’s Champions League studio panel are back and ready to irritate each otherKate Scott, Thierry Henry, Jamie Carragher and Micah Richards discuss their oft-viral approach to covering soccer for a US audienceJeff RueterMon 7 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 07.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt takes something special for a sports broadcast to outshine the action on the field. Yet that is often what happens on CBS Sports, where theChampions Leaguestudio show has struck a rare chord with viewers, most often broadcast on streaming branch Paramount+.The usual group (Kate Scott,Jamie Carragher, Thierry Henry, and Micah Richards), have become fixtures on the American TV circuit, thanks in large part to their on-air chemistry. Scott guides the show expertly – all with with a mass of banter and ribbing along the way.“I think it’s just authentic,” Scott tells the Guardian earlier this month, “and I think that’s why it works. There was one time on an intro where I used an analogy of a family and kind of the squabbles that can exist within a family, but the underlying thing being a mutual appreciation and love.The French aristocrat and the all-American idiot: Henry v Lalas is the World Cup’s most compelling battleRead more“There are times that we can rub each other the wrong way, and that can maybe play out on air … Enjoyment of irritating one another, that’s very sibling-like to me. There’s nothing I enjoy more than kind of irritating my brother and getting under his skin, and I think that can kind of apply within the group as well … But I think there’s always respect and love there that kind of underlines everything.”The Champions League hasn’t always been the most prized asset in American soccer broadcasting. BeforeCBSobtained the competition’s broadcast rights in 2021, they were passed around by a number of rivals for over a decade. ESPN, Fox Sports, and Turner Sports all broadcast the competition at some point between 2008 and 2020, at times undervaluing its possible pull. Studio shows weren’t a staple until the latter stages of the season. At times, it seemed like the Champions League was mostly a way for sports broadcasters to fill midweek daytime slots with live programming.Coinciding with the launch of a committed soccer channel on Paramount+, CBS turned heads when they announced their studio plans in 2021. Scott was already a trusted host after working on Turner’s Champions League broadcasts. Henry’s playing career spoke for itself, and he further endeared himself to American soccer fans in his four-year stint with the New York Red Bulls. Carragher and Richards were known entities to those who followed the Premier League from afar and caught their Sky Sports clips on YouTube.While the CBS team insist they don’t code-switch when speaking to US audiences, broadcasting an ocean away – they film from a studio in the UK – does offer room for fresh approaches.“I don’t think about that when we’re on air,” Carragher says, “thinking: ‘Oh, this is an American audience’. But, certainly from my point of view, the way I probably let myself go a little bit more or try and wind someone up a little bit more than I would on English TV is because it’s on American TV. Not because [viewers are] American, but because I think I don’t know anyone.“I don’t really care, and I don’t mean that in a bad way. But you know, if you’re acting the goat on English TV, all your friends and family are watching, or someone’s texting you, or it’s on social media. Because it’s so far away in America, you’re thinking, ‘Oh, I don’t know them. Don’t worry about it.’ I think there was always that feeling for me at the start where we could maybe take a few more chances.”Although known as a more cerebral pundit than the gregarious Carragher and Richards, Henry also stresses the importance of sincerity.“I try to do what I’m supposed to do for the show and for the team, in the way I actually like to see the game,” Henry says. “Whether I’m on French TV, American TV or English TV, I’ll usually go about what I need to say and how I need to say it. I’m obsessed with making people understand stuff, so that’s my thing. I know sometimes it looks like I’m a bit cold, but that’s the way I want to go about the thing that I think needs an explanation.”The relaxed nature, especially compared tomore buttoned-up presentations, makes it easy to feel like you’re hanging out with friends. Time has allowed them to established dependable running gags. Even in their conversation with the Guardian, Carragher deftly works in a (relevant) reference to the French club that has blessed this bunch with ample opportunities for double entendre.“There’s always a story in the Champions League,” Carragher says. “You love a big match-up, and one of the reasons why [Uefa chose] the new format was probably to get a bit more of that in the league phase rather than having to wait until, maybe, a quarter-final. So we see more of those match-ups, but the great stories that we’ve probably had and covered have been some of the smaller teams.“You think of Bodø/Glimt. You think of Brest, being in the competition as well. These type of teams, who probably most people sat at home have never heard of, become massive stories. We incorporate that in the show and they become a big part of the show as well”.And yet, it never feels like a team of joke writers snuck into the planning meetings.“Because we’re all authentic with it, nobody, I would say, is acting on the show,” Henry says. “I think sometimes you might have some awkward moments, and people are like: ‘Ooookay, let’s move on’. But because nobody is kind of acting – you were talking about captivating the US audience, but somehow we did captivate other audiences, in other countries, because I guess they can relate – whether to Kate or to Jamie, to Micah or to me – in a way because it is authentic. We are also making the show very relatable while explaining it and having fun.”Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueUS sportsUS sports mediaThierry HenryJamie CarragherCBSParamount+featuresShareReuse this content

title: Fitter, happier, more productive: Arsenal could hardly have started the season better | Premier League | The Guardian
description: It’s still very early but Mikel Arteta’s side are playing with an authority and freshness that eluded them at times last season
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: It’s still very early but Mikel Arteta’s side are playing with an authority and freshness that eluded them at times last season
Content: Martin Ødegaard, David Raya and Kai Havertz are part of an Arsenal team who have won all three of their opening Premier League matches.Composite: EPA, AP, GettyView image in fullscreenMartin Ødegaard, David Raya and Kai Havertz are part of an Arsenal team who have won all three of their opening Premier League matches.Composite: EPA, AP, GettySoccer with Jonathan WilsonPremier LeagueFitter, happier, more productive: Arsenal could hardly have started the season betterIt’s still very early but Mikel Arteta’s side are playing with an authority and freshness that eluded them at times last seasonSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 7 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree league games played,three games won. For Arsenal this season could only have started better if Manchester City, who look like being one of their two most serious challengers, had dropped points. But it’s not just about results: Arsenal have been comfortably the better side in each of those three games, approaching each of them in very different ways.After the controlled victory over Coventry City and the tight game against Aston Villa that was won thanks to ratcheting up the pressure in the 15 minutes after half-time, came success in a far more open game in which they conceded for the first time this season.Chelseatested Arsenal on Sunday, went ahead, and yet Mikel Arteta’s side still always looked like they would win – even if it did take a superb late save from David Raya to keep out an Estevão shot. But the goalkeeper too is part of their strength; even if an opposing team can work a shooting opportunity, Raya has the capacity for spectacular saves that can dispirit opponents.Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s actionRead moreArsenal threatened from set-pieces but also from open play; they can beat opponents in multiple different ways, even when Declan Rice, probably their player of the season last year, has an off day (his unpunished late trip on Morgan Rogers was cynical and nasty, one of those deliberate offences miles from the ball that the game would benefit from treating as a red card offence).The uplift may simply be confidence,the pressure of not having won the title, of those three successive second-place finishes, now lifted. But there are also individuals who look sharper, livelier, fresher than they did at any point last season. Martin Ødegaard is perhaps the most obvious. He struggled with injuries last season and scored only one goal; already this season he has two in the league and one in the Community Shield. Some players return from the World Cup and look exhausted or find the readaptation to the grind of the domestic game difficult; Ødegaard seems reinvigorated.There is an imagination to his play, a lightness, and he took his goal against Chelsea superbly. His link-ups with Kai Havertz, another at times mercurial presence, were often delightful, conjuring space and angles where none seemed to exist and bringing the winner. In a team that last season developed a reputation for uncompromising physicality, there is something almost otherworldly about seeing two such ephemeral talents combining, sprites glimmering on a castle wall.But it’s not just Ødegaard. For Bukayo Saka, last season felt like chickens coming home to roost. He is only 25 but Sunday brought what was already his 205th league start, while playing regularly for England as well. Fatigue had been stored up, which is always a worry for players who emerge as early as he did. Thomas Tuchel didn’t use him in the World Cup semi-final for reasons of tiredness or injury that remain opaque (the situation was promptly confused when he scored a hat-trick in the third-place game). But he seems back to something like his best in the early weeks of this season, fizzing in from the right-hand side and delivering dangerous corners on demand.The other standout in the early weeks of the season is Riccardo Calafiori, who has already developed a very promising relationship going forward with Christos Tzolis, even if a few issues remain to be resolved defensively on that flank. The Italian, who scored Arsenal’s opener in the Community Shield, is not only a threat from set-plays but is very good at breaking through the lines, making him a real weapon against low blocks.Chelsea are improving. Xabi Alonso’s side were far less open through midfield than they had been against Fulham and Brighton – easier as that can sometimes be to manage against sides who don’t instinctively cede possession. It may be, especially as the attrition of European fixtures strikes others later in the season, that they emerge as a very serious force. Arsenal, though, are very, very good now, and that means they could be several points clear by the time that putative Chelsea challenge emerges.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArteta’s side are not merely playing with great authority; the fixtures have also fallen well for them, getting Villa away and Chelsea at home while both sides are still finding their patterns of play. It’s still very early. We haven’t even got to the first international break yet. Pitfalls are always waiting, and football is not a sport that reacts well to being taken for granted. But for Arsenal, their title defence could hardly have started better. Things could change but, at this moment, it seems more likely that they’ll have it won with several games still to play than that their grasp on the title will have slipped.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueSoccer with Jonathan WilsonArsenalChelseanewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Fulham need a boost, Tottenham show some spirit and Jack Grealish offers Everton much-needed energy
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Fulham need a boost, Tottenham show some spirit and Jack Grealish offers Everton much-needed energy
Content: Álvaro Arbeloa, Sandro Tonali and Jack Grealish.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskView image in fullscreenÁlvaro Arbeloa, Sandro Tonali and Jack Grealish.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskTen talking points from the weekend footballPremier LeaguePremier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s actionFulham need a win, Tottenham show some spirit and Jack Grealish offers Everton much-needed energyGuardian sportMon 7 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Everton need Grealish’s energyWith 25 minutes to go againstManchester United, the Everton supporters had something to roar about as Jack Grealish made his return after rejoining on loan. The attacking midfielder remains universally popular thanks to his desire to entertain, getting the hosts back on their feet by creating dangerous situations within seconds of his arrival. Everton were limited in the final third for long periods as Thierno Barry sat on the periphery. If David Moyes is to keep his side pushing for a top-half finish, he will need Grealish to be a creative focal point.Will UnwinMatch report:Everton 2-2 Manchester United2Tzolis stands out among new facesThere was no shortage of highlights from the new arrivals as Arsenal battled back to beat Chelsea, Morgan Rogers setting the tone with a well-taken goal within two minutes. Emi Martínez got a hostile reception on his return to the Emirates but, while he may feel disappointed not to have kept out Kai Havertz’s opener, he made a handful of excellent saves, a diving stretch to deny Bukayo Saka the best of the bunch. Ezri Konsa, on his first start for Arsenal, had the home fans on their feet after a thunderous slide tackle to stop Rogers early in the second half, the standout moment of a solid performance. It was Christos Tzolis who really took the game by the scruff of the neck, however, harrying Chelsea’s defence with mazy dribbles and driving runs forward. He also provided the diagonal ball which, via Havertz’s audacious dummy, set up Martin Ødegaard to score the winner, earning a firstPremier Leagueassist.Will MageeMatch report:Arsenal 2-1 ChelseaView image in fullscreenArsenal’s Riccardo Calafiori (left) and Christos Tzolis team up to thwart Chelsea’s Pedro Neto.Photograph: John Walton/PA3Scott showcases England potentialIf Thomas Tuchel required a reminder of precisely how good Alex Scott is, theBournemouthmidfielder provided it at St James’ Park. The 23-year-old reads the game a little faster and a little better than those around him and his stellar passing range raised the tone in a game Marco Rose’s side really should have won after cantering into a 2-0 lead, with Scott helping to create both goals. While Newcastle’s manager, Matthias Jaissle, can be heartened by his team’s refusal to surrender and, courtesy of goals from Harvey Barnes and Jacob Ramsey, their ultimate collection of a point, for long periods his players found no answers to Scott’s questions. Surely a first senior England cap beckons. The forthcoming Nations League fixtures against Spain, Croatia and Czechia offer ideal openings for Tuchel to put Scott on the international stage his talent demands.Louise TaylorMatch report:Newcastle 2-2 Bournemouth4Arbeloa already seeking solutionsThe omens don’t look good for Álvaro Arbeloa. Only twice before have Fulham started a top-flight season with three successive defeats and it ended with relegation on both occasions: in 1951-52 and in 2020-21 under Scott Parker. Arbeloa tried to concentrate on the positives after throwing away the lead twice againstCrystal Palaceand ending up losing to Ben Chilwell’s winner. His side looked dangerous in attack, with Josh King having already developed an understanding with the summer signing Gonzalo García, even if the Spaniard played a comical role in Tyrick Mitchell’s second equaliser. Fulham’s defending is another matter entirely: Joachim Anderson’s lack of pace was repeatedly exposed by the high line they deployed against Palace and Arbeloa must find a solution before facing his former club Liverpool and then Manchester United. “We knew that this month would be very tough,” said Arbeloa. “But I told my players it will not define our entire season.”Ed AaronsMatch report:Fulham 2-3 Crystal Palace5Gakpo delivers creative edgeSeveral positives for Liverpool in Suffolk on Friday: Bradley Barcola showing off his lightning speed in his cameo, Ronald Araújo solid in the troublesome right-back position and Alexander Isak coming back to the boil with two well-taken goals. Receiving the most plaudits in post-match was Cody Gakpo, who appeared headed forManchester Cityor Tottenham in the transfer window but stayed on to supply both Isak goals. “Cody knows how much we value him,” said Andoni Iraola. The confirmed exit of the sporting director, Richard Hughes, on Saturday brought assessments of a mixed legacy. Eventually, Isak repeating the form of his Newcastle days may stamp the decision to pay a record fee for the striker. Florian Wirtz, another expensive Hughes purchase, continues to receive similarly mixed reviews. At Ipswich, attention was drawn to his losing possession 22 times. It was left to Gakpo, whose purchase and sale were deals Hughes did not do, to provide Liverpool’s creative edge.John BrewinMatch report:Ipswich 0-2 LiverpoolView image in fullscreenLiverpool’s Cody Gakpo tries to break clear of Ipswich’s Julio Enciso.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/Reuters6Ndiaye could not refuse City’s offerIliman Ndiaye enthused about working hard in his Manchester City debut after his £65m transfer fromEverton. “I ran my backside off for the team wanting to get the win and you have to do the dirty side sometimes,” said the Senegalese forward, who was removed on 87 minutes, and brushed off how he might have joined Tottenham instead. “It was always going to be City. I wanted Champions League [football] and to play for one of the best teams in the world. I’m not saying Tottenham is not but when Manchester City comes through you don’t say no. It’s been a good week for me and topped off with a win. I was just being patient and when City came through I was buzzing.”Jamie JacksonMatch report:Manchester City 1-0 Coventryskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion7Brighton find another diamondThere were plenty of questions for Fabian Hürzeler to answer after Brighton’s draw with Leeds, namely why it took them the best part of an hour to wake up. But, for consecutive weekends, the Brighton manager had the pleasure of lauding Malick Yalcouyé’s performance. The 20-year-old was barely known even by his own club’s fans at the start of the campaign, having spent seasons on loan at Sturm Graz and Swansea since joining from Gothenburg for a reported £6m in July 2024. He has since started againstChelseaand Leeds, excelling in an attacking midfield role. Hürzeler said: “He shows a lot of energy, a lot of effort, he is good in possession and out of possession.” The Brighton manager has previously flagged Yalcouyé’s physicality as an area to improve and it is notable just how slight he is at just 5ft 7in. The Ivorian’s confidence, eagerness to enter combat and close control are in no doubt. He could be the next player off the conveyor belt of young talent who Brighton sell for a vast profit.Ben BloomMatch report:Brighton 1-1 Leeds8Tonali duel sums up Tottenham’s spiritOn the eve of Tottenham firing blanks for the third straight game, Roberto De Zerbi joked Allan Dixon’s bodybuilder physique could help them threaten at set pieces. Tottenham’s player liaison, who is Daniel Levy’s brother-in-law, moved up the pecking order again after Spurs failed to score in their first three league games for the first time since 1974-75. The club spent more than £300m this summer, Sandro Tonali the pick of the new signings on a blunt outing at the City Ground. De Zerbi praised Spurs’ spirit in the stalemate, epitomised by Tonali during a first-half duel with Dan Ndoye which culminated in a Forest corner. “I think it will be an advertising clip for the Premier League,” said Forest’s head coach, Oliver Glasner. “This is what the league is famous for and everyone loves.”Ben FisherMatch report:Nottingham Forest 0-0 Tottenham9Sunderland’s agent of chaosNilson Angulo, who scored for Ecuador against Germany at the World Cup, remains an enigmatic presence, at once robust and delicate, cunning and naive, deft and clumsy. At times, not obviously related to the game going on around him, he will simply stop, and waggle his legs around as though stirring paint with his feet. One volleyed flick with the back of his ankle to return an overhit cross to the middle was remarkable. He is a master of accelerating and suddenly slowing to create space, control immaculate, then at other times he will simply charge out of play. The only thing harder than marking him, perhaps, is playing alongside him, trying to work out if a cross is ever going to come. He is a magnificent agent of chaos, that is clear; whether he is a high-grade footballer is less obvious.Jonathan WilsonMatch report:Brentford 1-1 SunderlandView image in fullscreenSunderland’s Nilson Angulo attempts to keep the ball in play against Brentford.Photograph: David Klein/Reuters10Teenage defender coming of ageNot many teenage centre-halves play regularly in the Premier League, but the Australia international Lucas Herrington is quietly establishing himself in Hull’s acclimatisation to the top flight. The summer signing from Colorado Rapids celebrated turning 19 on Saturday by coming off the bench againstAston Villato help the Tigers keep another clean sheet. Herrington is rated as one of the finest defensive prospects in world football and underlined his promise with a vital block to deny Tyrone Mings. In all three of Hull’s Premier League games this season, Herrington has featured from the bench and the Queenslander’s star should continue to rise throughout the season. The Hull manager, Sergej Jakirovic, said: “Herrington is excellent and has great potential, so all these minutes are invaluable for him. I don’t have any fear when he’s on the pitch and I believe in him 100%. Provided he stays healthy, anything is possible.”Ross HeppenstallMatch report:Hull 0-0 Aston VillaPosTeamPGDPts1Man City3592Arsenal3593Hull3374Chelsea3165Brentford3356Liverpool3257Newcastle3258Everton3259Leeds31510Brighton33411Man Utd31412Sunderland30413Crystal Palace3-4314Ipswich3-4315AFC Bournemouth3-1216Nottm Forest3-1217Aston Villa3-5118Tottenham Hotspur3-5119Fulham3-3020Coventry3-50Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTen talking points from the weekend footballEvertonManchester UnitedArsenalChelseaNewcastle UnitedBournemouthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Safety, security and service’: behind the scenes with police at Arsenal v Chelsea | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Facial recognition and spotters part of operation at Emirates that involved dozen incidents and two arrests
Author: Sam Dalling
Headline: Facial recognition and spotters part of operation at Emirates that involved dozen incidents and two arrests
Content: Met police officers try to defuse tension between rival fans as they leave the ground after the Premier League match between Arsenal and Chelsea.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMet police officers try to defuse tension between rival fans as they leave the ground after the Premier League match between Arsenal and Chelsea.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianSoccer‘Safety, security and service’: behind the scenes with police at Arsenal v ChelseaFacial recognition and spotters part of operation at Emirates that involved a dozen incidents and two arrestsSam DallingMon 7 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe concourses are silent when, deep in the Emirates Stadium’s bowels, Chief Inspector Pete Dearden’s briefing begins.Arsenal’s 4.30pm kick-off against Chelseais still hours away but the fixture carries significance as a London derby and because the Premier League champions are hosting a realistic challenger.Dearden is a senior officer in the Metropolitan police’s public order command and Sunday’s matchday commander. He is, to borrow football jargon, giving the pre-match team talk, running through intelligence and in-game tactics. “Set the right style and tone,” he says. After Dearden has finished, the police room becomes a pseudo-station for the afternoon, with all incidents triaged by the same crime officer. Football offences can be found in niche legislation, and the Met wants London’s matchdays to be, so far as possible, policed uniformly.Matchday is the iceberg’s tip. The Met’s 17 dedicated football officers (DFOs) each work full-time on one club, planning each fixture with the matchday commander. All 500-plus games the Met covers per season are risk-graded using factors such as risk level of supporters, proximity, recent history and kick‑off time. Dearden labels Sunday’s game “medium medium”.“Our mantra is safety, security and service,” Dearden says. “We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.”View image in fullscreenChief inspector Pete Dearden gives a briefing in the police room inside the stadium three hours before kick-off in the match between Arsenal and Chelsea.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPete Dearden: ‘We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThree police support units (PSUs), each containing an inspector, three sergeants and about 21 constables, have been assigned to the match. In addition, there are the senior team and 20 operational football officers, or “spotters”, on duty.Clubs also have their own in-house safety teams, with, in effect, both parties doing their homework before collaborating. Arsenal’s operation involves about 1,000 stewards and response team members. They are the first responders to any incidents within Arsenal’s footprint. When aChelseafan overzealously reacts to his team’s early lead, the response team remove him.Stadiums are not policed as standard, but clubs can request (and, if the request is accepted, pay for) special police services (SPS).Arsenalasked for one PSU to work within the Emirates for Chelsea’s visit but even then, police intervene only when required. Dearden estimates policing football costs the Met £23m a season, with approximately 10% recovered from clubs for SPS.The Met is looking to close that gap, with aspects such as road closures and hostile vehicle mitigation now managed, and financed, by clubs. Dearden says his department is looking at “mitigation measures to reduce risk, which means that we don’t have to have as many police resources and we don’t compromise safety and security”.Using spotters is one such measure. They work under the DFOs, are usually locally based for their day-to-day duties and operate consistently with one club. Dearden estimates that their expertise allows them to do the work of double the number of public order officers that would otherwise be needed. “They will go to pubs in the wider footprint where these people gather and try to identify what their plans are, get a good feeling for their mood and the numbers,” Dearden says.Some Chelsea spotters are in Holborn and will follow when supporters journey to Arsenal by tube. Fans being unwilling to engage with spotters may indicate they are planning something. “You can get a good idea of whether they are potentially going to cause problems at a game because of that lack of engagement,” Dearden says. “It’s that communication approach again – even with some of the supporters that cause us problems, albeit a minority, there’s still engagement to be had. There are still opportunities to say: ‘Don’t do that.’”Immediately before the match one spotter performed CPR on a supporter. The intervention was life-saving.View image in fullscreenArsenal fans walk past live facial recognition cameras on their way to the ground.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Premier League has invested millions of pounds into the intelligence-led live facial recognition pilot.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianOutside the Emirates, two blue vans contain officers monitoring the data from cameras scanning passersby as part of an intelligence‑led live facial recognition pilot. The trials were funded thanks to a multimillion-pound Premier League investment.Passing the cameras is voluntary, with signs alerting pedestrians to their presence. Faces are biometrically scanned and compared with a watchlist containing the several thousand people subject to football banning orders (FBOs) and individuals wanted for more serious crimes.“We are targeting high-harm offenders, sex offenders, those with FBOs, who, if they came to an event, could spoil it for others, commit crimes, or exploit opportunities such as crowded spaces,” Dearden says.The two-hour pilot yields six interventions, one while Guardian Sport is present. Officers intervene to speak to the individual, who is with their family. They have an FBO, although are not restricted from being around the Emirates. They have also recently been released from prison for human trafficking and are wearing a tag.Dearden feels half a dozen hits is proportional to what would be expected. “What we can’t measure is the deterrent effect,” he says.Noticeable is the relative lack of police visibility compared with recent years. That is by design, not accident. A heavy police presence does not necessarily make an event feel safe. “We don’t work on a ‘just in case’ basis these days,” Dearden says. “We deal with known knowns.” Arsenal fans in Naples on Wednesday are likely to meet a vastly different approach.Immediately before the match, the Guardian laps the ground with the day’s three-person violence against women and girls (VAWG) team. “We want to change the culture of what perhaps in the past was tolerated,” Dearden says, giving the example of staff being targeted with misogynistic abuse.“We’ve had people at football matches come forward and say: ‘I’ve heard you talk three or four times now and I’m now confident enough to report that I think I’m a victim of domestic abuse and controlling behaviour.’”The VAWG team are also watching for those who may target vulnerable individuals.View image in fullscreenA constable high-fives a young Arsenal fan as he patrols the podium level at the Emirates.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn officer acts as a spotter at the Emirates before kick-off.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianFor the match, Dearden heads to the command room with Arsenal’s safety team and the other emergency services. Proximity and open dialogue are vital. Because of the game’s risk level, there is a bronze commander, Inspector Rachel Duckett, at ground level. A half-time briefing allows all parties – including medical, the London fire brigade, the local authority, the Premier League, and British transport police – to compare notes and address issues. Dearden and Duckett then discuss the strategy for the game’s end.For all the planning, much of what happens at football is result-driven. With Arsenal 2-1 up and time running out, a late Chelsea equaliser might have changed the mood. Home and away fans cross paths after, outside the 3,000-strong Chelsea end, where there is no cordon. Arsenal supporters gloat; some Chelsea fans react. A pair of Chelsea content creators try to record in the middle of the departing crowd and receive an expletive-laden reaction from passing Arsenal fans. They are advised to move on for their own safety.Striking is the speed at which potential flashpoints are spotted and then defused. Officers are calm, not confrontational, and act as an external subconscious: “‘C’mon, think – do you really want to do that?’”View image in fullscreenA Chelsea supporter is escorted out of the ground by Arsenal stewards.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOfficers support a Chelsea content creator as he tries to record a piece after Arsenal’s 2-1 victory.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAn hour after the final whistle, the stadium is silent again, and Dearden and his senior team debrief pitchside. A dozen incidents occurred around the game, with two arrests made – one for assaulting a steward and another for racial abuse and assault. A further 10 people were reported for offences including drinking in view of the pitch, missile throwing, low-level assault of a steward, homophobic chanting and possession of drugs.Dearden says the number is “slightly higher than we’d like” but points out that it demonstrates proactivity. For example, stewards are told not to tolerate pushes as simply part of the job. Outcomes will be proportionate and consistency is key. In the days and weeks ahead, everything will be analysed, assessed, fed into data. Incremental improvement will be sought and further action may be required for the reported incidents.But, for a few hours at least, all involved can reflect on a matchday’s work completed well.Explore more on these topicsFootballArsenalChelseafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Emery ready to ignite Aston Villa’s season at Club Brugge after familiar slow start | Aston Villa | The Guardian
description: Manager remains calm despite his side taking one point and scoring no goals in opening three Premier League games
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Manager remains calm despite his side taking one point and scoring no goals in opening three Premier League games
Content: John McGinn keeps his eyes on the ball during training for Aston Villa’s match against Club Brugge.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenJohn McGinn keeps his eyes on the ball during training for Aston Villa’s match against Club Brugge.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAAston VillaEmery ready to ignite Aston Villa’s season at Club Brugge after familiar slow startManager remains calm despite his side taking one point and scoring no goals in opening three Premier League gamesBen Fisherin BrugesMon 7 Sep 2026 16.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnai Emery is not panicking. He may kick every ball on the touchline but, behind closed doors, Aston Villa’s players are used to him being the calmest person in the room, routinely more demanding after victory than defeat. John McGinn tells a story in which the Villa manager, early in his now almost four-year tenure, broke character and lost his cool during a half-time interval not owing to a lukewarm performance but because he witnessed his captain tearing into teammates. In Emery’s eyes, it was McGinn expending unnecessary energy rather than seeking solutions.Emery, McGinn and Villa have been here before. Just last season, in fact; at this point, they were pointless in the Premier Leagueand still another 157 minutes from registering their first goal. So in one sense Villa, who shook off a slow start to qualify for theChampions Leaguefor the second time in three seasons, are ahead of schedule. Villa’s goalless draw at Hull on Saturday was not the most absorbing display but there were enough green shoots to trust Emery when he says he is confident they can again exceed expectations.Maresca eyes rest for busy dad Haaland as Manchester City prepare for PortoRead moreIt is hard to disbelieve a man with Emery’s record, having overseen the most successful era in the club’s recent history. “When we started the project here, the ambition we had, it was [not even] in our highest expectations to be in Europe four years in a row,” the Villa manager says. “It was very difficult when we started working together but it was the ambition of the owner. We set our standards high with the players to be there and we are. Now is the moment to remember how we got here and the way we did. Now it is a different moment and chapter.”In these moments, Emery tends to double down on his methods. Last season they did not taste victory until their seventh game of the season in all competitions, McGinn scoring the only goal in a Europa League win against Bologna. Before that game, players assembled around 11.30am for the kind of opposition analysis meeting to which they have grown accustomed, so much so McGinn says they now walk in like robots.Emery lasers in on players’ positioning and tactical details. Jhon Durán, now on loan at Benfica from Al-Nassr after spells at Fenerbahce and Zenit St Petersburg, is famously the only player to have requested to leave mid-meeting.Villa face Club Brugge on Tuesday for the fourth time in the past two years, hoping Europe will again ignite their season.After that victory against Bologna last September, Villa embarked on an extraordinary run of 17 wins in 19 matches. Half of the 14 players involved in that game have departed but one of those who did feature, Emiliano Buendía, is hopeful that Emery’s new-look squad can put together a similar run. “It has not been the start we wanted, but we are trying to take the positive things from every match,” said the Argentinian, who has started all four Villa games this season. “We will try to change this momentum in terms of results and try to get our confidence back to perform well and [achieve] the results we want.”View image in fullscreenUnai Emery is remaining calm despite Aston Villa’s slow start to the season.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Stewart Kendall/Apl/SportsphotoAnother Champions League campaign should not be taken for granted and returning to this stage, after winning the Europa League last season, is arguably Emery’s greatest feat. The strides made under Emery will surely occupy the minds of supporters as they wander the cobbled streets of Bruges and when they explore Barcelona in November, too.Crucially, Emery is energised by the challenge, helped by the odd siesta at Villa’s Bodymoor Heath base. “Sometimes I need a good nap, after intensive work in the morning,” he said with a smile last week.For now, George Hemmings’s 13th‑minute shot against Hull represents Villa’s sole effort on target this campaign. In the same game it was the 19-year-old, who joined from Nottingham Forest aged 16, who supplied Buendía for a golden chance. It is easy to focus on the shortcomings but it would also be remiss to overlook Villa’s encouraging performance in the Super Cup against, in Emery’s view, the best team on the planet; defeat against Paris Saint-Germain was less than a month ago and Villa have only strengthened since.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne of the most exciting of their 11 summer arrivals, the 18-year-old Ibrahim Mbaye, was an unused substitute for PSG in Salzburg. Another talent signed this summer, Johan Manzambi, continues to step up his fitness after a knee injury and could feature as early as Saturday against Nottingham Forest.Only two of Villa’s new arrivals – Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson – started at Hull last time out. Matteo Ruggeri, Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho arrived from the bench. Taylor Harwood-Bellis, a £25m buy omitted from Villa’s Champions League squad, had a watching brief in Yorkshire. João Gomes was sent off on debut. Leon Goretzka, who joined on a free after leaving Bayern Munich, will not feature until at least October after a knee injury setback.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Emery often takes time to integrate signings. Youri Tielemans had to wait four months for his first Villa start before embedding himself as one of Emery’s undroppables. He demands a lot of his players and even more of himself. “In football, if you are expecting transition, maybe you are not in the right way,” he said last month.“We have to rebuild the team as fast as possible. I don’t know if we need time or not. We are progressing – still not enough because we are not getting good results – but tomorrow is a new test in Europe.”Explore more on these topicsAston VillaUnai EmeryChampions LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Maresca eyes rest for busy dad Haaland as Manchester City prepare for Porto | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City’s manager, Enzo Maresca, said Erling Haaland is a ‘complete’ person since the birth of his son and would soon need rest after a busy summer
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Manchester City’s manager, Enzo Maresca, said Erling Haaland is a ‘complete’ person since the birth of his son and would soon need rest after a busy summer
Content: Erling Haaland has matured into a complete person since the birth of his son, according to Enzo Maresca.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenErling Haaland has matured into a complete person since the birth of his son, according to Enzo Maresca.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersManchester CityMaresca eyes rest for busy dad Haaland as Manchester City prepare for PortoNorwegian forward has played every minute of seasonParenting duties have changed player’s ‘priorities’Jamie Jacksonin PortoMon 7 Sep 2026 17.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnzo Maresca believes Erling Haaland has become “complete” as his priorities have changed after the birth of theManchester CityNo 9’s son two years ago.Haaland has again started the campaign in prolific form, scoring three goals in City’s opening three Premier League victories. In three of the 26‑year‑old’s four previous seasons at City he has won the Premier League golden boot. Maresca pointed to how the birth of his son in 2024 changed the Norwegian’s motivation.Emery ready to ignite Aston Villa’s season at Club Brugge after familiar slow startRead moreThe manager said: “He’s a man now. He’s a dad. When he arrived here [in summer 2022] he was not a dad and now he’s a dad and life completely changes because the priority becomes his son. I’m happy for him because he was already top as a player and as a boy but now you can see that he is complete. He is a family man, he is still scoring goals so I’m very happy for him.”City are at Porto in the opening league‑phase game of theChampions Leagueon Tuesday. Haaland has played every competitive minute of the campaign so far, and Maresca said he will be rested at some point, particularly as as the striker was part of the Norway team that reached the World Cup quarter-finals.The Italian said: “It’s not easy for Erling or for any of the players that play for club and international teams. I think it is normal that you [may] see these players start to be tired. So, it’s correct to give them some rest. It can be one game out or one week away.“It depends on which moment we are in but the priority is to allow the players to be good and happy. When you see them tired the risk of injury increases, and we need players who are 100%.”While Maresca’s options if Haaland is rested against Porto would be selecting Antoine Semenyo at centre-forward, or fielding Phil Foden or Rayan Cherki as a false 9, he pointed to the in-game control the two latter players can give City when required.View image in fullscreenNico O’Reilly pulled up with an injury before the Coventry match but will ‘probably’ be available to face Porto.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA“There is always a gameplan and Rayan can drop a little bit to manage the tempo and the game,” the 46-year-old said.“We [also] need Rayan in the position to be dangerous – the last game against Coventry [a 1-0 win] we made contact with him five or six times between the lines and created chances.“It depends on the game. Against Coventry, it was good for him to drop a little bit and manage the tempo and not always be a reference for the other team. We need him in the right position because he gives us the quality. Phil can also do that – and the last pass between the lines is very good so we are lucky that we have two very good players that can do this.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn his first campaign as head coach, Francesco Farioli led Porto to their 31st title, and they have a maximum 15 points from their opening five Primeira Liga games.Maresca was asked if City will be favourites at the Estádio do Dragão. “We are here to do our best,” he said. “The game will dictate the favourite. This is a hard place to come. This season they started very good. In the last 14, 15 games in Europe they just lost one so we are going to try our best and try to win the game.“I know that Porto is very good in set pieces. I think it has become part of the game now so we need to do our best, defend in the right way, score goals as much as we can from set pieces because it’s part of the game and you need to be perfect because all teams are prepared for that.”Maresca said Nico O’Reilly would “probably” be available after missing the Coventry game with a late fitness problem, but the manager said he was “not sure” about Jérémy Doku’s availability after injury.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityErling HaalandChampions LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea’s midfield a headache for Alonso after Arsenal press advantage | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: There was a gulf between the teams in the middle of the park, with Moisés Caicedo’s absence hurting the visitors
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: There was a gulf between the teams in the middle of the park, with Moisés Caicedo’s absence hurting the visitors
Content: Xabi Alonso (second from right) leads his players in a round of applause for the away fans after Chelsea’s defeat against Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenXabi Alonso (second from right) leads his players in a round of applause for the away fans after Chelsea’s defeat against Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersChelseaChelsea’s midfield a headache for Alonso after Arsenal press advantageThere was a gulf between the teams in the middle of the park, with Moisés Caicedo’s absence hurting the visitorsJacob SteinbergMon 7 Sep 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere have been seasons when Chelsea have turned up at the Emirates Stadium and parked the bus. “You know, I think 10 years without a title is boring,” José Mourinho said in response to criticism from Arsenal fans aftera stultifying 0-0 draw in April 2015. On Sunday, though, there was no holding back from Chelsea. “I want to compete in the best possible way to win,” Xabi Alonso said after seeing his new sideedged out by Arsenal in a breathless encounter. “Today we didn’t want to sit deep from the first minute. We wanted to be active.”The plan worked at times. Chelsea maintained their habit of scoring early goals, going ahead through Morgan Rogers, and created further openings. But they were facing the championsand do not have Arsenal’s completeness. Shortcomings were exploited, particularly in midfield.
