title: Pixel 11 review: Google sets the bar for standard flagship phones | Google | The Guardian
description: Longer battery life, faster chip, actually useful AI tools and better cameras keep quality Android ahead of competition
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Longer battery life, faster chip, actually useful AI tools and better cameras keep quality Android ahead of competition
Content: The latest Google phone is most refined yet, offering the best balance of price and features for base-model flagship handsets.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe latest Google phone is most refined yet, offering the best balance of price and features for base-model flagship handsets.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.GoogleReviewPixel 11 review: Google sets the bar for standard flagship phonesLonger battery life, faster chip, actually useful AI tools and better cameras keep quality Android ahead of competitionSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 7 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle’s Pixel 11 continues to set the standard for what you should expect from the base model of a flagship phone with class-leading cameras, long software support and almost all the bells and whistles of its most expensive phones.The regular Pixel 11 costs £879 (€999/$899/A$1,499) making it £80 or equivalent more expensive than last year’s model as the cost ofRAMageddon continues to bite. It’s not cheap by any stretch of the imagination, but it comes with 256GB of storage and is £200 less than the Pixel 11 Pro, matching rivalSamsung’s Galaxy S26.At a glance the Pixel 11 looks very similar to theprevious twoGooglephone iterations: glass front and back with flat aluminium sides and large pill-shaped bar at the back, which is much slimmer this time. Stick it in a case and the protruding camera all but disappears.View image in fullscreenThe Pixel 11’s camera bar depth has been reduced by 40% compared with previous models for a sleeker look that doesn’t catch on your pocket quite as much.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 6.3in OLED screen is crisp and super bright with up to a 120Hz refresh rate to keep your scrolling smooth. The in-screen fingerprint scanner is fast and accurate, while thecamera-based face recognitionworks well during the day and is secure enough for use with banking apps, unlike similar systems on most Android rivals.SpecificationsScreen:6.3in 120Hz FHD+ OLED (422ppi)Processor:Google Tensor G6RAM:12GBStorage:256 or 512GBOperating system:Android17Camera:48MP+ 13MP UW + 10.8MP 5x tele; 10.5MP selfieConnectivity:5G, eSIM, wifi 6E, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6 and GNSSWater resistance:IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes)Dimensions:152.8 x 72.0 x 8.6mmWeight:197gFaster and more efficient Tensor G6 chipView image in fullscreenThe Pixel 11 takes less than 90 minutes to fully charge using a 30W or greater power adaptor (not included) hitting 53% in half an hour. It also supports 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThePixelhas a new generation of Google’s chip, the Tensor G6, which is up to 20% faster in tests. It significantly lags top-end rivals from Qualcomm and Apple, so won’t win any raw performance awards, but feels snappy in daily tasks and can handle mid-level gaming just fine.The battery life is also improved over previous models, lasting about 54 hours of light use between charges. That includes actively using the screen for more than seven hours for browsing, messaging, apps and photos across a mix of 5G and wifi.Gaming and more demanding use hits the battery harder, but the Pixel should be able to see out even the heaviest of use days.Android 17 with more proactive AIView image in fullscreenGoogle’s proactive AI tools pop up with timely information in chats and other situations to save you manually having to check your calendar, search for a restaurant or schedule an event.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Pixel 11 runs the latest Android 17 out of the box with operating system and security updates provided untilAugust 2033.The software is slick, nicely animated and well optimised, with plenty of colourful customisation if you want it. As with previous Pixels, it is a showcase for some of Google’s most advanced AI systems, many of which run on-device, making them fast.The most interesting of the tools remains Google’s proactive AI systems, which vary a bit depending on where you live. In the UK the expandedMagic Cuefromlast yearpops up in messages and a few other apps with information such as your schedule, flight or order details, and suggestions for good local restaurants from Google maps or photos to share in a chat. In the US, Canada, Australia and a few other regions, the feature is called “Gemini Proactive Assistance” but has similar powers. If you use a supported app, such as Google Messages, the suggestions are low-key great. Unfortunately it doesn’t work in WhatsApp, Signal or other third-party apps I’ve tried, which limits its usefulness.In the UK and US, Gemini can go further, proactively taking action for you, such asbooking a restaurant via OpenTable, which is the type of assistance that has long been promised by various AI agents.Another useful AI feature is built directly into Google’s keyboard called Rambler, which is voice typing on steroids. You can speak naturally to it and the system will remove your ums and ers and other deviations to produce a succinct, fully formed sentence or paragraph. It makes trying to dictate a rushed messaged while hustling for public transport a lot easier, although it doesn’t show your text until after you hit the stop button, unlike most other dictation tools.CameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app is fairly simple to use while being feature rich with plenty of tools and modes to make the best of your photography.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Pixel 11 has three cameras on the back and a solid 10.5-megapixel selfie camera in the screen.The improved main 48MP camera captures excellent photos across a range of lighting conditions, including low light where its larger sensor helps capture more of what’s available. The 13MP ultra-wide camera is one of the best on a phone of this class, helpful for fitting more in the shot or providing a different perspective. But it is the 10.8MP 5x telephoto camera that sets it apart from the competition, capable of meaningfully closing the distance to objects. In bright light it can digitally zoom to 30x magnification with surprisingly good results.Entirely new for the Pixel camera this year is the“Looks” feature, which allows you to customise how the phone captures and processes your photos for very different styles far beyond simple filters applied after the fact.There are three versions of the default look available – natural, vanilla and shadows – plus six more-distinctive looks, including “digi” that replicates the look of the old digital cameras that has recently become popular. Each look can be customised in colour, tone, grain and sharpness, so you can get arty or replicate a particular film style.If you are a Pixel user who has ever thought its photos look a little too cold, dramatic or overly processed, this is for you.The Pixel shoots great video at up to 4K at 60 frames a second. The newMagic Capturefeature is a one-button shooting mode that records video and photos automatically that is best used during events such as birthday parties where you want to be more in the moment but still capture the scene.Google has also added a “Creator Suite” mode to the video capture, which shoots straight to a folder you can quickly storyboard and trim to create a video. It also has a teleprompter mode for shooting face to camera, a social media grid to get the alignment correct and speech enhancement that cuts out background noise.All these features are in addition to Google’s popular Auto Best Take, Add Me and Camera Coachfrom last year, which makes the new Pixel camera one of the most feature rich available.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe Pixel 11 is available in a range of colours including the standard mat black (obsidian).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe batteryis rated to lastin excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repairwith manualsandparts available.The Pixel 11 is contains 33% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down thephone’s environmental impactin its report and willrecycle old devicesfor free.PriceThe Google Pixel 11 costs from£879(€999/$899/A$1,499) in a choice of four colours.For comparison, thePixel 10acosts£499, the Pixel 11 Pro costs£1,079, the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs£1,279, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from£1,799, theSamsung Galaxy S26costs£879and theApple iPhone 17costs£799.VerdictThe Pixel 11 isn’t the most advanced Google phone, nor is it the cheapest. But this middle-ground model offers more than enough to beat the competition and question whether you really need to spend more on a Pro phone.It offers, yet again, a very high-quality experience, great triple camera, long software support and very good battery life. It won’t win any raw performance awards, so those looking for a gaming phone should look elsewhere, but it feels fast and responsive in daily use.Google’s AI tools are second to none, particularly its Rambler dictation feature in the keyboard and the proactive Gemini features, which offer genuinely useful help even if they are not available in every third-party app.The new camera looks feature provides more control over photos than ever before on a Pixel, so you can tailor it to your preferences or get creative far beyond simple filters.It may not have changed all that much from last year’sequally excellent Pixel 10, and it isn’t quite thebargain the Pixel 10ais, but the Pixel 11 is the best phone you can get under £900.Pros:seven years of software updates, great camera with 5x telephoto, great screen, impressive local AI features, Qi2.2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, long battery life, good size, fast fingerprint and face recognition, 256GB starting storage.Cons:face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance short of rivals, no physical SIM card slot in the US, heavier than rivals, not a big upgrade on previous model, no wifi 7.View image in fullscreenThe combination of fast face recognition and in-screen fingerprint scanner with the slick screen keep the Pixel 11 feeling responsive in use.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsGooglePixelSmartphonesAlphabetMobile phonesAndroidreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Why Meta started losing in court - podcast | Meta | The Guardian
description: Katy McQue, who has spent years reporting on Meta and the potential harms its platforms pose to children, explains the tactics being used by prosecutors
Author: Annie Kelly
Headline: Katy McQue, who has spent years reporting on Meta and the potential harms its platforms pose to children, explains the tactics being used by prosecutors
Content: 00:00:0000:00:00Today in FocusMetaWhy Meta started losing in court - podcastKaty McQue, who has spent years reporting on Meta and the potential harms its platforms pose to children, explains the tactics being used by prosecutorsMore ways to listenApple podcastsSpotifyRSS FeedDownloadPresented byAnnie Kellywith Katy McQue; produced byRuth Abrahams,Guy SzafmanandBrian McNamara; executive producersSami KentandAlex AtackSun 6 Sep 2026 22.00 EDTShareFor years, the investigative journalistKaty McQuehas been reporting on the potential harms Meta’s platforms pose to children.Yet, as she explains toAnnie Kelly, despite the mountain of evidence compiled by journalists, prosecutors, bereaved families and others, it has been nearly impossible to bring Meta and other social media companies to court.Finally, in 2026, something seems to have changed. Already three landmark cases have brought Meta to trial in the US: in New Mexico, which cited Katy’s reporting on child sexual exploitation; in California, about the mental health harms to young people; and last week, an unprecedented case that Meta settled for $18bn.In all three, prosecutors seem to have found a new way to argue against Meta; an argument based not on the content it publishes, but on the very design of its platforms.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersExplore more on these topicsMetaToday in FocusSocial mediaLaw (US)Digital mediaChild protectionInternet safetyChildren's tech

title: Designers should not fear being replaced by AI, industry leaders say | UK news | The Guardian
description: Firms are more likely to use technology as ‘the intern in the office’ than as a replacement for skilled staff
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Firms are more likely to use technology as ‘the intern in the office’ than as a replacement for skilled staff
Content: Despite fears about the rapid growth of generative AI, industry leaders point to robust employment figures and argue that the tools have so far done little to reduce demand for design skills.Photograph: ktasimar/AlamyView image in fullscreenDespite fears about the rapid growth of generative AI, industry leaders point to robust employment figures and argue that the tools have so far done little to reduce demand for design skills.Photograph: ktasimar/AlamyUK newsDesigners should not fear being replaced by AI, industry leaders sayFirms are more likely to use technology as ‘the intern in the office’ than as a replacement for skilled staffPhillip InmanMon 7 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProfessional designers should not feel “threatened” by the rapid growth of generative AI, according to business leaders, despite fears over job losses in the sector.With design and film production companies and manufacturers all adopting AI at an accelerating pace, industry bodies said the technology would be used to enhance the work of designers rather than replace them.Mat Hunter, the chief executive of theDesignCouncil – a charity which champions the industry – said that while AI was increasingly being used by designers, “they are using it to add value”.He said: “We are aware that technology always displaces people with new ways of working. However, we believe in the imagination and inventiveness of designers to find opportunities. We believe the UK needs more professional designers, so overall employment should continue to grow.”Deborah Dawton, chief executive of the Design Business Association, said: “What protects great designers from AI is skill, experience, empathy and deep understanding of the sectors they operate in. So, no, [workers] shouldn’t feel threatened if they operate at this level.”Uncanny and unappetizing: appetites spoil as AI images take over food menusRead moreEarlier this yearresearch, conducted by The King’s Institute for Artificial Intelligence and the Policy Institute, showed 57% of the public think AI will lead to widespread unemployment. Last week, freelancers including designers told the Guardian they werepicking up “soulless” workcorrecting AI errors.The Design Council said on Monday that its analysis showed the sector – which covers everything from the design of household products and fashion to building and transport design – had grown by 40% between 2019 and the end of 2023, beating the economy’s 23% average rate of expansion and leapfrogging the size of the retail industry.Research funded by the council for its triennial overview –Design Economy 2026– showed that sectors like construction, services and manufacturing support 2.27m design jobs, and that there has been a 15% increase in employment between 2020 and 2025.While the figures estimating the size of the industry pre-date the arrival of dominant AI tools including ChatGPT and Claude, the employment figures to the end of last year indicate that their use has done little so far to affect the demand for workers with design skills.Hunter said design was often considered to be an add-on or nice-to-have, but was essential to industries from advanced manufacturing to digital services.“People don’t realise design is everywhere and is about trying to make things usable,” he said.He added that the government’s consolidation of hundreds of public sector websites into one consistent design was an example of improvements in a service that can be supported by designers.Dawton said AI was being used as a substitute for the work done by human designers, but “rip-offs have been happening for a very long time – AI hasn’t enabled that”.The industry went through a similar transition when companies began using computer-aided design software, displacing draughtspeople, but Dawton said modern workers could find jobs elsewhere in the industry as it expands.She added: “The key thing to remember is that these copycats look the same but they aren’t the same. The materials, finishes, methods of manufacture, assembly, colour, etc, mean that they are very different products.”Over the longer term, she said: “We have to adapt to any technological change that takes place around us. The difference with the design industry is that large chunks of it drive that change.“For most in business, efficiency/optimisation is the main conversation around AI. Designers have a second conversation with AI, which is about the potential it opens up in the hands of a creator.”I’m a father of three who studies the impact of artificial intelligence: this is what parents need to know about AIRead moreAndrew Duff, head of the Society of Garden and Landscape Designers, said many people working in his industry were nervous about AI. He said design companies were more likely to use AI as “the intern in the office” than as a replacement for skilled staff.The Design Council report said some regions had grown strongly over the last eight years, though from a low base. There was an 88% increase in income from design across all industries in Wales and a 67% rise in the north-east of England. The south-east remained the hub for design industries, accounting for £43.3bn of gross value added (GVA) – a calculation of income from economic activity – compared with just £3.1bn in the north-east from a UK total of £136.7bn.Its contribution was larger than the UK’s retail sector, worth £114bn, and nearly twice the size of the accommodation and food service industry, worth £70bn.Hunter said a lack of skilled workers was a bigger problem than AI after entries for design and technology GCSEs declined by 68% over the decade to 2024.Dawton said: “We need specialist teachers and equipment in schools if we’re going to inspire the next generation of world shapers at an early age.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsAI (artificial intelligence)DesignComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Mistrust’ of Palantir may affect NHS research, says health minister | Health | The Guardian
description: James Frith says patients may be less willing to share data as new figures show a rise in opt-outs
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: James Frith says patients may be less willing to share data as new figures show a rise in opt-outs
Content: Health workers protest outside the London headquarters of Palantir, in opposition to the company’s involvement with the NHS.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenHealth workers protest outside the London headquarters of Palantir, in opposition to the company’s involvement with the NHS.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAHealth‘Mistrust’ of Palantir may affect NHS research, says health ministerJames Frith says patients may be less willing to share data as new figures show a rise in opt-outsRobert BoothUK technology editorMon 7 Sep 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConcern is being raised about Palantir’s work with the NHS as new figures showed tens of thousands of patients have withdrawn their data from use in research projects.James Frith, the health innovation minister, said he was worried about “mistrust” of the US defence and health tech company and “the impact it could have on people’s willingness to share data with the NHS”.The government is deciding whether to axe the company’s £330m contract to operate the health service’s federated data platform, which is intended to improve efficiency and patient outcomes.Frith’s comment, in a letter toLayla Moran, the chair of the Commons health committee, follows a rise in patients opting out of allowing their medical data to be shared. In the two months from mid-May to mid-July, 60,000 more people withdrew their private information under a mechanism called the national data opt-out.Doctors and patients’ groups are calling for Labour to exercise a break clause in Palantir’s seven-year contract. They cite its work with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s ICE immigration agency and question the company’s claim to provide value for money.Palantir and its supporters say its AI-driven technology has cut NHS waiting lists for surgery. A spokesperson for the company said it was “helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 110,000 additional operations, a 15% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 6.8% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days”.NHS England has reported similar numbers butsaidit could not “draw conclusions about cause and effect”. The government’s statistics watchdog is investigating the data.Frith told Moran there had been an increase in NHS data opt-outs, in line with media interest in Palantir’s position.Palantir paid just £2m corporation tax in UK in 2024 despite lucrative public sector contractsRead morePalantir’s government contracts have been beset by controversy. Ministers apologised after it emerged that the company’s staff had access to identifiable patient data.London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, has also blocked the Metropolitan police from awarding Palantir a £50m contract to use its AI to support investigations. He said Londoners wanted to see public money paid only to companies that “share the values of our city”. Palantir issuingover the mayor’s decision.Frith said the rise in opt-outs was “modest” but would still be monitored. Opting out does not stop an individual’s records from being used for direct care, such as live operations. However, it prevents it being used for research and planning.Frith said: “It may not be possible to realise the benefits of the 10-year health plan if patients stop sharing their data.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFoxglove, a tech equity campaign, welcomed the minister’s acknowledgment of apparent public mistrust of Palantir. “Doctors and patients have been warning about the threat this poses to NHS care, and tens of thousands of people have opted out in just the last few months,” said Tom Hegarty, its head of communications.“People are right to be concerned given … its founder, Trump ally Peter Thiel, going on record to opine that the NHS makes people sick.”Frith indicated a policy shift on whether the Palantir-powered platform must be used by NHS trusts. In July, a health minister told parliament that health trusts would be told they “must use” parts of NHS England’s federated platform, which is controlled using Palantir technology. Now Frith has said “there is no requirement to use the FDP” and they may “prefer an alternative”.Moran, who is a Liberal Democrat MP, said she welcomed the “softened stance” on whether adoption of the FDP was mandatory but added: “We remain of the view that the government should switch provider and not extend the current contract. Given how long this process could take, ministers need to act decisively and quickly, and not put this decision off until February.”A spokesperson for the Department ofHealthand Social Care said: “There has been absolutely no change in position. The NHS federated data platform has never been mandatory and organisations have always been able to choose alternative solutions where they meet local needs.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsHealthNHSPalantirAI (artificial intelligence)Layla MoranSadiq KhannewsShareReuse this content

title: The death of ‘hello’: how gen Z – and scammers – put paid to the greeting | Social etiquette | The Guardian
description: If you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you’re sure there’s a human being on the line. Is this the end of an era?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: If you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you’re sure there’s a human being on the line. Is this the end of an era?
Content: With caller ID, gen Z don’t bother with the charade of a greeting.Photograph: Posed by model /Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWith caller ID, gen Z don’t bother with the charade of a greeting.Photograph: Posed by model /Getty ImagesPass notesSocial etiquetteThe death of ‘hello’: how gen Z – and scammers – put paid to the greetingIf you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you’re sure there’s a human being on the line. Is this the end of an era?Mon 7 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Hello.Age:200 years old.Status:Under threat of extinction.That’s ridiculous –we’ve been saying hello to each other for millions of years.Well, that isn’t true. As I just mentioned, the word appeared in print a couple of hundred years ago. But it’s a deviation of“holla”, “hollo”, “halloo” or “hillo”, all of which were used in English as attention-grabbing noises since at least the 16th century.But we use it all the time now.Only because of the telephone. After the phone’s invention by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876, Thomas Edison decided that a newstandardised greetingneeded to be invented.Why?Because previously people tended to greet each other with time-based salutations, such as “good morning” or “good evening”. But the telephone could instantly cross time zones, which made these redundant.But why hello?Because Edison preferred it to Bell’s favoured “Ahoy-hoy”.Shame.I know. Anyway, forget all that, because nobody says hello any more.But I like hello.Too late. Technology has marched on again: everyone has a smartphone with caller ID now. Why go through the charade of a “hello?” when you already know who’s calling you?I don’t know, basic politeness?Tell that to gen Z. The New York Times hasreportedon the death of hello, stating that young people now prefer to answer the phone with “Hi”, “What’s up?” or “Yeah?”.This sounds spurious.It isn’t. Asurveylast year revealed that 40% of 18-24 year-olds feel that it is acceptable to answer the phone without any form of greeting whatsoever.Isn’t that a bit weird?It sort of makes sense, though. Conversations have become free-form things spread across multiple formats. If you’ve just been texting, or DMing, or emailing with someone, a phone call is just a continuation and arguably doesn’t require anything as formal as a hello.Still, it’s nice.Only if you love AI scammers.What the hell? Where did that come from?You didn’t hear about this? Apparently scammers can now replicate your voice with AI, cloning it from your telephone greeting, and use it to beg your loved ones for money. This is a real thing that has been covered by theconsumer watchdog Which?, the BBC andthe Guardian.This is genuinely nightmarish.Guess what the best way to beat it is.I’ll guess rudeness.Correct! If you’re called by an unidentified number, the advice is to remain silent until you are sure that a friendly human being is on the other end of the line. Not saying hello first could save you a whole heap of trouble.Well, it looks like this is goodbye to hello.Don’t say goodbye. Say au revoir.Because it’s romantic?No, because the terrifying hordes of robot scammers might clone you into a French person, and your family would be confused.Do say:“Hello is becoming obsolete.”Don’t say:“Ahoy-hoy!”Explore more on these topicsSocial etiquettePass notesLanguageTelecommunications industryYoung peopleScamsCrimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lindsay Clancy’s case is a rorschach test | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: Clancy’s case became a referendum on mothers, healthcare, and the status of women
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: Clancy’s case became a referendum on mothers, healthcare, and the status of women
Content: ‘What is most haunting about the Clancy case is how ordinary and unsurprising were all the failures that led to her break.’Photograph: Greg Derr/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘What is most haunting about the Clancy case is how ordinary and unsurprising were all the failures that led to her break.’Photograph: Greg Derr/ReutersOpinionMassachusettsLindsay Clancy’s case is a rorschach testMoira DoneganClancy’s case became a referendum on mothers, healthcare, and the status of womenMon 7 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.33 EDTShareMost family annihilators are men. It’s a grim fact that such incidents are common enough to have a discernible pattern. The massacre is carried out by a husband and father, often one who is on the verge ofbankruptcyordivorce; typically, it forms the finale of a long reign ofdomestic violenceterror.Abouthalf the time, the perpetrator kills himself after slaughtering his family. Gun use is common – alarge numberof what are termed “mass shootings” in the United States are in fact family annihilation killings, in which a man turns his weapon on his family members. Other times, the killer uses knives, or fires.This kind of killing does not always make the news. When it does, news organizations often run family photos, in which the killer smiles on a beach or beside the Grand Canyon with his arm around the wife and children he will later shoot or strangle.Lindsay Clancy murder trial ends in dramatic deadlock – what comes next?Read moreIn this context of pervasive and normalized male domestic violence against women and children, the Lindsay Clancy case was always going to attract outside attention. Because in that case, when three Massachusetts children werestrangledof their family home in January of 2023 – Cora, who was five, Dawson, who was three, and Callan, who was just eight months old – the killer was their mom.As is fairly common for family annihilators, Clancyattempted suicideafter killing her children. But Clancy survived. Injuries left her paralyzed below the waist. At her murder trial, which lasted an unusually long six weeks andconcluded in a hung juryon Friday, she rolled to the defense table each morning in a wheelchair.The mistrial means that Clancy – along with her children’s father, their grandparents, and everyone else who loved them, to say nothing of the state – will now face the possibility of being subjected to a second trial. All because of a hung jury.Eleven of the 12 jurors accepted the argument put forward by Clancy’s defense, that Clancy, who does not contest that she killed her children, was suffering from anacute case of postpartum psychosis, and hence could not be held legally responsible for their deaths. But according to notes that the forewoman of the jury sent to the judge, one juror, a man, expressed “reasonable doubt” about Clancy’s culpability under the law, but refused to apply that doubt as is legally required.That this lone juror who wanted to convict Clancy was male is relevant, because the Clancy case itself became, in the distorting ways that such stories tend to when they are witnessed en masse through social media, a referendum on motherhood, mental healthcare, and the status of women.Some mothers have expressed deep sympathy for Clancy’s postpartum mental health crises, citing resonances with their own experiences and a hope that the case can bring greater attention to the rare but acute and debilitating kind of postpartum mental suffering that Clancy seems to have experienced; others say that medical neglect of the condition, and of the experiences of postpartum women more broadly, create the conditions for tragedies like that of the Clancy family.Some on the misogynist right, meanwhile, have seized upon Clancy’s actions and the support she has received as evidence that women are congenitally evil, disposed to violence, untrustworthy, and unfit for public life.Your opinion on the Clancy case will likely largely depend on whether you believe her defense team’s claim that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis that was severe enough that she experienced the kind of delusions, hallucinations, paranoia, rapid shifts in mood, and other departures from reality that would render her not responsible for her own actions. In other words, do you think she was really ill, or do you think that she killed her children in cold blood, and is lying?The facts suggest that she isn’t. Clancy had a history of postpartum psychological distress following the births of her first two children, in 2017 and 2019. She was prescribed medication after those births, and seems to have been a loving and attentive mother to them for years.But following the birth of her third child, a little boy named Callan, in 2022, reports suggest that Clancy began to experience something different, and much more serious, than her previous bouts with postpartum anxiety.She couldn’t sleep, wasn’t eating, and would experience bouts of sudden, acute terror. Going back to her job as a nurse in a labor and delivery unit seemed impossible; she could barely function. She sought help again and was diagnosed with anxiety.Later, she would speak to other mental health practitioners, too. A series of providers issued her a stunning array of psychiatric medications. As her sleeplessness continued, Clancy was prescribed increasingly powerful tranquilizers.More than a month before she killed her children, Clancy reported that she had begun to hallucinate. She kept seeking help, saying that she was thinking of killing herself; she told both her mother and her husband that she feared she would harm her children, though she had never mistreated them before.Clancy briefly checked herself in to inpatient treatment, but left after just a few nights. The Clancys seem to have thought that longer-term hospitalization was out of the question. After all, she had kids to take care of. Soon, she was hearing voices.Lindsay Clancy trial highlights gaps in postpartum psychosis research, experts sayRead moreThose who are most outraged by the Clancy case, and by the sympathy that a homicidal mother has received, are disturbed by the unnaturalness of a woman killing her children, disturbed by what they fear is a secret core of hate and depravity in women that could be unleashed at any time.But if I were a psychoanalyst, I might say that the right wing that imagines all women as potential Lindsay Clancys is projecting their own guilt: on some level, they know that what our culture asks mothers to do is unsustainable, cruel, and often quite literally maddening.Because to me, what is most haunting about the Clancy case is how ordinary and unsurprising all the failures were that led to her break.She was failed in ordinary ways by providers who saw a woman living in relative comfort and assumed her suffering could not be very serious; she was failed in ordinary ways by a community that understands motherhood to be a state of variously mild and acute suffering, and has so normalized women’s disappearance into the family that they can barely see the mother for the baby.She was failed by the expectation that women will persevere through their own suffering, even their most disturbing and agonizing moments, to care for their children; she was failed by the trivialization of women’s lives, and by the blithe assumption that the so-called “baby blues” were mere neurotic episodes, not psychotic breaks requiring serious clinical interventions. Her children were failed, too.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistIn the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsMassachusettsOpinionGenderWomenMental healthcommentShareReuse this content

title: For baseball’s Black and Latino players, it’s always 1926 somewhere | MLB | The Guardian
description: From home-run celebrations to tilted caps, players embracing joy continue to collide with an old guard devoted to Dust Bowl grimness
Author: Howard Bryant
Headline: From home-run celebrations to tilted caps, players embracing joy continue to collide with an old guard devoted to Dust Bowl grimness
Content: Oliver Marmol and Doug Eddings argue during Friday’s game.Photograph: David Zalubowski/APView image in fullscreenOliver Marmol and Doug Eddings argue during Friday’s game.Photograph: David Zalubowski/APMLBFor baseball’s Black and Latino players, it’s always 1926 somewhereHoward BryantFrom home-run celebrations to tilted caps, players embracing joy continue to collide with an old guard devoted to Dust Bowl grimnessMon 7 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 15.58 EDTShareOver the last several years, simultaneously lauded and paralyzed by its ironclad traditions, baseball has undergone various forays into reinvention, trying to free itself from itsunwritten rules of retaliation, its seeming aversion to joy, its demand that every generation of player of every culture and background play the game with the grimness of a Dust Bowl farmer.The sport even attempted to change those customs by promoting a cultural shift withan industry-wide motto:Let the Kids Play.But in a time of intense division within the aggressive backdrop of Trumpism, the result is a racial clash that is actually a generational and cultural one that predates current politics by a century.On Saturday night, Braves superstar Ronald Acuña Jr hit a third-inning home run off Zack Wheeler of the Phillies andfloated around the bases, arms wide, imitating an airplane, Euro-stepping past third base as if he were Manu Ginobili, and infuriating Wheeler and his manager Don Mattingly with his apparent disregard for the accepted customs of the game.A week before, in the midst of what would be a 16-1 rout, Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm swiped two meaningless bases in a blowout win over the Red Sox when the defense had conceded his presence – according to a 150-year-old custom, runners are expected to respect this courtesy by not advancing. Chisholm’s breach of protocol prompted Red Sox radio announcer Will Flemmingto suggest on the airthat a Yankee player drill one of Chisholm’s teammates for his insolence.‘I felt like Babe Ruth’: baseball’s 3ft 7in pinch-hitter, 75 years onRead moreFor the trifecta, during a Colorado-St Louis series this weekend, neither the Cardinals nor the Rockies had a problem with each other – but umpire Doug Eddings did, stopping the game to tell Cardinals rookie Hancel Rinconto adjust his hat. Eddings determined the rookie’s hat was too crooked (despite his later admission that Rincon had not violated any official rules) and Rincon would not disrespecthis gameonhis field.Eddings then issued a time violation to the Cardinals when manager Oli Marmol complained,thenejected Marmol, andthenmissed an obvious call at the plate against the Cardinals.In each of the incidents, the offended – Eddings, Wheeler (and to a lesser extent Mattingly), and Flemming – were white, while the alleged offenders – Acuña, Chisholm, Rincon, and Marmol – were Black or Latino. Periodically this season, baseball has found its way into the repellent culture wars, first during the World Baseball Classic earlier this year when the Americans soured the proceedings with their militia-like grimness when therest of the world was having fun. Maybe war is all America has to offer these days.In June, when participation was optional, several players decided to exercise their religious freedoms by crashing Pride Night bywriting Bible passages on their hats. When the players were warned over the incident, the Department of Justicethreatened to investigatewhether baseball was discriminating against Christians.If, however, it appears that baseball is an extension of Maga – and it very well may be – what Eddings and company have really resurfaced over the past is not exactly Trumpism per se, but what Trumpism tacitly demands: an incessant imposition of whiteness on American institutions, and an aggressiveness that emboldens the gatekeepers like Eddings to put the coloreds in their place.No league forces its historical whiteness on its players like Major LeagueBaseball. That whiteness is also known as “tradition,” ofplaying the game the right way.That tradition is practiced by players Black, white and Latino, who were raised in the old-school American baseball tradition with its ethnic, Depression-era seriousness. Other sports adjust to the new generations of players who enter the game. The NBA’s Nikola Jokić and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander are not expected to play like George Mikan and John Havlicek. In baseball, Bob Gibson and Pedro Martínez are proudly the spiritual extensions of Rube Waddell and Walter Johnson.Mattingly, wasn’t happy with Acuña, but judging by his postgame comments his conflicts were not racial, or racist, but instead resigned to a baseball becoming unrecognizable to him – a carnival of bat flips and unprofessionalism masquerading as fun. Mattingly has been in the game nearly 50 years. He was teammates with the ultimate showman, Rickey Henderson, whose on-field expressions were loathed, but Mattingly knew Henderson was no clown. He also managed Yasiel Puig, who was electric but whose respect for his craft wavered. Mattingly knows the difference between being professional and not, joy and disrespect, and seemed to be lamenting the desperate blurring of the two at the encouragement of the people who run the sport.In better times, when it didn’t appear umpires were looking for a fight, and when baseball especially did not appear to enlist itself in harassing players of color – Eddings might have been shrugged off as another power-tripping umpire having a bad day and taking it out on a kid making his big-league debut and the manager telling him to “fucking grow up,” as Marmol did.These are not better times. Eddings looked small and petty, and baseball’s strain of “playing the right way” is usually code for its eternal conflicts with how Black and Latino players express themselves in competition, how they dress, celebrate, emote. Even in 2026, somewhere in baseball – as evidence by Flemming’s comments and subsequent apology – it is always 1926.What, it should be asked, is this all about? It is an example of just how frayed the nerves of the country are, and what abuses of authority look like, especially as baseball in the backdrop of a Maga country feels like a hostile place. The Cardinals responded by protecting their player, and thumbing their nose at Eddings bytilting their hats as a team in solidarity. The small moments can provide the kind of kindling that can bring a team together (after five months of mediocrity, the Cardinals are trying to snag an 11th-hour playoff spot.)As for Eddings, who later apologized, he resembled the doomed, peacocking general surrounded by enemy forces. Umpires have few friends these days. The humorous YouTube channel Jomboy, once an innocuous value-add for Yankee fans for its clever lip-reading of on-field incidents, became a viral sensation, and MLB, desperate to attract a younger audience, realized the telegraph isn’t going to make a comeback andbought an equity stake in the company, transforming Jomboy from a clever fan site to an arm of MLB, which is not so innocuously trying to rid the game of human umpiring. In addition to Jomboy, numerous unofficial social media users virally spread umpires’ worst calls, intensifying the drumbeat that umpiring in its current form needs to go the way of the flannel uniform.Eddings spent this Labor Day weekend making another case for the robots, contributing simultaneously to baseball’s 100-year culture war and to the umpires’ digging of their own graves.Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America.He writes at Substack.Explore more on these topicsMLBBaseballUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: We’re the mayors of Paris, Milan and Phoenix. The heat crisis has us all facing the same question | Emmanuel Grégoire, Giuseppe Sala and Kate Gallego | The Guardian
description: Our three cities are learning from each other about how to protect residents. These climate policies are also public health measures
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Our three cities are learning from each other about how to protect residents. These climate policies are also public health measures
Content: ‘The city is planning for a future that would have been inconceivable to Parisians just a few decades ago.’Photograph: Apaydin Alain/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘The city is planning for a future that would have been inconceivable to Parisians just a few decades ago.’Photograph: Apaydin Alain/ABACA/ShutterstockOpinionClimate crisisWe’re the mayors of Paris, Milan and Phoenix. The heat crisis has us all facing the same questionEmmanuel Grégoire, Giuseppe Sala and Kate GallegoOur three cities are learning from each other about how to protect residents. These climate policies are also public health measuresMon 7 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTShareThis summer, mayors met in London during the heatwave that ironically threatened to derail London Climate Action Week.As temperatures broke records across the UK and Europe, leading some climate talks to besuspended or cancelled, we found ourselves seeking shelter and comparing how our cities prepare for extreme heat: how we protect vulnerable residents, communicate risk, and redesign neighbourhoods for hotter summers.At the same time, Paris was overseeing the city’s crisis response as another intense heatwave swept across France. Across Europe,more than 14,000 people lost their lives due to the heat.As mayors, we are confronting the same question: how do you protect millions of people when extreme heat is no longer an exceptional event, but an increasingly familiar part of summer?ForPhoenix, that question has shaped city government for decades. For Paris and Milan, it is now becoming one of the defining challenges of urban leadership.Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster | Michael MannRead moreIt may strike some people as unusual that two of Europe’s oldest and most prestigious cities are looking to a city in the Arizona desert for ideas. But rising temperatures are now a global challenge, and we don’t have time for each city to figure out what works on its own.Phoenix has learned, sometimes the hard way, that extreme heat cannot be treated as simply a weather event. It shapes decisions about transport, housing, public health, public space, and emergency planning. Preparing for summer begins long before temperatures start to rise.Phoenix established one of the world’s first city offices dedicated to heat response and mitigation, reflecting an approach that focuses on both immediate relief from extreme heat, especially for those most vulnerable, and building resilience in the medium-long-term by implementing cooling solutions to make the city safer and more comfortable.The city’s shade plans require 75% shade coverage in new development in areas with high pedestrian activity, and programs that support schools, transit users, and those most vulnerable. To further reduce the urban heat island effect, Phoenix is applying cool surface treatment to buildings and roadways, including on more than 300 kilometers of neighborhood streets.The city leads its region in heat response, including providing a 24-hour cooling center with wraparound support to connect people with resources such as housing, medical services, and even job placement. Landlords are required by law to maintain a safe indoor temperature (28C/82F or lower), and companies that contract with the city must implement heat safety plans to keep workers healthy and comfortable. These measures save lives: during the summer of 2024, which was the hottest on record in Phoenix, the city’s coordinated heat response measures contributed to a 20% year-over-year decline in heat-related 911 calls.Paris and Milan bring different expertise as well as unique challenges.Both are historic European cities where streets, buildings and public spaces were designed for a different time and a different climate. Today, both cities are adapting.Every Parisian now lives within a seven-minute walk of a cool spot. The city now has more than 1,400 of these spaces where people can cool down during a heatwave, including parks, gardens and other public facilities. The city also extends opening hours for parks, swimming pools, and public baths during high temperatures. The city has mobilised a network of 27,000 climate volunteers to raise awareness within their communities of the climate crisis and heatwave adaptation strategies, alongside preventive actions.The city is also planning for a future that would have been inconceivable to Parisians just a few decades ago: “Paris at 50°C” was organised in October 2023 to test the responsiveness of the municipality and its partners, as well as improve planning and coordination for future heat emergency responses. This involved the whole community, utilities, media and schools and directly inspired Barcelona to carry out the same exercise in 2027.double quotation markAs mayors, we are confronting the same question: how do you protect millions of people when extreme heat is no longer an exceptional event, but an increasingly familiar part of summer?No city can simply import another’s model. Geography, history and politics are different everywhere. But every mayor owes it to their residents to gather the best ideas from cities around the world; and through the C40 Cities network, nearly 100 of the world’s biggest cities are sharing climate solutions for our residents and businesses. Cities have always learned from one another. We have adapted successful transport systems, housing policies and public health measures for generations. Heat adaptation should be no different.If one city discovers a better way to protect outdoor workers, cool public spaces or communicate risk to residents, others should not spend years reinventing it. Good ideas should travel.Inspired by Barcelona and Paris cool spaces initiatives, Milan is expanding its Piazze Aperte (Open Squares) and School Streets programme to integrate cool spaces by planting trees, replacing hard surfaces with permeable green space and creating shaded areas. The Municipality also provides a helpline and support services for the elderly and vulnerable residents through Milano Aiuta (Milano Helps). Milan’s Air and Climate Plan outlines a binding goal to limit local temperature increases to 2C by 2050; they are one of the only cities in the world that has set a temperature-related target, which is very ambitious.Extreme heat already claims more than half a million lives every year, making it the deadliest climate hazard. Cities are particularly exposed because buildings, roads and pavements absorb heat during the day and release it long into the night, meaning residents get no respite and struggle to cool down properly. Older residents, young children, outdoor workers and lower-income communities often face the greatest risks.From bone-dry to soaked to the bone, welcome to the age of climate whiplash | Aditya ChakraborttyRead morePlanting trees, cooling schools, redesigning streets, improving buildings, and expanding early warning systems are often described as climate policies. They are also public health measures, investments in local economies, and practical improvements that make cities more liveable throughout the year.Meanwhile, heating and cooling account fornearly halfof all energy use in Europe, with about70%of heating still generated by fossil fuels. Cities have the power to lead a fair transition to clean heat. By investing in renewable energy and cleaner heating systems, they can cut emissions, improve air quality, and create local jobs, ensuring the benefits reach those who need it most.Cities are often the first to experience climate impacts but the last to receive the powers, funding and flexibility needed to respond. National governments should work with cities to develop more effective adaptation strategies, expand early warning systems, and make it easier for local leaders to access the finance needed to protect residents. Those investments can save lives, strengthen economies and reduce future costs across the entire country.This summer has given Europe a glimpse of what those living in desert climates feel so often, and what we can all expect to become our norm in the age of climate crisis.Extreme heat is not an individual burden; it is an existential challenge we must all rise to. The responsibility cannot fall on the shoulders of an isolated pensioner, a vulnerable child or a construction worker. Heat is a political crisis that demands bold political action.We must prepare and fight back. The climate crisis is redefining what our definition of “normal” is at a rapid rate. Our ability to learn from one another must move even faster.Emmanuel Grégoire, Giuseppe Sala and Kate Gallego are the mayors of Paris, Milan and PhoenixExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionParisPhoenixItalyEuropeFranceExtreme weathercommentShareReuse this content

title: A Reform UK without Nigel Farage used to be unthinkable. Not any more | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The scandals are building, his touch perhaps not quite what it was. And, most of all, his party rivals are beginning to sense an opportunity, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The scandals are building, his touch perhaps not quite what it was. And, most of all, his party rivals are beginning to sense an opportunity, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, Nigel Farage and the party’s shadow home secretary, Zia Yusuf, sing the national anthem at Reform’s conference at the NEC in Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenReform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, Nigel Farage and the party’s shadow home secretary, Zia Yusuf, sing the national anthem at Reform’s conference at the NEC in Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionReform UKA Reform UK without Nigel Farage used to be unthinkable. Not any moreGaby HinsliffThe scandals are building, his touch perhaps not quite what it was. And, most of all, his party rivals are beginning to sense an opportunityMon 7 Sep 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.42 EDTShareNigel Farage didn’t know. He wasn’t told.Sure, he was right there at the table when theundercover reporterhe believed to be a rich American’s sonspelled out very clearly how he hoped to channel his father’s money to Reform, in ways that certainly don’t sound too lawful.But hewasn’tlistening,you understand.God forbid that the man who insists his party takes compliance very seriously, and who never stops warning that the establishment is out to get him by any means possible, should actually pay attention to the details of a donation offered bang in the middle of a byelection that was fought over – of all the luck, eh? – some other questionable donations.Farage’s defence is essentially that he was present but not involved, asJeremy Corbyn once famously saidof attending an event where someone laid a commemorative wreath for members of the terrorist group behind the 1972 Munich Olympics atrocity.It didn’t work for Corbyn, any more than claiming to have tried cannabis butnever inhalingworked an age ago for Bill Clinton, in part because some people just didn’t believe it. But mostly, perhaps, because critics found it revealing even that Corbyn would be at the kind of gathering where such things might happen. Most aspirant prime ministers take good care to avoid moving in circles where someone might end up venerating terrorists, or explaining exactly how they intend to get around the law. For good reason, it turns out.What we are being asked to accept, in the instance caught on camera, is that at best Farage has been astonishingly sloppy; that he just turned up, tuned out, thanked the guy without even really knowing what for, and then went happily on his way. Take Farage at his own word and he is describing someone curiously semi-detached. Someone who, despite repeatedly claiming his enemies will stop at nothing to stitch him up, puzzlingly doesn’t seem to take such basic precautions against entrapment as noticing what’s actually going on around him. Someone for whom fighting a byelection in which nobody else of note is standing, bar a talking bin, is apparently so all-consuming that he can’t possibly be expected to concentrate on talking to donorsas well.If that degree of walking and chewing gum is a stretch, imagine what a shock running the country might be. No wonder some in Reform are starting to ask themselves if, deep down, that’s what he even wants.What would Reform look like without Nigel Farage? Once upon a time that would have been a ridiculous question – without him, it would simply fall apart – but the party now is not quite what it used to be. Among the faithful, the fact he doesn’t seem to take the job too seriously is still part of his charm, and many Reform supporters will be nothing but indignant on his behalf at the undercover tactics used to catch him out.But there are also people in Reform these days who have seen the very real possibility of seizing power to enact an agenda not seen before in Britain, just as Alternative für Deutschlandisstarting to doin Germany and as the National Rally’sJordan Bardella(the star turn at Reform’s party conference this year) and Marine Le Pen threaten to do next year in France. They won’t want to let that opportunity slip through their fingers.Having lost its lead in the polls, Reform finds itself ironically in a version of the dilemma Labour faced a few months ago: torn between those who think recovery depends on tacking left (in this case towards Tory voters who are Reform-curious but worry that it seems too extreme or sleazy) or tacking right (towards Rupert Lowe’s Restore, now consistently taking small but damaging chunks out of them, and other far-right groupings). Events like last weekend’s sinister black-shirted, paramilitary-style show of force in Dover by the previously little known Patriot Platform group – which even the government took a surprisingly long time to condemn in the decisive terms that chief secretary to the TreasuryEmma Reynolds eventually didon Monday morning, after what looked like copycat demonstrations in Portsmouth – may now start to push those tensions into the open.Are these their people, or not? Having ripped open Pandora’s box by saying what others would not on immigration, there would be a grim irony in Reform struggling to deal with the furies unleashed, if only the whole thing wasn’t so frightening for everyone else. Farage ended up calling the Dover mob “disgusting” because of their balaclavas, while suggesting he absolutely shared their anger about small boat crossings (now, of course, down to aseven-year low). But is covering your face at a protest the only line Reform won’t cross?Some of its supporters clearly do want a leader prepared to say what Farage won’t, a niche that Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesperson,evidently aims to fill. Others more recently arrived from the old Conservative party might prefer a leader who treads a hard line on immigration, welfare and woke, but with some rougher edges sanded off (or so Robert Jenrick clearly hopes). Crucially, some in both camps will see the departure ofclose aideDan Jukes – who along with head of policy, James Orr,has taken the rapfor this latest donor scandal, though both deny wrongdoing – as an opportunity to replace Farage’s loyal and protective sidekicks with people less tied to him personally.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHistorically, anyone daring to fly this close to Farage’s sun has got their wings scorched. But what if that sun doesn’t burn quite so brightly any more? What if the political judgment that always served him so well in the past is now fractionally off-key? For now, the idea that there could be an electionany minute – forced, perhaps, by some future bond market crisis – is perhaps imposing a measure of discipline on the party. But what if that imaginary snap election never materialises?For now, these are all still very much “what ifs”. Given his miraculous capacity for resurrection, it is a mistake to underestimate Farage or count him out when he is down.But until recently, even the idea of Reform without its leader seemed ridiculous; hewasReform, to the point that without him it would cease to meaningfully exist. In the current climate, that assumption may no longer be safe. Bardella, after all, got his big break when Le Pen wasbrought down by a financial scandal. It’s time the other parties thought harder about the shape Reform might take without its maker, rather than assuming the battle begins and ends with him.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: We have fact sheets for many health conditions. Why isn’t there one for ‘What to do on the day your loved one dies’? | Ranjana Srivastava | The Guardian
description: The best doctors understand something that is easy to lose in the machinery of a hospital: death does not turn a person into an administrative task
Author: Ranjana Srivastava
Headline: The best doctors understand something that is easy to lose in the machinery of a hospital: death does not turn a person into an administrative task
Content: ‘For a routine death, there is a well-established process: ward, mortuary, funeral home,’ writes Ranjana Srivastava. ‘But families will remember how we treated them.’Photograph: Tetra Images/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘For a routine death, there is a well-established process: ward, mortuary, funeral home,’ writes Ranjana Srivastava. ‘But families will remember how we treated them.’Photograph: Tetra Images/AlamyOpinionHealthWe have fact sheets for many health conditions. Why isn’t there one for ‘What to do on the day your loved one dies’?Ranjana SrivastavaThe best doctors understand something that is easy to lose in the machinery of a hospital: death does not turn a person into an administrative taskMon 7 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 19.34 EDTShare“If you don’t mind, can we start with the patient who has died?”“But he has died,” I say to the resident, eyeing our long list of the living.“The family is getting agitated.”I hear “agitated” and my senses sharpen. We approach the patient’s room, knock and enter as a team.The death was expected, but its certification hadn’t occurred yet. It had been delayed for several hours for the usual reasons: many patients, too few doctors.The room is overflowing with family. Despite my apprehension, it is only right that I take responsibility.“I am sorry for your loss, and especially sorry that it has taken us hours to get here,” I say. “It shouldn’t have been this way.”Australians in end-of-life agony can’t always see a doctor. Telehealth can help them die with dignity | Andrew DentonRead moreThe family nods. To my relief, no one looks angry. They are just exhausted.My eyes settle on the patient, whom I had met on his last admission. He had presented with sepsis and survived against the odds but never recovered enough to return home. Age and frailty, compounded by his equally vulnerable wife, kept him in hospital for weeks while his family searched for a suitable nursing home. He lasted just two days there, barely long enough to become accustomed to the new bed, before being sent back to hospital by ambulance.This time, sepsis took his life.It is the only time I have seen him at peace. He looks asleep, without doctors and nurses probing and prodding him. I suspect no one in the room regrets that his suffering is over, which is not to say they do not mourn his loss.I look at his forlorn wife, sitting closest to him. How long has she been perched on her walking frame? What will that posture do to her bent back? Around her, children and grandchildren are gathered. No one is crying. Everyone is anticipating.It dawns on me that, although some of them are in their 50s, this may be their first “milestone” death: the first time they have had to navigate the practical aftermath of someone they love dying.Sure enough, the questions come tumbling out.“What happens now?”“We don’t have a funeral plan.”“Is there a deadline to get him out?”“Do you need this bed?”Even at this moment, the family is worrying about everyone else.“Please don’t stress,” I say gently. “You can stay in this room for as long as you need. We are used to taking care of the details.”This simple orientation, offered at a time of enormous disorientation, seems to calm them.We have fact sheets for constipation. Why isn’t there one for “What to do on the day your loved one dies”?For a routine death, there is a well-established process: ward, mortuary, funeral home. Necessary, orderly and administrative.But families may remember something else.They will remember how we treated them. And, importantly, how we treated the person they loved.I ask the family to step outside for a few moments while we certify the death, and I instruct one of the two interns to stay behind to do so, while the rest of us return to our other patients.Just then, the resident whispers, “They haven’t done this before.”The compassion in her voice stops me.How is that possible? How have not one, but two seasoned interns managed to avoid the unavoidable – a death in their first few weeks on the job?Trusting my resident to teach them, I leave to see the other patients. When we eventually meet again, there is no time to debrief.The next day, though, I ask after them.A death generates an extraordinary amount of administration, mainly for the family.For doctors, the death certificate is the clinical part: date, time, cause of death, signature.But certifying that death is also a deeply human act.Before reducing the fullness of a life to the sterility of an online form, how do we pause to acknowledge the person? How do we perform our final act with humility, remembering that this patient was once someone with experiences, ambitions, mistakes, relationships and memories?A wise boss once taught me to first close the door to the patient’s room and stand still for a minute.Take in the last book someone was reading. The last “get well soon” drawing tacked to the wall. The fading flowers sent by a friend. The last menu, left blank.Ads call ovarian cancer a ‘silent killer’. But does urging women to undergo early detection testing do more harm than good? | AntiviralRead moreFrankly, a minute is an awfully long time to feel confronted by mortality. But it has never failed to humble me.My interns tell me that the nurses and social workers had swung into action, just as promised. When they re-entered the room to certify the death, some relatives were still there.If the interns felt self-conscious, they did not let it show.“At each step, we talked to our patient as if he was listening,” they say, “explaining what we were doing. It felt right.”Of all the details, this is the small revelation that moves me most.These young doctors understood something that is easy to lose in the machinery of a hospital: death does not turn a person into an administrative task.There is a final act of medicine after treatment has ended. It is to pause, to explain, to make room for grief, and to treat the dead with the same dignity we aspired to when they were alive.Public perception increasingly casts doctors as impatient, even harsh. But this was the art of medicine at its best: compassion for a grieving family and empathy for a patient who will file neither complaint nor compliment.In my final week of rounds, I tell my team how proud I am of their work. One day, they will remember their first death as I remember mine.In a profession increasingly measured by what we do, perhaps grace resides in how we act when there is nothing left to do.Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the PublicExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionDeath and dyingHospitalscommentShareReuse this content

title: Dover and Portsmouth showed us a new kind of far right – and the authorities were caught out | Joe Mulhall | The Guardian
description: This is a new and dangerous development: a network of vigilantes who have mobilised as politicians and police have failed to act, says Joe Mulhall of Hope Not Hate
Author: Joe Mulhall
Headline: This is a new and dangerous development: a network of vigilantes who have mobilised as politicians and police have failed to act, says Joe Mulhall of Hope Not Hate
Content: On Saturday morning, balaclava-clad men piled out of the back of vans and blocked roads around Dover port.Photograph: Ay_audits/YouTubeView image in fullscreenOn Saturday morning, balaclava-clad men piled out of the back of vans and blocked roads around Dover port.Photograph: Ay_audits/YouTubeOpinionFar rightDover and Portsmouth showed us a new kind of far right – and the authorities were caught outJoe MulhallThis is a new and dangerous development: a network of vigilantes who have mobilised as politicians and police have failed to actMon 7 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.17 EDTShareSadly, we’ve become used to far-right protests in recent years. Whether it’s the vast demonstrations led by Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (AKA Tommy Robinson) in central London, or the hundreds of local protests outside hotels and HMOs housing asylum seekers, the sight of far-right activists chanting anti-migrant slogans has become all too common.What we saw in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend feels different. At roughly 7am on Saturday morning,hundreds of balaclava-clad men, dressed all in black, began piling out of the backs of vans and blocked roads around Dover port. Shockingly, the policeappear to have known nothingabout it in advance.Then, on Sunday evening, a group of mengathered near a Portsmouth beachto “block” the arrival of asylum seekers on a boat. The group had been monitoring maritime apps and tracking the progress of boats towards Britain. They put out a call for people to join them and dozens answered, including well-known activists from the neo-Nazi movement.What we have seen over the past three days marks a dangerous new development in the far right. While previous protests – many of which descended into ugly racist violence – have been worrying enough, we are now faced with a new, more clandestine and confrontational threat.Hope Not Hate was the first to identify that the Dover disturbance was organised by a far-right groupcalled Patriot Platform. The balaclava-clad men blocking roads were part of a new network founded by Tommy Robinson’s right-hand man Daniel Thomas (AKA Danny Tommo).Launched in June, the group unites a web of smaller localised anti-migrant groups into a single body. Current members hail from theKentPatriots, Watford Patriots, South London Patriots, South-East Patriots, North-West Patriots, Surrey Patriots and Chertsey Patriots, to name just a few.Patriot Platform is a self-professed Christian “army of patriots” formed to, in Thomas’s words, “reclaim our borders, restore order and send a clear message: Britain belongs to the British people”. The group functions as a vigilante unit to combat immigration and revive what it says are Christian values, ready to spring into action across the country at Thomas’s word.Worryingly, there is an unusual degree of discipline to Patriot Platform’s organising. Rather than being a single entity, it operates as a network for the local groups. These groups utilise various social media platforms, most commonly Instagram, X, Facebook and TikTok, for their promotional output.However, unlike organisers of previous public anti-migrant protests, Patriot Platform operates clandestinely, with event planning happening via closed groups and direct personal communication.Its means of operation have more in common with football hooligan gangs than with traditional anti-migrant protest groups. This is how its supporters managed to arrive in their hundreds in Dover unnoticed.Rather than being met with the usual mealy-mouthed condemnations and talk of “legitimate concerns”, these “protests” need to be called what they are: far-right vigilantism. These aren’t fearful locals, they are organised far-right activists led by Thomas, a man whopleaded guiltyto attempted kidnapping and was sentenced to two years in prison after taking part in an armed attempt to abduct a man during a drugs-related dispute.Since the riots of 2024, Thomas has repeatedly spoken about the need to take to the streets and take direct action. He has been upfront abouthis intention to createa “patriotic army that is able to take control of the United Kingdom”.Despite warnings from Hope Not Hate, the authorities have failed to act. They have allowed Thomas to agitate, organise and mobilise large groups around the country. Last weekend was the consequence of police inaction, and I fear that without decisive action things will only get worse.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClearly, the government needs to be far more robust in dealing with far-right vigilantism. The Home Office is so preoccupied with being seen to be tough on immigration that it has neglected the safety of the very migrants and asylum seekers being targeted.And the police response exposes serious failings in the authorities’ approach to far-right anti-immigrant violence more broadly. Time and again, they appear unaware of the strength of protests and unprepared for the violence that sometimes results.The events in Dover andPortsmouthshould be a wake-up call for anyone who believes that far-right extremism can be managed through inaction. This is no longer simply about angry protests or offensive rhetoric. We are seeing organised groups willing to mobilise quickly, operate covertly and confront those they see as enemies. The longer authorities fail to recognise the seriousness of this threat, the bolder these groups will become.The government must act now, before vigilantism becomes normalised and far-right activists feel they can operate with impunity on Britain’s streets.Joe Mulhall is director of research at the anti-fascism organisation Hope not HateExplore more on these topicsFar rightOpinionImmigration and asylumPolicePortsmouthKentEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: The AfD’s win in Germany is a dark day for Europe. Time is running out to stop the far right | Cas Mudde | The Guardian
description: This party is among the most extreme in Europe. To protect our democracies, liberal parties must urgently change their tactics, says Cas Mudde, author of The Far Right Today
Author: Cas Mudde
Headline: This party is among the most extreme in Europe. To protect our democracies, liberal parties must urgently change their tactics, says Cas Mudde, author of The Far Right Today
Content: Supporters of the AfD celebrate after exit poll results were announced in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, Magdeburg, Germany, 6 September 2026.Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSupporters of the AfD celebrate after exit poll results were announced in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, Magdeburg, Germany, 6 September 2026.Photograph: Ronny Hartmann/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionThe far rightThe AfD’s win in Germany is a dark day for Europe. Time is running out to stop the far rightCas MuddeThis party is among the most extreme in Europe. To protect our democracies, liberal parties must urgently change their tacticsMon 7 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTShareThe far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) narrowly failed to secure an outright majority in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. But nobody should take comfort from that. The party still won by a landslide. Decades of far-right election gains have made them seem normal to the point where only the biggest victories are deemed newsworthy. But 44% of the vote for a party that is officially classified as “extreme right” is not normal. It is a black day for European democracy, even if it occurs in a small east German state.While Saxony-Anhalt (andGermanyitself) may have dodged the worst outcome because the AfD won’t automatically fulfil its ambition of forming the first far-right state government in Germany since the Nazi era, there is no reason to assume it will be so lucky at the next election. Neither will other German states, such as Mecklenburg-Vorpommern in two weeks’ time, or other countries, such as France next year. No country is immune from the far right and, perhaps even more worryingly, no far-right party or politician is too extreme for political success (as the US has shown). We must therefore update our analyses and strategies.Although Saxony-Anhalt, and east Germany in general, is an extreme case, it reflects similar trends in the rest ofEurope. Far-right parties are going from strength to strength, with old dominant parties decimated, and party systems fragmented. Consequently, coalition formation is becoming increasingly complicated, particularly if we want to keep the far right out of power.
