In many countries, provinces and cities, most democratic parties are having to govern together to exclude the far right. This often leads to inefficient and unstable coalitions, in turn feeding yet more political dissatisfaction and far-right support.Far-right AfD celebrate ‘dream result’ in key German state as Merz reportedly holds crisis talks – Europe liveRead moreSunday’s results will only intensify an ongoing debate in Germany about the so-calledBrandmauer(a firewall maintained by mainstream parties against cooperating with the AfD). Actually, Germany is one of the few EU countries to still have a far-rightcordon sanitaire. Throughout Europe, from Italy to Sweden, far-right parties have been normalised and integrated into the political mainstream. In most cases, the (rightwing) parties that collaborate with the far right claim that the latter have moderated and are now “conservative” – a claim that is factually wrong, but increasingly popular with the electorates and members of these parties, and much of the media.This will remain almost impossible to claim in Germany. The AfD is among the most extreme parties in Europe, and its most successful branches, including the one in Saxony-Anhalt, are among the AfD’s most extreme. This will not prevent some rightwing politicians from claiming that the AfD is less of a problem than the left, and there is even a fear that some parliamentarians from the conservative CDU in Saxony-Anhalt will defect to give the AfD a majority in the state. On the other side of the political spectrum, calls for an AfD ban will become even louder, and while this might be legally possible, it could create a massive popular backlash, going well beyond Saxony-Anhalt.Both approaches share a too-limited interpretation of the problem. The idea of maintaining theBrandmaueris that the only (or main) problem is outside the system. Yet the system is falling apart as it is. Yes, the AfD (and the far right in general) is a fundamental threat to liberal democracy, but so is the fact that a sizeable and growing part of the population no longer feels represented by its politicians. While many still come out to vote for democracy, they increasingly vote against a party rather than for one.Even worse, most mainstream politicians have accepted that they are unpopular and try to remain in power by arguing that they are the lesser evil and mobilising people to come out to vote against the far right. Ultimately, this is unsustainable. If democratic parties do not develop inspiring manifestos for what they want to achieve in government, liberal democrats will refuse to come out to vote and the far right will win a majority of votes – even if they represent only a minority of the population.Developing such manifestos will require realism from politicians, but also from the media and voters. In fragmented party systems with large far-right parties, no party will be able to implement most of its preferred policies. There are no majorities for social democratic, Christian democratic or Green parties and policies. But this should also not be the main concern at this moment. When the far right gets close to governing alone, or dominating coalitions, the main goal should be to strengthen liberal democracy – in terms of institutions and values. This should be something that all liberal democratic parties can agree on.This does not simply entail strengthening democratic institutions – the judiciary and regulating social media,for example – and promoting inclusion and tolerance. It also means listening to the many concerns and preferences of the majority of voters who do not vote for the far right. In other words, mainstream politicians need to go beyond crime and immigration and focus also on such things as increasing housing provision and public spending, limiting economic and income inequality, fighting the climate crisis and strengthening European integration.And it means accepting that you don’t get everything you want – now or in the near future.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOf course, many countries are not as close to a far-right majority as Saxony-Anhalt is. But we should not forget that in the state’s 2021 election, the AfD had “only” 20% – and the average score of the far right now isroughly 25%across Europe. In other words, there may not be much time left. And, as we can see in countries such as Hungary and the US, the democratic struggle becomes harder and less fair once the far right establishes power.Democratic politicians must therefore realise that today’s key fight is for democracy, rather than for party or power. This requires both fighting the far right and strengthening democracy. Neither the banning nor the normalisation of the far right can achieve this. Democracy neither be strengthened in isolation, nor by the politics of fear. It requires a collective effort from democratic politicians, citizens and journalists, who must show realism, resilience and restraint. And the time for that fight is now.Cas Mudde is the author of The Far Right Today, and is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of GeorgiaExplore more on these topicsThe far rightOpinionAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)GermanyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: I had an amazing experience as a disabled person at school in the 70s. Since then, discrimination has got far worse | Mik Scarlet | The Guardian
description: Toxic narratives around ‘benefit scrounging’, fed by successive governments, have become embedded in the national psyche, says Mik Scarlet, campaigner and co-CEO of the national charity Phab
Author: Mik Scarlet
Headline: Toxic narratives around ‘benefit scrounging’, fed by successive governments, have become embedded in the national psyche, says Mik Scarlet, campaigner and co-CEO of the national charity Phab
Content: Mik Scarlet: ‘An accessible, inclusive society helps us all.’View image in fullscreenMik Scarlet: ‘An accessible, inclusive society helps us all.’OpinionDisabilityI had an amazing experience as a disabled person at school in the 70s. Since then, discrimination has got far worseMik ScarletToxic narratives around ‘benefit scrounging’, fed by successive governments, have become embedded in the national psycheMon 7 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 05.32 EDTShareAs a disabled person, you’re forced to repeatedly explain your medical history – but for this article, I think it’s important. I was born with a very rare type of cancer called a neuroblastoma. In 1965, it was pretty much a death sentence. Luckily, I took part in a clinical trial and, with only days to live, I had major surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy with a new drug. Despite being given no more than five years to live, on my last birthday I celebrated hitting 60. I doubt anyone in 1965 would have imagined how attitudes towards disabled people would improve as I grew up. It is devastating to see how those same attitudes have reversed in the past decade or two.Mik Scarlet as a childThe cancer left me with a paralysed right leg, so I wore a leg brace, but otherwise I was a pretty normal kid. I was lucky to be starting school in 1970 when theChronically Sick and Disabled Persons Actcame into force, which made it possible for disabled children to attend mainstream schools, if they could manage it. My parents moved across Luton to be near the only school that would accept me on a trial run and then as a pupil. When I was a child, if you could manage living like non-disabled people then you were allowed to do so. Not the fully inclusive practice I later campaigned for, but an acknowledgment that disabled people shouldn’t be written off.At 15, my spine collapsed and crushed the nerves to both legs, an unforeseen side effect of chemo. After months in hospital I came home a full-time wheelchair user. I was lucky our town centre in Luton was very wheelchair accessible and, during my time in hospital, my high school put in some serious adaptations to ensure I could return. Accessible toilets and a lift meant I could take my exams without any real difficulty, thanks to Putteridge high school and the then headteacher, Mr Price. At Luton sixth form college, adaptations were made again, this time under my guidance. Through the course of my childhood ideas around disability had changed from “if they can, let them try” to “what can we do to help them succeed?” and even “what do they want us to do?”That was the overarching attitude I encountered for the next 20 years. Some viewed being disabled as a tragedy, others as part of life. Most people saw any help that we received as important and something a healthy society should be offering. The exception was the workplace. I tried two jobs, both of which ended in me being sacked because I took a couple of days off. One was because I broke my foot in a lift that was too small for my wheelchair, the other was following a car accident. Both times, taking sick leave was seen as proof that disabled people couldn’t manage the world of work. So I focused on my hobby, music, and was soon touring the UK and Europe playing in bands. This led to my discovery by a TV producer. I ended up on the BBC, ITV and Channel 4, where my show Beat That won an Emmy. My media career, as one of the first disabled celebrities, lasted more than 15 years and only ended during a period of ill health.In the late 90s and early 00s, I found attitudes became twisted towards an angrier, almost jealous view of disabled people. My Motability vehicle was vandalised repeatedly, because local people were upset about my “free car”. This morphed into “free car, free house and loads of benefits” as Tony Blair’s government, from 1998 onwards, implemented cuts to the benefits bill that scapegoated disabled people. I was attacked twice, my car was vandalised every week and my wife was beaten to a pulp by three people wearing masks. When they threatened to burn our flat down, we packed up and left our fully adapted home to rent somewhere that was safe from violence but totally unsuitable. The police? Useless.My own brother even once spouted that it was “all right for you with your free car, free house and benefits cash”. It was especially galling as I had worked most of my adult life, paying taxes. The only time I stopped work was when I was very ill. My wife cared for me during this time, and we went from earning about £50,000 in joint income to being paid £15,000 in benefits to cover everything, including our rent. Luckily I got well again, retrained and went back to work as an access consultant.But those toxic narratives seem to be getting worse, and have become embedded in the national psyche. Successive governments and the media have continued to tell the public lies, such as the much repeated accusations of huge amounts of fraud within the so-called “disability benefits” system that has led to terrifying levels of anger. Only a week ago I was punched in the street for being a “scrounger”.View image in fullscreenMik Scarlet plays live with his band Freak UK.I call them lies because that’s what they are. Motability isnota free car. It is a vehicle that is leased for a set fee over a three- or five-year period. We don’t get a free Mercedes or BMW. We make a huge upfront payment and it costs the same per week as a tiny little car. Andpersonal independence payment(Pip) isnotan out-of-work benefit. It is paid to support independent living, based on people’s ability and support needs. No one is getting it for tennis elbow. In fact, Pip and its forerunners allowed me to work, and my Motability vehicle lets me travel the UK working as co-CEO of the national charityPhab. The access to work scheme saves employers money by paying towards the adaptations and support a disabled worker might need. It brings in £1.48 for every £1 paid out, with the wider economy benefiting by £3.86, according to research carried out by the Royal National Institute of Blind People.As we mark 31 years since theDisabilityDiscrimination Act and 16 since that was superseded by the Equality Act, please don’t believe the hype around disabled people. Try to imagine a day walking in our shoes, or pushing our wheels. Before you allow the hype around “the freebies” we get, do some research. My wheelchair alone cost me £6,500, for example. No support; that was all out of my pocket.As I visit the clubs and events Phab supports I meet many disabled people who can only dream of having a life like mine. But shouldn’t all disabled people have the chance to shine? When I was young I had hoped that the future would allow disabled people to fulfil their potential, and let them lead the discussion around making society more accessible and inclusive for everyone. An accessible, inclusive society helps us all. Take the lift, the ability to text and voice-to-text software. All designed to help disabled people, but now a boon to us all. If disabled people are listened to, everyone benefits.I doubt many of us considered that things would get worse, but if disabled people are allowed to tell the reality of our lives maybe we can get back to a positive place. One where being disabled is just part of daily life. Not sad or tragic, or a licence for free government handouts. Just normal.Mik Scarlet is co-CEO of the national charityPhab, a campaigner and a music journalist forBlitzed magazineExplore more on these topicsDisabilityOpinionWelfareBenefitsWork & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: Friendships meant everything to me as a child. I worry today’s young people are being robbed of that | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: We sat in the park, laughing for hours, talking about nothing. Today’s childhoods are digital – and the result is an epidemic of loneliness, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: We sat in the park, laughing for hours, talking about nothing. Today’s childhoods are digital – and the result is an epidemic of loneliness, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: ‘The art of friendship is as much the art of doing nothing.’Photograph: Image Source/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The art of friendship is as much the art of doing nothing.’Photograph: Image Source/Getty ImagesOpinionFriendshipFriendships meant everything to me as a child. I worry today’s young people are being robbed of thatRhiannon Lucy CosslettWe sat in the park, laughing for hours, talking about nothing. Today’s childhoods are digital – and the result is an epidemic of lonelinessMon 7 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIsaw an old friend recently – the kind you’ve known for so long that you clear a whole day for them, as you might a family member. We laughed and laughed like we were teenagers again, and drank martinis before lunch, and it felt almost like it always did when we were young, except we could afford better than cheap cider, and he owns a house and I’m someone’s mother.Another old friend – one I’ve known even longer, since I was six – described me and the other girls who made up our little group as “fake siblings”. That is how lifelong friendships feel. There’s an easiness and acceptance that comes with longstanding intimacy. You know each other’s secrets,you’ve been inside each other’s parents’ houses, shared beds and cigarettes, witnessed heartbreak and foolishness, tears and whiteys, before the more serious stuff piles up: weddings, births, illnesses, life crises, deaths. You talk about the serious stuff, of course (there has always been some serious stuff, but teenage friendships often provide a refuge from it), but when you need it that old friendship is a portal, transporting many of us to a time of lightness and freedom that is otherwise hard to access.I don’t know where I’d be without these friendships, which is why it makes me sad to read that young people today aren’t making them, or at least not in the same way. According to a new report from the Institute for Public Policy Research titledThe Loneliest Generation, the number of young people with no close friends has risen fivefold since 2014, with 11- to 24-year-olds becoming dramatically more isolated. One in 20 16- to 21-year-olds say that they have no close friends at all.The report cites digital childhoods and austerity measures such as youth club closures as factors in eroding the foundations of a good adolescence. My own friendships owed much to the digital realm (specifically MSN Messenger), but they were still largely and crucially face to face, and that seems to be one of the things that has changed. We did not have internet childhoods, and so the skill – and I do believe it’s a skill – of making friends was crucial, and acquired young. The things that bonded us – circumstances, subcultures, music and, most of all, humour – took place mostly offline. We spent hours sitting in parks or around campfires, just talking and joking. We went to gigs and club nights and festivals. We rode our bikes or begged lifts or walked five miles home. It’s strange seeing these ways of relating to one another being idealised by younger people, spoken of wistfully in social media posts and comments as though something has been lost. I suppose we idealise the countercultures of our parents’ eras. People simply conversing without a phone present shouldn’t be seen as radical, but it’s being framed that way.We are right to be worried about this mass loneliness among young people. To spend adolescence without friends can leave a lifelong trace. Even the friendships that didn’t last affect us, even – perhaps especially – those that were not so straightforward. Therapists are fond of the phrase “rupture and repair” because it’s accurate – falling in and out and in again with friendship groups can be educative. It can teach you to be kinder to one another, to tolerate difference, and to learn what behaviour you are and aren’t willing to put up with. These are important life lessons but they are increasingly overstated –the online language of friendship, which emphasises what a friend “gives” you or “adds” to your life seems intense and transactional to those of us raised in lesspsychobabblytimes.These sorts of bonds take time and energy to establish. Many, many hours of sitting and fooling around. The art of friendship is as much the art of doing nothing. Of mooching. Hanging out. Watch an old sitcom such asSeinfeldand friends are always running errands together. When did you last go to the dry-cleaner’s with somebody?Much has been written aboutthe decline in third spacesand its impact on social relationships. Places to hang out, outside home or work, are essential to the art of real-world friendship. So is time to talk, to wander and to linger together. When it comes to the crisis in friendship,a social media ban for under-16sis a good thing: it makes relating to one another in person more of a priority, and leaves more time for those activities that bond us together.It’s only as you get older that you realise how precious those adolescent years are. People don’t talk about fun enough – how important it is to wellbeing and survival. So much about technology makes our lives smoother and quicker, but I am not sure it makes it more fun. Not like gathering four or five or six people around a campfire and drinking cider before all jumping naked into a river, or exploring an abandoned house (not something I would ever endorse, but something we used to do). Memories of adolescence and the people we spent it with have been found to be more vivid. They call itthe “reminiscence bump”. It is a crucial time for development and, as I’ve found myself, those memories carry us through our lives. In my dreams, I still explore abandoned houses with those kids, my fake siblings.What will be the long-term wellbeing impact if those years are filled instead with the flickerings of other lives on a screen, gobbled up and then swiped past, forgotten? We must preserve the art of friendship before it’s lost for ever.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsFriendshipOpinionLonelinessYoung peopleChildrenSocial mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: Israeli ministers keep telling everyone their brutal plans – so why doesn’t the world take them seriously? | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: Schemes to forcibly remove Palestinians from Gaza are not being promoted by fringe voices. But the international community continues to avert its eyes, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Schemes to forcibly remove Palestinians from Gaza are not being promoted by fringe voices. But the international community continues to avert its eyes, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Israel’s national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, at the Mahaneh Yehudah Market, Jerusalem, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAView image in fullscreenIsrael’s national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, at the Mahaneh Yehudah Market, Jerusalem, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAOpinionIsraelIsraeli ministers keep telling everyone their brutal plans – so why doesn’t the world take them seriously?Nesrine MalikSchemes to forcibly remove Palestinians from Gaza are not being promoted by fringe voices. But the international community continues to avert its eyesMon 7 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 03.10 EDTShareThe gap between what is being inflicted on Palestinians and the appropriate reaction on the part of the international community has always been vast. But now it yawns so wide that it swallows reality itself. As arms export licences for Israel from statessuch as Germany surge, talk of harsher measures and sanctions on the part of other European countriesremains talk. People continue to be killed in Gaza, Palestinian families remain besieged in the West Bank, and the Israeli political right has been removing all doubt that these violations are intentional, by telling the world of its hopes and plans.A sample from only the past few days. On Thursday, Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir,detailed a schemefor the illegal ethnic cleansing of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip. He also posted an AI-generated video, now deleted, of Palestinian men entering a conveyor belt into detention, emerging emaciated and tearful. Also a few days ago, the defence minister, Israel Katz, stated that the country was “organised and prepared” to expel Palestinians from Gaza “by every way possible”.This macabre theatre continues to unfold, its performances less plausible by the day. The Board of Peace promises Gaza will be “redeveloped for the benefit” of its people, while the notion that those same Palestinians in Gaza cannot be allowed to thrive is expressed by Israeli politicians with consistency and a frequency that makes a mockery of the declarations. Last month, the former head of Israel’s national security council, Giora Eiland, pointed out the fact that Israel’s acceptance of Donald Trump’s 15-point plan was a matter of temporary military tactics, rather than long-term peace. “Israel has no interest in Gaza being rebuilt, it’s better for us that it be destroyed for generations to come,”he said.Moshe Feiglin, previously a “far-right outcast” according to the Times of Israel, is now within reach of a cabinet position as a result of an alliance with the finance minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionist party. In a recent interview, Feiglin said that those who didn’t want to leave Gaza should be compelled to by “every way possible. We’ll shut off his water pipes, for example.”This sort of talk, from within the very ranks of government, is often dismissed asunrepresentative of the Israeli stateand, as there are elections ahead, is written off as the lurid but ultimately unserious rhetoric of electioneering. But people such as Ben-Gvir and Katz are not fringe voices, they are ministers with high-impact executive briefs – security and defence – that they have indeed used to push policy that matches their statements.Ben-Gvir has reopened theunderground Rakefet prison, one closed in the 1980s for being inhumane. He has successfullypushed for the death penaltyfor Palestinians convicted of terror attacks, andcelebrated the legislationwith a noose-themed cake. Torture and sexualabuse in Israeli prisonsare widely documented, the latterearning Israel a spoton the UN’s sexual violence in war zones blacklist. As Ben-Gvir himself is fond of saying, “we promised, we delivered”.Katz hasapprovedthe biggest settlement expansion in the West Bank in decades and justified the move on the grounds that it “prevents the establishment of a Palestinian state that would endanger Israel”; he recentlyadvancedlegalisation of outpost settlement farms in the West Bank, and instructed the IDF to hand over law enforcement in the West Bank tothe Israeli police, which is a stealth move towards annexation.As the Knesset member Ahmad Tibi wrote in Haaretz earlier this year, a fiction exists at the heart of Israeli politics, where politicians’ efforts to explain and justify policy to international opinion proceed as though “the racism and extremism now driving government policy exist only on the margins”. When really, it lies at the heart of the state.And if some of the more extreme statements are just electioneering, what does that say about the parameters of discourse in the country if your campaign is mass ethnic cleansing? What does that say about not only the future of Gaza, but all Palestinians in occupied territories who are labouring underhome demolitions, militant settlers and thede facto annexationof the West Bank?Even if these figures are a minority, both in terms of the seats held in the Knesset and the relative number of people who have voted for them, they still hold the levers of power, there is no substantial domestic mobilisation against them, and the rest of the system is unable or unwilling to stop them. The distinctions around how big their constituency may be or how representative they are of Israelis in general matters not a jot to the fate of Palestinians over whom they have been given executive dominion.The question now is, why are these people not being taken at their word? Why is there no sense of urgency and outrage. Why are these policies and stated goals from the Israeli state not taken seriously and met with appropriate sanctions, trade and arms embargos, and international censure? There is a wild asymmetry when it comes to the perceived potency of Israeli rhetoric and action. “From the river to sea”, for example, as expressed by Palestinians and their supporters has becomestigmatisedand its use censured. But the most extreme interpretation of that phrase, that it means only onesovereign people in the mentioned land, is commonplace in Israel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBen-Gvir posts Palestinians on conveyor belts to detention camps. The world is silent | Arwa MahdawiRead moreThefounding charterof Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party states that “between the sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty”. Netanyahu himself last weekattended a gatheringat a religious-Zionist yeshiva, nodding along to a Kahanist song belted out by the attenders. “Remember me, please, give me strength just this time, O God, to take revenge, if only for one of my two eyes, on Palestine,” they sang, adding “May their name be erased!” “There are no more red lines,” was how a Haaretz writer described the scene.The international community has averted its eyes as red lines are trampled over. This can only be a combination of cowardice and acceptance, barely obscured by feeble statements of condemnation here and there, and grounded in the belief or resignation that Palestinian lives shall be consigned to hell. The facts are clear and plentiful. The Israeli right has a plan and a sense of direction, one that it has nursed for a very long time, and now given nourishment by the 7 October attacks.Some may not be realisable (ethnic cleansing of Palestinians inGazais limited by the fact there are no countries that can or will receive them), but much of it is. The direction of travel is clear and there have been some huge successes so far. There is a line connecting the hundreds of thousands of Palestinians expelled or forced to flee in 1948 and today. The security and carceral state that Palestinians exist in, the destruction of their homes and infrastructure, the settlement and fracturing of their territories, and the extension of Israeli sovereignty over them in ways that dehumanise and oppress, all serve to ensure that a future in which Palestinians are free, let alone thriving in self-governance, never emerges.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsIsraelOpinionGazaPalestineMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: TV has never been so nerve-jangling: 10 years of the agonising Motherland | Television | The Guardian
description: The rage, the wine, the power mums, the PTA horror – the BBC sitcom was a spot on send-up of life at the school gates. A decade on, we remember its most awkward bits
Author: Rachael Sigee
Headline: The rage, the wine, the power mums, the PTA horror – the BBC sitcom was a spot on send-up of life at the school gates. A decade on, we remember its most awkward bits
Content: ‘The most frazzled woman on television’ …Anna Maxwell Martin, centre, with Paul Ready, Lucy Punch and other cast members in Motherland.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The most frazzled woman on television’ …Anna Maxwell Martin, centre, with Paul Ready, Lucy Punch and other cast members in Motherland.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyTelevisionTV has never been so nerve-jangling: 10 years of the agonising MotherlandThe rage, the wine, the power mums, the PTA horror – the BBC sitcom was a spot on send-up of life at the school gates. A decade on, we remember its most awkward bitsRachael SigeeMon 7 Sep 2026 07.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 10.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIfUncut Gemswas about the school run instead of gambling debts, it would look like Motherland. It is now 10 years since the BBC sitcom jangled the already frayed nerves of all parents watching and turned Anna Maxwell Martin into the most frazzled woman on television in the name of skewering middle-class motherhood.Whether she was marching her children to buy school shoes the night before term started (“Don’t be closed. Pleeeeeaaaaase don’t be closed”) or having a meltdown at temporary traffic lights en route to a school drop-off that proved redundant because she’d forgotten it was half-term, Maxwell Martin’s Julia would undoubtedly have a more chilled-out time in the kitchen ofThe Bearthan raising her kids.Originally created by Sharon Horgan, Holly Walsh, Helen Serafinowicz and Graham Linehan (with Barunka O’Shaughnessy joining from series two, after Linehan departed), Motherland arrived into a TV landscape where mothers were no longer images of parenting perfection. But while the likes ofMalcolm in the Middleand Outnumbered had embraced the humour in the warts and all of child-rearing, the experience of mothering on television was still mostly centred on the kids themselves: tantrumming toddlers, precocious primary schoolers and stroppy teenagers.Motherland took a different tack. It was never about the offspring, who rarely amounted to more than the occasional school uniform bobbing into view (rare is a Motherland fan who can name all – or indeed any – of the sprogs). Instead, it was more like a workplace comedy, focusing on the adult experience of motherhood: the passive aggression, the barely disguised competition, the begged-for favours, the ulterior motives, the whingeing and the copious bottles of wine. While it had been considered progress to see women on television who were more than just mothers, Motherland acknowledged an uncomfortable truth: that the mothering bit can really take over, at least for a while there. That being a mother sometimes – often – feels like a constant fight against being flattened into two dimensions.View image in fullscreen‘Like a workplace comedy focusing on the adult experience of motherhood’ … Punch and Anna Maxwell Martin in Motherland.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyAlongside Maxwell Martin’s perma-stressed Julia was unflappable Liz (Diane Morgan), token dad Kevin (Paul Ready), long-suffering Anne (Philippa Dunne) and Amanda (Lucy Punch), a vividly heinous alpha-mum creation who always saw herself as the centre of the universe and now literally is, in spin-offAmandaland. The series two introduction of Meg (Tanya Moodie), a high-flying Black woman who appeared to have it all together, gave us a more diverse group but Motherland was carefully hyper-specific to its well-off west London demographic. The horrors here took place at interminable PTA fundraisers, joylessly non-competitive sports days and skin-crawling swimming pool birthday parties (devastatingly, not a drop-off situation).In Motherland, panic rises faster than house prices in a good school catchment area, and there is always someone to witness you making a colossal balls-up such as panicking about forgetting World Book Day and sending your child in holding an umbrella … as the novel Umbrella by Will Self. Obviously.The show gamely took on the utter weirdness of mother-to-mother relations: attempting variously to bond with, impress and one-up a group of people who just happen to have given birth around the same time as you. The thwarted efforts to join carpools and get your kids into after-school clubs, all the while doing just enough to appease this gaggle of onlookers eager to judge (if only to convince themselves they are doing OK).Amanda may be the obvious villain, but Motherland never stopped reminding us that motherhood will, at times, make sinners of us all. Having children does not suddenly wash away our foibles; if anything, it probably magnifies them. Motherland understood that being a mother frequently involves your spirit hovering somewhere above your body, watching yourself mutter Latin gibberish in an attempt to get your kids into a Catholic school, and silently screaming: “How did it come to this?”As the series progressed and the bonds formed at the school gates transitioned into real friendships, the stakes got higher. But Motherland never lost sight of the relentless nature of parenthood: even as divorce, illness and death reared their heads, lunches still had to be packed (and probably left at home).Anna Maxwell Martin looks back: ‘I was bullied a little bit, but it didn’t affect me because I was a happy weirdo’Read moreView image in fullscreen‘An act of catharsis’… Philippa Dunne with Maxwell Martin, Ready and Morgan in Motherland.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyIt’s a show that really should have had parents diving for the remote rather than spend their evenings reliving a hellish half-term cottage break or attempting to curb a nit epidemic. As Julia hissed when she ended up back at Anne’s house for an afterparty (a special bottle of cava and some dubious homemade paté): “This is my worst nightmare come true – surrounded by mums at night.”But while it’s too close to the bone to be a comfort watch, sitting down in front of Motherland is an act of catharsis – a reassurance that even when you’re trying reallyreallyhard, you still might lose someone else’s child while trick-or-treating. If you no longer identify as a Carrie or a Samantha, perhaps being a Liz or a Kevin feels more appropriate.It stands up as a triumphantly messy monument to a stage of life that passes in a blur of doctor’s appointments and sponsored bike rides and forgotten swimming kits. Less laugh till you cry and more laugh to stop yourself crying, Motherland holds out a hand to mothers watching. Not to help, of course, but to cling on to across a pub table as you try to fathom how on earth you’ve agreed to sort out the collection for the school’s poorly caretaker.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionBBCDiane MorganAnna Maxwell MartinfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The more famous I got, the bigger my beehive got’: how Mari Wilson made Just What I Always Wanted  | Culture | The Guardian
description: ‘I was trying to bring back some glamour. The backcombed hair was like architecture really. It took more than 45 minutes to style’
Author: Jack Watkins
Headline: ‘I was trying to bring back some glamour. The backcombed hair was like architecture really. It took more than 45 minutes to style’
Content: ‘Headphones had to go under my chin’ … Mari Wilson in 1983.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Headphones had to go under my chin’ … Mari Wilson in 1983.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesHow we madeCulture‘The more famous I got, the bigger my beehive got’: how Mari Wilson made Just What I Always Wanted‘I was trying to bring back some glamour. The backcombed hair was like architecture really. It took more than 45 minutes to style’Interviews byJack WatkinsMon 7 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMari Wilson, leadand backing vocalsJust What I Always Wanted had already been in our live set, but with different verses. When we’d gone onDavid Essex’s Showcaseearlier in 1982, in the middle eight I sang “A wink from Wilbur, a kiss from Kurt, don’t tell Hank, he might get hurt” – all names of my backing band the Wilsations. But when it came to recording, I said to Tot Taylor, who wrote most of my early singles, including Love Man and Baby It’s True, “We can’t sing that because no one will know who they are. What about, ‘A mink from Paris, a ring from Rome, a whole new wardrobe in my home?’” Tot, such a brilliant writer, took it from there.We’d brought in Tony Mansfield, whose futuristicNew Musikhad enjoyed hit singles with Living by Numbers and This World of Water, to produce the song and my debut album Showpeople. He brought a modern feel but captured our warmth and sense of fun. The trumpet solo was actually a synth, as was the timpani, but Paul Bultitude recorded his very loud snare drum fills in a studio corridor. I’m at the top of my range at the end of the middle eight – something a lot of Motown artists did to make the voice sound more plaintive.double quotation markI walked from my local Post Office to Tesco – and heard the song in both placesMy older sister had a beehive which I’d loved. When I first got mine in 1980, I remember walking through Brent Cross shopping mall and everyone staring. It wasn’t long after punk and no one wanted that look. However, the more famous I became, the bigger it got! It took more than 45 minutes to style, the hair backcombed to buggery – it was like architecture really. I was trying to bring back some glamour.I’d just come from an interview when I laid down the vocal part in Pete Townshend’s Eel Pie Studios, so I was already in character. I was wearing a crimplene dress and because of my beehive, the headphones had to go under my chin.The artwork for the single and album covers was inspired by classic Julie London and Peggy Lee LPs of the 1950s. I never wanted to be just an 80s pop singer and later I shifted to jazz. Some people come to my shows and say: “I didn’t know you could sing like that.” My new album combines pop, jazz and soul – a hybrid of what I’ve been performing live all my life.My earlier singles had reflected my love of 60s soul. I remember being in a studio with the Wilsations when Just What I Always Wanted was discussed onBBC Radio 1’s Round Table. We were excited and had the broadcast relayed through the speakers, but they were saying: “She’s meant to be retro, but she’s gone synthy.” Fortunately, the public were more enthusiastic and it became my biggest seller.Tot Taylor, songwriter, backing vocals, pianoI knew something was up when I walked from my local Post Office to Tesco and heard the single playing loud and clear over the sound systems in both places. Mari and her 12-piece band had been playing live in London for around a year. We’d released a couple of – now rare – singles on my record label the Compact Organization. This operated out of a cupboard in my one-bedroom flat, with a tiny backroom office off Portland Place in London. One of Mari’s singles,Beat the Beat, was an airplay hit and we thought Just What I Always Wanted was probably a likely UK indie hit, if lucky.View image in fullscreen‘An Ashworth snap’ … Wilson in the photo shoot that provided the 1982 single’s cover.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyBut massive radio play and a Top 10 position for three weeks exceeded all expectations. The initial idea for the song came to me when the band were at the BBC for a Radio 1 live session. I sat down at their beautiful Steinway grand piano in a tea break and out of nowhere this short-phrased tune came floating by. I grabbed it, and played it over and over so I could remember it.Frankie! Eurythmics!  Tina Turner! Peter Ashworth’s 80s pop mavericks - in picturesRead moreThen, on the bus going home, I got a lyric idea for a shopping list of best things – real-life items, or examples of things that were happening to Mari. “A tune from Teddy,” came from my songwriting pseudonym, Teddy Johns. “An Ashworth snap,” referred to Pete Ashworth,the cult photographerwho took the – much imitated – photos for the sleeve.I’ve always believed the song did so well because it followed the list formula, as with Cole Porter’s You’re the Top. It brings a natural structure. Tony Mansfield’s outer space and out of sight production sounded good – and loud – on the radio. And Mari’s vocal is so figured out and “up” attitude-wise. It really shows off her velvet sound.Mari Wilson’s new album Girl About Town is out now. She plays Cadogan Hall, London on 4 October, then toursExplore more on these topicsCultureHow we madePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Handsome, boyish – and he can cook!’ Richard O’Sullivan landed on TV like a lovable alien | Television | The Guardian
description: It was taken as read in the 1970s that all women, given the chance, would go out with him. But the star wasn’t just a new man – he was a radical presence
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: It was taken as read in the 1970s that all women, given the chance, would go out with him. But the star wasn’t just a new man – he was a radical presence
Content: ‘Dishy but not macho’ … Richard O’Sullivan on The Sweepstakes Game, 1976.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Dishy but not macho’ … Richard O’Sullivan on The Sweepstakes Game, 1976.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockTelevision‘Handsome, boyish – and he can cook!’ Richard O’Sullivan landed on TV like a lovable alienIt was taken as read in the 1970s that all women, given the chance, would go out with him. But the star wasn’t just a new man – he was a radical presenceZoe WilliamsMon 7 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRichard O’Sullivan, who has died at the age of 82, arrived in acting by accident. As a boy, he’d come back from a family holiday in Ireland with a strong accent, and his parents sent him to the Corona Theatre School in London to soften it. This origin story was very much in keeping with his adult self-fashioning: blokey, lovable, down to earth, cheeky – not the kind of guy who would go to drama school for the purposes of drama. But his work as a child star was almost back to back. He filmed his first feature aged eight, as an extra in The Yellow Balloon, and the next role he landed was the lead in The Stranger’s Hand, released the following year (1954). He played Audrey Hepburn’s younger brother in The Nun’s Story in 1959, and Elizabeth Taylor’s in Cleopatra four years later. It’s famously not that easy, making the child-to-adult actor transition, and the higher your profile as a junior the harder it is. It was while straddling the awkward between-years that O’Sullivan appeared in two Cliff Richard flicks, The Young Ones and Wonderful Life in the early 60s, and his facility with that pastel-shaded wholesomeness fed into but only partly described the comic actor he would become.Richard O’Sullivan obituaryRead moreHis first lead role as an adult was opposite Beryl Reid in Alcock and Gander, in 1972. Creators Johnnie Mortimer and Brian Cooke found their muse in O’Sullivan. Man About the House aired the following year, with O’Sullivan playing Robin Tripp, a trainee chef. The setup sounds so unremarkable now that it’s hard to fathom it as a break from any norm: two women (played by Paula Wilcox and Sally Thomsett) are looking for a flatmate. It’s assumed it’ll be another woman who’s all ready to move in; instead, O’Sullivan appears in their bath after a party. It was almost an ET archetype – thisalienarrives, this man who can cook, and spices up all their lives, to great merriment – and they can only get him past the landlord by pretending he’s gay.View image in fullscreenUnthreatening … with Paula Wilcox (left) and Sally Thomsett in Man About the House.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThere was a timeless innocence to it all – the girls insist the flatshare must always be platonic, so there’s a lot of forbidden flirtation, like a Shakespearean subplot. But it was also distinctively second-wave feminist, which is to say, determined to shake up norms and yet the guy, mysteriously, ended up on top. Tripp was a new kind of masculine ideal – handsome, boyish, unthreatening. Happy to pretend to be gay to keep the peace, constitutionally unable to batten down his heterosexual magnetism, always in a good mood. When you put it all together, what’s not to like?In the spin-off, Robin’s Nest, he’s grown up, but only on paper. Now in a relationship with Vicky Nicholls (played by Tessa Wyatt), he’d love to make an honest woman of her but she’s not having it. This was radical, being as they were the first unmarried cohabiting couple in a British sitcom, and it was O’Sullivan’s plausibly sweet nature that made it work, managing to convey that a new era had arrived, but everyone in it was still basically OK.O’Sullivan and Wyatt were a couple in real life, which didn’t do any harm – though he’d also been going out with Thomsett during Man About the House. This seems to have been adiaphoron to O’Sullivan fans, who were legion – his on-screen relationships either could or could not have been true in real life. It was taken as given during the 70s that all women, given the chance, would go out with him. He wrote recipe books – Man About the Kitchen, Roastin’ With Richard – and he appeared in adverts for British Gas. He was the ultimate new man, who could suddenly cook, while at the same time laugh at himself.View image in fullscreenRascally … with Michael Deeks in Dick Turpin.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockWhen Robin’s Nest ended, O’Sullivan took the title role in Dick Turpin. This was a stamp of his universalism, as it’s quite a different vibe, with the derring-do and all that, but no matter – if a main guy was called for, O’Sullivan was that guy. Dick Turpin ran into the early 80s, after which came Me and My Girl. O’Sullivan never tired of the business and would take smaller roles well into the 1990s, but his leading man years were over, and he was in poor health throughout that decade, suffering a stroke in 2003.He remained the embodiment of the 70s domestic dream – rascally but not roguish, dishy but not macho. It was a transitional era, out of the sitcom past where men were mainly grumpy, into who knew what? Richard O’Sullivan persuaded a nation that, wherever it was headed, it would probably be fine.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Can breath be art? Liz Larner on sculpting with hair, lashes, leather – and international group exhalation | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The Californian once cultivated petri dishes breathed on by artists that turned ‘murky and scary’. But now, in our dystopian age of space technocrats, she’s taking inspiration from Nasa shots of asteroids
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Californian once cultivated petri dishes breathed on by artists that turned ‘murky and scary’. But now, in our dystopian age of space technocrats, she’s taking inspiration from Nasa shots of asteroids
Content: ‘We don’t even see them, all these different forms’ … Contrary Brunette by Liz Larner.Photograph: © Liz Larner. Courtesy Galerie Max Hetzler, Anton Kern Gallery, The Modern Institute, Regen ProjectsView image in fullscreen‘We don’t even see them, all these different forms’ … Contrary Brunette by Liz Larner.Photograph: © Liz Larner. Courtesy Galerie Max Hetzler, Anton Kern Gallery, The Modern Institute, Regen ProjectsArt and designInterviewCan breath be art? Liz Larner on sculpting with hair, lashes, leather – and international group exhalationDaniel CulpanThe Californian once cultivated petri dishes breathed on by artists that turned ‘murky and scary’. But now, in our dystopian age of space technocrats, she’s taking inspiration from Nasa shots of asteroidsMon 7 Sep 2026 10.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Ihad artists from all over the world breathe over petri dishes,” says Liz Larner. “It was a piece of international art made from breath bacteria.” The American sculptor is reminiscing about her 1988 work Every Artist Gave a Breath, a fragile and strangely evolving work of art grown on agar. Exhibited in a 2022 show, it has since transformed in various ways: some bacteria has morphed into “beautiful, dried wafers in colour”, while other dishes “turned into a really weird blackish-green, really murky and a little scary”.Larner is no stranger to making alluring work out of strange materials, from human hair and false eyelashes to leather and surgical gauze. For her first major exhibition in the UK – A Hard Line to Bend at Camden Arts Centre in London – the sculptor has been transforming single-use plastic into pieces that bristle with seductiveness and menace. “I was living in LA at the time when China stopped accepting American plastic, which was where we were sending it all to be recycled,” she says. “I started taking it to my studio – it got so huge, I had to hang it from my ceiling.”View image in fullscreenMarthe, by Liz Larner,.Photograph: © Liz Larner. Courtesy Galerie Max Hetzler, Anton Kern Gallery, The Modern Institute, Regen ProjectsAssemblages such as Meerschaum Drift (2020-21) suggest a haunting analogue to our plastic-choked oceans. “I realised there’s so many smart people designing these objects made of plastic that are made to be discarded. We don’t even see them, all these different forms. We can’t see it. We just use it.”Born to a California farming family in 1960, Larner recalls how the state “sprayed DDT [a toxic insecticide since banned] over our house for the first seven years of my life”. Engaging in recent years with eco-feminism (such as Rosi Braidotti’s 2019 book Posthuman Knowledge), she acknowledges her own ambiguous position. “Maybe I’m implicated because I’m a sculptor. But I feel like we need to see these materials in different ways. To try and imagine something different.”In our dystopian age of SpaceX technocrats (“There are all these movies about disaster, except our lives are the biggest movie about disaster”), it’s not only Earth that’s being eyed as a commodity. Larner’s ceramic “asteroids”, such as 2022’s Nyx, transpose official Nasa photos into 3D forms, their glazed surfaces crenellated and mesmeric. Yet for all her precision, Larner is as preoccupied with what’snotthere as what can be captured. When it comes to colour, she paraphrases Wittgenstein: how do we know if two people are ever seeing the same shade of yellow? “In sculpture, colour is usually subservient to form. And I want to make my work not to do that. I want them to be together and to each have their interaction with each other.”View image in fullscreen‘We’re in such a different time now’ …  Liz Larner.Photograph: Laure JolietThe show’s eponymous work was inspired by the Burney Relief, a Babylonian terracotta plaque said by some to depict the mythological Lilith. She fled the Garden of Eden (sometimes portrayed as a snake), refusing her fate as Adam’s wife. “What I find interesting about her is that she’s not a fighter. She just says no. And that’s powerful for everyone, not just women.” We’re speaking on the day that Gloria Steinem’s death is announced, and Larner namechecks the feminist pioneer – alongside Dolly Parton – as similarly trailblazing. “I find something ‘Lilith’ about them both. They went their own way but with such style and grace. They took a different path.”I ask Larner about her time studying at the California Institute of Arts with John Baldessari. “Art school could be tense, people having their positions. But John let all that flow together,” she says. Later, she ran with LA’s 80s art crowd, where artists, poets and writers (including Dennis Cooper, Bob Flanagan and Mike Kelley) would gather at Beyond Baroque arts centre. It’s far from today’s terminally online glare and the flattening grid of Instagram. “I was so lucky to grow up in that scene,” Larner says. “We’re in such a different time now, where everything is seen before you experience it. There’s so much pre-knowledge.”She herself never joined social media (“There’s only so much time in every day. You have to decide what you want it to be about”). But despite refusing any easy categories for herself or her work, she still believes in the power of making objects to reshape reality. “That’s why I like sculpture. You have to walk in there and move around, while you’re thinking and seeing. And maybe talk to somebody too. Or watch somebody.” She smiles. “I wonder what they’re thinking by how they’re moving around.”Liz Larner: A Hard Line to Bend isat Camden Art Centre, London, from 11 September to 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designInstallationPlasticsArtinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sharks are my film stars’: how the Jacques Cousteau of the North Sea finally unlocked its beauty  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Epic plankton blooms make filming in the North Sea notoriously difficult. But a new documentary gives a rare glimpse of the kaleidoscopic life – seals, sharks, tuna, orcas and shorthorn sculpins – lurking beneath its waves
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Epic plankton blooms make filming in the North Sea notoriously difficult. But a new documentary gives a rare glimpse of the kaleidoscopic life – seals, sharks, tuna, orcas and shorthorn sculpins – lurking beneath its waves
Content: Rare sighting … a basking shark in North Sea, Nature Untamed.Photograph: Joost van Uffelen/©Dutch Maritime ProductionsView image in fullscreenRare sighting … a basking shark in North Sea, Nature Untamed.Photograph: Joost van Uffelen/©Dutch Maritime ProductionsMovies‘Sharks are my film stars’: how the Jacques Cousteau of the North Sea finally unlocked its beautyEpic plankton blooms make filming in the North Sea notoriously difficult. But a new documentary gives a rare glimpse of the kaleidoscopic life – seals, sharks, tuna, orcas and shorthorn sculpins – lurking beneath its wavesPatrick BarkhamMon 7 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 03.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe North Sea, as even its greatest admirers will concede, often glowers an unappetising grey or brown. And we assume that its dull exterior is matched by sediment-filled waters where little life dwells. For years, the friends and family of Peter van Rodijnen wondered why the Dutch cinematographer and diving fanatic spent so much time exploring “this murky bowl of soup”. But, inspired by a childhood of watching Jacques Cousteau’s adventures in rather more enticingly temperate waters, Van Rodijnen’s dedication to North Sea diving gradually revealed its hidden wonders.Over 20 years, as camera technology improved, Van Rodijnen obtained more and more amazing footage of marine life near his home on the Netherlands coast. Nearly a decade ago, he teamed up with director Mark Verkerk. “We started with the idea,” says Van Rodijnen, “that if somebody can make a movie about the North Sea, it’s got to be us.”double quotation markIt’s no accident that there are virtually no films about the North SeaNorth Sea, Nature Untamedwill startle anyone who has ever set eyes on – or dipped a toe in – the shallow sea shared by the coastal nations of north-west Europe. Despite decades of intensive fishing, oil extraction and multiple other exploitations, parts of the North Sea are still alive with luminous pinks, purples and greens; starfish, lobsters, brittle stars, kelp forests, seals and basking sharks. This hidden wilderness may be almost as spectacular as a tropical reef, even if the Great Barrier Reef, where Van Rodijnen began his diving career, is much more accessible.View image in fullscreenRough seas … four out of five planned dives were cancelledPhotograph: Joost van Uffelen/Dutch Maritime ProductionsPart of the reason we rarely comprehend the marine riches of the North Sea is because of epic plankton blooms that, as the film explains, are actually the foundation of this living ecosystem. These annual eruptions feed its whole pyramid of marine life but, combined with the shallow waters and big tides, frequently make underwater visibility too poor to film. “It’s no accident that there are virtually no films about the North Sea,” grimaces Verkerk. “This is really one of the first big attempts. It is incredibly difficult.”Van Rodijnen, who narrates the film in a charmingly personal way, meticulously assembled his underwater stories from decades of North Sea diving. But during their seven-year shoot, the film-makers faced multiple last-minute cancellations of carefully scheduled trips to join fishers or windfarm construction sites alongside even less predictable attempts to intercept dolphin, bluefin tuna and basking sharks. Four out of every five planned dives in the North Sea were cancelled because of rough seas.“The visibility can be poor, there can be lots of currents, it is cold,” says Van Rodijnen. “You’ve got depth and the limitations of your scuba devices, so you have 20 or 30 minutes of filming per dive. It’s about patience but it’s more about persistence. You need to just keep pushing to get the shots. I had some sleepless nights, I can tell you.”Although North Sea, Nature Untamed is awash with charismatic characters – from supersmart orcas to the conscientious shorthorn sculpins that nurse neon-pink eggs until they grow eyes and squiggle out into the dark water – the documentary does not lead with obvious or familiar marine stars. “The big idea is to show the whole system working,” says Verkerk. “It’s fantastic to see the bluefin tuna come back and orcas thriving, but they only do that because of this massive system supporting all of that life.”Unlike the British natural history film-making tradition, where wild animals are often portrayed in a world without humans, people are shown as key engineers of this living system, for better and for worse. Fishing and overfishing continues to shape the North Sea, and the film reveals the impact of sand eel decline on puffins and follows Van Rodijnen on to a Dutch fishing boat. The boat is a clean, conscientious operation that prides itself on its sustainable methods, eschewing beam or bottom trawling, in which heavy beams and nets plough – and obliterate – the seabed and much of its life. But even this boat’s fishing is a challenging watch as Van Rodijnen witnesses “my subjects, my film stars” – beautiful little sharks and rays – discarded as bycatch.Later, he joins a mackerel fishing boat off Shetland, a supremely efficient, industrial enterprise. A pod of orcas recognise the sound of the vessel’s winch and pick off any mackerel that evade its vast net. While the orca pod can devour 1,000 mackerel in a day, fishers far outdo that. It is shocking to see the sheer scale of the operation: thousands of fish sucked up giant tubes into a huge steel vat.View image in fullscreenFull of life … lobsters, kelp forests and curious seals feature in North Sea, Nature Untamed.Photograph: Joost van Uffelen/©Dutch Maritime ProductionsVan Rodijnen says he still finds the images upsetting, “but once you get on the boat with those guys and you’re living together for a couple of days, you don’t always agree but you start to understand their situation”. The film is not a polemic. Van Rodijnen believes it is “naive” to hope we can “make one big Marine Protected Area out of the North Sea. That just won’t happen. There’s lots of nuance to understand.”He opposes bottom trawling and bycatch but the mackerel fishery deploys nets that don’t damage the seabed; nor does it appear to catch large quantities of non-target species. In this case, he says in the film, fishing quotas “seem to work”. However, he would still like to see marine life better protected, particularly by nations such as his own, Denmark and Norway, which he fears could revive destructive deep-sea mining proposals.For decades, the North Sea has also been challenged by extraction. While the film-makers do not turn their cameras on its oil and gas industries, they do explore the positives and negatives of the offshore windfarm boom. Underwater is “not just a world that you don’t see, but it’s also a world that you don’t hear,” says Verkerk. The film reveals the pounding noise that reverberates through the ocean during construction. “The sound is pretty deafening above the water but underwater it can be 20 times louder,” says Verkerk. “Because visibility is not so good in the North Sea, a lot of marine life is geared for sound. The impact is not just on whales but right down to the actual development of a fish egg.”View image in fullscreen‘Give nature a chance and it responds’ … Peter van Rodijnen.Photograph: Rosalie van der Does/Dutch Maritime ProductionsAs well as providing clean energy, though, there may be an unforeseen upside to the North Sea windfarms. Van Rodijnen’s most surprising dive is to some rocks that accidentally fell from a ship 30 years ago. Similar to those used at the base of windfarms, the rocks have over three decades had their grey surface transformed by multicoloured marine life – a profusion of seaweeds and sea creatures have attached itself to this artificial reef.With bottom trawling and other commercial fishing prevented within sizeable windfarm areas, de facto marine parks have been established. More mini artificial reefs could flourish over the coming decades. “Give nature a chance and it responds,” says Van Rodijnen. “It’s good to keep a constant eye on how the system reacts to these many windfarms being built. But in the end, they can absolutely have a positive effect on marine life.”Verkerk and Van Rodijnen sound surprised and delighted by the success of their film, which they have been touring for two years across the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany and even countries with no North Sea coast such as Austria and Switzerland. There’s now interest in China, Japan, Argentina and Italy, perhaps because it is ultimately a universal film about the life-giving miracle that is the sea.“It’s very much out of sight out of mind, isn’t it?” says Verkerk. “Even for those of us who live around the North Sea, it’s a little underwhelming. But it is actually an incredibly interesting sea. A lot of the problems facing seas and oceans all around the world are at their most acute here – the North Sea is leading the way in exploitation but also in solutions.”“There’s a lot of parties wanting to get something out of the oceans,” adds Van Rodijnen, “and there are a lot of discussions about the North Sea. What we’re trying to do with the film is spark wonder by showing what’s down there. Then you bring about a bit of love and understanding.”North Sea, Nature Untamedis in cinemas UK wide from 25 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsOceansEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Will I screw this up?’ How I played timpani for the Philharmonia Orchestra – with no experience | Classical music | The Guardian
description: He hasn’t seen the score and can’t actually play his instrument. But with the help of a virtual headset, our writer joins the revered orchestra for the rollicking finale of Rossini’s William Tell Overture
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: He hasn’t seen the score and can’t actually play his instrument. But with the help of a virtual headset, our writer joins the revered orchestra for the rollicking finale of Rossini’s William Tell Overture
Content: ‘The Royal Festival Hall is packed to the rafters!’ … a participant in the Philharmonia’s Virtual Orchestra.Photograph: Marc GascoigneView image in fullscreen‘The Royal Festival Hall is packed to the rafters!’ … a participant in the Philharmonia’s Virtual Orchestra.Photograph: Marc GascoigneClassical music‘Will I screw this up?’ How I played timpani for the Philharmonia Orchestra – with no experienceHe hasn’t seen the score and can’t actually play his instrument. But with the help of a virtual headset, our writer joins the revered orchestra for the rollicking finale of Rossini’s William Tell OvertureTim JonzeMon 7 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 03.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m about to perform with the Philharmonia Orchestra and I’ve not rehearsed my part. In fact, I’ve not even seen the score. Or played my instrument before. Nervously taking my place among the virtuosos, I look around: the brass, string and woodwind sections are all warmed up and ready to be led by the energetic conductor, Santtu-Matias Rouvali. Then I glance up at the audience: the Royal Festival Hall is packed to the rafters. Gulp!“Are you OK there?” asks Marta Génova, the Philharmonia’s head of digital product and experience, “or do I need to tighten your headset?” This, you see, is Virtual Orchestra, a VR experience designed by the Philharmonia that lets you play percussion during the rollicking finale of Rossini’s William Tell Overture. You’re offered the choice of triangle, cymbal and timpani (the last is “definitely the most fun”, Génova assures me) and after a quick run-through of the sounds you can get from your instrument, courtesy of Philharmonia percussionist Tom Edwards, you’re thrown into a rehearsal and then the actual performance. I’ve barely had time to say “How do I hold these sticks again?” before the strings start swelling, Rouvali waves his baton and a musical score starts hurtling across the bottom of my vision. Oh God, I think, am I about to screw this up?View image in fullscreenEducational … feedback from children was overwhelmingly positive.Photograph: Marc GascoigneThe Philharmonia have a history of using cutting-edge technology to help them stand out from the other big London orchestras. They were founded in 1945 as a “recording orchestra”, back when such a thing was still a novelty, and more recently they’ve provided immersive digital orchestral experiences, lighting up the walls of places such as the Science Museum. The move to interactive headsets is the next logical step in trying to engage new audiences – no previous musical or VR experience is required to join this orchestra.The headsets’ main purpose, however, is educational. The Philharmonia have developed a programme of activities that can be completed as part of the national curriculum. The aim is not for students to fully learn instruments virtually (I’m impressed with how realistic the mimicry is but it can’t completely replace the subtleties of an actual instrument). Rather, the hope is that it sparks interest in playing – and encourages users to seek out the real thing. The scheme was spurred on by recent research highlighting declining music participation in schools, withGCSE Music entries falling 27% since 2010.The Philharmonia is signed up to the Orchestra in Every School programme, a scheme designed to ensure every child in the UK has access to live music-making and high-quality music education. “But we thought, we can’t possibly take our orchestra into all the schools in the country,” says Thorben Dittes, the Philharmonia’s CEO. “With headsets, it’s a very different situation.”Earlier this year, the headsets were piloted in 12 schools across Leicestershire, Derbyshire and Lincolnshire. The feedback from the 428 children in year 7 involved was overwhelmingly positive. According to Dittes, 75% of the children had never attended a classical concert before, yet 96% said they were now likely to, with 60% saying they felt inspired to learn an instrument. It’s early days, of course, but as Dittes notes: “They were happy to stay in the headsets for hours, learning about notation, about rhythm, about the joy of being part of a big orchestra.”“We didn’t want it to be just a video game,” adds Génova. “We wanted it to be something that’s actually useful, where you pick up a few skills that are transferable to the real thing.” Ultimately, the dream is to have a variety of instruments and pieces children can trial using the headsets.double quotation markI achieved 84% on ‘hard’ mode – I do feel quietly impressed with myselfBack in my own orchestra, I’m not doing so badly. The experience will be familiar to anyone who’s ever played Guitar Hero – we might technically be playing off sheet notation, with crochets, quavers and rests to be observed, but the coloured notes denoting which timpani to bash arrive at the clef whenever it’s time to strike them.It’s intuitive, but it’s also frantic stuff. The trickiest bits are the drum rolls, where you have to relax your wrists and let the sticks gently flutter up and down. I’ve mastered the left side but on my right the rhythm feels awkward and stilted. I finish with a flourish of quick quavers which I feel are executed perfectly … until I realise I’m actually hitting the wrong timpani for each one.Still, when former Clean Bandit star Love Ssega pops up in front of me to tell me that I achieved 84% on “hard” mode, I do feel quietly impressed with myself. How, I wonder, does it compare with others? “I can’t share with you my score,” laughs Dittes, “because it was actually rather bad. And the people here have gotten quite competitive over their scores.”Does this mean I might have a shot at joining the Philharmonia for real? Génova did mention they had auditions coming up. “Well, if you can do it repeatedly, then yes, why not?” says Dittes. “Who knows, maybe this will be how we find our next great percussionist.”Virtual Orchestra is part ofCreative Intelligence at the Southbank Centre, London, 11-13 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicThe Philharmonia OrchestraVirtual realitySouthbank CentrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hawking by Graham Farmelo review – the dark side of genius | Biography books | The Guardian
description: A biography of the physicist recognises his achievements, but also reveals the selfish narcissist underneath
Author: Philip Ball
Headline: A biography of the physicist recognises his achievements, but also reveals the selfish narcissist underneath
Content: Stephen Hawking in 2005.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStephen Hawking in 2005.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianBook of the dayBiography booksReviewHawking by Graham Farmelo review – the dark side of geniusA biography of the physicist recognises his achievements, but also reveals the selfish narcissist underneathPhilip BallMon 7 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I wrote an unadoring review of Stephen Hawking’s final book, a collection of essays published posthumously in 2018, New Scientist suppressed some of my criticisms on the grounds that it was “too early” to voice anything other than praise for the physicist who died, aged 76, that March. It was apparently still too early in 2021, when no British publisher would touch Charles Seife’s exposé of Hawking’s bullying and self-aggrandising behaviour, Hawking Hawking.In this new biography, veteran science writer Graham Farmelo takes a different approach. It is a comprehensive and accessible portrait of a brilliant scientist and an extraordinarily determined man who also possessed deep personal flaws to which the scientific community and the public mostly turned a blind eye. The uncomfortable but unavoidable truth is that Hawking’s overweening ambition and self-promotion, his repeated failure to acknowledge the work of others, his sexism and controlling behaviour were largely ignored because of his disability. I think it is indeed going to take us years to process that.As this book was authorised by the Hawking family, and as Farmelo (whose superb biography of Paul Dirac, The Strangest Man, won a Costa award in 2009) is a generous and kind writer, I had feared the warts would be omitted. But instead Farmelo handles them mostly by letting others’ words speak for themselves.But let’s start with the science, which offers a genuinely inspirational tale. As Farmelo says, while Hawking’s longevity against all odds was surely due in part to the exceptional care and treatment he received, “it was his unconquerable will, resilience and fortitude that did most to make his remarkable career possible”. His scientific achievements would be impressive by any measure; when accomplished in the face of debilitating and ultimately paralysing motor neurone disease, they are extraordinary.Like many scientists of his calibre, Hawking was a slow and rather lackadaisical starter. But once installed at Cambridge for a PhD under the supervision of astrophysicist Dennis Sciama, his sharp intelligence emerged. It was there in early 1963 that, after a series of falls, he was diagnosed and given less than 10 years to live. Undeterred, and despite steadily declining mobility and speech, he was electrified by the work of physicist Roger Penrose, 10 years his senior, on the gravitational collapse of dead stars into what had become known as black holes.That process was predicted by Einstein’s 1915 theory of general relativity, but Penrose was the first to show convincingly that it should lead to a “singularity” where all the star’s matter condenses to zero volume: an object with mass but no matter. Hawking had the brilliant insight that this same process, happening in reverse, could explain the big bang, in which the entire universe came into being from “nothing” 13.8bn years (as we now know) ago.That was his first triumph, described in a 1970 paper with Penrose. The best came four years later, when Hawking proposed that, thanks to the peculiar quantum-mechanical nature of spacetime, black holes are not really black because they should constantly radiate a dim glow of particles – now called Hawking radiation – that will eventually lead to their evaporation. That work was a virtuosic blend of four fundamental ideas in physics: general-relativistic gravity, quantum mechanics, thermodynamics and information theory.It was the high point of his research career: Hawking’s scientific achievements were largely done by the time he became a global celebrity, appearing on Star Trek and TheSimpsons and becoming the subject of the 2014 Oscar-winning biopic The Theory of Everything. It is “as a truly great elucidator of black holes” that he will be remembered, Farmelo rightly judges.I’m not alone in thinking Hawking’s work on black-hole thermodynamics and the discovery of Hawking radiation were worthy of a Nobel prize. (Hawking became obsessed to an unseemly degree with getting one.) But let’s keep it in proportion. Anyone who compares Hawking to Einstein knows nothing about Einstein or physics. Einstein made wide-ranging contributions to the discipline, but Hawking’s expertise was narrow and his forays outside it were sometimes embarrassing. Even in the closely related field of particle physics he said things that were, as Peter Higgs (of Higgs boson fame) said, “total crap”. “He made pronouncements about things he had no understanding of,” Higgs said – in the confident knowledge that it would make newspaper headlines the next day, uncritically lapped up by reporters.Which brings us to the problematic stuff. While professional colleagues mostly spoke about Hawking with reverence and affection, it is often those closest to him who speak of another side. His father, Frank, worried that the teenaged Stephen “was developing into a selfish character … like a small boy who took everything but gave little in return”. There was evidently no love lost with his sister Mary, who called him “one of the most self-centred people I’ve ever met”. At Oxford, some friends found him rather lazy and entitled, and at Cambridge “annoyingly haughty”. His youngest son recounted how his father was “hugely competitive” and never let him or his siblings win at board games.His unsparing ridicule of his first wife Jane’s religious beliefs contributed to their marital tensions, and the sacrifices she made often went unremarked by him. The pressure of going from lover to carer would never have been easy, but Hawking’s “authoritarian” demands and indifference to Jane’s interests added to her isolation. His adoptive brother, Edward, admitted “I’ve never really felt close to Stephen … he seems very cold.” And his mother, Isobel, complained how he would ignore people when it suited him. “I suppose what in other people would just be bad manners is excusable great-mannishness in him,” she wrote bitterly in her diary.Sometimes the indulgence gets creepy. Who else’s Marilyn Monroe obsession would be pampered by hiring a lookalike to croon “I want to be loved by you” to him in a “whispery voice” on his birthday? What Farmelo calls “flirting” might have been seen as something else if Hawking had not been using a wheelchair. He does not mention the nights at Stringfellows strip club and makes light of the trip to (pre-conviction) Jeffrey Epstein’s island. But we do hear how Hawking’s victory in a scientific bet was celebrated by making his opponents deliver lectures in T-shirts showing scantily clad women. Hilarious.Hawking was scandalously bad at giving due scientific credit to others, a trait evident from the outset when he failed to indicate his debt to Penrose. Worse was his treatment of physicist Jacob Bekenstein, whose idea about the connection between the area and the entropy of a black hole he mercilessly derided before discovering for himself that Bekenstein was right – and then essentially claiming the idea as his own, which Farmelo says “disappointed some of Stephen’s friends”.
