Hawking could clearly be a supportive and kind adviser to his own students, but when one discovered an argument for why Hawking was wrong about a conjecture concerning black holes, he tried to get him dismissed from the Cambridge PhD programme.Some of his colleagues, Farmelo says, “believed that Stephen’s talks were ‘all about him’ and that he rarely gave much public credit to his peers”. Farmelo suspects they rarely grumbled because “such comments would have been interpreted as mean-spirited”. But mean-spiritedness rarely deters academics; what he surely means is mean-spirited about a scientist with a disability. And there’s the problem. If we were to start finally treating Hawking as we do any other scientist, it would be a positive step for disability in science (which is still poorly accommodated). The effect on Hawking’s legacy is another matter.Hawking: His Life and Work by Graham Farmelo is published by John Murray (£30). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsBiography booksBook of the dayStephen HawkingPhysicsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: End of the Road festival review – Pulp and CMAT lead indie landmark’s joyous birthday party  | End of the Road festival | The Guardian
description: Hitting 20, this festival has grown into a warm, genre-hopping powerhouse where fringe experimental acts are greeted as warmly as the star headliners
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: Hitting 20, this festival has grown into a warm, genre-hopping powerhouse where fringe experimental acts are greeted as warmly as the star headliners
Content: Cathartic farewell … CMAT performs at the End of the Road festival.Photograph: Burak ÇıngıView image in fullscreenCathartic farewell … CMAT performs at the End of the Road festival.Photograph: Burak ÇıngıEnd of the Road festivalReviewEnd of the Road festival review – Pulp and CMAT lead indie landmark’s joyous birthday partyLarmer Tree Gardens, WiltshireHitting 20, this festival has grown into a warm, genre-hopping powerhouse where fringe experimental acts are greeted as warmly as the star headlinersDaniel Dylan WrayMon 7 Sep 2026 07.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 07.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a celebratory feeling in the air atEnd of the Road festivalthis year as it turns 20. The piano stage has been turned into a giant birthday cake with candles on top, one man is dressed as a toilet to commemorate the porcelain anniversary, and Jarvis Cocker leads a spirited singalong of Happy Birthday while wishing for 20 more years.Retaining a core identity while also expanding and evolving has been key to that longevity. While early days were centred more on alt-folk and Americana, EOTR is now a genre-hopping powerhouse, blending everything from pop fun to noisy experimentation via global grooves, and with an equal focus on the familiar and the unknown.View image in fullscreenHappy birthday … Jarvis Cocker performs with Pulp.Photograph: Burak ÇıngıRepresenting the former,Geesemanage to pull in record audience attendance levels for their Thursday headliner show, while Pulp use theirs to announce a hiatus and they bow out with a set of deep, deep cuts and B-sides (including a beautifully sprawling and pulsing live debut of Deep Fried in Kelvin). It could have backfired spectacularly – with not even a nod to a hit song until almost an hour in – but while it was steadfastly uncompromising it was also a joyous rummage through the archive of true art-pop pioneers.CMAT also announces she won’t be playing the UK for two years during her headline set, which wraps up with the singer shirtless and deep in the audience for some collective cathartic screaming to say goodbye. Angine de Poitrine’s microtonal math-rock, as though styled by Alejandro Jodorowsky on a B-movie budget, may be still firmly in the leftfield camp but they are on the main stage after their huge breakthrough year, turning their frantic and frenetic instrumental workouts into an oddly big-crowd-friendly routine.Beyond the heavy hitters, the lineup has a deeply impressive wingspan. Factory Floor are in phenomenal form as they knock out a pummeling set of industrial electro-techno. Experimental electronic duo Another Country $$$ span everything from drum’n’bass to post-rock, while Cleo Reed’s queer country-soul (cuntry, as she calls it) is playful and sweet but also angry and impassioned. James K creates swirling electronic sounds that are so richly layered, dynamic and immersive, it’s like being pulled in and out of a dream state. Model/Actriz unleash a ferocious noise that manages to be as heavy as it is groove-locked – almost recalling a sweet spot between Perfume Genius and Gilla Band – as well as theatrical, with vocalist Cole Haden either doing endless ballet twirls or down in the audience whipping them into a frenzied state. But what’s especially infectious and energising at End of the Road is how everything, big or small, weird or poppy, is proportionally and enthusiastically attended. Everything is lapped up with the same appetite and gusto.Twenty years on from its inception, the festival may be hitting a major milestone and delivering a vintage year, but it exists as a crowning achievement in a wider context. A medium-sized event (15,000 capacity) free of big corporate sponsors as money from brands and multinationals pours into identity-less festivals elsewhere, this is a rare yet deserved success story, testament to the enduring power and beauty of independent music.Explore more on these topicsEnd of the Road festivalMusic festivalsIndieFestivalsJarvis CockerPulpGeeselive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘She’ll outdo herself’: Céline Dion fans camp out for glimpse of star before sold-out Paris comeback | Céline Dion | The Guardian
description: Singer has rewarded patience of hundreds waiting outside hotel with regular appearances and even some dancing
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Singer has rewarded patience of hundreds waiting outside hotel with regular appearances and even some dancing
Content: Céline Dion acknowledges fans as she arrives at her hotel in Paris for her first shows in six years.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCéline Dion acknowledges fans as she arrives at her hotel in Paris for her first shows in six years.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesCéline Dion‘She’ll outdo herself’: Céline Dion fans camp out for glimpse of star before sold-out Paris comebackSinger has rewarded patience of hundreds waiting outside hotel with regular appearances and even some dancingAngelique Chrisafisin ParisMon 7 Sep 2026 11.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNoëlla Lamy, 52, who described herself as one ofCéline Dion’s biggest fans, was preparing to spend all night on a Paris pavement without a tent but wearing a sweatshirt printed with the singer’s face for comfort.“Céline Dion is a force of bravery and an inspiration,” she said.Lamy, who works in catering for a private clinic, had travelled from her village near Amiens in northernFranceto wait for 36 hours behind a metal barrier outside the Canadian star’s Paris hotel to get a glimpse of her.Céline Dion fan Noëlla Lamy outside the singer’s Paris hotel.Photograph: Angelique Chrisafis/The GuardianHundreds of Dion fans have been gathering each day to catch sight of the singer, as she rehearses for along-awaited return to the stagein a series of sold-out Paris shows that begin this weekend.Dion, 58, announced in 2022 that she had been diagnosed with the rare and incurable autoimmune disorder,stiff-person syndrome. She took a break from performing, later describing how the condition meant she had suffered muscle spasms so strong that her ribs were broken as a result. In the 2024 documentaryI Am: Céline Dionshe provided insight into the severity of her pain from the condition, including having a seizure.Celine Dion sings with fans outside Paris hotel“She is resilient, humane and humble,” said Lamy, who had seen Dion perform several times in the US and France and has tickets for a Paris show. “I’m happy she’s back on stage and I hope it’s a gentle comeback for her. I know it won’t necessarily be the same type of shows she put on before, because of her health, but I know she’ll outdo herself and it will still be very grand.“I feel like she’s been there for me for every challenge in my life. I lost my husband around the same time she lost her husband, and her songs really helped me through. I first watched her singing on a French TV chatshow when she was 14 years old and I was eight and I’ve been a fan since then.”Dion, who grew up the youngest of 14 children in a small town near Montréal in French-speaking Quebec, has a massive fanbase in France. Although she is famous worldwide for her 1997 songMy Heart Will Go On, which featured in the Oscar-winning film Titanic and became the second-bestselling single by a woman in music history, in France she is known for her many French-language songs. Her 1995 album D’eux became the biggest-selling Francophone album of all time. In 2024, she sang an Edith Piaf song from the Eiffel Tower at theParis Olympics opening ceremony.View image in fullscreenThe Eiffel Tower illuminated in March as the singer announces her Paris shows.Photograph: Pierre Suu/Getty ImagesDion has made a point of greeting fans outside her Paris hotel, often dancing for them and chatting to them as they wait for her to come and go from evening rehearsals. She told fans a few days after arriving at the hotel that she was not going out in Paris except to rehearse because: “I’m trying to conserve my energy to give the best of myself.”The pavement outside Dion’s hotel has become a gathering place that often resembles a street party, with office workers in the next-door building putting speakers on their balcony to blast her hits while the crowd dances along.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarina, 31, a chemist for a cosmetics company, who has tickets for one of Dion’s Paris shows, said: “I thought I just have to get down here to her hotel as the mood seemed so good outside. My mother had all her CDs when I was a child and I also watched Titanic when I was small. Even if you don’t specifically listen to Céline Dion, you’re constantly surrounded by her music in France. It’s really positive that she showed her health condition so honestly. Lots of stars clearly feel they mustn’t show any difficult moments, but they’re human like us. I think it made her more real and close to her fans.”View image in fullscreenDion performing in 2017.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesSylvie Lugans, a retired cafe worker, had been a fan since Dion won Eurovision in 1988 representing Switzerland. “She’s a wonderful diva on stage, but in real life, she’s so down to earth,” Lugans said.Augustin, 21, who worked in the last remaining wallpaper factory in France, had also travelled from northern France to stand outside the hotel and had seen Dion wave at the crowd as she left.“She’s brave enough to speak about the hardest moments of her life, and that’s very moving,” he said.Explore more on these topicsCéline DionFranceEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Netflix announces production of third Inbetweeners film | Netflix | The Guardian
description: Creators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris return as writers and directors, with the original cast reprising their roles
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Creators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris return as writers and directors, with the original cast reprising their roles
Content: A scene from the first Inbetweeners film in 2011, in which the group of friends head to Crete for a post-sixth form break.Photograph: Bwark Prods/Kobal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA scene from the first Inbetweeners film in 2011, in which the group of friends head to Crete for a post-sixth form break.Photograph: Bwark Prods/Kobal/ShutterstockNetflixNetflix announces production of third Inbetweeners filmCreators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris return as writers and directors, with the original cast reprising their rolesNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 10.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 14.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNetflix has announced that production has begun on a new Inbetweeners film, with the original cast members reprising their roles.It will be a continuation of the popular Channel 4 sitcom, which aired on E4 from 2008 to 2010, followed by two films in 2011 and 2014.The actors Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will star as Will McKenzie, Jay Cartwright, Neil Sutherland and Simon Cooper. The coming-of-age comedy followed the misadventures of the four teenage friends at the fictional Rudge Park comprehensive as they navigated school life, friendship and failed sexual encounters.Thetrailer announcing the new filmbegins with a garage door being opened and pairs of feet making their way towards a car, revealed to be Simon’s yellow Fiat Cinquecento. The four men are then seen in the car, and when it fails to start Simon says: “Ah, for fuck’s sake.”He gets the engine going and drives the car out of the garage with the number three written on the rear windscreen. The trailer ends with the announcement: “Now in production.”The Inbetweeners creators, Damon Beesley and Iain Morris, will return to write and direct the film. They said: “It’s been super-fun hanging out with our friends again, and we’re going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans.”In the first film, which grossed £65.1m at the box office, the group of friends head to Crete in Greece for a post-sixth form break. It made history as the biggest opening weekend for a UK comedy at the time, according to Netflix.The 2014 follow-up, which grossed £46.6m, reunited Will, Simon, and Neil as they travelled to Australia to visit Jay during his gap year.It is not known whether Emily Atack will return in her role as Charlotte Hinchcliffe, or if Emily Head will come back as Carli D’Amato.Explore more on these topicsNetflixComedy filmsComedynewsShareReuse this content

title: Oasis recordings up for auction despite band’s objections | Oasis | The Guardian
description: Guide price of archive documenting concerts, rehearsals, soundchecks and conversations between £1.2m and £1.6m
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Guide price of archive documenting concerts, rehearsals, soundchecks and conversations between £1.2m and £1.6m
Content: The archive includes recordings of candid conversations between Noel and Liam Gallagher.Photograph: Tiziana Fabi/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe archive includes recordings of candid conversations between Noel and Liam Gallagher.Photograph: Tiziana Fabi/AFP/Getty ImagesOasisOasis recordings up for auction despite band’s objectionsGuide price of archive documenting concerts, rehearsals, soundchecks and conversations between £1.2m and £1.6mNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentMon 7 Sep 2026 08.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn archive of more than 100 hours of Oasis recordings, including concerts, rehearsals and candid conversations between Noel andLiam Gallagher, is to be auctioned for up to £1.6m despite objections from the band.The collection was amassed by the band’s sound engineer Huw Richards, who worked withOasisfrom the release of their 1994 debut album, Definitely Maybe, until 2001. It comprises 209 DAT tapes, 73 analogue cassettes and three MiniDiscs, and is being sold by Richards’s son, Owain.Littleton Auctions in Evesham,Worcestershire, has given the archive a guide price of between £1.2m and £1.6m, with the sale due to take place on 3 October.Ben Homer, the auction house’s managing director, said Oasis had expressed concerns about the sale.View image in fullscreenLiam and Noel Gallagher at their Loch Lomond gig, 1996. The collection includes what is believed to be the only recording of this show.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian“The Oasis camp is aware of the auction and has expressed concerns, which is entirely understandable given the scale and significance of the material,” he said in a statement to the Guardian.Homer said the auction house was handling the sale through the appropriate legal process and the recordings were being offered with verified provenance. He said the archive would give collectors and institutions the opportunity to acquire material documenting an important period in British music.The collection includes what is believed to be the only recording of Oasis’s 1996 concert on the banks of Loch Lomond in Scotland. It also contains recordings of numerous rehearsals and soundchecks, as well as informal conversations involving the Gallagher brothers and members of the touring crew.Owain Richards, who is also a sound engineer, said he had previously been in discussions with Oasis’s management after the band sought some of the recordings.He told the Times those discussions had ultimately “fizzled away” and that the band wanted the tapes returned rather than sold elsewhere.Richards said his father had meticulously preserved the recordings, which date from a period when concertgoers were far less likely to make their own recordings on mobile phones. “It really is a piece of history,” he said.View image in fullscreenLiam (L) and Noel Gallagher at a press conference in London in August 1999.Photograph: Fiona Hanson/PARichards said the audio remained in sufficiently good condition to be mastered for a live album. The recordings cannot, however, simply be released by whoever buys them. Oasis retain the intellectual property rights, meaning the archive cannot be commercially exploited without the band’s cooperation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLittleton Auctions has described the collection as a significant record of the band’s live career and said it could be of interest to collectors, scholars and museums.The auction comes as interest in Oasis continues to grow since the band’s reunion last year, when Noel and Liam Gallagher returned to the stage together for the first time in 15 years.Oasis became one of the biggest British rock bands of the 1990s, with albums including (What’s the Story) Morning Glory? and Be Here Now. Their career was marked by the fractious relationship between the Gallagher brothers, whose arguments eventually contributed to the band’s split in 2009.The reunion saw Oasis play sold-out dates in Britain, North America, Australia and Asia. The brothers were also pictured together at the Venice film festival this weekend, whereOasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger, a film documenting their return, was premiered.The Littleton auction will also feature other Oasis memorabilia, including a pair of Adidas Kegler Super Ostrich trainers given toNoel Gallagher. Oasis were approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsOasisWorcestershirePop and rockLiam GallagherNoel GallaghernewsShareReuse this content

title: Chris Langham obituary | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Actor and writer best known for his role in TV’s The Thick of It who was jailed in 2007 for downloading child pornography
Author: Anthony Hayward
Headline: Actor and writer best known for his role in TV’s The Thick of It who was jailed in 2007 for downloading child pornography
Content: Chris Langham in 2011. The Thick of It cemented Langham’s reputation as a naturalistic performer in satirical comedy and he was garlanded with honours.Photograph: Felix ClayView image in fullscreenChris Langham in 2011. The Thick of It cemented Langham’s reputation as a naturalistic performer in satirical comedy and he was garlanded with honours.Photograph: Felix ClayTelevision & radioObituaryChris Langham obituaryActor and writer best known for his role in TV’s The Thick of It who was jailed in 2007 for downloading child pornographyAnthony HaywardMon 7 Sep 2026 10.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 10.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe actor and writer Chris Langham, who has died of pancreatic cancer aged 77, starred as the inept government minister Hugh Abbot in The Thick of It, the BBC television political satire created byArmando Iannucci. During its first two series, he was at the centre of chaos as the secretary of state in the fictional Department of Social Affairs, finding himself outmanoeuvred by his own political advisers and civil servants.“Chris Langham is a master at acting the guy missing the point, out of his depth and striving to keep his head above water while sharks nibble his nether regions,” wrote the Sunday Times in 2005.It seemed that Langham had put past demons behind him, but his time in the spotlight was abruptly cut short when he was arrested and thenin 2007 jailedfor downloading child pornography.A quarter of a century earlier, alcoholism and cocaine addiction had led to Langham being sacked from Not the Nine O’Clock News, at the end of its first series in 1979 (and replaced by Griff Rhys Jones). Time in rehab was followed by writing for Alas Smith & Jones, which paired Jones withMel Smith(1984-88). Langham later appeared in sketches alongside them in Smith & Jones (from 1989 to 1992).“I was frightened that, clean and sober, I wouldn’t be talented any more,” Langham told the journalist Pauline Wallin in 1999. But his rehabilitation – and the satire – continued when he wrote Look at the State We’re In! (1995), a BBC series of six 10-minute skits confronting the laws and state powers governing modern life, with appearances from stars such as John Cleese, Hugh Laurie, Dawn French andRik Mayall.Hot on its heels, Langham was performing again, in John Morton’s award-winning BBCRadio 4mockumentary People Like Us (1995-97), playing Roy Mallard, a bumbling journalist meeting people in different walks of life. The show then switched to television (1999-2001).His big TV breakthrough in front of the camera was by then already under way, with him and Morton scripting the BBC sitcom Kiss Me Kate (1998-2001). He fed his own experience into the series, which starred Caroline Quentin as Kate Salinger, a counsellor, and Langham as her constantly depressed business partner, Douglas Fielding.As this new-found fame made him in demand for press interviews, which inevitably brought up his troubled past, Langham reflected: “I could say I wish I wasn’t an alcoholic, but I am. It’s like being a diabetic. It’s not a moral failing on my part – it’s just the hand I’ve been dealt.”He remained on an upward path. The BBC asked him to star as a psychotherapist in a sitcom, with his patients played by celebrities. He suggested: “Perhaps all the clients should be played by the same actor, in a Kind Hearts and Coronets sort of way.” So, in Alec Guinness mode, Paul Whitehouse stepped in, co-scriptedHelp(2005) with Langham (as Peter Strong) and not only took the roles of all the grotesque patients, with different wigs, prosthetic noses and accents, but also that of Peter’s own therapist.The Thick of It then cemented Langham’s reputation as a naturalistic performer in satirical comedy and the honours rained on him at the 2006 Bafta awards, where he took the best comedy performance title for that programme and best comedy programme or series award for Help.But Langham’s world had already started falling apart – he was arrested in 2005 on charges of downloading images and videos of child abuse. In court two years later, he denied the offences, saying he himself had no interest in children, but was researching material for a future episode of Help. Langham also claimed he had been sexually abused by a family friend as a child and that watching the videos was also an attempt to “reach something that I was blocking out”.Langham was found guilty on all 15 counts, and not guilty on further charges of having sex with an under-age girl. He was sentenced to 10 months in prison, reduced to six on appeal. On his release he found work in just a handful of low-budget films. “Everybody in the country hates me – and I can’t get a job,” Langhamtold the Guardianin 2011.He was born in London, toMichael Langham, a director in repertory theatre and later artistic director of the Stratford festival in Canada, and Helen Burns, an actor. Chris attended St Paul’s school, Barnes, while his parents worked in North America, and said he said dropped out of an English and drama course at Bristol University after suffering a nervous breakdown because of their subsequent marriage breakup.He acted in fringe theatre and found work writing and appearing in sketches in Spike Milligan’s surreal TV programmes, including Milligan In… ( 1973) and Q5 (1975). Then, as a scriptwriter on The Muppet Show (from 1978 to 1981), he shared in a 1981 Primetime Emmy award.As an actor, he had small roles in the films The Pink Panther Strikes Again (1976), Life of Brian (1979) and Carry on Columbus (1992), and character parts on television in Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1985), The McGuffin (1986), Bergerac (1989) and Making Out (1990).His marriage to the actor and singer Sue Jones-Davies ended in divorce. He is survived by his second wife, Christine Cartwright, a choreographer, whom he married in 1991, their children, Emily and Harry, and the three sons, Siencyn, Dafydd and Glyn, from his first marriage.Christopher Langham, actor and writer, born 14 April 1949; died 24 June 2026Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioComedyTV comedyThe Thick of ItArmando IannucciTelevisionRadio 4obituariesShareReuse this content

title: Radiohead announce 2027 tour with shows in Australia and Japan  | Radiohead | The Guardian
description: UK band will play 16 shows across Perth, Melbourne and Sydney, as well as five shows in Saitama
Author: Adeshola Ore
Headline: UK band will play 16 shows across Perth, Melbourne and Sydney, as well as five shows in Saitama
Content: Thom Yorke performing with Radiohead. The band will play 16 shows in Perth, Melbourne and Sydney, and five in Saitama, Japan.Photograph: Hayley Madden/RedfernsView image in fullscreenThom Yorke performing with Radiohead. The band will play 16 shows in Perth, Melbourne and Sydney, and five in Saitama, Japan.Photograph: Hayley Madden/RedfernsRadioheadRadiohead announce 2027 tour with shows in Australia and JapanUK band will play 16 shows across Perth, Melbourne and Sydney, as well as five shows in SaitamaAdeshola OreMon 7 Sep 2026 05.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 05.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRadiohead will return to Australia to play 16 shows across three cities next year, marking the band’s first tour of the country in 15 years.On Monday afternoon, the British rock band unveiled the itinerary for its May 2027 tour, which also includes five shows inJapan.The series of shows will kick off at Perth’s RAC Arena on 3 May for four performances in the city. This will be followed by six shows at Melbourne’s Rod Laver Arena and Sydney’s Afterpay Arena.The band last toured Australia after their 2011 album the King of Limbs, although frontman Thom Yorke visited Australia for solo shows in 2024. During a Melbourne performance, Yorkewalked off stageafter being heckled by a pro-Palestine protester in the crowd. He returned a few minutes later to perform his final song of the evening, Radiohead’s 1997 hit Karma Police.Last year, Radiohead reunited after seven years for astring of showsin European cities.The band will alsoreturn to Japanfor the first time in 19 years with five concerts at the GMO Arena Saitama near Tokyo.The band has not recorded a studio album since 2016’s A Moon Shaped Pool. But the absence of new material has not quelled demand, with a frenzied rush for tickets when the shows were announced.Radiohead first toured Australia in 1994 after the band’s debut album Pablo Honey, which contained their breakthrough hit Creep.Fans can register interest for tickets to the Australian shows on anonline portal– run by co-promoter Frontier Touring – that opened on Monday evening. It will create a ballot-like process to “help give fans fair access to tickets and minimise automated and unauthorised purchases.”Tickets are capped at four for each city the band is performing in, the portal said.“There’s no benefit to registering earlier. Every completed registration received by the deadline will be treated equally,” the website said.Registration closes on Thursday at 5pm AEST. Successful registrants will be emailed with next steps from Friday and given a chance to buy tickets next week.Explore more on these topicsRadioheadThom YorkeJapannewsShareReuse this content

title: Susan Sarandon says she is losing movie roles because of her support for Palestine | Susan Sarandon | The Guardian
description: Oscar-winning actor says she and other outspoken critics of Israel have found it ‘impossible’ to get hired by major studios
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Oscar-winning actor says she and other outspoken critics of Israel have found it ‘impossible’ to get hired by major studios
Content: Actor Susan Sarandon at the premiere of The Echo Chamber at the Venice film festival in Italy on Sunday.Photograph: Fabio Frustaci/EPAView image in fullscreenActor Susan Sarandon at the premiere of The Echo Chamber at the Venice film festival in Italy on Sunday.Photograph: Fabio Frustaci/EPASusan SarandonSusan Sarandon says she is losing movie roles because of her support for PalestineOscar-winning actor says she and other outspoken critics of Israel have found it ‘impossible’ to get hired by major studiosReutersSun 6 Sep 2026 20.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Oscar-winning actorSusan Sarandonhas said she is still losing work because of her outspoken support for Palestinians, despite what she ⁠described as a broader shift ⁠in public opinion against ​US support for Israel.Speaking at theVenice film festival, where she is promoting her latest movie The Echo Chamber, Sarandon said some parts of the film industry continued to ⁠shun her over her activism.“I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of the historical relevance ofPalestineand the ties of Zionists with America and our politics,” ⁠she said. “That has been a major revelation for people, how much money the United States gives to Israel, nobody really ​understood that.“US opinion pollshave shown support ‌for Israel softeningand sympathy for ‌Palestinians rising since the start of the Gaza war in 2023.But the 79-year-old actor said her support for the Palestinian ‌cause continued to carry professional consequences.“I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still,” she told reporters. “But that’s the power structure. I think [among] people, certainly internationally, I feel welcome.“An Academy Award winner for Dead Man Walking, Sarandon rose to prominence in films including The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Bull Durham and Thelma and Louise.‘Many of us in Israel live in a state of shock at the savagery’: veteran director Amos Gitai returns to GazaRead moreShe wasdropped by her longstanding talent agency UTA in 2023after ‌remarks she made while attending pro-Palestinian rallies one month after the Hamas attack on Israel, including: “There are a lot of people afraid of being Jewish at this time, and are getting a taste of what it feels like to be a Muslim in this country.”The conflict has spilled into this year’s Venice film festival, with activists ​calling on organisers to raise the Palestinian flag in recognition of Palestinian directors screening at the event.The festival’s artistic director, Alberto Barbera, has said this is impossible because Italy does not formally recognise the state of Palestine, but he has pointed to several films being shown on the Lido that show the struggle of ordinary Palestinians.Sarandon said resistance to hiring outspoken critics ofIsrael⁠remained particularly strong among major studios.“If it is a major studio, I think ​it’s not just with me but with ​other people who have been told ​that that is impossible,” she said, thanking Andrea Pallaoro, the director of The Echo Chamber, for casting ​her.“I found my family, ‌I found my people ​and I’m OK,” she ​said, sparking prolonged applause at the news conference.In her latest film, adapted from the final screenplay by Italian film-maker Bernardo Bertolucci, Sarandon plays an ageing singer who hires a music producer recovering from drug addiction to work on a comeback album.The Echo Chamber is one of 21 films competing for Venice’s Golden Lion award, which will be presented on 12 September.Explore more on these topicsSusan SarandonVenice film title: TV tonight: the final series of hit Aussie romcom Colin from Accounts  | Television | The Guardian
description: A chance encounter brings Gordon and Ashley together again in this wonderfully messy comedy. Plus: a chaotic University Challenge. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: A chance encounter brings Gordon and Ashley together again in this wonderfully messy comedy. Plus: a chaotic University Challenge. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Miraculous … Harriet Dyer as Ashley and Patrick Brammall as Gordon in Colin From Accounts.Photograph: BBC/© 2024 CBS Studios Inc., Easy Tiger Productions Pty Ltd, Foxtel Management Pty Ltd, Create NSWView image in fullscreenMiraculous … Harriet Dyer as Ashley and Patrick Brammall as Gordon in Colin From Accounts.Photograph: BBC/© 2024 CBS Studios Inc., Easy Tiger Productions Pty Ltd, Foxtel Management Pty Ltd, Create NSWTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: the final series of hit Aussie romcom Colin from AccountsA chance encounter brings Gordon and Ashley together again in this wonderfully messy comedy. Plus: a chaotic University Challenge. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Jack SealeandSimon WardellMon 7 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColin from Accounts10pm, BBC TwoThree years have passed since Gordon’s misjudged proposal and the final season of this miraculous Aussie sitcom gets off to a melancholy start. Gordon and Ashley have unsatisfactory new partners and the brewery is struggling. Still, at least Colin seems well. A chance encounter brings the pair together again and the feelings are still strong, but there’s baggage to discard first. It’s not without plotting contrivances but, crucially, continues to feel wonderfully messy and real in emotional terms. The comedy and drama balance immaculately and the chemistry between Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer is as perfect as you’d expect from a real-life couple. Still the sweetest thing on TV.Phil Harrison9/11: The Saudi Connection8pm, BBC OneA quarter of a century after the 2001 attacks on the US, the origin stories of the perpetrators remain far from settled. This documentary explores the implications of thousands of newly released documents that, some argue, suggest the involvement of the Saudi Arabian government. The revelations centre on Omar al-Bayoumi, who has been accused of being a middle man between the Saudis and the first two hijackers (al-Bayoumi and the Saudi government deny these claims).PHFred’s Ultimate Hotels8pm, Channel 4Fred from the First Dates restaurant, TV’s favourite maître d’, continues his fancy hotel tour in a South African safari lodge. But service is never far from his mind, as he offers to help the team prepare a “bush braai” outdoor barbecue. There’s also time for an encounter with an elephant.Hollie RichardsonMy Life Is Murder8pm, U&AlibiView image in fullscreenDid he zip up? … Rhys Darby guests in My Life Is Murder.Photograph: Matt Klitscher/UKTVCrushed by a gargoyle thrown from a balcony is one hell of a way to go. Worse still if it happens during your nightly “ablution stop” in a garden. That’s what happens to a toy inventor this week, and it’s up to Alexa to work out who did it: “I hope he managed to zip up first.”HRUniversity Challenge8.30pm, BBC TwoAmol Rajan hosts another brain-off between two student teams: Birmingham and an adorably chaotic quartet from Leicester. Highlights include a spectacular mishearing of a famous novel’s title and a classics question that’s much easier than it would have been a few years ago.Jack Seale999: What Happened Next9pm, Channel 4Another new series of copaganda, this one exploring the aftermath of 999 calls. It begins with a fascinating case: a train passenger has noticed something deeply troubling on a fellow traveller’s phone and informed the police. The unfolding investigation is bigger than anyone could have expected, involving a network of child exploitation.PHFilm choiceView image in fullscreenDramatic force … Juanita Moore as Annie in Imitation of Life.Photograph: Channel 4Imitation of Life (Douglas Sirk, 1959),4.25pm, Film4Douglas Sirk’s melodrama is remarkable in that it bats around a number of knotty, topical questions about racism, sexism and class but is also a powerfully intimate drama about the bond between two mothers and their daughters. Lana Turner headlines as actor Lora, whose independent spirit leads to theatre fame, despite being a single parent to Sandra Dee’s Susie. But it’s the other pairing that provides the main dramatic force: Juanita Moore as Annie, Lora’s Black maid, and Susan Kohner as her unhappy child Sarah Jane, who can, fatefully, pass for white.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightAmol RajanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Boatbuilders review – a gentle study of craftsmen’s quiet expertise | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Luke Lorentzen’s light-touch documentary follows a team of Maine craftsmen constructing a high-spec sailboat for a super-rich guy who seems kind of nice
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: Luke Lorentzen’s light-touch documentary follows a team of Maine craftsmen constructing a high-spec sailboat for a super-rich guy who seems kind of nice
Content: Taking a bow … Trent Glisson in Brooklin Boat Yard in Boatbuilders.Photograph: Luke LorentzenView image in fullscreenTaking a bow … Trent Glisson in Brooklin Boat Yard in Boatbuilders.Photograph: Luke LorentzenVenice film festivalReviewBoatbuilders review – a gentle study of craftsmen’s quiet expertiseVenice film festival:Luke Lorentzen’s light-touch documentary follows a team of Maine craftsmen constructing a high-spec sailboat for a super-rich guy who seems kind of niceXan Brooksin VeniceMon 7 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Brooklin Boat Yard stands in a quiet harbour on the coast of Maine and makes high-spec yachts for rich men and women to sail. Its latest client is Graham Green, a millionaire financier who has commissioned the team to build him a 56ft cruising sailboat, the Kiandra, complete with maple worktops and a Sonos sound system. Green plans to sail the boat around the world, while its creators will stay in Brooklin, raise their kids and make boats. These men know their place. “We’re just the fucking help,” one confides.Boatbuilders is directed with the lightest of touches by 33-year-old Luke Lorentzen, who has already proved himself a past master in unhurried, observational documentaries about work.Midnight Family, his 2019 debut, spotlighted the travails of a private ambulance business in Mexico City, while 2023’s A Still Small Voice trailed a chaplain at Mount Sinai hospital in New York. Neither, though, immersed themselves in their subject to quite the level of Boatbuilders, which covers the process from lumber cutting to launch and from one summer through to the following spring. The leaves turn to gold, then the snow starts to fly, but down at the boatyard the job continues on schedule. The craftsmen plane and glue and discuss their lives.Folded in amid the heat and hubbub of this year’sVenice film festival, Lorentzen’s serene piece of slow cinema provides both a cool palate cleanser and a paean to the pleasures of practical work. If you’ve ever watched Witness and wished that the barn-raising sequence was longer, then do seek this out: your cup will runneth over.Is Lorentzen’s main focus the boat or the team of New Englanders who make it? Almost certainly both, in that the two are indivisible, with each dependent on the other. And while the boatyard’s soft-spoken boss, Brian Larkin, never actually goes so far as to say that ‘there is no I in team’, it’s the coded message of every one of his pep talks as he seeks to gently elevate a Jesus-bearded carpenter, Trent Glisson, to the role of project manager. Trent – an amiable young father, still dithering over baby names – is the closest Lorentzen’s film has to a hero. He fears that he’s floundering, worries the boat has gone over budget and knows that he needs to be more decisive. When the millionaire client video-calls for a progress report, Trent’s responses are so awkward that the conversation soon stalls. Flummoxed, Green elects to put a brave face on it. “You guys are like the ducks on the pond,” he says. “You look super-mellow on top, but you’re paddling like crazy.”Is it wrong to wish for more conflict and strife? Lorentzen’s approach is discreetly respectful, occasionally to a fault. When, midway through the film, an obstinate craftsman has to be fired, we learn of it via the team meeting that follows and the offending employee is never referred to by name. “It’s a small community,” says Larkin by way of explanation. The boss spares his blushes and the director plays ball.Is this a political film? Certainly not in an obvious sense. These men are happy in their work and desire little more than the opportunity to keep doing it. They punch the clock and sweep the shavings and fit the planks around the frame. They measure their year by the turn of the seasons, gathering apples in autumn, ice-fishing in winter, while the older builders help their younger colleagues gain strength. Nonetheless, there is an undertow of Marxist melancholia to what should be the film’s euphoric final scenes, when Green rocks up in his Ray-Bans to take possession of the Kiandra. Green’s a nice guy and will no doubt treat her well. But he laughs too much and is way out of his depth; a master among servants who know infinitely more than he does.As for Trent, our plucky project manager, the launch marks the end of a momentous 12 months. He’s earned his spurs and provided for his family; welcomed one baby and said goodbye to another. Job done, clock punched, he climbs into his tiny skiff, fires up the outboard motor and putters home across the bay.Boatbuilders screened at the Venice film festivalExplore more on these topicsVenice film festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Last Bath review – self-mortifying nun struggles with profoundly uneasy sexual awakening | Movies | The Guardian
description: Anabela Moreira is an impressively intense lead as the sister who finds herself in charge of her wayward teenage nephew
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Anabela Moreira is an impressively intense lead as the sister who finds herself in charge of her wayward teenage nephew
Content: Passionate … The Last BathView image in fullscreenPassionate … The Last BathMoviesReviewThe Last Bath review – self-mortifying nun struggles with profoundly uneasy sexual awakeningAnabela Moreira is an impressively intense lead as the sister who finds herself in charge of her wayward teenage nephewPhil HoadMon 7 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsharp, self-abnegating performance from Anabela Moreira elevates this passionate – largely in the religious sense – Portuguese debut, which is only now arriving in the UK after festival screenings dating back to 2020. As senior nun Josefina, she wears a permanent cowl of careworn melancholy, suggesting a woman for whom, even after she is summoned to look after her bereaved 15-year-old nephew Alexandre (Martim Canavarro), holding the world at arm’s length is standard practice. Watching him slam into girl drivers on the fairground dodgems, it seems clear that desire is for other people.Or maybe not. Josefina is called back to her childhood village after the death of her father, who – in her wantaway sister’s absence – was Alexandre’s guardian. Traumatised by finding the body and spoiled because he was the first birth in the locality for years, the teenager requires mollycoddling. So Josefina finds herself in uncomfortable proximity to this coltish overgrown boy, who looks like a male model in waiting; bathing him, letting him sleep in her bed after he has wet his, inspecting his penis infection. She suffers it, presumably for love and our Lord. But when it becomes clear that he may be shipped off to a foster home if she doesn’t stick around, her inner motivations come into sharper focus.From the opening, symbolically charged image of Alexandre running haplessly around a maze of terraced vineyards, director David Bonneville has a keen sense of the higher implications of his story. He’s clearly interested in the boundaries and pathways behind spiritual, familial and physical love; finding a used condom in a bed at her convent, employing a self-mortifying garter, Josefina obviously regards the last of these as off-limits. But caring so intimately for Alexandre reawakens powerful feelings. The daily baths perhaps aren’t purely a devotional act; the photographs she takes of him sleeping testify to an adoration tipping into something transgressive.This growing possessiveness comes to a head with the return of Alexandre’s mother Angela (Margarida Moreira), a caricatured irresponsible glamourpuss who turns his head. The Last Bath’s resolution feels forced, which is a shame given the amount of faith Bonneville hitherto places in his audience in not giving them easy answers and letting this domestic mystery play breathe – a sign of the film’s spiritual strength.The Last Bath is on digital platforms from 14 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsPortugalEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: In the Shadows of Nuremberg review – trial-adjacent thriller aims to be Russian answer to Saving Private Ryan | Movies | The Guardian
description: A trivial personal plotline and a strain of maudlin patriotism undermine Nikolay Lebedev’s shaky telling of the Soviet side of the story
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: A trivial personal plotline and a strain of maudlin patriotism undermine Nikolay Lebedev’s shaky telling of the Soviet side of the story
Content: Web of intrigue … In the Shadows of NurembergView image in fullscreenWeb of intrigue … In the Shadows of NurembergMoviesReviewIn the Shadows of Nuremberg review – trial-adjacent thriller aims to be Russian answer to Saving Private RyanA trivial personal plotline and a strain of maudlin patriotism undermine Nikolay Lebedev’s shaky telling of the Soviet side of the storyPhil HoadMon 7 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 06.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaking place in the wings of the Nuremberg trial, this Soviet-side political thriller, first released back in 2023, features a scene in which the crowd turns on a boa-draped Hollywood floozy in town to entertain the troops. A case ofmea culpafor director Nikolay Lebedev, who trivialises the momentous issues emerging from the courtroom by dressing the legal stuff up with a tenuous and shakily handled plotline about a missing soldier, in an attempt to make his film the Russian answer toSaving Private Ryan.After his brother goes MIA in the vicinity of the soon-to-be-historic city, Red Army intelligence officer Igor Volgin (Sergey Kempo) wangles a post translating for the Soviet delegation. He’s approached by Lena (Lyubov Aksyonova), a Russian wastrel with a perfectly coiffed bob despite months of forced labour in a German munitions factory; she claims to have run into his sibling, an artist, in captivity. But she is also feeding information to Helmut (Wolfgang Cerny), a Nazi resistance diehard who believes Göring (Carsten Norgaard) and company should be accountable only to German courts.A serious film unveiling the Soviet perspective on the trial, to accompany the likes of last year’sRussell Crowe vehicle Nuremberg, would have been fascinating. But if Lebedev felt his thriller needed a compelling personal throughline, Volgin’s quest isn’t it; the manhunt is only tangentially tied into the Nazi network, via a connection to art connoisseur Helmut that is mostly there to enable platitudes about beauty transcending war. And the underground elements are erratically threaded through to the bigger judicial picture, with Helmut’s attempt to reach Göring by blackmailing a key witness seemingly forgotten about by the end.Despite his track record with Russian blockbusters, Lebedev struggles to find a confident foothold in this haphazard web of intrigue. His twitchy camerawork can’t sit still, as if preferring the epic vistas of blitzed cityscapes over his protagonist. Without being overtly propagandist (despite its Russian state backing), the film displays a strain of maudlin patriotism – insisting how the Soviets are disdainfully treated by the allies and slandered by the Nazis at the tribunal – at odds with the film’s message: that Nuremberg was a moment when universal human justice took precedence over national interests. Not a capital crime, but Lebedev is unconvincing taking the stand.In the Shadows of Nuremberg is on digital platforms from 14 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmWar filmsSecond world warRussiaEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Swiftly enchanted’: why Bedknobs and Broomsticks is my feelgood movie | Movies | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers recommending their most rewatched comfort films is a reminder that Disney’s kids fantasy is more than a Mary Poppins knock-off
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest in our series of writers recommending their most rewatched comfort films is a reminder that Disney’s kids fantasy is more than a Mary Poppins knock-off
Content: A still from Bedknobs and Broomsticks.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenA still from Bedknobs and Broomsticks.Photograph: Moviestore Collection Ltd/AlamyMy feelgood movieMovies‘Swiftly enchanted’: why Bedknobs and Broomsticks is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers recommending their most rewatched comfort films is a reminder that Disney’s kids fantasy is more than a Mary Poppins knock-offGary RyanMon 7 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 13.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Filigree, apogee, pedigree, perigee!” – the four incantatory words I blame for receiving a shonky Paul Daniels magic set as a child in the 80s. In Bedknobs and Broomsticks, it’s the spell that Angela Lansbury’s patriotic Nazi-vanquishing witch Eglantine Price casts to transform people into fluffy rabbits; a trick I yearned to pull off.‘Sometimes you just need a good cry’: why Little Women is my feelgood movieRead moreWhen it became clear I wouldn’t deter the Third Reich with three plastic thimbles, a deck of playing cards and a flaccid wand, my conjuring kit was mothballed – but my irrational love of the Disney film remains to this day. For me, it originally fell into the category of the crackling VHS that your parents taped off ITV at Christmas then would repeatedly plonk you in front of to shut you up – to the point Ican even recall the adverts.Still, Bedknobs has a flying nanny-shaped shadow over it; its ignoble reputation as a knock-off Mary Poppins was perhaps coded into its DNA. Put into production as a back-up plan when acquiring the rights to his beloved Poppins was looking shaky, Walt’s second-favourite attitude towards Bedknobs was captured by its screenwriter Don DaGradi, who sketched his boss asleep during a 1963 story conference, exaggerated zzzs tumbling out of his mouth, as the Sherman brothers previewed the rousing love song Eglantine. When it premiered in 1971, the Shermans and Lansbury felt the picture had been hobbled by cuts, while critics found the use of Nazis in a kids’ movie tonally jarring, akin to show tunes and a kick line erupting in The Hills Have Eyes.But (non-Paul Daniels-branded) cards on the table: I’m a ’Knobstruther. As a working-class nipper, turning my bed into a DFS-based Tardis and hanging out with Jessica Fletcher-with-an-English-accent appealed more than a bossy nanny healing a posho family. Even now, I prefer its more offbeat, darker tone, and how its spoonfuls of sugar are strictly wartime-rationed.Lansbury’s Miss Price is introduced to us rocking up to the village post office in a heraldic puff of luridly coloured motorcycle fumes, to collect a broomstick from a witchcraft correspondence course (a scam run by huckster magician Emelius Browne, a twinkly portrayal by Poppins alumnus David Tomlinson), only to end up reluctantly housing three London orphan evacuees. Together, they embark on a quest to locate a levitation spell to send inanimate objects into battle, thus preventing human casualties.Objectively, I realise Bedknobs is an oddly paced jamboree of set pieces and styles, but the greatest comfort feelgood movies trip the critical switch in your brain. Simply typing the song titles – the Poppins offcut The Beautiful Briny (soundtracking a dazzling underwater animated dance competition), Substitutiary Locomotion and the market-based cockney rave-up Portobello Road, featuring sailors on shore leave from HMS Choreography - means they’ll be lodged in my head. Best of all is the sumptuous sorrow of The Age of Not Believing, lamenting the receding of childhood wonder directed at sceptical 11-year-old Charlie Rawlings, which handily doubles as a midlife crisis anthem for adults. In the wake of the death of Disney in 1969, the Shermans channelled their existential angst into the number and it shows. It makes Feed the Birds resemble the Macarena.Revisiting it decades later, despite possessing a cynical anti-nostalgia firewall, I was nevertheless swiftly enchanted. It also proved funnier than I remembered. Particularly a hilarious cartoon/live action football match on an animal-ruled island, where stretcher-carrying vulture paramedics excitedly flap on to the pitch at the first sign of injury. A climactic battle where Miss Price, clad in a Brodie helmet and brandishing a sword while gliding atop a Union Jack-adorned broom, summons a phantom army of medieval suits of armour to repel a platoon of invading Nazis is played for slapstick yuks, like a bizarre cross between Went the Day Well? and the Three Stooges.In fact, the sole difference is I now snigger at eight-year-old Paul Rawlings’s exclamation of “What’s that got to do with me knob?” (I’m not proud) and understand a reference to Mr Browne’s familiarity with sex workers on Portobello Road that had previously whooshed over the innuendo no-fly zone above my head.Lately, a friend’s four-year-old son has become obsessed with Bedknobs. Talk of getting in touch with my inner child usually makes me want to find my inner King Herod, but seeing it through his eyes is like a mirror back to being a kid convinced that if he pointed at someone and reallybelieved, I could turn nemeses into nose-twitching bunnies.Bedknobs and Broomsticks is available on Disney+ in the US, UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmMy feelgood movieAngela LansburyAction and adventure filmsComedy filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A crucial look at the disappearance of Austin Tice: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The US marine turned journalist went missing in Syria 14 years ago – and now, a suspenseful new pod uncovers essential evidence. Plus, the charming Julie Andrews serenades audiences with Jane Austen’s Emma
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: The US marine turned journalist went missing in Syria 14 years ago – and now, a suspenseful new pod uncovers essential evidence. Plus, the charming Julie Andrews serenades audiences with Jane Austen’s Emma
Content: Austin Tice photographed in Cairo, 2012.Photograph: Christy Wilcox/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustin Tice photographed in Cairo, 2012.Photograph: Christy Wilcox/AFP/Getty ImagesBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioA crucial look at the disappearance of Austin Tice: best podcasts of the weekThe US marine turned journalist went missing in Syria 14 years ago – and now, a suspenseful new pod uncovers essential evidence. Plus, the charming Julie Andrews serenades audiences with Jane Austen’s EmmaHannah J DaviesandHollie RichardsonMon 7 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekI’m Not a Monster Presents: Where Is Austin Tice?It has been 14 years since US marine turned journalist Austin Tice went missing in Syria. Much has changed in the embattled nation since then – not least the end of Bashar al-Assad’s regime – but Tice is yet to be found. Inthis series, Josh Baker and Sara Obeidat uncover crucial new evidence, some of which has already made headlines. Sensitive and highly suspenseful.Hannah J DaviesWidely available, episodes weeklyDrive Thru MagicFans of Heated Rivalry will surely love this new queer indiedrama podwritten by and starring Briggon Snow (The Bright Sessions), with Daniel J Kim (Cobra Kai) as his fellow lead. Its irresistible, bite-size instalments – set at a drive-thru takeaway – fizz with young love, while also tackling tough topics such as grief and dementia.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyJane Austen Stories: EmmaView image in fullscreenSharp Regency lit … Julie Andrews narrates Emma.Photograph: Michael Kovac/Getty Images for AFIAsecond seriesof sharp Regency lit from the Noiser podcast stable, as narrated by the ever-charming Julie Andrews. This unabridged version of the novel about a committed meddler and matchmaker (described by Austen as “a heroine whom no one but myself will much like”) has original music and immersive sound design to boot.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyFault Line: HadithaFilm-maker Michael Epstein hasn’t been able to forget the Haditha massacre of 2005, when 24 unarmed civilians were slain by US marines. His dedication topursuing the true storybehind a shocking chapter of the Iraq war is clear in this iHeart show, as he expertly pulls on forgotten threads, drawing on years of investigation and interviews.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEnd of the WorldThe zombie apocalypse alarm goes off and broadcasting mates Dan Noble and Will Short get a comedian into their bunkerto chatabout their survival plan of action. title: Going for gold: an early autumn road trip across Finland’s sparkling lake district | Finland holidays | The Guardian
description: On a self-drive break in search of Lake Saimaa’s autumn colours, we encountered blue skies, cosy lakeside cabins and saunas, great food – and lots of stubbornly green trees
Author: Annabelle Thorpe
Headline: On a self-drive break in search of Lake Saimaa’s autumn colours, we encountered blue skies, cosy lakeside cabins and saunas, great food – and lots of stubbornly green trees
Content: Finland’s Lake Saimaa at sunriseView image in fullscreenFinland’s Lake Saimaa at sunriseFinland holidaysGoing for gold: an early autumn road trip across Finland’s sparkling lake districtOn a self-drive break in search of Lake Saimaa’s autumn colours, we encountered blue skies, cosy lakeside cabins and saunas, great food – and lots of stubbornly green treesAnnabelle ThorpeMon 7 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 02.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwasn’t sure what to expect from an autumn trip to Finland, my first ever to the country, but spending an afternoon sprawled on a deck chair beneath blazing blue skies certainly wasn’t part of it. After a morning walking beneath the leafy canopy at theMustila Arboretum– the oldest, most extensive botanical garden in the country – and a lunchtime wine-tasting (more of which later), my friend Sara and I pitched up at the Sahanlahti resort, deep in the FinnishLakeland, only to find sun-drenched scenery that felt far more Mediterranean than Nordic.Sahanlahti was the second stop on a mid-September road trip from Helsinki to the shores of Lake Saimaa; a journey in search ofruska, the spectacular autumn colours that blaze for a few short weeks before the long Finnish winter sets in. However, on our opening drive east from the airport to the Radalla resort, set on Lake Urajärvi, most of the thousands of trees we drove past were resolutely green, with just the very tips of the leaves tinged with auburn, like a foliage balayage.View image in fullscreenEnjoying the peace at Sahanlahti resort on Lake Saimaa.Photograph: Annabelle Thorpe“You’re too early,” the waitress told us, cheerfully, after we had checked in to our chic waterfront cabins, and were tucking into hefty plates of crispy garlic chicken, scattered with freshly picked chanterelles, in Radalla’s quiet dining room. “But you might get some sun tomorrow.” Later, walking back to our cabins through thick drizzle, we agreed she was most probably just being kind.The Radalla resort is just one of dozens of lakeside hotels scattered across southern Finland – many with self-catering cabins, sauna complexes and gleaming metal steps that lead from wooden piers down into the chilly waters of the lake. The grey drizzle we awoke to made a dip less than appealing, and instead we decided to set off for our next stop, taking in the arboretum en route before finding a place for lunch.double quotation markResolutely green trees rolled past us for mile after mile, until slowly the fields began to melt into lakesDriving in southern Finland turned out to be quite different from other countries. Most settlements fringe the lakesides, so they tend to be tucked away down side roads leading off from the main highway. Instead, trees – those resolutely green trees – rolled past us for mile after mile, until slowly the fields began to melt into lakes, one after another, the road snaking alongside the blue-grey waters, or stitching together small islets that lay scattered between them.Googling somewhere for lunch, Sara came across theOllinmäki winery, an unexpected find in a country that grows absolutely no grapes. Instead, berry wines are hugely popular, and once settled in at our table, we were persuaded to try a flight of six, accompanied by a bowl of hearty elk soup (which tasted considerably better than it looked) and a leaf salad with local cheese. One wine, the white currant and berry Myllärin Matti was particularly delicious, with the tang of a crisp sauvignon – although I wouldn’t want to find out what a Finnish hangover feels like.From the winery it was an easy drive to Sahanlahti, by which time the weather had cleared and pin-sharp blue skies gleamed above the shores of Lake Saimaa. The main house – painted butterscotch-yellow and dating back to the mid-18th century, when the owners presided over the local sawmill – had a languidly old-fashioned air, but dinner at theKoskivahti restaurantwas anything but: rich mushroom soup, slivers of goose confit with lingonberry sauce, wafer-thin beetroot carpaccio with tangy goat’s cheese.View image in fullscreenAnnabelle Thorpe and friend foraging for wild mushrooms.Photograph: Annabelle ThorpeIt might have been too early for the leaves to turn, but we had arrived right in the middle of harvest season, when heading out into the fields and islands to pick wild mushrooms and berries (of which there are 35 different varieties) is practically a national sport. We had barely set down our bags at our final stop, Järvisydän resort, before we were whizzing out across Saimaa on a small motor boat, baskets tucked between our feet, to hunt for chanterelles and look for rare ringed seals and ospreys.double quotation markWe had arrived in the middle of harvest season, when heading out into the fields and islands to pick wild mushrooms and berries is practically a national sportThe sky was flawlessly blue as we whipped across the water, disembarking first to pick the mushrooms – slashes of bright yellow among the green undergrowth. We were guided in our harvesting by Sebastian, the 12th generation of the Heiskanen family to be running Järvisydän. “Back in 1654,” he told us, “my family were given a portion of land by the Russian tsar, to build a tavern on the route between St Petersburg and Helsinki.” More than 350 years later, the tavern has morphed into a 100-room resort, offering everything from starkly modern glass-walled cabins, high in the forest, to hexagonal log houses with bedrooms set off a central, fire-lit atrium, and camping pods.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe ‘Hobbit-like spa’ at Järvisydän resortIt’s an extraordinary place: everything – from the vast reception, dwarfed by a replica Viking longship hull hung above reception, to the restaurants, bar and the Hobbit-like spa – is built entirely from local stone and timber. A visit to the spa seemed the perfect way to warm up after our chilly boat trip, with six different saunas to dip into – although the “sunken log” sauna, where the temperature reached 70C, gave me some sense of how an ice-cream might feel if left out in the sun.Of the three resorts we visited, Järvisydän was the standout – for its history, for the spectacular scenery of Lake Saimaa that surrounds it, for the delicious mushroom soup and for the long, sunlit walk we took on our final afternoon, through the dense pine forest, where red squirrels skittered around in the branches above. It was a wrench to leave on our last morning, but as we sped back along quiet roads to Helsinki, we agreed Finland had – in spite of our foliage fail – outstripped our expectations. It was more beautiful, more peaceful, more sunkissed than we could ever have imagined.Ruska(the vibrant colours of autumn foliage) begins in the northof the country in early to mid-September, reaching the Lake Saimaa region in the south by early October.The trip was provided byDiscover the World. A four-nightbespoke self-drive tripstaying atRadalla,SahanlahtiandJärvisydänresorts startsat £794pp, including B&B and car hire, but not flights.Explore more on these topicsFinland holidaysScandinavia holidaysRoad tripsScandinavian food and drinkEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for courgette and preserved lemon herby giant couscous | Food | The Guardian
description: A seasonal special featuring both summer vibes and autumn comfort
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: A seasonal special featuring both summer vibes and autumn comfort
Content: Georgina Hayden’s courgettes with preserved lemon and herby couscous.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden’s courgettes with preserved lemon and herby couscous.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.FoodGeorgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for courgette and preserved lemon herby giant couscousA seasonal special featuring both summer vibes and autumn comfortGeorgina HaydenMon 7 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile I dig my head in the sand at September’s arrival and the back-to-school dread, I’m trying to hold on to summer flavours for as long as possible. And this salad does just that: it’s summer and autumn, vibrant and comforting, all at the same time. It can also be served a multitude of ways: still warm, at room temperature with the feta added at the last minute, or even as leftovers (it’s great for lunchboxes, say).Courgette and preserved lemon herby giant couscousIf your courgettes are homegrown and on the larger side, use just two or three. And although it’s not a necessity, I like to cut them into irregular shapes, because that gives them more surface area to char and flavour.Prep10 minCook30 minServes44 courgettes,trimmed and roughly chopped2 preserved lemons,halved, flesh and seeds removed and discarded, peel finely chopped4 garlic cloves,unpeeled1 heaped tsp groundcoriander½ tsp sweet smokedpaprikaSea salt andblack pepperExtra-virgin olive oil200g wholewheat giant couscous, rinsed½25g packflat-leaf parsley, finely choppedA few mint sprigs, leaves picked and finely chopped1 bunch of spring onions, trimmed and finely sliced200gfetaHeat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9. Put the courgettes, preserved lemon peel, garlic cloves, ground coriander and paprika in a large roasting tray and season generously.Drizzle over two tablespoons of the oil, toss well to coat, and roast for 20 minutes, until everything is a little charred. Leave to cool a little, then press the garlic flesh into any juices in the tray, and remove and discard the skins.Meanwhile, bring a pan of salted water to a boil and cook the couscous for about eight minutes (or according to the packet instructions). Drain and rinse under cold water, then transfer to a large bowl.When everything is ready and has cooled a little, mix the courgettes and any tray juices into the couscous. Add the chopped herbs and spring onions, mix again, then taste and adjust the seasoning as required. Just before serving, finish by crumbling over the feta.Explore more on these topicsFoodSaladCheeseVegetablesSummer food and drinkFruitCereals and grainsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Cheese pie, seed crackers and prawn rolls: Ravinder Bhogal’s recipes for cooking with filo | Food | The Guardian
description: Making your own filo is notoriously faffy but, luckily, there are great ready-made versions out there that make these crunchy, golden savoury treats a doddle
Author: Ravinder Bhogal
Headline: Making your own filo is notoriously faffy but, luckily, there are great ready-made versions out there that make these crunchy, golden savoury treats a doddle
Content: Ravinder Bhogal’s cheese and spring onion pie.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.View image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s cheese and spring onion pie.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Georgia Rudd.FoodCheese pie, seed crackers and prawn rolls: Ravinder Bhogal’s recipes for cooking with filoMaking your own filo is notoriously faffy but, luckily, there are great ready-made versions out there that make these crunchy, golden savoury treats a doddleRavinder BhogalMon 7 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlove this gossamer-thin pastry for its lightness and crunch, not least because it can be used for both sweets and savouries. Once, on a trip to Athens, I learned how to make filo from scratch: it needs to be rolled very, very thin, so, unless you are skilled with a rolling pin, it’s hard and time-consuming. Luckily there are good ready-made varieties out there (if you’re using the frozen variety, make sure it’s fully defrosted). And always keep the pastry you are not working with under a damp cloth, because it dries out very quickly and will probably crack.Cheese and spring onion pie (pictured top)This boasts four varieties of cheese and a ruffly top of crisp, golden filo that requires no complicated technique.Prep15 minCook1 hr, plus coolingServes6300gfeta, crumbled250g firm ricotta, crumbled200g halloumi, grated150g gruyere or a sharp cheddar, grated150ml single cream3 eggs25g chives, finely chopped25g dill, finely chopped25g flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped1 large bunch spring onions(8-10), trimmed and finely slicedFinely grated zest of1 unwaxed lemonNutmegSea salt and black pepper125g butter, melted8 sheets filoSesame seeds, to scatterHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. In a large bowl, combine the cheeses, cream, eggs, herbs, spring onion, lemon zest and a good grating of nutmeg, then season to taste.Line the base of a 20-23cm cake tin with baking paper and grease the sides with melted butter. Lay a sheet of pastry in the bottom of the tin, allowing the excess to hang over the sides. Brush generously with butter, then lay on another sheet of pastry at a slight angle, so it doesn’t completely overlap the first sheet, and brush that with butter, too. Repeat until you have six filo sheets covering the base and sides of the tin.Spoon the filling into the pastry base and flatten it out with the back of the spoon. Brush another piece of pastry with butter, fold it in half and lay it on top of the filling, tucking in the excess pastry. Repeat with the last sheet of pastry, then fold in all the overhanging filo to create a lovely textured top. Brush with the remaining butter, sprinkle over the sesame seeds, then bake for 45 minutes, until golden. Leave the pie to rest and cool for 15 minutes before serving.Seeded filo crackersView image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s seeded filo crackers.These require no dough making or rolling: they’re simply made by layering ready-made filo pastry. They have an addictive crunch, and are ideal for swiping through your favourite dips.Prep5 minCook20 min, plus coolingServes61tbsp fennel seeds1tbsp caraway seeds1tbsp coriander seeds2tbsp sesame seeds2tbsp nigella seeds1tsppul biber½tsp onion powder1tsp flaky sea salt4 sheets filo pastry100ml extra-virgin olive oilIn a mortar, lightly crush the fennel, caraway and coriander seeds, then stir in the sesame and nigella seeds, pul biber, onion powder and salt.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Put a sheet of baking paper the size of your baking tray on a work surface, and top it with a sheet of filo. Brush with olive oil, then lay over a second sheet of filo, pressing it down lightly to get rid of any air pockets, and brush with oil. Repeat with the remaining two filo sheets, brush the top with the remaining olive oil and scatter over the spiced seed mix generously and evenly, pressing it in gently, so it sticks.Using a sharp knife, cut the filo into strips, triangles or squares – whatever you like – then slide the baking paper on to a baking tray and bake for 10 minutes. Leave to cool on the baking sheet to crisp up, then serve with your favourite dip.Saffron prawn boreksView image in fullscreenRavinder Bhogal’s saffron prawn boreks.With the addition of saffron, these crisp prawn rolls feel rather lavish. Perfect to pass around at a party with a glass of something fizzy.Prep15 minCook40 min, plus coolingMakes16 small boreks2tbsp olive oil1 onion, peeled and very finely chopped1 red pepper, halved, pith and seeds removed, and flesh finely chopped1 carrot, coarsely grated1green bird’s eyechilli, finely chopped½tsp pul biber1 pinchsaffron threads, steeped in 1 tbsp warm water for 5-10 minutes200g raw prawns, peeled, deveined, half blitzed in a food processor, half roughly chopped25g coriander, leaves very finely choppedFinely grated zest of1 unwaxed lemon, plus the juice of ½ lemonSea salt4 sheets filo75g butter, melted1tsp fennel seeds mixed with½ tsp pul biber, to garnishPut the oil in a pan on a medium heat, then saute the onion, pepper and carrot until soft but not coloured. Add the green chilli, pul biber and saffron, stir-fry briefly, then take off the heat and tip into a bowl. Leave to cool slightly, then stir in the blitzed and chopped prawns, coriander, lemon zest and juice, and season with salt.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. On a clean surface, lay out a filo sheet and brush it with melted butter. Using a sharp knife, cut the filo into four equal rectangles. Spread a log of the filling mix along the short end of one rectangle, leaving a 1½cm gap on each side, then roll up the pastry, tucking in the ends to secure the filling. Put the roll seam-side down on a lined baking sheet and brush with more melted butter. Repeat with the remaining three sheets of filo and filling, then sprinkle over fennel seed and pul biber mix.Bake for 15-20 minutes, until golden brown and crisp, and serve hot or at room temperatureExplore more on these topicsFoodPastryVegetablesHerbs and spicesNuts and seedsCheesePierecipesShareReuse this content
